0.title: The Fear of the LORD Is the Beginning of Wisdom
0.overview:
Proverbs is the Bible's most practical book — and its most misread. It is habitually approached as a collection of timeless life-tips, a biblical self-help manual for the successful and the prudent. But Proverbs is not primarily about success; it is about wisdom. And wisdom in Proverbs is not a technique or a set of principles. It is a person. "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom" (9:10) — wisdom begins in a relationship, in the right posture before the living God, and every practical instruction in the book flows from that foundation. Timothy Keller puts it well: the wisdom Proverbs offers is not a ladder you climb to a better life, but a reorientation of the whole person — mind, heart, will, and desire — toward the God who made you and the world he made you for.

The book is not a random anthology. It has a deliberate architecture. Chapters 1–9 are not proverbs at all but extended wisdom poems — a father's passionate, sustained appeal to his son to choose the path of wisdom over the path of folly. Lady Wisdom calls from the highest point of the city; Lady Folly calls from her doorway. Both are inviting; both promise life. Only one delivers. These nine chapters are the theological and moral foundation for everything that follows. They establish what wisdom is (the fear of the LORD, 1:7), who wisdom is (a figure present at creation, 8:22–31), and what is at stake (life and death, 8:35–36).

Chapters 10–31 are the proverbs proper — individual observations, comparisons, and commands drawn from every domain of human life: work and laziness, wealth and poverty, speech and silence, marriage and family, friendship and conflict, pride and humility, justice and oppression. The collections are not random: 10:1–22:16 are the proverbs of Solomon; 22:17–24:34 are the words of the wise; 25–29 are Solomonic proverbs compiled by Hezekiah's scribes; chapter 30 contains the words of Agur; and chapter 31 closes with the words of King Lemuel and the famous portrait of the excellent wife — who is, in the book's final irony, the embodiment of Lady Wisdom herself.

The christological dimension of Proverbs is signalled in chapter 8, where Wisdom speaks of herself as present with God before creation, as the craftsman beside him, as his delight (8:22–31). The New Testament identifies this Wisdom with Jesus Christ: "Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24); "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Col 2:3); "who became to us wisdom from God" (1 Cor 1:30). When Proverbs calls you to pursue wisdom at all costs — "Get wisdom; whatever you get, get insight" (4:7) — it is, in the fullest biblical sense, calling you to pursue Christ. Every failure of human wisdom that Proverbs exposes is implicitly pointing to the one who is Wisdom incarnate, the one who lived the perfectly wise human life, and the one who gives wisdom generously to all who ask (Jas 1:5).

This commentary follows the approach of Timothy Keller, whose work on Proverbs insists that wisdom is not moralism. The fool in Proverbs is not simply the immoral person; the fool is the person who lives as if God does not exist — who makes decisions about money, relationships, speech, and ambition without reference to the Creator. And the wise person is not simply the prudent, disciplined achiever; the wise person is the one whose whole life is ordered around the fear of the LORD, whose practical decisions flow from a heart reoriented by grace. The path from folly to wisdom is not self-improvement; it is the path that leads, ultimately, to Christ.

1.title: The Fear of the LORD Is the Beginning of Knowledge

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Why This Book Was Written
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A heading and a purpose statement: The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel (v. 1) were collected to know wisdom and instruction, to give prudence to the simple and discretion to the youth (vv. 2-4), and even the wise are told to keep learning (vv. 5-6). Then the motto of the whole book: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom in Proverbs is skill for living in God's world, and it starts not with a technique but with a posture before God.

verseByVerse.quote: The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel:

The book opens with a name and a pedigree. Solomon was the king who, when God offered him anything he asked, asked for an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil (1 Kgs 3:9). God gave it, and the history records that He also spoke 3,000 proverbs (1 Kgs 4:32). What we have here is a selection, and not all of it is his. Later headings name the men of Hezekiah who copied more of Solomon's sayings more than two centuries after him (25:1), and two otherwise unknown men, Agur and King Lemuel (30:1; 31:1).

So the book's authority does not rest on Solomon's brilliance. Solomon himself ended badly, his heart turned by the very things this book warns against. Its authority rests on the God who gave him wisdom and then gave these sayings to his people. The word proverbs translates the Hebrew mashal, which means a comparison or likeness: a saying that sets two things side by side so that one throws light on the other. That is exactly how most of this book works.

And there is one more name behind this one. Jesus said of himself, something greater than Solomon is here (Matt 12:42). The queen of the South crossed the known world to hear Solomon. The reader of Proverbs has the wiser King close at hand, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3).

verseByVerse.quote: To know wisdom and instruction, to understand words of insight, to receive instruction in wise dealing, in righteousness, justice, and equity; to give prudence to the simple, knowledge and discretion to the youth—
verseByVerse.commentary:
To know wisdom and instruction, to understand words of insight, to receive instruction in wise dealing, in righteousness, justice, and equity;

Before a single proverb, the book states its purpose, and the purpose is stacked up word on word: wisdom, instruction, insight, wise dealing. Notice what sits inside the list: righteousness, justice, and equity. Wisdom in this book is not cleverness. A con man can be clever. Wisdom here is the skill of living rightly, and it is never separated from being good.

The word instruction appears twice, and it translates musar, which carries the idea of discipline and correction. Wisdom is not only information received; it is a shaping that sometimes hurts. The same word returns in 3:11, quoted in Hebrews 12, about the Lord's discipline of his sons.

to give prudence to the simple, knowledge and discretion to the youth—

Two audiences are named. The simple are not the mentally slow. The word pictures someone open in every direction, a door that swings with any wind, the person who believes whatever he hears last. The youth is the young man standing at the start of life with every road still open. Proverbs is written for exactly the person who does not yet know which voices to trust. That makes it a book for teenagers, and for every adult who is honest about how easily he is still persuaded.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the wise hear and increase in learning, and the one who understands obtain guidance, to understand a proverb and a saying, the words of the wise and their riddles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the wise hear and increase in learning, and the one who understands obtain guidance,

Then, in case the wise reader thinks the book is for other people, the purpose statement turns to him. The wise are to hear and increase. One mark of wisdom is that it knows it has not arrived. The fool in this book is always sure; the wise man is always learning.

Try it as a test. When did you last change your mind about something important because someone corrected you? If you cannot remember, the verse is aimed at you.

to understand a proverb and a saying, the words of the wise and their riddles.

Proverbs have to be understood, not merely memorised. A proverb is compressed. It states a truth about how life usually goes, in a form short enough to carry. It is not a promise with a guarantee attached, and reading it as one breaks both the proverb and the reader. Part of wisdom is knowing which proverb fits which moment, which is why 26:4 and 26:5 can sit side by side and say opposite things about answering a fool.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction.

This is the motto of the whole book, and it comes back at the end of the first section in almost the same words (9:10). The rest of Scripture repeats it: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (Ps 111:10), and Job's great poem on the search for wisdom ends, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom (Job 28:28).

What is the fear of the LORD? It is not cringing terror, as though God were a tyrant. Nor is it only respect, as though he were a distinguished elder. It is the settled awareness that the God of Israel, the LORD, is really there, is holy, sees everything, and is the one you will answer to. It is the reverence of a child who loves his father and would not for the world grieve him, and who also knows his father is not to be trifled with. Both together.

And it is the beginning. The Hebrew word can mean the first step or the chief part, and here it means both. You cannot start being wise without it, and you never graduate beyond it. This means that a person can be highly educated, successful and articulate, and still not have begun. The first question Proverbs asks is not how smart you are but where you stand before God.

The second line gives the alternative. Fools despise wisdom and instruction. The fool in Proverbs is not stupid. He is someone who will not be told. The problem is not in his head but in his will.

For a Christian the motto has a face. God has made Christ wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30). To fear the LORD now is to bow before the Son, and that is where real knowledge begins.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A father speaks. Hear, my son, your father's instruction, and forsake not your mother's teaching (v. 8). The first danger he names is a gang with a proposal: easy money, shared risk, one purse (vv. 10-14). Do not walk with them (v. 15), for they run to blood (v. 16), and a bird at least has the sense to avoid a net it can see (v. 17). The ambush they set is for themselves: Such are the ways of everyone who is greedy for unjust gain; it takes away the life of its possessors (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The first temptation in the book is not lust but belonging, and the first lie is that greed can be shared without cost.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, my son, your father's instruction, and forsake not your mother's teaching, for they are a graceful garland for your head and pendants for your neck.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear, my son, your father's instruction, and forsake not your mother's teaching,

The voice changes. From here to the end of chapter 9, most of the book is a father speaking to his son. Wisdom is not taught in a lecture hall first; it is taught at the kitchen table. And the father names the mother alongside himself: your mother's teaching. In a world where a mother's voice could be discounted, the book gives her teaching the same weight as the father's.

Timothy knew what that looks like. Paul reminds him of the faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice (2 Tim 1:5), and that from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings (2 Tim 3:15). A mother reading Scripture to a child is doing the work of Proverbs 1.

for they are a graceful garland for your head and pendants for your neck.

Parental instruction is not a weight hung round the neck but jewellery. A young man often feels his parents' teaching as a chain; the father says it is a crown. The picture returns in 4:9, where wisdom herself places a graceful garland on the head of the one who holds to her.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent. If they say, "Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood; let us ambush the innocent without reason; like Sheol let us swallow them alive, and whole, like those who go down to the pit; we shall find all precious goods, we shall fill our houses with plunder; throw in your lot among us; we will all have one purse"—
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent.

The first specific warning in the book is short and plain. Not "try to resist" but do not consent. Temptation is not sin. The enticement comes from outside, and the son cannot stop sinners from asking. What he can control is his answer. The whole battle comes down to one word, and it is the word no.

If they say, "Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood; let us ambush the innocent without reason; like Sheol let us swallow them alive, and whole, like those who go down to the pit;

The father does not keep the temptation vague. He puts the gang's pitch in their own words, so that his son will recognise it when he hears it. And the first word of the pitch is Come with us. Before it is an offer of money, it is an offer of belonging. A lonely young man is offered a crew.

They speak of their victims as if they were death itself, swallowing people alive, and whole. It sounds exciting said quickly. Said slowly, it is the language of murderers.

we shall find all precious goods, we shall fill our houses with plunder; throw in your lot among us; we will all have one purse"—

Then the money. All precious goods, full houses. And the clinching promise: we will all have one purse. Shared risk, shared reward, loyalty.

The Gospels show how that purse ends. Among the Twelve, Judas was the one having charge of the moneybag, and he used to help himself to what was put into it (John 12:6). He sold innocent blood for thirty pieces of silver, and then came back saying, I have sinned by betraying innocent blood. The priests who had paid him answered, What is that to us? See to it yourself (Matt 27:4). That is the loyalty of the one purse. The gang that promises to share everything leaves you alone with the guilt.

verseByVerse.quote: my son, do not walk in the way with them; hold back your foot from their paths, for their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed blood. For in vain is a net spread in the sight of any bird, but these men lie in wait for their own blood; they set an ambush for their own lives. Such are the ways of everyone who is greedy for unjust gain; it takes away the life of its possessors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
my son, do not walk in the way with them; hold back your foot from their paths,

The counsel is physical: do not walk, hold back your foot. Sin is usually reached by steps, not leaps. The father does not tell his son to argue with the gang or out-think them. He tells him not to go with them in the first place. Some temptations are resisted by debate; most are resisted by not being there.

for their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed blood.

Isaiah says nearly the same of a whole nation, Their feet run to evil, and they are swift to shed innocent blood (Isa 59:7), and Paul gathers those words into his indictment of the human race: Their feet are swift to shed blood (Rom 3:15). The gang in Proverbs 1 is not an unusual kind of human being. It is what every heart is capable of when greed and company are allowed to run together.

For in vain is a net spread in the sight of any bird,

A bird that watches you spread the net will not fly into it. The point is sharp: a bird has more sense than these men. They can see the trap. They are building it. And they walk into it anyway.

but these men lie in wait for their own blood; they set an ambush for their own lives. Such are the ways of everyone who is greedy for unjust gain; it takes away the life of its possessors.

The ambush they planned for the innocent turns out to be set for themselves. Their greed takes away the life of its possessors. It does not merely cost them their money; it owns them and then kills them. Judas again: he acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and died in it (Acts 1:18).

Paul says the same about the respectable version of this sin: those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare (1 Tim 6:9). The snare is the same, whether it is a mugging in an alley or a dishonest deal in an office. Ask the question the proverb puts: is there any gain in my life that I could only have by someone else's loss? That is the net, and I can see it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–33 — Wisdom Cries Aloud in the Street
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom is not hidden; she shouts in the markets and at the city gates (vv. 20-21). How long, O simple ones, will you love being simple? (v. 22). She offers her spirit and her words to anyone who turns (v. 23), but those who refuse will call when calamity comes, and she will not answer (vv. 24-28). They chose their way and will eat its fruit (vv. 29-31). For the simple are killed by their turning away, but whoever listens to me will dwell secure (vv. 32-33).
verseByVerse.theology: The same voice that pleads also warns that the day of pleading ends. The New Testament hears that voice in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom cries aloud in the street, in the markets she raises her voice; at the head of the noisy streets she cries out; at the entrance of the city gates she speaks:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom cries aloud in the street, in the markets she raises her voice; at the head of the noisy streets she cries out; at the entrance of the city gates she speaks:

Now a new voice. Wisdom is pictured as a woman, and where does she speak? Not in a temple, not in a classroom, not in a hermit's cave, but in the street, the market, the noisy junction, the city gate where business and lawsuits were settled. She goes where the gang goes. The sinners of verse 11 called the young man in the street; Wisdom shouts in the same street.

Wisdom is not a secret for the initiated. She is shouting over the traffic. Nobody in this chapter perishes because the truth was hidden from him.

The New Testament hears this voice in Jesus. On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). He described himself in Wisdom's terms: wisdom is justified by her deeds (Matt 11:19). And where Luke records the Wisdom of God said, 'I will send them prophets and apostles (Luke 11:49), Matthew records Jesus saying in his own person, Therefore I send you prophets and wise men and scribes (Matt 23:34). The Wisdom who calls in the street took flesh and walked into it.

verseByVerse.quote: "How long, O simple ones, will you love being simple? How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing and fools hate knowledge? If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you; I will make my words known to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"How long, O simple ones, will you love being simple? How long will scoffers delight in their scoffing and fools hate knowledge?

Three kinds of people, and they are a descending staircase. The simple are drifting. Scoffers have learned to mock what they have not considered. Fools have come to hate knowledge. The chilling word is love: the simple love being simple. They are not trapped in their ignorance; they prefer it, because staying unformed means staying uncommitted.

And the question is How long? Not how can you, but how long will you? Wisdom speaks with the impatience of love, like a mother calling a child in from the road.

If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you; I will make my words known to you.

The offer is astonishing. Wisdom does not ask the simple to become wise first and then come. She asks them to turn, and then she will give herself: her spirit and her words. The turning is repentance; the gift is grace.

Read that promise with the whole Bible open. God said through Joel, I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh (Joel 2:28), and Peter declared it fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:17). Jesus' cry at the feast was about exactly this: Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive (John 7:39). What Wisdom offers in the street, Christ poured out on his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Because I have called and you refused to listen, have stretched out my hand and no one has heeded, because you have ignored all my counsel and would have none of my reproof, I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when terror strikes you, when terror strikes you like a storm and your calamity comes like a whirlwind, when distress and anguish come upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because I have called and you refused to listen, have stretched out my hand and no one has heeded,

Now the tone changes, and it is frightening. Wisdom has called and stretched out my hand, the gesture of someone reaching to pull a person out of danger. Paul uses the same picture of God with Israel: All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people (Rom 10:21).

because you have ignored all my counsel and would have none of my reproof, I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when terror strikes you,

How can Wisdom laugh at anyone's disaster? It sounds cruel until you see what is being laughed at. It is not the suffering person but the folly that thought it could defy God and win. Psalm 2 uses the same figure of the kings who plot against the LORD and his Anointed: He who sits in the heavens laughs (Ps 2:4). The laughter is the absurdity of rebellion exposed. Every warning the fool dismissed as overcautious has come true.

when terror strikes you like a storm and your calamity comes like a whirlwind, when distress and anguish come upon you.

Storm, whirlwind, distress, anguish. The consequences of folly are not delivered gently or gradually at the end. They arrive like weather: suddenly, from every side at once. A marriage that ends, a body that fails, a career that collapses in a week, after years of warnings ignored.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they will call upon me, but I will not answer; they will seek me diligently but will not find me. Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the LORD, would have none of my counsel and despised all my reproof, therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way, and have their fill of their own devices.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they will call upon me, but I will not answer; they will seek me diligently but will not find me.

This is a hard sentence, and it must be read carefully. Proverbs 8 promises, those who seek me diligently find me (8:17). Here, the same seeking finds nothing. What is the difference?

The difference is what they are seeking. Verse 29 explains: they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the LORD. They are not seeking God; they are seeking rescue from the storm. They want the consequences removed, not the heart changed. It is the cry of Esau, who found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears (Heb 12:17). He wanted the blessing back, not the God of the blessing.

There is a real then. Jesus told of the master of the house who has risen and shut the door, and those outside knocking and calling Lord, open to us (Luke 13:25). The door does not stay open forever. That is why the Bible's urgency always falls on the present: Seek the LORD while he may be found (Isa 55:6); behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor 6:2).

Pastorally, it matters to say this plainly: if you are anxious that you have sought God too late, your anxiety is itself evidence that you are not the person of verse 29. The people in this verse do not grieve that they hated the fear of the LORD. They only grieve the storm.

Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the LORD, would have none of my counsel and despised all my reproof,

Notice the verb choose. The fear of the LORD is presented as a choice people make. The fool was not unlucky; he decided, again and again, until the decisions became who he was.

therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way, and have their fill of their own devices.

God's judgment here is not an arbitrary punishment dropped on them from outside. It is being given what they chose, in full. They wanted their own devices; now they have their fill of them. The worst thing God can do to a person who insists on his own way is to let him have it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the simple are killed by their turning away, and the complacency of fools destroys them; but whoever listens to me will dwell secure and will be at ease, without dread of disaster."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the simple are killed by their turning away, and the complacency of fools destroys them;

Two killers are named, and neither is dramatic. Turning away: not open rebellion, just walking off when Wisdom is talking. And complacency: the ease of a person who assumes tomorrow will look like today. Jesus told of a rich man who said to his soul, relax, eat, drink, be merry. But God said to him, 'Fool! This night your soul is required of you (Luke 12:19-20). Most people are not destroyed by one great act of defiance. They are destroyed by being comfortable.

but whoever listens to me will dwell secure and will be at ease, without dread of disaster."

The chapter ends on the other side, and the promise is rest. The fool was at ease in a false way and destroyed by it. The one who listens to Wisdom is truly at ease, without dread of disaster. Not without disaster, necessarily. Without dread of it. His security rests on something the storm cannot take.

Wisdom called in the street; Christ called in the same way, with the same offer: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt 11:28). Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Heb 3:15). The whole book of Proverbs is an extended invitation to be the person of verse 33, and it begins by bowing before the Lord who is himself the wisdom of God.

1.overview:
Proverbs opens with its heading and purpose. These are the proverbs of Solomon, collected so that the simple and the young may gain wisdom, and so that the wise may grow wiser (vv. 1-6). Then the motto of the whole book: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction (v. 7).

A father warns his son about a gang that offers belonging and easy money. Their ambush is really set for themselves, because greed takes the life of those who possess it (vv. 8-19).

Then Wisdom herself shouts in the streets. She pleads with the simple to turn and receive her spirit, warns that those who refuse will call on her in calamity and not be answered, and promises security to all who listen (vv. 20-33).
1.theology:
Wisdom begins with the fear of the LORD, the reverent and loving awareness of the holy God (v. 7; 9:10; Ps 111:10). Folly is a matter of the will, not the intellect: fools despise wisdom. Wisdom is inseparable from righteousness, justice and equity (v. 3).

Temptation offers belonging before it offers gain, and sin is self-destructive: the ambush is set for the ambushers (vv. 10-19; Rom 3:15; 1 Tim 6:9).

Wisdom calls publicly and freely, offers her spirit to those who turn (v. 23; Acts 2:17), and warns that the time of calling ends (vv. 24-31; Luke 13:25). The New Testament presents Christ as the Wisdom of God who cries out and gives rest (Luke 11:49; John 7:37; 1 Cor 1:24, 30; Col 2:3).
1.examples:
Solomon's prayer for an understanding mind.

The simple as a door that swings in any wind.

A mother reading Scripture to a child: Lois and Eunice.

The gang's first word: Come with us.

Judas and the one purse.

A bird watching the net being spread.

Wisdom shouting in the market; Jesus crying out at the feast.

The rich fool who said, Relax.

Not without disaster, but without dread of it.

2.title: If You Seek It Like Silver

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Search and the Gift
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The father builds one long sentence. If you receive my words, if you call out for insight, if you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures (vv. 1-4), then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God (v. 5). The seeker finds, because the LORD gives wisdom and guards the way of his saints (vv. 6-8). Wisdom comes into the heart and becomes a pleasure, and discretion stands guard (vv. 9-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The effort is ours and the gift is God's, and neither cancels the other.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if you receive my words and treasure up my commandments with you, making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding; yes, if you call out for insight and raise your voice for understanding, if you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures,
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, if you receive my words and treasure up my commandments with you, making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding;

Proverbs 2 is, in Hebrew, one long sentence of twenty-two verses, and it is built like an argument: if this, then that. The father starts with the conditions, and they climb.

First, receive and treasure up. A word heard and forgotten has not been received. To treasure it is to store it the way a person stores what is valuable, somewhere safe, where he can get at it again. Then making your ear attentive and inclining your heart, the picture of leaning toward a speaker so as not to miss a word. Ear and heart together: hearing that goes inward.

yes, if you call out for insight and raise your voice for understanding,

In chapter 1, Wisdom raises her voice in the street (1:20). Now the son is to raise his voice for her. She calls; he calls back. Wisdom is a conversation, and the one who wants it must be willing to ask out loud, which means admitting he lacks it. If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God (Jas 1:5).

if you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures,

Now the image that governs the chapter. Think about how men have searched for silver: tunnels cut into rock, lamps lowered into shafts, years spent on the hope of a seam. Job 28 describes exactly that, Surely there is a mine for silver, and then asks, But where shall wisdom be found? (Job 28:1, 12).

Here is a test the verse puts to any reader. What do you search for with that kind of energy? A promotion, a house, a sports result, a relationship? The verse does not say those are wrong. It says wisdom deserves at least as much. Jesus told of a man who found treasure hidden in a field, Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field (Matt 13:44). For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matt 6:21).

verseByVerse.quote: then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God. For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding; he stores up sound wisdom for the upright; he is a shield to those who walk in integrity, guarding the paths of justice and watching over the way of his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God.

And here is the then. Notice what the searcher finds. He went looking for wisdom and found God. Chapter 1 said the fear of the LORD is where wisdom begins (1:7); chapter 2 says it is also where the search ends. The treasure at the bottom of the mine is not a technique for living but the knowledge of God: not facts about him, but knowing him.

For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding;

Verse 6 is the hinge of the chapter, and it turns everything the right way round. After four verses of seeking, searching, calling and digging, the reason anyone finds wisdom is that the LORD gives it. The search is real, but it is not a wage. Nobody earns wisdom by effort, the way a miner earns silver by labour. It is a gift, and it comes from his mouth, which means it comes by his word.

The New Testament keeps both halves in the same way: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Phil 2:12-13). The effort does not cancel the grace, and the grace does not make the effort pointless. God gives his wisdom to people who want it badly enough to dig. Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find (Matt 7:7).

he stores up sound wisdom for the upright; he is a shield to those who walk in integrity, guarding the paths of justice and watching over the way of his saints.

The son was to treasure up the father's words (v. 1); here God stores up wisdom for the upright. He is laying up a supply for his people before they need it. And he is a shield, guarding, watching over. The son who walks this road is not walking it alone.

His saints are not an elite of especially holy people. The word describes those bound to God in his covenant love. Every believer walking the path of justice has God on watch over that path.

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will understand righteousness and justice and equity, every good path; for wisdom will come into your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul; discretion will watch over you, understanding will guard you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then you will understand righteousness and justice and equity, every good path;

The second then. The first was about knowing God (v. 5). This one is about knowing how to live. The order matters. Proverbs never offers moral skill cut off from God; it comes after, and out of, knowing him. Righteousness and justice and equity are the same three words from the book's purpose statement (1:3). The father is saying: this is where the book was heading.

Every good path is a generous phrase. Wisdom does not only tell a person what to avoid. It opens up every good road there is.

for wisdom will come into your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul;

Something changes inside. At first the son searches for wisdom as a duty, digging because his father told him to. But wisdom will come into your heart, and then it becomes pleasant. What was hard work becomes a taste. This is what God does to the desires of those he teaches. The psalmist could say, The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces (Ps 119:72). The search for silver ends with the searcher preferring what he found to silver.

If obedience still feels like a mine shaft to you, keep digging. The promise is that it will not always feel that way.

discretion will watch over you, understanding will guard you,

God watched over the way of his saints (v. 8). Now the wisdom he gave does the watching from inside. Discretion is the ability to see a situation for what it is before you are in the middle of it: to recognise the smooth voice on the first sentence rather than the fifth. That is what the rest of the chapter needs.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — Delivered from Two Ways of Death
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom delivers from two dangers. First, men of perverted speech, who rejoice in evil and walk crooked paths (vv. 12-15). Second, the forbidden woman with her smooth words, who has broken faith with her husband and her God, whose house sinks down to death (vv. 16-19). The wise walk in the way of the good: the upright will inhabit the land, but the wicked will be rooted out of it (vv. 20-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The two great seductions of a young man, crooked company and illicit sex, both speak smoothly and both lead down.

verseByVerse.quote: delivering you from the way of evil, from men of perverted speech, who forsake the paths of uprightness to walk in the ways of darkness, who rejoice in doing evil and delight in the perverseness of evil, men whose paths are crooked, and who are devious in their ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
delivering you from the way of evil, from men of perverted speech,

Wisdom's first rescue is from a kind of man, and he is identified by his speech. Perverted speech is talk that twists things, that makes the wrong sound reasonable and the right sound naive. The gang of chapter 1 was dangerous because of what it said: Come with us. Most young people are not dragged into evil. They are talked into it.

who forsake the paths of uprightness to walk in the ways of darkness,

The word forsake matters. These men once knew the paths of uprightness. They are not ignorant; they walked away. And they prefer darkness, where what they do cannot be seen.

who rejoice in doing evil and delight in the perverseness of evil, men whose paths are crooked, and who are devious in their ways.

Here is the last stage of corruption: not doing evil reluctantly, but enjoying it, and enjoying it in others. Paul describes the same end of the road: they not only do them but give approval to those who practice them (Rom 1:32). When a group laughs together about wrongdoing, that is the verse.

And their paths are crooked. A crooked path is hard to follow and easy to get lost on, and you cannot see where it bends next. Wisdom's value is that it lets you see the bend before you take it.

verseByVerse.quote: So you will be delivered from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words, who forsakes the companion of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
So you will be delivered from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words,

Wisdom's second rescue. The ESV notes that the Hebrew behind forbidden woman is "strange", and behind adulteress, "foreign woman". She may be an Israelite by birth; she is "strange" and "foreign" because she stands outside the boundary God set around marriage. She belongs to someone else.

And like the men of verse 12, she works by speech: smooth words. Chapter 5 will say her lips drip honey and her speech is smoother than oil (5:3). Sexual temptation almost never introduces itself as adultery. It introduces itself as being understood, admired, listened to. The discretion of verse 11 is what hears the flattery for what it is.

Both dangers in this chapter work through words, which means both are defeated by a better word: the father's commandments treasured up in the heart (v. 1). A man who has Scripture stored away has something to answer the smooth voice with.

who forsakes the companion of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God;

She has done two things. She has left the companion of her youth, her husband, the one she married when they were both young. And she has forgotten the covenant of her God. Marriage in the Bible is never merely a private arrangement between two people. God is party to it. Malachi says it outright: the LORD was witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant (Mal 2:14).

So adultery is not a sin against one person. It breaks faith with a spouse and with God at the same time. Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled (Heb 13:4).

verseByVerse.quote: for her house sinks down to death, and her paths to the departed; none who go to her come back, nor do they regain the paths of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for her house sinks down to death, and her paths to the departed;

Her house looks like a house. It has a door, a bed, perfume. But the father sees what the young man cannot: the whole building is sinking, and it goes down to death. The ESV notes that the departed is in Hebrew "the Rephaim", the shades of the dead, the same word Isaiah uses when Sheol rouses the shades to greet a fallen king (Isa 14:9). Chapter 7 ends with the same picture: Her house is the way to Sheol (7:27).

none who go to her come back, nor do they regain the paths of life.

This is a warning about where the road goes, and it is meant to frighten. Adultery rarely stays one act. It rewires a person's desires, breaks trust that is almost never fully rebuilt, wrecks children, and often ends a life's direction. Many who go down that road never come back to where they were. He who commits adultery lacks sense; he who does it destroys himself (6:32).

But a reader who has already been down that road needs to hear the rest of the Bible too. Proverbs describes the destination of the path, not the limit of God's mercy. David went to another man's wife and took her. When Nathan confronted him, David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD." And Nathan said to David, "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die (2 Sam 12:13). Paul wrote to Corinthians who had been adulterers, And such were some of you. But you were washed (1 Cor 6:11). No one regains the paths of life by his own strength. Christ brings people back who could not come back.

verseByVerse.quote: So you will walk in the way of the good and keep to the paths of the righteous. For the upright will inhabit the land, and those with integrity will remain in it, but the wicked will be cut off from the land, and the treacherous will be rooted out of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So you will walk in the way of the good and keep to the paths of the righteous.

After the two warnings, the positive goal. Wisdom does not just keep a person out of the ditch; it puts him on a road with good company. The men of verse 12 had their crooked paths; here are the paths of the righteous, and others walking them. The best protection against bad company is good company. Flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart (2 Tim 2:22).

For the upright will inhabit the land, and those with integrity will remain in it, but the wicked will be cut off from the land, and the treacherous will be rooted out of it.

For an Israelite, the land meant the inheritance God had promised Abraham, the place of God's blessing and presence. To be cut off from it was to lose everything the covenant offered. Psalm 37 says the same, The righteous shall inherit the land and dwell upon it forever (Ps 37:29).

Jesus took that promise and widened it: Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth (Matt 5:5). The land was always a picture of something larger, the whole creation renewed and given to God's people.

So the chapter ends with two futures. The treacherous are rooted out, pulled up like a plant that looked established and had no hold. The upright remain. The world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever (1 John 2:17). The silver the young man was told to dig for turns out to be a place in God's world forever.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>My son, if you receive my words and treasure up my commandments with you,<sup>2</sup>making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding;<sup>3</sup>yes, if you call out for insight and raise your voice for understanding,<sup>4</sup>if you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures,<sup>5</sup>then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God.<sup>6</sup>For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding;<sup>7</sup>he stores up sound wisdom for the upright; he is a shield to those who walk in integrity,<sup>8</sup>guarding the paths of justice and watching over the way of his saints.<sup>9</sup>Then you will understand righteousness and justice and equity, every good path;<sup>10</sup>for wisdom will come into your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul;<sup>11</sup>discretion will watch over you, understanding will guard you,<sup>12</sup>delivering you from the way of evil, from men of perverted speech,<sup>13</sup>who forsake the paths of uprightness to walk in the ways of darkness,<sup>14</sup>who rejoice in doing evil and delight in the perverseness of evil,<sup>15</sup>men whose paths are crooked, and who are devious in their ways.<sup>16</sup>So you will be delivered from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words,<sup>17</sup>who forsakes the companion of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God;<sup>18</sup>for her house sinks down to death, and her paths to the departed;<sup>19</sup>none who go to her come back, nor do they regain the paths of life.<sup>20</sup>So you will walk in the way of the good and keep to the paths of the righteous.<sup>21</sup>For the upright will inhabit the land, and those with integrity will remain in it,<sup>22</sup>but the wicked will be cut off from the land, and the treacherous will be rooted out of it.
2.overview:
Proverbs 2 is one long conditional sentence. If the son receives his father's words, calls out for insight and searches for wisdom like silver (vv. 1-4), then he will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God, because the LORD gives wisdom and guards his saints (vv. 5-8). Then he will understand every good path, wisdom will become pleasant to him, and discretion will guard him (vv. 9-11).

Wisdom delivers him from men of perverted speech who delight in evil (vv. 12-15), and from the forbidden woman with smooth words who has broken her marriage covenant and whose house sinks down to death (vv. 16-19). The upright will remain in the land; the wicked will be rooted out (vv. 20-22).
2.theology:
The search for wisdom requires real effort (vv. 1-4), yet wisdom is God's gift from his mouth (v. 6); human seeking and divine giving work together (Phil 2:12-13; Jas 1:5). Its goal is knowing God himself (v. 5), and moral understanding follows from that (v. 9). God changes desire, so that wisdom becomes pleasant (v. 10).

Evil and sexual sin both work through deceptive speech (vv. 12, 16). Marriage is a covenant before God, so adultery breaks faith with God as well as a spouse (v. 17; Mal 2:14). The road of adultery leads to death (vv. 18-19), but the gospel restores the repentant (2 Sam 12:13; 1 Cor 6:11). The inheritance of the land anticipates the meek inheriting the earth (v. 21; Matt 5:5).
2.examples:
Miners following a seam of silver.

The man who sold everything for the field.

Searching for wisdom and finding God.

A duty that becomes a taste.

Recognising the smooth voice on the first sentence.

A house that looks like a house and is sinking.

David and Nathan: the road's end is not the limit of mercy.

Good company as protection.

3.title: Trust in the LORD with All Your Heart

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Trust, Honour and the Father's Discipline
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The father asks his son to keep his teaching, which adds length of days and years of life and peace (vv. 1-2), and to bind steadfast love and faithfulness round his neck (vv. 3-4). Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths (vv. 5-6). Humility before God is health (vv. 7-8); honouring him with the firstfruits brings plenty (vv. 9-10). My son, do not despise the LORD's discipline, for the LORD reproves him whom he loves (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Every line in this section is about the heart's posture toward God: trusting him, honouring him, and not resenting him when he corrects.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, do not forget my teaching, but let your heart keep my commandments, for length of days and years of life and peace they will add to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, do not forget my teaching, but let your heart keep my commandments,

The father begins where he always does, with memory and the heart. Do not forget. Most people who abandon what they were taught do not reject it in a single decision. They forget it slowly, by not returning to it. So the command is not only to learn but to keep, and to keep it in the heart, where it shapes what a person wants and not just what he knows.

for length of days and years of life and peace they will add to you.

The reason given is life. Not only more years, but peace, the Hebrew shalom, which means wholeness: life that is well in every part. This is how Proverbs speaks throughout. The commandments are not a fence around life to keep good things out; they are the shape of life as God made it to work.

Is this a promise that every godly person lives to old age? The book itself does not read it that way, and neither does the rest of Scripture. Proverbs describes how God's world generally runs: a life of honesty, self-control and peace with neighbours tends to be longer and fuller than a life of drunkenness, violence and deceit. Abel was righteous and died young. The deepest fulfilment of length of days lies beyond this life, in the one who promises eternal life to all who trust him.

verseByVerse.quote: Let not steadfast love and faithfulness forsake you; bind them around your neck; write them on the tablet of your heart. So you will find favor and good success in the sight of God and man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let not steadfast love and faithfulness forsake you; bind them around your neck; write them on the tablet of your heart.

Steadfast love and faithfulness are two of the richest words in the Old Testament, hesed and emet. They are the words God used for himself when he passed before Moses on the mountain: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod 34:6). The father is telling his son to have the character of God: loyal love that does not quit, and truthfulness that can be relied on.

Then two places to keep them: outside, around your neck, like a necklace everyone sees; and inside, on the tablet of your heart, where no one sees but God. The phrase recalls the law written on tablets of stone. What God wrote on stone at Sinai, the father wants written on his son's heart. That is precisely what God promised to do in the new covenant: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jer 31:33). Paul told the Corinthians they were a letter written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts (2 Cor 3:3).

And when the Word became flesh, John saw the two words walking in a human life: full of grace and truth (John 1:14).

So you will find favor and good success in the sight of God and man.

A loyal and truthful person is trusted by people as well as by God. The ESV notes that good success may be rendered "repute": a good name. Luke says the boy Jesus increased in favor with God and man (Luke 2:52), the clearest picture there is of this verse lived.

verseByVerse.quote: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding.

These may be the most loved verses in the book, and they deserve to be read slowly.

Trust means to rely on, to put your weight down on something. With all your heart excludes the divided trust that relies on God for eternity and on itself for Tuesday. It is the same wholeness God asked for in the great command, You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart (Deut 6:5).

The second line gives the alternative: do not lean on your own understanding. It does not say, do not use your understanding. Proverbs is full of commands to think, plan, consider and learn. It says, do not lean on it, do not make it the thing that holds your weight. Your understanding is a useful tool and a terrible foundation. It is limited, because you do not know what tomorrow holds, and it is bent, because your heart tilts it toward what you want.

Here is a test. Think of the decision in front of you that you are most anxious about. Where is your weight resting at this moment: on your ability to work it out, or on God's faithfulness whichever way it goes?

In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths.

Acknowledge translates the ordinary Hebrew word for know. It means more than a nod in God's direction before you do what you had already decided. It means knowing him, recognising him, bringing him into all your ways: the career decision and the conversation at lunch, the budget and the marriage.

And the promise: he will make straight your paths. The picture is of a road being levelled, as when Isaiah calls for a highway in the desert where the uneven ground shall become level (Isa 40:4). It does not promise a map of the whole journey in advance, or a road without hills. It promises that God clears the way ahead of the one who trusts him, and gets him where he is meant to go. The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps (16:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD, and turn away from evil. It will be healing to your flesh and refreshment to your bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD, and turn away from evil.

Verse 7 says negatively what verse 5 said positively. Leaning on your own understanding, in practice, looks like being wise in your own eyes: the man who does not ask advice because he already knows, who does not pray about a decision because it is obvious. Isaiah pronounced a woe on exactly him: Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes (Isa 5:21). Paul told the Romans, Never be wise in your own sight (Rom 12:16).

And the cure is three words long in English: fear the LORD. The fear of the LORD, which chapter 1 called the beginning of knowledge (1:7), is here the antidote to self-made wisdom, and it shows itself practically: turn away from evil. A person who says he trusts God and keeps walking toward evil is still wise in his own eyes.

It will be healing to your flesh and refreshment to your bones.

The ESV notes two things here: flesh is literally "navel", and healing may be "medicine". The navel may picture the centre of the body, or the cord through which a child in the womb is fed. Either way, humility before God is not only good for the soul. A person who is not carrying the burden of being his own god carries less strain in his body. Pride is exhausting.

verseByVerse.quote: Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your produce; then your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will be bursting with wine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your produce;

Trust in God shows up in the bank account. Under the law, Israel brought the first and best of the harvest to God: The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of the LORD your God (Exod 23:19). The firstfruits were given before the farmer knew how big the rest of the harvest would be. That is what made it an act of trust. Giving God what is left over after the bills requires no faith at all.

For a Christian the principle stands without the agricultural calendar: giving to God first, deliberately, and gladly. Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor 9:7).

then your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will be bursting with wine.

Is this the prosperity gospel, give to get? No. It is the same pattern Malachi describes, where God invites his people to bring the tithe and see whether he will not pour down for you a blessing until there is no more need (Mal 3:10). God is no man's debtor. But Proverbs is describing how his world generally works, not offering a formula to manipulate him. Job feared God, gave to the poor, and lost everything in a day, and said, The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD (Job 1:21).

Paul gives the New Testament form of the promise, and notice what the abundance is for: God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work (2 Cor 9:8). The full barn is given so that the giving can continue.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, do not despise the LORD's discipline or be weary of his reproof, for the LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, do not despise the LORD's discipline or be weary of his reproof,

Having promised full barns, the father immediately faces the other side. What about when life hurts? There are two wrong responses, and the verse names both. To despise discipline is to treat it lightly, to shrug off hardship as bad luck and learn nothing. To be weary of it is to be crushed by it, to resent God and give up. One takes it too lightly, the other too heavily.

for the LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights.

And the reason neither response is right: discipline is love. A father who never corrects his son does not love him more; he cares about him less. God's correction is proof that he has claimed you as his own.

The letter to the Hebrews quotes these two verses to Christians who were suffering and ready to give up: My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives (Heb 12:5-6). Hebrews follows the ancient Greek translation of the verse, and the sense is the same. It goes on to say what discipline produces: he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness (Heb 12:10), and For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness (Heb 12:11). The risen Christ says the same to a lukewarm church: Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline (Rev 3:19).

Not all suffering is punishment for a specific sin, and Job is the Bible's long proof of that. But all of a believer's suffering is in the hands of a Father who is training his son. That changes the question from "Why is this happening to me?" to "What is my Father teaching me in this?"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–26 — Blessed Is the One Who Finds Wisdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Blessed is the one who finds wisdom, whose value is beyond silver, gold and jewels (vv. 13-15). She holds long life, riches and honour; her paths are peace; She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her (vv. 16-18). By this same wisdom the LORD founded the earth and established the heavens (vv. 19-20). So keep her: she gives security by day and sweet sleep by night, and freedom from the fear of sudden terror, for the LORD will be your confidence (vv. 21-26).
verseByVerse.theology: The wisdom that holds the universe together is offered to a young man to hold his life together.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the one who finds wisdom, and the one who gets understanding, for the gain from her is better than gain from silver and her profit better than gold. She is more precious than jewels, and nothing you desire can compare with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the one who finds wisdom, and the one who gets understanding, for the gain from her is better than gain from silver and her profit better than gold.

A new section opens with a beatitude. Blessed, the word that opens the Psalter, describes the person who is truly well off, whatever his circumstances look like. And the language is commercial: gain, profit. The father is speaking the language of the market to a young man who is about to enter it. Compare the returns, he says. Wisdom beats silver and gold.

She is more precious than jewels, and nothing you desire can compare with her.

Nothing you desire. Take the verse at its word and run through the list: the house, the salary, the spouse, the reputation, the retirement. Nothing on it compares. That is either an exaggeration or the most important financial advice a young person will ever get. Paul would say it is the second: godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come (1 Tim 4:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Long life is in her right hand; in her left hand are riches and honor. Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace. She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her; those who hold her fast are called blessed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Long life is in her right hand; in her left hand are riches and honor.

Wisdom is pictured holding gifts in both hands. In her right hand, the hand of greater honour, is long life; in her left, riches and honor. The order matters. Life comes first, and riches second. The man who chases riches and honour directly usually loses both. The one who pursues wisdom finds them given to him as extras. Jesus put it in the same order: But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matt 6:33).

Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace.

Many people imagine a godly life as dreary. The verse says otherwise. The road of wisdom is pleasant. The paths of folly are exciting at the start and full of regret. The paths of wisdom are sometimes hard at the start and full of peace.

She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her; those who hold her fast are called blessed.

A tree of life takes the reader back to Eden. After the fall, God guarded that tree lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever (Gen 3:22). Humanity lost access to it. Now Proverbs says that wisdom is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her, the very reaching out that was barred in Eden.

The Bible ends where it began, with the tree restored: on either side of the river, the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit, and The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations (Rev 22:2). The way back to the tree is through the one who is the wisdom of God. And the verse ends as it began, with blessed: the section is framed by the word.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD by wisdom founded the earth; by understanding he established the heavens; by his knowledge the deeps broke open, and the clouds drop down the dew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD by wisdom founded the earth; by understanding he established the heavens;

Now the father lifts his son's eyes from the marketplace to the universe. The wisdom he has been urging is not a small, private thing. It is the wisdom by which God built the world. O LORD, how manifold are your works! In wisdom have you made them all (Ps 104:24).

That changes how to think about living wisely. Wisdom is not an arbitrary set of rules laid over a neutral world. It is the grain of the universe. To live wisely is to go with the grain of the way God built things, and folly is going against it. A person who lives against the grain of creation will find that creation pushes back.

by his knowledge the deeps broke open, and the clouds drop down the dew.

From the great waters under the earth to the gentle dew each morning, the same wisdom is at work. It governs the flood and the drop of water on a blade of grass.

The New Testament names this creative wisdom. All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made (John 1:3). For by him all things were created, and in him all things hold together (Col 1:16-17). Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24). Chapter 8 will develop this at length. For now, the father's point is this: the wisdom that holds galaxies in place is on offer to a young man to hold his life in place.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, do not lose sight of these— keep sound wisdom and discretion, and they will be life for your soul and adornment for your neck. Then you will walk on your way securely, and your foot will not stumble. If you lie down, you will not be afraid; when you lie down, your sleep will be sweet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, do not lose sight of these— keep sound wisdom and discretion, and they will be life for your soul and adornment for your neck.

After the cosmic view, back to the son. Do not lose sight of these: keep them in view. The two words sound wisdom and discretion are practical ones: good judgement, and the ability to plan well. They are life for your soul inside and adornment for your neck outside, the same double picture as verse 3.

Then you will walk on your way securely, and your foot will not stumble.

By day, security. The wise person is not immune from difficulty, but he is not tripping over his own folly. Many of the disasters that wreck lives are the foreseeable results of choices. Wisdom removes a great many stones from the road.

If you lie down, you will not be afraid; when you lie down, your sleep will be sweet.

By night, rest. Many people know what it is to lie awake at three in the morning with the mind racing: the debt, the conflict, the lie that might come out, the fear of what tomorrow will bring. The verse promises the wise something that money cannot buy, sweet sleep. In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety (Ps 4:8). For he gives to his beloved sleep (Ps 127:2).

The most vivid picture of this verse in the Bible is a boat in a storm on Galilee. The disciples were terrified. Jesus was in the stern, asleep on the cushion (Mark 4:38). He slept because he trusted his Father completely. Those who belong to him can learn to sleep the same way.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be afraid of sudden terror or of the ruin of the wicked, when it comes, for the LORD will be your confidence and will keep your foot from being caught.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be afraid of sudden terror or of the ruin of the wicked, when it comes,

The ESV notes that ruin is literally "storm". It is the same storm as in chapter 1, where terror strikes the fool like a storm (1:27). The storm that destroys the wicked will come. The wise person is told not to be afraid of it. That does not mean it will not touch him. It means he will not be swept away by it.

for the LORD will be your confidence and will keep your foot from being caught.

Yet the ground of his safety is not his own wisdom, finally, but the LORD. The LORD will be your confidence. The chapter began with trust (v. 5) and returns to it here. The wise man does not trust his wisdom. He trusts the God who gave it. His foot is kept, not because he is clever enough to spot every trap, but because God is watching over his steps.

Try the verse on the fear that most often wakes you. Then say it aloud: the LORD will be my confidence.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom turns outward to the neighbour. Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in your power to do it, and do not put off till tomorrow what you can give today (vv. 27-28). Do not plot against a trusting neighbour or quarrel without cause (vv. 29-30), and do not envy the violent (v. 31). The LORD's curse and blessing rest on houses (vv. 32-33): Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor, and The wise will inherit honor, but fools get disgrace (vv. 34-35).
verseByVerse.theology: Trust in God that does not open the hand to a neighbour is not the trust of verse 5.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in your power to do it. Do not say to your neighbor, "Go, and come again, tomorrow I will give it"—when you have it with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in your power to do it.

The chapter now turns, sharply, to the neighbour. Faith in God (v. 5) and honouring him with wealth (v. 9) are tested at the front door. The Hebrew, as the ESV's footnote records, reads Do not withhold good "from its owners". The good you could do for someone who needs it belongs, in a sense, to him. Wages owed, a debt due, help needed that you could easily give: to hold it back is a kind of theft.

Notice the condition, when it is in your power to do it. The verse does not ask you to meet every need in the world. It asks you not to refuse the need in front of you that you could meet. So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone (Gal 6:10). Owe no one anything, except to love each other (Rom 13:8).

Do not say to your neighbor, "Go, and come again, tomorrow I will give it"—when you have it with you.

Here is the polite way of withholding good: postponement. Come back tomorrow. It sounds generous. It costs nothing today. But the neighbour's need is today, and tomorrow is not promised to either of you. Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring (27:1).

James saw the same thing in the church: a brother or sister without food, and a believer saying, Go in peace, be warmed and filled, without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that? (Jas 2:16). The kind words that replace help are an insult. Is there a need you have been saying "tomorrow" to?

verseByVerse.quote: Do not plan evil against your neighbor, who dwells trustingly beside you. Do not contend with a man for no reason, when he has done you no harm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not plan evil against your neighbor, who dwells trustingly beside you.

Your neighbour dwells trustingly beside you. He does not lock his gate against you. He assumes you are safe. To take advantage of that trust, to plot against someone who is not on guard, is a particular kind of evil. It is the evil of the office colleague who seems friendly and is quietly positioning against you, or the business partner who is moving the money.

Do not contend with a man for no reason, when he has done you no harm.

Some people pick fights. They argue for the pleasure of winning, take offence where none was meant, and treat every disagreement as a war. The verse says: if he has done you no harm, leave him alone. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Rom 12:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways, for the devious person is an abomination to the LORD, but the upright are in his confidence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways,

Why would anyone envy a violent man? Because he often seems to win. He gets his way, people fear him, he takes what he wants. A young man watching him may think, that is how the world works. Psalm 73 is the long confession of a believer who nearly slipped this way: For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked (Ps 73:3). Envy is the first step toward choosing his ways.

for the devious person is an abomination to the LORD, but the upright are in his confidence.

Here is what the envious young man cannot see. The devious person is an abomination to the LORD, one of the strongest words of revulsion in the Old Testament. And the upright are in his confidence: the word pictures a close circle of friends who share secrets. The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him, and he makes known to them his covenant (Ps 25:14).

The violent man has power. The upright man has God's friendship. Jesus said to his disciples, but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you (John 15:15). Which of the two would you rather be?

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD's curse is on the house of the wicked, but he blesses the dwelling of the righteous. Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor. The wise will inherit honor, but fools get disgrace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD's curse is on the house of the wicked, but he blesses the dwelling of the righteous.

The chapter ends with three contrasts, and the first is about houses. The wicked man's house may be large and the righteous man's small. But God's curse rests on one and his blessing on the other. What a house is made of matters much less than what rests on it.

Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor.

God answers people in kind. The scorner mocks God and is mocked. The humble bend low and are lifted. The ESV notes that favor may be rendered "grace", and that is exactly how the verse passed into the New Testament, where it is quoted twice in its Greek form: God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (Jas 4:6; 1 Pet 5:5). James introduces it with the words But he gives more grace.

This is the gospel in a proverb. Grace is not given to the deserving. It is given to the humble, the people who know they are not deserving. The door to God is low, and only those who bend can get through it.

The wise will inherit honor, but fools get disgrace.

The last line looks to the end. The wise inherit honour: it comes to them as a gift, like an inheritance. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew word behind get is uncertain, but the contrast is plain. Honour at the end for the humble; disgrace for the fool who grasped at honour and lost it. The chapter that began with trusting God with all your heart ends by showing where that trust leads.
