3.overview:
The father urges his son to keep his teaching and to bind steadfast love and faithfulness on his heart (vv. 1-4). Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding, and God will make his paths straight (vv. 5-6). He is to fear the LORD rather than be wise in his own eyes, honour the LORD with his firstfruits, and not despise the LORD's discipline, which is the discipline of a loving father (vv. 7-12).

Wisdom is more valuable than silver, gold or jewels; she is a tree of life (vv. 13-18). By wisdom the LORD founded the earth (vv. 19-20). Keeping wisdom brings security by day and sweet sleep by night, because the LORD is the wise person's confidence (vv. 21-26).

Wisdom does not withhold good from a neighbour, does not postpone help, plot against the trusting, pick quarrels or envy the violent (vv. 27-32). God curses the house of the wicked and blesses the righteous; he is scornful to scorners and gives grace to the humble (vv. 33-35).
3.theology:
Trust in God is wholehearted reliance that does not rest its weight on human understanding (vv. 5-6), and it is expressed in humility (v. 7), generosity (vv. 9-10) and acceptance of discipline (vv. 11-12). God's discipline is evidence of his fatherly love (Heb 12:5-11).

The wisdom by which God created the world (vv. 19-20) is fulfilled in Christ, through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Col 1:16-17). Wisdom is a tree of life, restoring what was lost in Eden (v. 18; Gen 3:22; Rev 22:2).

Love of neighbour is the proof of trust in God (vv. 27-30). God gives grace to the humble (v. 34; Jas 4:6; 1 Pet 5:5). The promises of long life and prosperity describe the general pattern of God's world, not a formula (Job 1:21).
3.examples:
Relying on God for eternity and on yourself for Tuesday.

A road levelled in the desert.

Firstfruits given before the size of the harvest is known.

Two wrong responses to hardship: shrugging it off and being crushed by it.

Jesus asleep in the stern.

"Come back tomorrow" to a neighbour in need.

Envying the man who gets his way.

A low door that only the humble can get through.

4.title: Keep Your Heart with All Vigilance

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A father calls his sons to listen (vv. 1-2), and tells them what his own father taught him when he was a boy: Let your heart hold fast my words; keep my commandments, and live (vv. 3-4). Get wisdom; get insight; love her and she will guard you (vv. 5-6). The beginning of wisdom is this: Get wisdom, and whatever you get, get insight (v. 7). Prize her, and she will bestow on you a beautiful crown (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom is handed down from grandfather to father to son, and the first step toward it is simply wanting it more than anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, O sons, a father's instruction, and be attentive, that you may gain insight, for I give you good precepts; do not forsake my teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear, O sons, a father's instruction, and be attentive, that you may gain insight,

The address has widened from my son to O sons. The teaching that was a private word to one boy is now for every son who will listen, which includes every reader of the book, daughters as surely as sons. The ESV notes that gain insight is literally "know insight". Wisdom is not only understood; it is known the way a person knows a friend.

for I give you good precepts; do not forsake my teaching.

The father makes a simple claim: what I am giving you is good. Not merely strict, or traditional, or what his generation believed. Good. A young person often assumes that his parents' instruction is there to limit him. The father asks him to consider that it might be a gift, and then warns him not to forsake it, as the men of chapter 2 forsook the paths of uprightness (2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: When I was a son with my father, tender, the only one in the sight of my mother, he taught me and said to me, "Let your heart hold fast my words; keep my commandments, and live. Get wisdom; get insight; do not forget, and do not turn away from the words of my mouth. Do not forsake her, and she will keep you; love her, and she will guard you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I was a son with my father, tender, the only one in the sight of my mother,

Now something moving happens. The father stops lecturing and tells a story about himself. He was once a boy too, tender, young and impressionable, and cherished by his mother as though he were the only one. He is not asking his son to do anything he did not have to learn himself.

If the father speaking is Solomon, the grandfather is David, and we have a record of the kind of thing he said: And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind (1 Chr 28:9).

he taught me and said to me, "Let your heart hold fast my words; keep my commandments, and live.

Three generations are in these verses: the grandfather who taught, the father who remembers, the son who hears. Wisdom in Scripture is meant to travel that way, from one generation's mouth to the next generation's heart. And what the grandfather said is short enough for a boy to carry: keep my commandments, and live.

That raises a question for any parent reading. What are the sentences your children will quote to their own children? They will not remember most of what you say. They will remember a few things said often and lived out in front of them.

Get wisdom; get insight; do not forget, and do not turn away from the words of my mouth. Do not forsake her, and she will keep you; love her, and she will guard you.

Get is a word from the market; it means to buy, to acquire. Wisdom is something to be obtained, at a cost. And then the language turns personal. Wisdom is her, someone to love, who in return will keep and guard you. The son who guards her is guarded by her. That is the shape of every relationship with God's wisdom: what you hold on to ends up holding you.

verseByVerse.quote: The beginning of wisdom is this: Get wisdom, and whatever you get, get insight. Prize her highly, and she will exalt you; she will honor you if you embrace her. She will place on your head a graceful garland; she will bestow on you a beautiful crown."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beginning of wisdom is this: Get wisdom, and whatever you get, get insight.

This sounds circular: the beginning of wisdom is to get wisdom. But that is the point. The first step toward wisdom is not cleverness or experience. It is deciding that you want it above everything else. The fool never starts, because he does not think he needs it.

Whatever you get ranks everything else a person might acquire beneath this one thing. Degrees, money, friends and experience all have their place, but insight comes first, and a wise person would spend the rest to have it. Jesus told of a merchant who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it (Matt 13:46). The kingdom and the wisdom of God are not an add-on to a life already full of other priorities. They are worth the whole purse.

A practical test: if someone looked at how you spend your money and your hours, would they conclude that wisdom is what you are trying to get?

Prize her highly, and she will exalt you; she will honor you if you embrace her. She will place on your head a graceful garland; she will bestow on you a beautiful crown."

Prize her, and she will exalt you. Embrace her, and she will honor you. The language is almost that of courtship, and the gift at the end is a crown. The grandfather's words end at verse 9 with a coronation. The person who treasures wisdom is not diminished by submitting to it; he is made royal.

Paul saw a crown at the end of his own race: Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing (2 Tim 4:8).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The father has led his son on straight paths, where he will not stumble (vv. 10-13). Do not enter the path of the wicked; avoid it, turn from it (vv. 14-15), for the wicked cannot sleep until they have done wrong and feed on violence (vv. 16-17). But the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, which shines brighter and brighter until full day. The way of the wicked is like deep darkness; they do not know over what they stumble (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: One road grows lighter with every step; the other grows darker until a person cannot see what trips him.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, my son, and accept my words, that the years of your life may be many. I have taught you the way of wisdom; I have led you in the paths of uprightness. When you walk, your step will not be hampered, and if you run, you will not stumble. Keep hold of instruction; do not let go; guard her, for she is your life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear, my son, and accept my words, that the years of your life may be many.

The father returns to his own voice, and to one son again. Accept is stronger than hear: it means taking hold of what is offered, as a person takes a gift into his hands.

I have taught you the way of wisdom; I have led you in the paths of uprightness.

Two verbs, taught and led. The father has not only explained the path; he has walked it with his son. Instruction without example is a map; instruction with example is a guide. The father can say I have led you because he has been on the road himself.

When you walk, your step will not be hampered, and if you run, you will not stumble.

Walking and running. There are seasons of life that are steady and seasons that go at a sprint, when decisions come fast and there is no time to deliberate. Wisdom learned in the walking seasons keeps a person from falling in the running ones. A man who has thought through his convictions before the crisis does not have to invent them in it.

Keep hold of instruction; do not let go; guard her, for she is your life.

The grip language is urgent: keep hold, do not let go, guard. The father talks about instruction the way a man hanging over a cliff talks about a rope. For she is your life. Moses said the same of God's word: For it is no empty word for you, but your very life (Deut 32:47).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not enter the path of the wicked, and do not walk in the way of the evil. Avoid it; do not go on it; turn away from it and pass on. For they cannot sleep unless they have done wrong; they are robbed of sleep unless they have made someone stumble. For they eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not enter the path of the wicked, and do not walk in the way of the evil. Avoid it; do not go on it; turn away from it and pass on.

Count the commands: do not enter, do not walk, avoid it, do not go on it, turn away, pass on. Six ways of saying one thing. The father is not being repetitive by accident. He knows that the danger lies less in a single decision to become wicked than in the first step onto the path, and the second, and then the discovery that one is a long way down it.

Notice also that the counsel is not "walk down the path a little way to understand it". It is avoid it. Some evil is best understood from a distance. There are films not to watch, websites not to open, parties not to attend, and conversations to walk out of. Pass on.

For they cannot sleep unless they have done wrong; they are robbed of sleep unless they have made someone stumble.

Here is a chilling picture of what evil does to a person over time. At first, a wicked act keeps him awake with guilt. In the end, not doing it keeps him awake. He is robbed of sleep until he has hurt someone. Evil has become an appetite. Micah pronounced woe on those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it (Mic 2:1).

Compare the sweet sleep promised to the wise in 3:24. Both kinds of people lie awake or sleep according to what their hearts love.

For they eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence.

Wickedness is their food. It is what sustains them, what they cannot do without. Jesus described what fed him in exactly the opposite terms: My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work (John 4:34). Every person lives on something. The question is what.

verseByVerse.quote: But the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, which shines brighter and brighter until full day. The way of the wicked is like deep darkness; they do not know over what they stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, which shines brighter and brighter until full day.

This is one of the most beautiful images in Proverbs. Think of dawn: at first only a grey line on the horizon, barely distinguishable from night. Then colour. Then the sun's edge. Then, steadily, brighter and brighter until full day. The righteous life is not bright all at once. It grows.

That is an encouragement to anyone who feels his faith is still at the grey-line stage. It is supposed to start there. The question is not how bright the light is but which direction it is moving. Paul describes the Christian life in the same way: we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Cor 3:18).

And the light has a source. Jesus said, I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life (John 8:12). The righteous path grows brighter because it leads toward him.

The way of the wicked is like deep darkness; they do not know over what they stumble.

The other path runs the other way, into deep darkness. And the worst of it is not the stumbling but the not knowing why. The wicked keep falling and cannot see what trips them. The broken marriages, the lost jobs, the friendships that end: they blame luck, other people, the system. They cannot see that the obstacle is their own path. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going (John 12:35).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Keep my words in your heart, for they are life and healing (vv. 20-22). Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life (v. 23). Then guard the mouth (v. 24), the eyes (v. 25) and the feet: Ponder the path of your feet; Do not swerve to the right or to the left; turn your foot away from evil (vv. 26-27).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole person is kept by keeping the heart, and the heart is kept by what the mouth, eyes and feet are allowed to do.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, be attentive to my words; incline your ear to my sayings. Let them not escape from your sight; keep them within your heart. For they are life to those who find them, and healing to all their flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, be attentive to my words; incline your ear to my sayings. Let them not escape from your sight; keep them within your heart.

The last section of the chapter begins, and it moves through the body: ear, eyes, heart. Then it will go to the mouth, the eyes again, and the feet. The father wants his words to reach every part of his son.

Let them not escape from your sight is a warning about how easily truth slips away. It does not need to be refuted. It only needs to be not looked at for long enough. A Bible left closed for a month does not argue with you; it just fades.

For they are life to those who find them, and healing to all their flesh.

The ESV notes that the Hebrew reads all "his" flesh, individualising the promise: each person who finds these words finds them to be life and healing for himself. The father's words are not only rules; they are medicine.

verseByVerse.quote: Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.

This is the centre of the chapter, and perhaps the most important single verse for understanding how Proverbs thinks about a person.

In the Bible the heart is not only feelings. It is the control room of a person: where he thinks, chooses, loves and believes. Everything else in life flows out of it the way water flows out of a spring. From it flow the springs of life. If the spring is poisoned, every stream downstream is poisoned too.

Jesus taught exactly this: For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery (Mark 7:21). And again, out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks (Luke 6:45). The problem with human beings is not first their circumstances or their behaviour. It is their hearts.

That is why the verse says with all vigilance. A person guards what is most valuable most carefully. Guarding the heart is not a matter of protecting your feelings from being hurt. It means watching what goes into it, what it is allowed to love, what it dwells on, and what it is being trained to want. A man does not wake up one day an adulterer; he has let his heart dwell on another woman for months. A person does not become bitter overnight; he rehearsed the grievance a thousand times.

Run the test honestly. What have you allowed into your heart this week, through your eyes, your phone, your thoughts before sleep? Those are the springs your life will flow from next week.

And there is a limit to what anyone can do. No one can make his own heart new. That is what God promises to do: to give a new heart and put his Spirit within (Ezek 36:26-27). The command to keep the heart is given to people whose hearts God has already begun to change.

verseByVerse.quote: Put away from you crooked speech, and put devious talk far from you. Let your eyes look directly forward, and your gaze be straight before you. Ponder the path of your feet; then all your ways will be sure. Do not swerve to the right or to the left; turn your foot away from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put away from you crooked speech, and put devious talk far from you.

After the heart, the mouth, because the mouth is where the heart comes out first. Crooked speech and devious talk are words that twist: flattery, half-truths, gossip dressed up as concern, sarcasm that wounds. Put them far from you, as far as you would put a poison. Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up (Eph 4:29).

Let your eyes look directly forward, and your gaze be straight before you.

Then the eyes. The picture is a man walking a narrow road who does not keep glancing at every distraction on either side. Much temptation begins with the eyes lingering. And the Christian knows what to look at: let us run with endurance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith (Heb 12:1-2). No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62).

Ponder the path of your feet; then all your ways will be sure.

Then the feet. Ponder means to think carefully about where the next step goes. The ESV notes it may be rendered "Make level", and that is the form in which the verse is quoted in the New Testament: and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed (Heb 12:13). There the point is that a Christian's steady walk helps the weaker believers walking behind him.

Do not swerve to the right or to the left; turn your foot away from evil.

The chapter ends with the language Moses used to Israel: You shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left (Deut 5:32). There are two ditches on either side of the path, and people fall into both: into careless sin on one side and proud rule-keeping on the other. The wise person keeps walking straight ahead, with his heart guarded, his mouth clean, his eyes forward and his feet on the road that grows brighter and brighter until full day.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Hear, O sons, a father's instruction, and be attentive, that you may gain insight,<sup>2</sup>for I give you good precepts; do not forsake my teaching.<sup>3</sup>When I was a son with my father, tender, the only one in the sight of my mother,<sup>4</sup>he taught me and said to me, "Let your heart hold fast my words; keep my commandments, and live.<sup>5</sup>Get wisdom; get insight; do not forget, and do not turn away from the words of my mouth.<sup>6</sup>Do not forsake her, and she will keep you; love her, and she will guard you.<sup>7</sup>The beginning of wisdom is this: Get wisdom, and whatever you get, get insight.<sup>8</sup>Prize her highly, and she will exalt you; she will honor you if you embrace her.<sup>9</sup>She will place on your head a graceful garland; she will bestow on you a beautiful crown."<sup>10</sup>Hear, my son, and accept my words, that the years of your life may be many.<sup>11</sup>I have taught you the way of wisdom; I have led you in the paths of uprightness.<sup>12</sup>When you walk, your step will not be hampered, and if you run, you will not stumble.<sup>13</sup>Keep hold of instruction; do not let go; guard her, for she is your life.<sup>14</sup>Do not enter the path of the wicked, and do not walk in the way of the evil.<sup>15</sup>Avoid it; do not go on it; turn away from it and pass on.<sup>16</sup>For they cannot sleep unless they have done wrong; they are robbed of sleep unless they have made someone stumble.<sup>17</sup>For they eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence.<sup>18</sup>But the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, which shines brighter and brighter until full day.<sup>19</sup>The way of the wicked is like deep darkness; they do not know over what they stumble.<sup>20</sup>My son, be attentive to my words; incline your ear to my sayings.<sup>21</sup>Let them not escape from your sight; keep them within your heart.<sup>22</sup>For they are life to those who find them, and healing to all their flesh.<sup>23</sup>Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.<sup>24</sup>Put away from you crooked speech, and put devious talk far from you.<sup>25</sup>Let your eyes look directly forward, and your gaze be straight before you.<sup>26</sup>Ponder the path of your feet; then all your ways will be sure.<sup>27</sup>Do not swerve to the right or to the left; turn your foot away from evil.
4.overview:
A father calls his sons to listen, and passes on what his own father taught him as a boy: hold fast to my words and live; get wisdom above everything, love her, and she will guard you and crown you (vv. 1-9).

He has led his son in straight paths. He urges him not even to set foot on the path of the wicked, who cannot sleep until they have done wrong. The path of the righteous is like the dawn, growing brighter until full day; the way of the wicked is deep darkness where they cannot see what trips them (vv. 10-19).

Finally, the father's words are life and healing. Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life. Guard the mouth, the eyes and the feet, and do not swerve to the right or the left (vv. 20-27).
4.theology:
Wisdom is passed down through the generations in the family (vv. 3-4; 1 Chr 28:9). The first step toward wisdom is to desire it above all else (v. 7; Matt 13:45-46).

Sin is progressive and becomes an appetite (vv. 16-17); righteousness is progressive and grows toward full light (v. 18; 2 Cor 3:18; John 8:12).

The heart is the source of all of life, so it must be guarded above all (v. 23; Mark 7:21-23; Luke 6:45). The guarding of heart, mouth, eyes and feet belongs together (vv. 24-27), and the New Testament applies verse 26 to walking steadily for the sake of weaker believers (Heb 12:13).
4.examples:
Three generations: grandfather, father, son.

The sentences your children will quote to theirs.

Selling everything for a pearl.

The wicked man who cannot sleep until he has done wrong.

Dawn: a grey line, then full day.

Stumbling in the dark and blaming the furniture.

The heart as a spring that feeds every stream.

Eyes forward on a narrow road.

5.title: Drink Water from Your Own Cistern

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Honey That Turns to Wormwood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The father calls for attention (vv. 1-2). For the lips of a forbidden woman drip honey, and her speech is smoother than oil, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword (vv. 3-4). Her steps go down to Sheol, and she does not ponder the path of life; her ways wander, and she does not know it (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Adultery is sweet at the beginning and bitter at the end, and the one who leads others astray is lost herself.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, be attentive to my wisdom; incline your ear to my understanding, that you may keep discretion, and your lips may guard knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, be attentive to my wisdom; incline your ear to my understanding, that you may keep discretion, and your lips may guard knowledge.

Chapter 2 warned about the forbidden woman in two verses. Chapter 5 gives her a whole chapter, and chapter 7 will give her another. The father knows which temptation is most likely to wreck his son, and he spends his words accordingly.

He begins, as usual, with attention. And he wants his son's lips to guard knowledge. That is a pointed phrase, because the danger in this chapter comes through lips too. Her lips drip honey (v. 3). His lips must be full of something better. A man whose mouth is stocked with truth has an answer ready when flattery comes.

verseByVerse.quote: For the lips of a forbidden woman drip honey, and her speech is smoother than oil, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword. Her feet go down to death; her steps follow the path to Sheol; she does not ponder the path of life; her ways wander, and she does not know it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the lips of a forbidden woman drip honey, and her speech is smoother than oil,

The ESV notes that forbidden is literally "strange", and that speech is "palate", the mouth itself. Everything about her approach is sweet and smooth: honey, oil. The father does not pretend temptation is ugly. If he told his son that sin looks disgusting, the son would conclude on the first attractive temptation that his father did not know what he was talking about. So he admits it: it is sweet.

but in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword.

And then the two words that change everything: in the end. Wormwood is a plant so bitter that the Bible uses it as a picture of grief and judgment. The same experience that was honey becomes wormwood. The same smooth speech becomes a sword that cuts both ways.

This is the whole strategy of temptation: it sells the beginning and hides the end. Before any choice, ask the question the father asks: how does this taste in the end? Think past the evening to the morning, past the affair to the divorce court, past the secret to the moment it comes out.

Her feet go down to death; her steps follow the path to Sheol; she does not ponder the path of life; her ways wander, and she does not know it.

The ESV notes that her steps "lay hold of" Sheol, as if grasping at the grave. And the tragedy of verse 6 is that she herself is lost. She does not ponder the path of life. She is not a mastermind; her ways wander, and she does not know it. The person who leads others into sexual sin is usually someone who has never stopped to think where she is going. Compare the command to the son in 4:26, Ponder the path of your feet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Keep your way far from her, and do not go near the door of her house (vv. 7-8). The price is honour, years, strength and earnings handed to strangers, and a ruined body at the end of life (vv. 9-11). Then the groan of regret: How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof!, and ruin in front of the whole community (vv. 12-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The father makes his son hear, in advance, the words he will say at the end if he does not listen now.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O sons, listen to me, and do not depart from the words of my mouth. Keep your way far from her, and do not go near the door of her house,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, O sons, listen to me, and do not depart from the words of my mouth.

And now. The description is over; here is what to do. And the address widens again to O sons. No young man is exempt from this warning.

Keep your way far from her, and do not go near the door of her house,

The instruction is about distance. Not "go to her door and resist", but do not go near it. The strongest men in Scripture fell when they put themselves in reach. Paul's word is the same: Flee from sexual immorality (1 Cor 6:18). You do not negotiate with this temptation; you leave the building.

Practically, that means identifying the doors. The late-night conversation with a colleague that has become personal. The social media account you check. The trip where no one knows you. The app on the phone. Do not go near the door.

verseByVerse.quote: lest you give your honor to others and your years to the merciless, lest strangers take their fill of your strength, and your labors go to the house of a foreigner, and at the end of your life you groan, when your flesh and body are consumed,
verseByVerse.commentary:
lest you give your honor to others and your years to the merciless, lest strangers take their fill of your strength, and your labors go to the house of a foreigner,

Now the father itemises the cost, like a man reading out a bill. Your honor: your reputation, given away. Your years: the best of your life, given to people who will show no mercy. Your strength and your labors: your money and your work, going to the house of a foreigner. Adultery has always been expensive. Today the bill arrives as legal fees, divided property, maintenance payments, and a family home sold.

and at the end of your life you groan, when your flesh and body are consumed,

And at the end, the body. Sexual sin has physical consequences, sometimes in disease, always in the wearing out of a life spent on it. Paul says, the sexually immoral person sins against his own body (1 Cor 6:18). The groan at the end of life is the sound of a man who has discovered too late what he spent.

verseByVerse.quote: and you say, "How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof! I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my instructors. I am at the brink of utter ruin in the assembled congregation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and you say, "How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof! I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my instructors.

This is a remarkable piece of teaching. The father puts words into his son's mouth, the words the son will say decades later, if he does not listen now. He lets him hear his own future regret. How I hated discipline. Notice that the regret is not only about the woman. It is about not listening. The root sin was despising correction; the adultery was the fruit.

Every older person who has wrecked his life has some version of this speech. Most of them could name the teachers who warned them. A young reader can take this as a gift: here is the speech; you do not have to give it.

I am at the brink of utter ruin in the assembled congregation."

The ruin is public. In the assembled congregation means before the whole community of God's people. Sexual sin is conducted in secret, but it rarely stays there, and when it comes out it damages not only the man but the congregation that trusted him. That is especially sobering for anyone who leads in a church.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Rejoice in the Wife of Your Youth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Drink water from your own cistern; keep your springs for yourself (vv. 15-17). Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth, and be delighted in her love always (vv. 18-19). Why go to a stranger (v. 20)? For a man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and the wicked man is caught in the cords of his own sin, dying for lack of discipline (vv. 21-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The best defence against forbidden pleasure is not less pleasure but delight in the gift God has given.

verseByVerse.quote: Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well. Should your springs be scattered abroad, streams of water in the streets? Let them be for yourself alone, and not for strangers with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well.

Now the father turns from warning to invitation, and the picture is water. In a dry land a man's own cistern or well was precious. It was his, it was dug with labour, and it kept his household alive. The image is of a man's wife and the delight of sexual love within marriage. The Song of Songs uses the same picture of a bride: a garden fountain, a well of living water (Song 4:15), a spring locked, a fountain sealed (Song 4:12).

Notice what the father does not say. He does not say that sexual desire is shameful, or to be suppressed. He says: drink. From your own well.

Should your springs be scattered abroad, streams of water in the streets? Let them be for yourself alone, and not for strangers with you.

The picture reverses: a man's springs flowing out into the streets, wasted, shared with anyone. That is what promiscuity does. What was meant to water one home is spilled on the public road where it nourishes nothing. Sexual love is designed to be exclusive, for yourself alone. That is not a restriction on its joy; it is the condition of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth, a lovely deer, a graceful doe. Let her breasts fill you at all times with delight; be intoxicated always in her love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth,

Rejoice is a command. The father commands his son to be glad in his wife. The wife of your youth is the woman he married young, who will grow old with him. Malachi uses the same phrase in warning men who were abandoning their first wives: let none of you be faithless to the wife of your youth (Mal 2:15). The law even gave a newly married man a year's exemption from military service so that he could be happy with his wife whom he has taken (Deut 24:5).

a lovely deer, a graceful doe. Let her breasts fill you at all times with delight; be intoxicated always in her love.

Here the Bible speaks with a frankness that surprises some readers. The father tells his son to find physical delight in his wife's body, at all times, always. God is not embarrassed by the marriage bed. He designed it. Paul says married couples are not to deprive one another (1 Cor 7:5).

And the ESV notes a striking thing: be intoxicated is literally "be led astray". The same verb that describes a man wandering off to sin (v. 23) is used here of being carried away by love for his own wife. The father is saying: be led astray, but at home. Let her love be the thing that takes you out of yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: Why should you be intoxicated, my son, with a forbidden woman and embrace the bosom of an adulteress? For a man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and he ponders all his paths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why should you be intoxicated, my son, with a forbidden woman and embrace the bosom of an adulteress?

Having painted the joy of married love, the father asks a simple question: Why? Why would a man leave that for this? The word is the same again, "led astray", and adulteress is literally "a foreign woman", as the ESV notes. Why be led astray by a stranger, when you could be led astray by your wife?

This is the strategy of the whole chapter. The best defence against forbidden pleasure is not grim willpower but a greater delight. A husband who cultivates love for his wife, who pursues her, who keeps enjoying her, has far less appetite for honey from other lips. Husbands and wives who neglect each other are leaving the gate open.

A word for readers for whom this is painful: the single, the widowed, those whose marriages are cold or broken. The chapter's command to flee still stands for you, and so does its promise that God sees every path (v. 21). The deepest fulfilment of the love the chapter describes is not found in any human marriage but in Christ, who loved the church and gave himself up for her (Eph 5:25). That love is offered to every believer, married or not.

For a man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and he ponders all his paths.

And here is the reason beneath all the others. Adultery depends on secrecy. But nothing is secret. No creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account (Heb 4:13). The woman of verse 6 did not ponder her path. The LORD ponders every path, and the ESV notes that the word may mean he "makes level" them. He sees the road and he governs where it leads.

verseByVerse.quote: The iniquities of the wicked ensnare him, and he is held fast in the cords of his sin. He dies for lack of discipline, and because of his great folly he is led astray.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The iniquities of the wicked ensnare him, and he is held fast in the cords of his sin.

The wicked man thinks he is free, doing what he wants. In fact he is tied up, and the ropes are his own sins. Every indulgence adds another cord. Jesus said, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin (John 8:34). Anyone who has fought a pornography habit knows how true this is. It began as a choice and became a cord.

He dies for lack of discipline, and because of his great folly he is led astray.

The chapter ends with the word it has been playing on: led astray. The man who would not be led astray by his wife's love is led astray by his own folly, all the way to death. And the cause is named, lack of discipline, the thing he confessed at verse 12 that he hated. Desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death (Jas 1:15).

But the cords can be cut. The Christ who was bound and led away for sinners came to set captives free. You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body (1 Cor 6:19-20).

5.text: <sup>1</sup>My son, be attentive to my wisdom; incline your ear to my understanding,<sup>2</sup>that you may keep discretion, and your lips may guard knowledge.<sup>3</sup>For the lips of a forbidden woman drip honey, and her speech is smoother than oil,<sup>4</sup>but in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a two-edged sword.<sup>5</sup>Her feet go down to death; her steps follow the path to Sheol;<sup>6</sup>she does not ponder the path of life; her ways wander, and she does not know it.<sup>7</sup>And now, O sons, listen to me, and do not depart from the words of my mouth.<sup>8</sup>Keep your way far from her, and do not go near the door of her house,<sup>9</sup>lest you give your honor to others and your years to the merciless,<sup>10</sup>lest strangers take their fill of your strength, and your labors go to the house of a foreigner,<sup>11</sup>and at the end of your life you groan, when your flesh and body are consumed,<sup>12</sup>and you say, "How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof!<sup>13</sup>I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my instructors.<sup>14</sup>I am at the brink of utter ruin in the assembled congregation."<sup>15</sup>Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well.<sup>16</sup>Should your springs be scattered abroad, streams of water in the streets?<sup>17</sup>Let them be for yourself alone, and not for strangers with you.<sup>18</sup>Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth,<sup>19</sup>a lovely deer, a graceful doe. Let her breasts fill you at all times with delight; be intoxicated always in her love.<sup>20</sup>Why should you be intoxicated, my son, with a forbidden woman and embrace the bosom of an adulteress?<sup>21</sup>For a man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and he ponders all his paths.<sup>22</sup>The iniquities of the wicked ensnare him, and he is held fast in the cords of his sin.<sup>23</sup>He dies for lack of discipline, and because of his great folly he is led astray.
5.overview:
The father warns his son about the forbidden woman. Her lips drip honey, but in the end she is bitter as wormwood, and her path goes down to death while she herself wanders without knowing it (vv. 1-6).

He must keep far from her door. Adultery costs honour, years, strength and wealth, and ends in a groan of regret and public ruin (vv. 7-14).

Instead, he is to drink from his own well: keep sexual love for his own marriage, rejoice in the wife of his youth, and be delighted in her love always (vv. 15-20). The LORD sees every path, and the wicked are bound by the cords of their own sin and led astray to death (vv. 21-23).
5.theology:
Temptation offers sweetness at the start and hides its bitter end (vv. 3-4). Sexual sin is costly in every dimension of life (vv. 9-14), and at root it grows from despising correction (v. 12).

Sexual delight within marriage is God's gift and is commanded (vv. 15-19; 1 Cor 7:3-5); delight in that gift is the positive defence against adultery (v. 20). God sees all human ways (v. 21; Heb 4:13), and sin enslaves (v. 22; John 8:34). Marriage points beyond itself to Christ's love for the church (Eph 5:25, 31-32).
5.examples:
Honey at the start, wormwood at the end.

Identifying the doors not to go near.

The bill for adultery, itemised.

The speech of regret you do not have to give.

Water spilled in the street.

Led astray, but at home.

A habit that began as a choice and became a cord.

6.title: Go to the Ant, O Sluggard

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Rash Pledge and the Lazy Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two traps with money. If you have guaranteed a neighbour's debt, you are caught by your own words, so go at once, without sleep, and get free like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter (vv. 1-5). And the opposite danger: Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise. With no one to command her, she gathers in summer (vv. 6-8). A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber (vv. 9-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom avoids reckless promises and idle hands alike, and both begin as small, pleasant decisions.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if you have put up security for your neighbor, have given your pledge for a stranger, if you are snared in the words of your mouth, caught in the words of your mouth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, if you have put up security for your neighbor, have given your pledge for a stranger,

The chapter opens with a very practical piece of financial advice. Security and pledge describe what we would call co-signing a loan or guaranteeing someone else's debt. The father's son has shaken hands on a promise to pay if the borrower does not. The Bible does not forbid lending, generosity or bearing another's burden (Bear one another's burdens, Gal 6:2). What it warns against, here and repeatedly in Proverbs, is binding yourself to an open-ended obligation you cannot control.

if you are snared in the words of your mouth, caught in the words of your mouth,

The trap was made of words. A quick promise, a handshake, a signature: snared, caught. Many people have lost their homes because of a moment's eagerness to help a friend or look generous. The words took a second; the debt took years.

verseByVerse.quote: then do this, my son, and save yourself, for you have come into the hand of your neighbor: go, hasten, and plead urgently with your neighbor. Give your eyes no sleep and your eyelids no slumber; save yourself like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter, like a bird from the hand of the fowler.
verseByVerse.commentary:
then do this, my son, and save yourself, for you have come into the hand of your neighbor: go, hasten, and plead urgently with your neighbor.

The remedy is urgent and humbling. You have come into the hand of your neighbor: your future now belongs to someone else's choices. So go, hurry, and plead with him to release you. The ESV notes that plead urgently may be rendered "humble yourself". Pride will want to keep the promise rather than admit it was foolish. The father says: swallow your pride and get out.

Give your eyes no sleep and your eyelids no slumber; save yourself like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter, like a bird from the hand of the fowler.

A gazelle does not negotiate with the hunter. It runs. Do not go to bed, says the father, until this is dealt with. Some problems grow quietly while we sleep, and a debt obligation is one of them.

There is a striking reversal of this warning in the New Testament. The one pledge Proverbs tells a son never to make, Christ made for us. He bound himself to pay the debt of people who could not pay. Judah once said to his father about Benjamin, I will be a pledge of his safety (Gen 43:9). Hebrews says that Jesus is the guarantor of a better covenant (Heb 7:22). He did not run from the obligation; he paid it in full.

verseByVerse.quote: Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise. Without having any chief, officer, or ruler, she prepares her bread in summer and gathers her food in harvest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.

From the man who promises too much to the man who does too little. Sluggard is Proverbs' word for the lazy man, and he appears again and again in this book, usually in comic scenes. Here he is sent to school, and the teacher is an ant. There is humour in that: a grown man learning from an insect.

Wisdom is written into creation. God's world is full of lessons for anyone willing to consider. Agur will return to the ants later: the ants are a people not strong, yet they provide their food in the summer (30:25).

Without having any chief, officer, or ruler, she prepares her bread in summer and gathers her food in harvest.

Two lessons. First, the ant works without a supervisor. No one stands over her. A great many people work hard only when someone is watching. The ant does the work because it needs doing. Paul told Christian workers to labour heartily, as for the Lord and not for men (Col 3:23).

Second, the ant works ahead. She gathers in summer for winter. She does not wait until she is hungry. Wisdom plans for seasons that have not yet arrived: saving, preparing, putting in effort now whose reward comes later.

verseByVerse.quote: How long will you lie there, O sluggard? When will you arise from your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How long will you lie there, O sluggard? When will you arise from your sleep?

Now the father addresses the sluggard directly, and it sounds like a parent at a bedroom door at eleven in the morning. How long?

A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest,

Listen to the sluggard's voice in this verse. He does not say, I intend to ruin my life. He says, just a little. A little more sleep. Five more minutes. The word little appears three times. Laziness never presents itself as a life decision. It is always only a little. That is what makes it dangerous.

and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man.

And the little decisions add up to a sudden arrival. Poverty comes like a robber, without warning, and like an armed man, whom you cannot resist. The sluggard is surprised. He should not be. These two verses appear again, word for word, at the end of the sluggard's vineyard in 24:33-34, as if the lesson needed saying twice.

The New Testament is equally plain: If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat (2 Thess 3:10). Work is not a curse; it is how God provides for us and lets us provide for others, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need (Eph 4:28). A word of care is needed too: the depressed, the exhausted and the sick are not sluggards, and this proverb is not aimed at them. It is aimed at the man who could get up and chooses not to.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The worthless man speaks crookedly, signals with eyes, feet and finger, and keeps sowing discord; calamity will break him suddenly (vv. 12-15). There are six things that the LORD hates, seven that are an abomination to him: proud eyes, a lying tongue, murderous hands, a scheming heart, feet running to evil, a false witness who breathes out lies, and one who sows discord among brothers (vv. 16-19).
verseByVerse.theology: God's hatred is aimed at what destroys people and community, and the list starts with pride and ends with division.

verseByVerse.quote: A worthless person, a wicked man, goes about with crooked speech, winks with his eyes, signals with his feet, points with his finger, with perverted heart devises evil, continually sowing discord; therefore calamity will come upon him suddenly; in a moment he will be broken beyond healing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A worthless person, a wicked man, goes about with crooked speech, winks with his eyes, signals with his feet, points with his finger,

Now a different kind of man, and a vivid portrait of him. He is a troublemaker, and he works in code. His speech is crooked, and his body is full of signals: a wink, a movement of the feet (the ESV notes the Hebrew is "scrapes"), a pointing finger. He communicates with his allies behind the backs of the people he is working against. Psalm 35 prays against enemies who wink the eye (Ps 35:19). Every office and every church has seen this man: the raised eyebrow in a meeting, the knowing look, the whispered aside.

with perverted heart devises evil, continually sowing discord;

Beneath the signals is the heart, which devises evil. And his main product is discord. He divides people. He plants a suspicion here, repeats a remark there, and watches friendships split. He does it continually; it has become a way of life.

therefore calamity will come upon him suddenly; in a moment he will be broken beyond healing.

He works slowly and secretly, but his end is sudden: in a moment. The man who broke others will be broken beyond healing. God's patience is not indifference. While people are saying, "There is peace and security," then sudden destruction will come upon them (1 Thess 5:3).

verseByVerse.quote: There are six things that the LORD hates, seven that are an abomination to him: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood, a heart that devises wicked plans, feet that make haste to run to evil, a false witness who breathes out lies, and one who sows discord among brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are six things that the LORD hates, seven that are an abomination to him:

The pattern "six things, seven" is a Hebrew way of building to a climax; the seventh item is the one the list is aiming at. And the language is strong. The LORD hates. Some readers are uncomfortable with a God who hates. But a God who loved people and did not hate what destroys them would not be good. A doctor who loves his patient hates the cancer.

haughty eyes, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood,

Notice how the list moves down the body: eyes, tongue, hands, heart, feet. The whole person can be put to the service of evil.

It begins with haughty eyes, the look of a person who sees himself above others. Pride is first, because pride is where most of the others start. Jesus told of a Pharisee who looked down on a tax collector, and ended, everyone who exalts himself will be humbled (Luke 18:14). Then a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood. Some readers find it strange that pride stands in the same list as murder. God does not.

a heart that devises wicked plans, feet that make haste to run to evil,

The scheming heart and the eager feet. These are the same as the troublemaker of verse 14 and the gang of chapter 1, whose feet run to evil (1:16).

a false witness who breathes out lies, and one who sows discord among brothers.

The last two are about destroying community. A false witness destroys justice. And the climactic seventh is one who sows discord among brothers, the exact phrase from verse 14. The section began and ends with discord. God hates it most because it attacks what he loves most: the unity of his people.

That should give every church member pause. Gossip, faction, the whispered complaint about the elders, the stirring up of one group against another, all belong on this list. Paul says, watch out for those who cause divisions (Rom 16:17). And Jesus pronounced the opposite blessing: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God (Matt 5:9). Ask which of the two your words this week have been.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–35 — Fire Carried in the Lap
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Keep your parents' teaching bound on your heart; it will lead, guard and speak to you, For the commandment is a lamp and the teaching a light (vv. 20-23), keeping you from the adulteress (v. 24). Do not desire her beauty (v. 25). Can a man carry fire next to his chest and his clothes not be burned? (vv. 27-29). A hungry thief repays sevenfold, but He who commits adultery lacks sense; he who does it destroys himself, and a husband's jealousy will accept no compensation (vv. 30-35).
verseByVerse.theology: Adultery is not a private risk but playing with fire, and it provokes a wound that money cannot settle.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, keep your father's commandment, and forsake not your mother's teaching. Bind them on your heart always; tie them around your neck. When you walk, they will lead you; when you lie down, they will watch over you; and when you awake, they will talk with you. For the commandment is a lamp and the teaching a light, and the reproofs of discipline are the way of life,
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, keep your father's commandment, and forsake not your mother's teaching. Bind them on your heart always; tie them around your neck.

The father returns to his great theme, and the language echoes Moses: these words that I command you today shall be on your heart, and You shall bind them as a sign on your hand (Deut 6:6, 8). Parental teaching in Proverbs carries the weight of God's law because it passes on God's law.

When you walk, they will lead you; when you lie down, they will watch over you; and when you awake, they will talk with you.

The ESV notes that the Hebrew says "it" three times, as if the teaching were a single companion. It walks with the son by day, watches over him at night, and is there to talk to him when he wakes. This is what it looks like to have Scripture stored in the heart. When you are walking into a meeting, it guides. When you lie awake, it guards. When you wake, the first thought can be God's word rather than the day's anxiety.

Moses had described the same three moments: when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise (Deut 6:7).

For the commandment is a lamp and the teaching a light, and the reproofs of discipline are the way of life,

A lamp shows the next step in the dark. Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path (Ps 119:105). And the father adds something less comfortable: the reproofs of discipline are the way of life. Correction is part of the light. The person who wants God's guidance but not his rebukes wants a lamp that shows only pleasant things.

verseByVerse.quote: to preserve you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the adulteress. Do not desire her beauty in your heart, and do not let her capture you with her eyelashes; for the price of a prostitute is only a loaf of bread, but a married woman hunts down a precious life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
to preserve you from the evil woman, from the smooth tongue of the adulteress.

And here is where the lamp is most needed. The ESV notes that by a change of vowels the Hebrew may read "from the wife of a neighbor", and that adulteress is literally "the foreign woman". The warning of chapters 2 and 5 returns, and once again she works by her smooth tongue.

Do not desire her beauty in your heart, and do not let her capture you with her eyelashes;

The battle is located precisely: in your heart. Adultery is not first an act; it is a desire entertained. Jesus said the same: everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt 5:28). David's fall began with a look from a rooftop at a woman bathing; and the woman was very beautiful (2 Sam 11:2).

And the weapon named is small: her eyelashes. A glance, a look held a second too long. The father wants his son to know how little it takes.

for the price of a prostitute is only a loaf of bread, but a married woman hunts down a precious life.

The verse is a comparison of costs, and the ESV notes that it may also be read, "for a prostitute leaves a man with nothing but a loaf of bread". Either way, the point is the same: sin with a prostitute is costly and degrading, but sin with another man's wife (the Hebrew is "a man's wife") costs far more. It hunts down a precious life. The verse is not approving of prostitution. Paul answers anyone who thinks it harmless: Do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? (1 Cor 6:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Can a man carry fire next to his chest and his clothes not be burned? Or can one walk on hot coals and his feet not be scorched? So is he who goes in to his neighbor's wife; none who touches her will go unpunished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can a man carry fire next to his chest and his clothes not be burned? Or can one walk on hot coals and his feet not be scorched?

Two questions, and both answer themselves. You cannot hold fire against your body and not be burned. You cannot walk on coals and not be scorched. The father uses questions because he wants his son to reach the conclusion himself. Every man who begins an affair believes he will be the exception. He will keep it secret, keep it contained, keep his marriage and his reputation. He is a man carrying fire in his shirt and insisting it will not burn.

So is he who goes in to his neighbor's wife; none who touches her will go unpunished.

None. No exceptions. The consequences may be slow or quick, public or private, but the fire burns everyone who carries it.

verseByVerse.quote: People do not despise a thief if he steals to satisfy his appetite when he is hungry, but if he is caught, he will pay sevenfold; he will give all the goods of his house. He who commits adultery lacks sense; he who does it destroys himself. He will get wounds and dishonor, and his disgrace will not be wiped away. For jealousy makes a man furious, and he will not spare when he takes revenge. He will accept no compensation; he will refuse though you multiply gifts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People do not despise a thief if he steals to satisfy his appetite when he is hungry, but if he is caught, he will pay sevenfold; he will give all the goods of his house.

Now a comparison with theft. A starving man who steals bread gets a measure of sympathy. Still, he must repay sevenfold, a number for full and complete restitution. (The law required fourfold or fivefold for stolen livestock, Exod 22:1, and Zacchaeus promised fourfold, Luke 19:8.) It may cost all the goods of his house. But it can be paid. The debt has a limit.

He who commits adultery lacks sense; he who does it destroys himself.

Adultery is different. The thief was hungry; the adulterer had a wife. He lacks sense, and the damage is not to his purse but to himself: he who does it destroys himself.

He will get wounds and dishonor, and his disgrace will not be wiped away.

Wounds, dishonour, and a disgrace that lasts. Even when forgiven, and it can be, the adulterer's reputation carries a mark for years. Many a gifted man has discovered that he cannot return to the place of trust he once held.

For jealousy makes a man furious, and he will not spare when he takes revenge. He will accept no compensation; he will refuse though you multiply gifts.

And here is the final difference from theft. You can repay a thief's victim. But you cannot pay off a husband whose wife you have taken. He will accept no compensation. What was stolen was not property; it was a one-flesh union. The Song of Songs says jealousy is fierce as the grave (Song 8:6).

That is a sobering place to end the chapter, and it is meant to be. But it also shows why the gospel is such good news. The sins that no human compensation can cover, the blood of Christ can. He did not pay in gifts or goods; he paid with his life, and what money could never wipe away, his cleansing does.
