he who does it destroys himself.<sup>33</sup>He will get wounds and dishonor, and his disgrace will not be wiped away.<sup>34</sup>For jealousy makes a man furious, and he will not spare when he takes revenge.<sup>35</sup>He will accept no compensation; he will refuse though you multiply gifts.
6.overview:
A son who has rashly guaranteed a neighbour's debt must humble himself and get free at once (vv. 1-5). The sluggard is sent to learn from the ant, who works without a supervisor and prepares ahead, because a little sleep brings poverty like a robber (vv. 6-11).

The worthless man signals and schemes and sows discord, and will be broken suddenly (vv. 12-15). The LORD hates seven things: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, murderous hands, a scheming heart, feet quick to evil, a false witness, and one who sows discord among brothers (vv. 16-19).

Parental teaching, bound on the heart, guides and guards like a lamp (vv. 20-23), and protects from the adulteress (vv. 24-26). Adultery is carrying fire in one's lap; unlike a thief's debt, it destroys the man who does it and provokes a jealousy no compensation can settle (vv. 27-35).
6.theology:
Wisdom governs money: avoiding reckless financial obligations (vv. 1-5) and working diligently without supervision (vv. 6-11; 2 Thess 3:10; Col 3:23). The one pledge Proverbs warns against, Christ made as the guarantor of the new covenant (Heb 7:22).

God hates what destroys people, and the list of seven begins with pride and ends with discord among brothers (vv. 16-19; Luke 18:14; Rom 16:17). God's word, stored in the heart, accompanies the believer at every moment (vv. 20-23; Deut 6:6-8).

Adultery begins in the heart (v. 25; Matt 5:28), always burns (vv. 27-29), and does damage that cannot be repaid by human means (vv. 30-35).
6.examples:
Co-signing a loan in a moment of eagerness.

A gazelle running from the hunter.

An ant with no supervisor.

Five more minutes.

The wink and the whisper in a meeting.

A doctor who loves the patient hates the cancer.

Scripture that walks, watches and talks.

A man carrying fire in his shirt.

A thief can repay; an adulterer cannot.

7.title: The Young Man Lacking Sense

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Keep My Words as the Apple of Your Eye
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: My son, keep my words and treasure up my commandments with you; keep my commandments and live, guarding them like the pupil of the eye and writing them on the heart (vv. 1-3). Say to wisdom, "You are my sister," so that she may keep you from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The father's defence against seduction is a closer relationship with wisdom than the seductress can offer.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, keep my words and treasure up my commandments with you; keep my commandments and live; keep my teaching as the apple of your eye; bind them on your fingers; write them on the tablet of your heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, keep my words and treasure up my commandments with you; keep my commandments and live;

The fourth and last major warning about the forbidden woman opens with the father's familiar words. But notice keep my commandments and live. It is the same sentence the grandfather said in 4:4. The father is passing on what he received, word for word.

keep my teaching as the apple of your eye;

The apple of your eye is the pupil, the most sensitive and protected part of the body. Anything that comes near it makes you blink. Moses said God kept Israel as the apple of his eye (Deut 32:10). The father wants his son to guard God's teaching with that same reflex, flinching at anything that threatens it.

bind them on your fingers; write them on the tablet of your heart.

On the fingers, where the hands do their work, and on the heart, where desire is formed. Hand and heart, action and affection. A man who has God's word only on his fingers keeps rules he does not love; a man who has it only in his heart has feelings that never become obedience. The father wants both.

verseByVerse.quote: Say to wisdom, "You are my sister," and call insight your intimate friend, to keep you from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Say to wisdom, "You are my sister," and call insight your intimate friend,

Here is a beautiful strategy. Wisdom is to be the son's sister and intimate friend. In the Song of Songs "my sister" is a term of tender affection for a bride. The father is not asking his son merely to know about wisdom. He is asking him to be close to her, to love her, to be at home with her. The best defence against a false intimacy is a true one.

to keep you from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words.

The ESV notes again that these are "the strange" and "the foreign" woman. And again, her weapon is smooth words. A young man who has made wisdom his closest friend will recognise a counterfeit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–23 — What the Father Saw from His Window
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Looking through his lattice at dusk, the father sees a young man lacking sense walking toward her corner as night falls (vv. 6-9). She meets him dressed for it, loud and restless (vv. 10-12), kisses him, and makes her offer: sacrifices paid, a feast, a perfumed bed, and my husband is not at home (vv. 13-20). With much seductive speech she persuades him, and All at once he follows her, as an ox goes to the slaughter; he does not know that it will cost him his life (vv. 21-23).
verseByVerse.theology: The fall is not sudden; it is a walk that began with a young man choosing which street to take at dusk.

verseByVerse.quote: For at the window of my house I have looked out through my lattice, and I have seen among the simple, I have perceived among the youths, a young man lacking sense, passing along the street near her corner, taking the road to her house in the twilight, in the evening, at the time of night and darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For at the window of my house I have looked out through my lattice,

Now the father tells a story. He stands at his window, looking through the lattice, the wooden screen that let a person see out without being seen. He is an eyewitness. What follows is not theory; he has watched it happen.

and I have seen among the simple, I have perceived among the youths, a young man lacking sense,

He picks out one young man in the crowd. He is not wicked, not a hardened criminal. He is simple, one of the open-door people of chapter 1, and lacking sense, literally lacking heart. There is nothing at his centre holding him steady. That is the most dangerous condition a young person can be in: not rebellious, just empty.

passing along the street near her corner, taking the road to her house

Watch his feet. He does not go to her house, not yet. He is passing along the street near her corner. He is not planning to sin. He is just walking near where sin lives. Maybe he tells himself it is the shorter route. Maybe he is curious. But he has chosen the street.

This is how most falls happen. No one wakes up planning to commit adultery. He chooses the street: the lingering conversation, the website opened "just to see", the drink with a colleague after everyone else has gone home. Paul's counsel is to make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires (Rom 13:14). Do not walk near her corner.

in the twilight, in the evening, at the time of night and darkness.

Notice the progression of time: twilight, evening, night, darkness. The light is fading as he walks, and so is his judgment. The darkness is literal, but it is also a picture. Sin prefers the dark, where no one sees. People loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil (John 3:19).

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, the woman meets him, dressed as a prostitute, wily of heart. She is loud and wayward; her feet do not stay at home; now in the street, now in the market, and at every corner she lies in wait.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, the woman meets him, dressed as a prostitute, wily of heart.

And behold. The father's voice tightens, as if he wants to shout a warning through the window. She comes out to meet him. Her clothing announces what she is, and her heart is wily. The ESV notes the Hebrew is "guarded in heart". She shows everything on the outside and hides everything on the inside. He is exposed; she is calculating.

She is loud and wayward; her feet do not stay at home; now in the street, now in the market, and at every corner she lies in wait.

She is restless, never settled, always out. And she is hunting: at every corner she lies in wait. The same verb was used of the gang in chapter 1 who lie in wait for blood (1:11). The seductress and the violent man are hunters of the same kind. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour (1 Pet 5:8).

verseByVerse.quote: She seizes him and kisses him, and with bold face she says to him, "I had to offer sacrifices, and today I have paid my vows; so now I have come out to meet you, to seek you eagerly, and I have found you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She seizes him and kisses him, and with bold face she says to him,

She moves fast. She seizes him and kisses him before he has said a word, and speaks with bold face, without any shame. Temptation often works this way: it moves before the person has had time to think, and it acts as if what is happening is perfectly normal.

"I had to offer sacrifices, and today I have paid my vows; so now I have come out to meet you, to seek you eagerly, and I have found you.

Her opening line is religious. The ESV notes the sacrifices were "peace offerings", and under the law the meat of such an offering had to be eaten that day or the next (Lev 7:15-16). She is saying two things. First, there is a feast at home. Second, she is a religious woman; she has done her duty to God. Religion becomes the cover for sin. That has not changed. Some of the most destructive affairs have been conducted by people who never missed church.

Then flattery: to seek you eagerly, and I have found you. You, specifically. For an empty young man, nothing is more intoxicating than being wanted.

verseByVerse.quote: I have spread my couch with coverings, colored linens from Egyptian linen; I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon. Come, let us take our fill of love till morning; let us delight ourselves with love. For my husband is not at home; he has gone on a long journey; he took a bag of money with him; at full moon he will come home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have spread my couch with coverings, colored linens from Egyptian linen; I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.

Now she describes the bed, and everything about it is luxurious and imported: Egyptian linen, expensive spices. She appeals to every sense. She has prepared for this.

Myrrh and aloes appear elsewhere in Scripture in two very different places. The king in Psalm 45 has robes fragrant with myrrh and aloes and cassia on his wedding day (Ps 45:8). And when Jesus was buried, Nicodemus brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight (John 19:39). The same scents belong to a wedding and a burial. Her bed smells like a wedding. It is a grave.

Come, let us take our fill of love till morning; let us delight ourselves with love.

She calls it love. It is not. Chapter 5 described love: rejoicing in the wife of your youth, delighted in her always (5:18-19). She offers a night, till morning. Love is measured in decades; this is measured in hours.

For my husband is not at home; he has gone on a long journey; he took a bag of money with him; at full moon he will come home."

And finally the reassurance: no one will find out. The husband is away, he took enough money for a long trip, and he will not be back until full moon. It is safe. Every affair makes this promise. Every affair is built on the belief that it will stay hidden. She refers to him coldly, not as "my love" but my husband, a man to be timed around.

verseByVerse.quote: With much seductive speech she persuades him; with her smooth talk she compels him. All at once he follows her, as an ox goes to the slaughter, or as a stag is caught fast till an arrow pierces its liver; as a bird rushes into a snare; he does not know that it will cost him his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With much seductive speech she persuades him; with her smooth talk she compels him.

Much speech. She keeps talking, and every sentence removes an objection. The feast, the flattery, the bed, the safety. By the end he is not so much persuaded as compelled. There comes a point in temptation where resistance feels impossible. The time to resist was on the street, three hours and one corner ago.

All at once he follows her, as an ox goes to the slaughter, or as a stag is caught fast till an arrow pierces its liver; as a bird rushes into a snare; he does not know that it will cost him his life.

Three animals, and each one tells the same truth. An ox walks placidly to the slaughterhouse, thinking it is going to pasture. A stag is caught and waits for the arrow. A bird rushes into a snare, eagerly. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew of the middle line is difficult, and gives the probable reading.) None of them knows what is happening. He does not know that it will cost him his life.

The Bible has its own case study. Samson laid his head on Delilah's knees, and his strength left him (Judg 16:19). And it has its counter-example. When Potiphar's wife caught Joseph by his garment and said, Lie with me, he left his garment in her hand and fled and got out of the house (Gen 39:12). Joseph lost a coat and kept his life. The young man in Proverbs 7 kept his coat and lost everything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–27 — Many a Victim Has She Laid Low
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And now, O sons, listen to me (v. 24). Let not your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths (v. 25), for many a victim has she laid low (v. 26). Her house is the way to Sheol, going down to the chambers of death (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The strong have fallen here too, so no reader may assume he is the exception.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O sons, listen to me, and be attentive to the words of my mouth. Let not your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, O sons, listen to me, and be attentive to the words of my mouth.

The story is over, and the father turns from the window to his sons. Once more, O sons. He has not told the story to entertain them but to arm them.

Let not your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths,

Two steps again: first the heart turns aside, then the feet stray. The fall begins inside. James describes the same order: each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire (Jas 1:14). This is why the father spent so much of the book on the heart. Guard it, and the feet will follow.

Practically, that means paying attention to where the heart's imagination drifts, and turning it back early. It means friends who ask hard questions: exhort one another every day, that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Heb 3:13). And it means prayer, because Jesus said, Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak (Matt 26:41).

verseByVerse.quote: for many a victim has she laid low, and all her slain are a mighty throng. Her house is the way to Sheol, going down to the chambers of death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for many a victim has she laid low, and all her slain are a mighty throng.

The final warning is statistical. Many have fallen here, and her slain are a mighty throng, which may also carry the sense of strong men. She has brought down people who were stronger, wiser and more gifted than the young man on the street. Samson was strong; David was a man after God's own heart. No one is too strong for this temptation. Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall (1 Cor 10:12).

Her house is the way to Sheol, going down to the chambers of death.

The chapter that began with a perfumed bed ends in the chambers of death. The bedroom was the graveyard's front room.

But the last word of the Bible on temptation is not death. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape (1 Cor 10:13). There is always a door out, and very often it is the door of your own house, which you can walk back through before dark. And for those who have already gone into her house, the Christ who went down into death for sinners came up again, and brings back with him all who turn to him.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>My son, keep my words and treasure up my commandments with you;<sup>2</sup>keep my commandments and live; keep my teaching as the apple of your eye;<sup>3</sup>bind them on your fingers; write them on the tablet of your heart.<sup>4</sup>Say to wisdom, "You are my sister," and call insight your intimate friend,<sup>5</sup>to keep you from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words.<sup>6</sup>For at the window of my house I have looked out through my lattice,<sup>7</sup>and I have seen among the simple, I have perceived among the youths, a young man lacking sense,<sup>8</sup>passing along the street near her corner, taking the road to her house<sup>9</sup>in the twilight, in the evening, at the time of night and darkness.<sup>10</sup>And behold, the woman meets him, dressed as a prostitute, wily of heart.<sup>11</sup>She is loud and wayward; her feet do not stay at home;<sup>12</sup>now in the street, now in the market, and at every corner she lies in wait.<sup>13</sup>She seizes him and kisses him, and with bold face she says to him,<sup>14</sup>"I had to offer sacrifices, and today I have paid my vows;<sup>15</sup>so now I have come out to meet you, to seek you eagerly, and I have found you.<sup>16</sup>I have spread my couch with coverings, colored linens from Egyptian linen;<sup>17</sup>I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.<sup>18</sup>Come, let us take our fill of love till morning; let us delight ourselves with love.<sup>19</sup>For my husband is not at home; he has gone on a long journey;<sup>20</sup>he took a bag of money with him; at full moon he will come home."<sup>21</sup>With much seductive speech she persuades him; with her smooth talk she compels him.<sup>22</sup>All at once he follows her, as an ox goes to the slaughter, or as a stag is caught fast<sup>23</sup>till an arrow pierces its liver; as a bird rushes into a snare; he does not know that it will cost him his life.<sup>24</sup>And now, O sons, listen to me, and be attentive to the words of my mouth.<sup>25</sup>Let not your heart turn aside to her ways; do not stray into her paths,<sup>26</sup>for many a victim has she laid low, and all her slain are a mighty throng.<sup>27</sup>Her house is the way to Sheol, going down to the chambers of death.
7.overview:
The father urges his son to guard his teaching like the pupil of the eye and to make wisdom his sister, as protection from the forbidden woman (vv. 1-5).

From his window he tells what he saw: a young man lacking sense, walking at dusk near her corner (vv. 6-9). She meets him dressed as a prostitute, kisses him, and offers a feast from her peace offerings, a perfumed bed, and the assurance that her husband is away (vv. 10-20). With smooth talk she persuades him, and he follows her like an ox to the slaughter, not knowing it will cost his life (vv. 21-23).

The father warns his sons not to let their hearts turn toward her ways, for she has brought down many, and her house leads down to death (vv. 24-27).
7.theology:
Sin works gradually and through small choices: a street chosen at dusk (vv. 8-9). Temptation appeals to every sense, flatters, uses religion as cover, and promises secrecy (vv. 13-20). The heart turns before the feet stray (v. 25; Jas 1:14).

The defence against false intimacy is a true intimacy with wisdom (v. 4), God's word treasured and written on the heart (vv. 1-3), flight rather than negotiation (Gen 39:12), watchful prayer (Matt 26:41), and the faithfulness of God who provides a way of escape (1 Cor 10:13). No one is strong enough to be safe from this sin (v. 26; 1 Cor 10:12).
7.examples:
The pupil of the eye, which blinks at any threat.

Watching through the lattice.

Choosing the street near her corner.

Twilight, evening, night, darkness.

Religion as cover for an affair.

Myrrh and aloes: a wedding and a burial.

An ox walking calmly to the slaughter.

Joseph lost his coat and kept his life.

8.title: Wisdom Calls: I Was Beside Him

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Wisdom Calls at the Crossroads
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Does not wisdom call? Does not understanding raise her voice? She stands on the heights, at the crossroads and the city gates (vv. 1-3), and calls to all people, even the simple and the fool (vv. 4-5). Her words are noble, true and straight, with nothing twisted or crooked in them (vv. 6-9). Take my instruction instead of silver, for wisdom is better than jewels (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The seductress of chapter 7 whispered at a corner in the dark; Wisdom calls in the open, to everyone, and has nothing to hide.

verseByVerse.quote: Does not wisdom call? Does not understanding raise her voice? On the heights beside the way, at the crossroads she takes her stand; beside the gates in front of the town, at the entrance of the portals she cries aloud:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does not wisdom call? Does not understanding raise her voice?

Chapter 7 ended in the chambers of death. Chapter 8 opens with a question that answers the whole of chapter 7. The young man lacking sense went looking for a voice at dusk, and found the wrong one. But was there not another voice calling? Does not wisdom call? She was calling all along.

On the heights beside the way, at the crossroads she takes her stand; beside the gates in front of the town, at the entrance of the portals she cries aloud:

Look where she stands. The seductress was at every corner lying in wait (7:12), in the twilight. Wisdom stands on the heights, where she can be seen, at the crossroads, where decisions are made, and beside the gates, where everyone passes. The two women stand in the same city. One whispers in the dark; the other calls aloud in the open. One has something to hide; the other has nothing.

Every reader stands at a crossroads, and there are two voices. The question is not whether wisdom is calling. It is whether you are listening.

verseByVerse.quote: "To you, O men, I call, and my cry is to the children of man. O simple ones, learn prudence; O fools, learn sense.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"To you, O men, I call, and my cry is to the children of man.

Wisdom's call is universal. Not to Israelites only, not to the educated or the religious, but to the children of man, all humanity. No one is outside the range of her voice.

O simple ones, learn prudence; O fools, learn sense.

And she calls the very people who seem least likely to respond: the simple and the fools. She does not wait for them to improve before she invites them. The invitation is precisely for those who lack what she offers. This is the shape of grace. Jesus said he came to call not the righteous but sinners, and Wisdom's voice sounds exactly like his.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, for I will speak noble things, and from my lips will come what is right, for my mouth will utter truth; wickedness is an abomination to my lips. All the words of my mouth are righteous; there is nothing twisted or crooked in them. They are all straight to him who understands, and right to those who find knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear, for I will speak noble things, and from my lips will come what is right, for my mouth will utter truth; wickedness is an abomination to my lips.

Wisdom describes her own speech, and every word is a contrast with the seductress. Hers were smooth words and flattery; Wisdom's are noble things, what is right, truth. The lips of the forbidden woman dripped honey (5:3). Wisdom's lips find wickedness disgusting.

All the words of my mouth are righteous; there is nothing twisted or crooked in them. They are all straight to him who understands, and right to those who find knowledge.

Nothing twisted. You never have to read Wisdom's words twice to find the trick. And they are straight to him who understands. The words are clear, but it takes an understanding heart to see how clear they are. To the proud they seem foolish or narrow; to the humble, obvious.

Here is a test for any voice you are listening to, whether a friend, an advertisement or your own desires. Is there anything twisted in it? Does it need to hide its ending, the way the seductress hid the chambers of death? Wisdom never does.

verseByVerse.quote: Take my instruction instead of silver, and knowledge rather than choice gold, for wisdom is better than jewels, and all that you may desire cannot compare with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take my instruction instead of silver, and knowledge rather than choice gold, for wisdom is better than jewels, and all that you may desire cannot compare with her.

The comparison with silver, gold and jewels has come before (3:14-15). Wisdom repeats it here in her own voice. Notice the word instead. She is not saying, have both. She is saying, if you must choose, choose me. And sometimes the choice is real. The honest businessman who loses a deal because he would not lie has taken instruction instead of silver. The student who will not cheat for a grade has taken knowledge rather than gold. Wisdom says they have the better bargain.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom lives with prudence and hates pride and evil, for The fear of the LORD is hatred of evil (vv. 12-13). She has counsel and strength; By me kings reign, and rulers decree what is just (vv. 14-16). I love those who love me, and those who seek me diligently find me (v. 17). She gives lasting riches and righteousness, granting an inheritance to those who love me, and filling their treasuries (vv. 18-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Every just ruler governs by a wisdom that is not his own, and that wisdom gives herself to anyone who loves her.

verseByVerse.quote: "I, wisdom, dwell with prudence, and I find knowledge and discretion. The fear of the LORD is hatred of evil. Pride and arrogance and the way of evil and perverted speech I hate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I, wisdom, dwell with prudence, and I find knowledge and discretion.

Wisdom lives in a household with prudence, knowledge and discretion. They are her companions. A person who takes wisdom into his life finds that she brings her family with her: good sense, foresight, the ability to plan well.

The fear of the LORD is hatred of evil. Pride and arrogance and the way of evil and perverted speech I hate.

Here is a definition that should surprise anyone who thinks of the fear of the LORD as merely a feeling. The fear of the LORD is hatred of evil. You cannot revere God and be comfortable with what he hates. A person who says he fears God but enjoys cruelty, lies easily and laughs at purity has not understood the words. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good (Rom 12:9).

And the first things on Wisdom's hate list are pride and arrogance, just as haughty eyes stood first among the seven things the LORD hates (6:17). Pride is the opposite of wisdom because pride will not learn.

verseByVerse.quote: I have counsel and sound wisdom; I have insight; I have strength. By me kings reign, and rulers decree what is just; by me princes rule, and nobles, all who govern justly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have counsel and sound wisdom; I have insight; I have strength.

Wisdom is not weak. I have strength. Many people think of goodness as soft and of power as belonging to the ruthless. Wisdom says she holds both the counsel and the strength.

By me kings reign, and rulers decree what is just; by me princes rule, and nobles, all who govern justly.

Every just government that has ever existed has ruled by wisdom that is not its own. The ESV notes that many manuscripts read all who "govern the earth". Kings think their power comes from armies, elections or birth. It comes from God. He removes kings and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise (Dan 2:21). There is no authority except from God (Rom 13:1).

That is a humbling truth for anyone in authority, whether a president, a manager, an elder or a parent. The wisdom to rule well is borrowed. And it is a comforting truth for everyone under authority: no ruler is outside the rule of the one whose robe bears the name King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev 19:16).

verseByVerse.quote: I love those who love me, and those who seek me diligently find me. Riches and honor are with me, enduring wealth and righteousness. My fruit is better than gold, even fine gold, and my yield than choice silver. I walk in the way of righteousness, in the paths of justice, granting an inheritance to those who love me, and filling their treasuries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I love those who love me, and those who seek me diligently find me.

After speaking of kings, Wisdom speaks of anyone at all. I love those who love me. Wisdom is not a cold principle but someone who returns love. And those who seek me diligently find me.

Put this beside chapter 1, where those who ignored Wisdom's call will seek me diligently but will not find me (1:28). The same words, opposite outcomes. The difference is the heart. The people of chapter 1 sought rescue from the storm; the people of chapter 8 seek Wisdom because they love her. Anyone who seeks God for God's sake will find him.

Riches and honor are with me, enduring wealth and righteousness. My fruit is better than gold, even fine gold, and my yield than choice silver.

Wisdom does bring riches and honour, but look at the adjective: enduring wealth. And it stands beside righteousness. The riches of folly are quick and passing; Wisdom's are slow and lasting. Her fruit and her yield are the language of a harvest, something that grows over seasons.

I walk in the way of righteousness, in the paths of justice, granting an inheritance to those who love me, and filling their treasuries.

She fills treasuries, but only by walking in the paths of justice. Wisdom never makes anyone rich by crooked means. And what she gives is an inheritance, something received as a gift and kept in a family. Isaiah extends the same invitation in the voice of the LORD: Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy? Incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live (Isa 55:2-3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–31 — Before the Beginning of the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his work; she was set up, at the first, before the beginning of the earth (vv. 22-23), before the depths, springs, mountains and fields (vv. 24-26). When God set the heavens in place, marked the horizon on the deep and gave the sea its limit, I was there (vv. 27-29). Then I was beside him, like a master workman, and I was daily his delight, rejoicing before him always, rejoicing in his inhabited world and delighting in the children of man (vv. 30-31).
verseByVerse.theology: The New Testament hears in this portrait the eternal Son, through whom all things were made and in whom the Father delights.

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his work, the first of his acts of old. Ages ago I was set up, at the first, before the beginning of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his work, the first of his acts of old.

Now Wisdom's speech rises to its highest point, and the reader should slow down. Wisdom takes us back before creation.

The word possessed is the subject of one of the most important debates in church history. The ESV notes that it may be rendered "fathered", and that the ancient Greek translation read "created"; it also notes that work is literally "way". In the fourth century Arius and his followers used the Greek "created" to argue that the Son of God was a creature, the first and greatest thing God made. The church rejected that teaching, and rightly.

The first thing to see is that Proverbs 8 is poetry. Wisdom is personified, as Folly is in chapter 9. The point of the passage is that God's wisdom is older than the world, that it was there before anything was made, and that everything was made by it. God was never without his wisdom. There was no moment when he was foolish and then acquired wisdom.

The second thing is that the New Testament does see Christ in this chapter. Paul calls Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24). But the New Testament is careful about how. John does not say the Word was made at the beginning; he says, In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God (John 1:1). The Son is not the first of God's works; he is the one through whom are all things (1 Cor 8:6). When the risen Christ calls himself the beginning of God's creation (Rev 3:14), he means its source and ruler, not its first product.

Ages ago I was set up, at the first, before the beginning of the earth.

Set up is the language of installing a king. Before there was an earth, Wisdom was enthroned. Micah said of the ruler to be born in Bethlehem, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days (Mic 5:2). And Jesus prayed, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed (John 17:5).

verseByVerse.quote: When there were no depths I was brought forth, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains had been shaped, before the hills, I was brought forth, before he had made the earth with its fields, or the first of the dust of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When there were no depths I was brought forth, when there were no springs abounding with water.

Brought forth is birth language. The poem uses it to say that Wisdom did not come after the world. Before the oceans, before a single spring, Wisdom was. The church's confession says of the Son that he is "begotten, not made", and that is the right direction to take this language when it is applied to Christ: not that he had a beginning, but that he is eternally from the Father, as a son is from a father.

Before the mountains had been shaped, before the hills, I was brought forth, before he had made the earth with its fields, or the first of the dust of the world.

The poem goes down the list of the oldest things anyone can imagine. Mountains seem eternal. Wisdom is older. The first of the dust of the world, the very first grain of soil, came after her. Everything a person can see or touch is younger than the wisdom of God.

verseByVerse.quote: When he established the heavens, I was there; when he drew a circle on the face of the deep, when he made firm the skies above, when he established the fountains of the deep, when he assigned to the sea its limit, so that the waters might not transgress his command, when he marked out the foundations of the earth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he established the heavens, I was there; when he drew a circle on the face of the deep,

I was there. Wisdom was not a spectator in the stands but present at the work. God drew a circle on the face of the deep, the horizon, where the sky seems to meet the waters. Genesis says that at the beginning darkness was over the face of the deep (Gen 1:2). Wisdom saw God mark out order in that darkness.

when he made firm the skies above, when he established the fountains of the deep, when he assigned to the sea its limit, so that the waters might not transgress his command, when he marked out the foundations of the earth,

The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew of verse 28 is uncertain, but the picture is clear. God set limits. He gave the sea a boundary it may not cross. To the ancient mind the sea was the great symbol of chaos. God speaks and it stops: Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed (Job 38:11). I placed the sand as the boundary for the sea, a perpetual barrier that it cannot pass (Jer 5:22).

That is exactly what wisdom does in a human life. It sets boundaries. The commands of God that seem to limit us are like the shoreline: without them, chaos floods everything. A person who throws off every limit does not become free; he becomes a flood.

verseByVerse.quote: then I was beside him, like a master workman, and I was daily his delight, rejoicing before him always, rejoicing in his inhabited world and delighting in the children of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
then I was beside him, like a master workman, and I was daily his delight, rejoicing before him always,

This may be the most beautiful verse in the chapter. Wisdom was beside him, close at God's side, and like a master workman, the skilled craftsman at the builder's elbow. John says, All things were made through him (John 1:3), and speaks of God the only Son, who is at the Father's side (John 1:18).

And the mood of creation was joy. I was daily his delight, and the ESV notes this may be "daily filled with delight". Wisdom was rejoicing before him always. Creation was not a grim task. It was carried out in delight, the Father delighting in his Wisdom and Wisdom rejoicing before him.

When Jesus was baptised, a voice from heaven said, This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased (Matt 3:17). And Jesus prayed of the glory the Father had given him because you loved me before the foundation of the world (John 17:24). The delight of verse 30 is older than time.

rejoicing in his inhabited world and delighting in the children of man.

And then this. Wisdom's delight moved outward, to the inhabited world and above all to the children of man. Of all that God made, Wisdom took special pleasure in human beings.

Read that in the light of the gospel. The Son who was the Father's delight before the world began delighted in the children of man so much that he became one of them. He emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men (Phil 2:7). The Wisdom who rejoiced over the world at creation came into that world to save it. That is how much God's wisdom delights in you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–36 — Whoever Finds Me Finds Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: And now, O sons, listen to me: blessed are those who keep my ways (v. 32). Blessed is the one who waits daily at Wisdom's doors (vv. 33-34). For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the LORD, but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death (vv. 35-36).
verseByVerse.theology: Life and death depend on one thing: whether a person finds wisdom, and in the fullest sense that means finding Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, O sons, listen to me: blessed are those who keep my ways. Hear instruction and be wise, and do not neglect it. Blessed is the one who listens to me, watching daily at my gates, waiting beside my doors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And now, O sons, listen to me: blessed are those who keep my ways.

And now. It is the same phrase the father used after the story of the seductress (7:24). Now Wisdom uses it. After the vision of creation, she comes back to the crossroads, to her sons, and draws the conclusion: listen to me. The wisdom that made the world is the wisdom that will make your life.

Hear instruction and be wise, and do not neglect it.

Do not neglect it. The danger for most people is not open rejection of wisdom. It is neglect: letting the voice go unheard because other voices are louder and closer.

Blessed is the one who listens to me, watching daily at my gates, waiting beside my doors.

The picture is of someone waiting outside a house every morning for the door to open, like a servant waiting for his master, or a lover for the beloved. Daily. The blessing belongs to the person who makes seeking wisdom a daily habit, not a crisis measure.

What would that look like? A time each day, however short, spent with God's word open, waiting at the door. The remarkable thing is that the door is Christ himself: I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved (John 10:9). And he is also the one who knocks on ours: Behold, I stand at the door and knock (Rev 3:20).

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the LORD, but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the LORD,

Here is the promise the whole chapter has been building toward. Whoever finds me finds life. Not only a better life, but life itself. And favor from the LORD, which is grace.

Few sentences in Proverbs sound more like the gospel of John. Whoever has the Son has life (1 John 5:12). And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6). To find Wisdom, finally, is to find Christ.

but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death."

And the other side. He who fails to find me injures himself. Rejecting wisdom is self-harm. No one else needs to punish the fool; he wounds himself.

The last phrase is shattering: all who hate me love death. Nobody thinks he loves death. The young man of chapter 7 thought he loved pleasure. But to reject the source of life is, whether one knows it or not, to choose death. Whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him (John 3:36).

So the chapter ends where the book always ends up: at a choice between two ways. But here the choice has a face. The Wisdom who stood beside the Father at creation, delighting in the children of man, stands at the crossroads and calls. Whoever finds him finds life.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>Does not wisdom call?
