Pride and arrogance and the way of evil and perverted speech I hate.<sup>14</sup>I have counsel and sound wisdom; I have insight; I have strength.<sup>15</sup>By me kings reign, and rulers decree what is just;<sup>16</sup>by me princes rule, and nobles, all who govern justly.<sup>17</sup>I love those who love me, and those who seek me diligently find me.<sup>18</sup>Riches and honor are with me, enduring wealth and righteousness.<sup>19</sup>My fruit is better than gold, even fine gold, and my yield than choice silver.<sup>20</sup>I walk in the way of righteousness, in the paths of justice,<sup>21</sup>granting an inheritance to those who love me, and filling their treasuries.<sup>22</sup>"The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his work, the first of his acts of old.<sup>23</sup>Ages ago I was set up, at the first, before the beginning of the earth.<sup>24</sup>When there were no depths I was brought forth, when there were no springs abounding with water.<sup>25</sup>Before the mountains had been shaped, before the hills, I was brought forth,<sup>26</sup>before he had made the earth with its fields, or the first of the dust of the world.<sup>27</sup>When he established the heavens, I was there; when he drew a circle on the face of the deep,<sup>28</sup>when he made firm the skies above, when he established the fountains of the deep,<sup>29</sup>when he assigned to the sea its limit, so that the waters might not transgress his command, when he marked out the foundations of the earth,<sup>30</sup>then I was beside him, like a master workman, and I was daily his delight, rejoicing before him always,<sup>31</sup>rejoicing in his inhabited world and delighting in the children of man.<sup>32</sup>"And now, O sons, listen to me: blessed are those who keep my ways.<sup>33</sup>Hear instruction and be wise, and do not neglect it.<sup>34</sup>Blessed is the one who listens to me, watching daily at my gates, waiting beside my doors.<sup>35</sup>For whoever finds me finds life and obtains favor from the LORD,<sup>36</sup>but he who fails to find me injures himself; all who hate me love death."
8.overview:
Wisdom calls publicly from the heights, the crossroads and the city gates, to all people, including the simple and fools. Her words are true and straight, and she is worth more than silver, gold and jewels (vv. 1-11).

She lives with prudence and hates pride and evil. By her kings reign and rulers govern justly. She loves those who love her, is found by those who seek her, and gives enduring riches and righteousness (vv. 12-21).

The LORD possessed Wisdom before the creation of the world. She was there before the depths, the mountains and the dust; she was present when God established the heavens and set the sea its limit; she was beside him as a master workman, his daily delight, rejoicing in the world and delighting in humanity (vv. 22-31).

Blessed are those who listen and wait daily at her doors, for whoever finds her finds life and favour from the LORD, and all who hate her love death (vv. 32-36).
8.theology:
God's wisdom is universally offered (vv. 4-5), perfectly truthful (vv. 6-9), and the source of all just authority (vv. 15-16; Dan 2:21; Rom 13:1). The fear of the LORD includes hatred of evil (v. 13).

Wisdom existed before creation and was the agent of it (vv. 22-31). The New Testament identifies Christ as the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24; Col 2:3), through whom all things were made (John 1:1-3; Col 1:16-17; Heb 1:2). Verse 22 must not be read, as Arius read it, to make the Son a creature; the Son is eternally with the Father (John 1:1; 17:5), begotten, not made.

The Father's eternal delight in his Wisdom (v. 30; Matt 3:17; John 17:24) overflows in delight in humanity (v. 31), fulfilled in the incarnation (Phil 2:6-7). Finding Wisdom is finding life; rejecting her is loving death (vv. 35-36; John 17:3; 3:36).
8.examples:
Two women in the same city: one whispering at a corner, one calling from the heights.

A businessman who loses a deal rather than lie.

Every just ruler governing with borrowed wisdom.

The same words in 1:28 and 8:17, with opposite outcomes.

The shoreline that keeps chaos out.

A master craftsman at the builder's elbow.

The Father's delight before time began.

Waiting daily at the door.

9.title: Wisdom Has Built Her House

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars. She has prepared meat and wine and set the table (vv. 1-2), and sends her young women to the heights of the town to call, Whoever is simple, let him turn in here! (vv. 3-4). Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed. Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom's invitation is a feast already prepared, offered free to people who have nothing to bring but their need.

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars. She has slaughtered her beasts; she has mixed her wine; she has also set her table.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars.

The first nine chapters of Proverbs end with a pair of pictures, and they are meant to be seen side by side. Two women, two houses, two invitations, two feasts. Everything in chapters 1 to 8 has been leading to this choice.

Wisdom's first act is to build. She has made a house, and a substantial one: seven pillars, cut from stone. Seven is the Bible's number of completeness. Her house is finished, solid, ready. Nothing about it is temporary. Proverbs will later say, The wisest of women builds her house (14:1). And Jesus spoke of the wise man who built his house on the rock, the house that did not fall (Matt 7:24-25).

The New Testament shows what house Wisdom has been building. Christ Jesus is the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord (Eph 2:20-21). Wisdom's house is the dwelling place of God among his people.

She has slaughtered her beasts; she has mixed her wine; she has also set her table.

Then the feast. Meat has been slaughtered, wine mixed with spices, the table laid. Everything is ready before a single guest has been invited. The cost has been paid by the host.

Jesus told a parable that sounds almost exactly like this. A king prepared a wedding feast for his son, and sent word: See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast (Matt 22:4). The gospel is not an invitation to come and help prepare the meal. It is an invitation to a table already set.

verseByVerse.quote: She has sent out her young women to call from the highest places in the town, "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" To him who lacks sense she says,
verseByVerse.commentary:
She has sent out her young women to call from the highest places in the town,

Wisdom sends messengers. Her invitation does not wait for people to find her house; it goes out to find them, calling from the highest places in the town, where the voice carries furthest. In the parable of the great banquet, the master said, Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city (Luke 14:21), and then, Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled (Luke 14:23).

Every Christian who speaks of Christ to a friend is one of Wisdom's messengers, calling from wherever he stands in the town.

"Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" To him who lacks sense she says,

Look at who is invited: whoever is simple, and him who lacks sense. That is the young man of chapter 7, exactly, the one who was lacking sense (7:7). Wisdom invites the very person who is most likely to walk into Folly's house. She does not demand that he become wise first. The qualification for her feast is knowing you need it.

Remember this invitation. Folly will repeat it word for word in verse 16.

verseByVerse.quote: "Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed. Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed.

The invitation is to eat and drink. Wisdom is not only studied; she is received, taken in, the way food becomes part of a body. Isaiah's great invitation sounds the same: Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! (Isa 55:1).

And Jesus took the words onto his own lips. I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst (John 6:35). I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever (John 6:51). The bread Wisdom offers is Christ himself. The Bible's last invitation is Wisdom's invitation still: let the one who desires take the water of life without price (Rev 22:17).

Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight."

But coming to the feast involves leaving something. Leave your simple ways. The ESV notes that this could be rendered "Leave the company of the simple". Either way, a person cannot sit at Wisdom's table and keep his old life and old companions unchanged. Grace is free, but it is not static. It changes the direction of a life: and live, and walk in the way of insight.

Three verbs sum up the gospel invitation: leave, live, walk. Leave the old way. Receive life. Walk in the new one.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse, but reprove a wise man, and he will love you (vv. 7-8). Teach the wise and he grows wiser (v. 9). The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight (v. 10). Wisdom adds years (v. 11), and each person bears the consequence of his own response: If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: How a person takes correction shows which banquet he is heading for.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse, and he who reproves a wicked man incurs injury. Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you. Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be still wiser; teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse, and he who reproves a wicked man incurs injury.

The picture of the two banquets is interrupted by a short collection of sayings, and at first they seem out of place. They are not. They explain why some people accept Wisdom's invitation and others do not. It comes down to how a person responds to correction.

The scoffer is the person who mocks what is serious. Correct him, and you will get abuse in return: insults, anger, perhaps worse. Jesus said the same: do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you (Matt 7:6).

Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you.

Here is one of the most practical tests of character in the whole book. Watch what happens when someone is corrected. The scoffer will hate you. The wise man will love you. The same rebuke produces opposite reactions, and the reaction reveals the heart.

So turn the test on yourself. When someone last pointed out a fault in you, a spouse, a colleague, a friend, did you love them for it or resent them? Faithful are the wounds of a friend (27:6). The psalmist could say, Let a righteous man strike me—it is a kindness; let him rebuke me—it is oil for my head (Ps 141:5).

Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be still wiser; teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning.

Wisdom grows by being corrected. The ESV notes that the Hebrew has no word for instruction; it simply says "give to a wise man". Give him anything, and he will make himself wiser with it. The wise man is not the one who knows the most; he is the one who keeps learning. The scoffer stays where he is forever.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight. For by me your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life. If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight.

And here, at the centre of the chapter, is the motto of the book again. Chapter 1 said, The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (1:7). Now, at the end of the first great section, it returns almost word for word. The first nine chapters are framed by this truth, like a door at each end.

But notice what is added: the knowledge of the Holy One is insight. Wisdom is not only fearing God; it is knowing him, the Holy One, personally. Everything in the book, every warning and every picture, leads back to this. The goal of Proverbs is not a clever life. It is a life that knows God.

For by me your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life.

Wisdom speaks again, and promises life. Folly's guests, as verse 18 will say, are among the dead. Wisdom's guests have years added. Both feasts have consequences that last far beyond the meal.

If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it.

This verse is intensely personal. No one else can be wise for you, and no one else will bear your scoffing. Your parents' faith will not save you, and your friends' folly will not excuse you. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon himself, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself (Ezek 18:20). For each will have to bear his own load (Gal 6:5).

Every reader, then, must make his own answer to the two invitations. That is what the chapter is pressing toward.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing (v. 13). She sits at her door on the heights and calls to passers-by with Wisdom's own words, Whoever is simple, let him turn in here! (vv. 14-16). Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant. But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Folly copies Wisdom's invitation word for word, but her table is set with stolen goods in a house of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing. She sits at the door of her house; she takes a seat on the highest places of the town, calling to those who pass by, who are going straight on their way,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing.

Now the other woman. Folly is personified just as Wisdom has been, and she looks very much like the forbidden woman of chapter 7, who was also loud (7:11). She is seductive, and she knows nothing. The ESV notes the alternative "full of simpleness". She has nothing to teach. She has a great deal to say, but there is nothing in it.

She sits at the door of her house; she takes a seat on the highest places of the town,

Compare the two women carefully. Wisdom built her house, hewed pillars, slaughtered, mixed, set, sent. Seven verbs of work. Folly sits. Nothing is said about her building anything. She has done no work, prepared nothing of her own. She simply takes a seat and waits.

And yet she has found a seat on the highest places of the town, exactly where Wisdom's messengers called (v. 3). Folly occupies the same public space as Wisdom. Her voice is just as easy to hear.

calling to those who pass by, who are going straight on their way,

Look at her target. Not people who are already lost, but those going straight on their way. Folly's business is to pull people off a good road. She calls to the young man who is doing well, the believer who is walking faithfully. No one is so far along the straight road that he is beyond her reach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" And to him who lacks sense she says, "Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant." But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" And to him who lacks sense she says,

And here is the most chilling detail of the chapter. Folly's invitation is word for word the same as Wisdom's (v. 4). The same words, from the same heights, to the same people.

That is how folly works. She does not announce herself as folly. She uses the language of wisdom. False teaching borrows the vocabulary of the gospel. Sin promises life, freedom, fulfilment, the very things God offers. The simple person cannot tell the two invitations apart by their words. He can only tell them apart by what is served, and by where the house leads.

"Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant."

And here is what is served. Wisdom offered meat and mixed wine. Folly offers water and bread, and it is stolen. She has nothing of her own. Her whole appeal is that it is forbidden. The water is not better water. It tastes sweet because it was stolen, and the bread is pleasant because it is eaten in secret.

This is the oldest temptation there is. The fruit in Eden was a delight to the eyes, and the woman took it (Gen 3:6); its attraction was sharpened by the fact that God had said no. Paul describes the same perverse effect: sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness (Rom 7:8). There is a thrill in the forbidden that has nothing to do with the thing itself. An affair, a theft, a secret habit: the secrecy is half the pleasure.

But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.

And the last verse of the first nine chapters. He does not know. The guests at Folly's table look around and see a party. They do not see what the father has been trying to show them since chapter 2: the dead are there. The ESV notes that the word is "Rephaim", the shades of the dead, just as at 2:18. Her guests are already in the depths of Sheol. They think they are dining; they are buried.

For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (Rom 6:23). That verse is Proverbs 9 in one sentence. Two tables. One sells stolen water that ends in death. The other gives bread for nothing that ends in life. Both hostesses are calling right now, in the same words, from the same heights. Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev 19:9).

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars.<sup>2</sup>She has slaughtered her beasts; she has mixed her wine; she has also set her table.<sup>3</sup>She has sent out her young women to call from the highest places in the town,<sup>4</sup>"Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" To him who lacks sense she says,<sup>5</sup>"Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed.<sup>6</sup>Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight."<sup>7</sup>Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse, and he who reproves a wicked man incurs injury.<sup>8</sup>Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you.<sup>9</sup>Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be still wiser; teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning.<sup>10</sup>The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight.<sup>11</sup>For by me your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life.<sup>12</sup>If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it.<sup>13</sup>The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing.<sup>14</sup>She sits at the door of her house; she takes a seat on the highest places of the town,<sup>15</sup>calling to those who pass by, who are going straight on their way,<sup>16</sup>"Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" And to him who lacks sense she says,<sup>17</sup>"Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant."<sup>18</sup>But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.
9.overview:
Wisdom has built a house with seven pillars, prepared a feast, and sent her young women to call from the heights: whoever is simple, come in, eat and drink, leave your simple ways and live (vv. 1-6).

A scoffer who is corrected will hate you, but a wise man will love you and grow wiser. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight; each person bears the consequences of his own wisdom or scoffing (vv. 7-12).

The woman Folly is loud and knows nothing. She sits at her door on the heights and calls to passers-by in Wisdom's own words, offering stolen water and bread eaten in secret. Her guests do not know that the dead are there (vv. 13-18).
9.theology:
Chapters 1 to 9 close with a choice between two invitations. Wisdom's feast is prepared at the host's cost and offered freely to the needy (vv. 1-6), prefiguring the gospel banquet (Matt 22:2-4; Luke 14:16-23) and Christ the bread of life (John 6:35, 51; Rev 22:17). Accepting it means leaving the old way (v. 6).

The response to correction reveals the heart (vv. 7-9). The fear of the LORD and the knowledge of the Holy One frame the whole first section (v. 10; 1:7). Each person is responsible for his own response (v. 12; Ezek 18:20).

Folly imitates Wisdom's words (v. 16), offers only what is stolen and secret (v. 17; Gen 3:6; Rom 7:8), and leads to death (v. 18; Rom 6:23).
9.examples:
A house with seven stone pillars.

A table set before the guests are invited.

Messengers calling from the highest places.

Leave, live, walk.

The same rebuke: hated by one, loved by another.

Wisdom builds; Folly sits.

Two identical invitations.

Stolen water that tastes sweet because it was stolen.

Guests who think they are dining and are buried.

10.title: The Proverbs of Solomon: Two Ways in Two Lines

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Righteous and the Wicked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A new heading begins the main collection: The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish son is a sorrow to his mother (v. 1). Ill-gotten treasure does not profit, and the LORD feeds the righteous (vv. 2-3). The diligent grow rich and the lazy son shames his family (vv. 4-5). Blessing rests on the righteous: The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: From here the book speaks in two-line contrasts, and the first ones set the two ways side by side in the family, the purse and the memory a life leaves behind.

verseByVerse.quote: The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish son is a sorrow to his mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish son is a sorrow to his mother.

With a new heading the book changes shape. For nine chapters a father has talked to his son in long, flowing speeches. From here to the middle of chapter 22, the book is a collection of short sayings, most of them two lines long, and most of them built on a contrast: the wise and the foolish, the righteous and the wicked, the diligent and the lazy. The first nine chapters were the lecture; these are the tools.

Reading this section well needs a different pace. A proverb is not meant to be read quickly in a row with its neighbours, the way a story is. It is meant to be picked up, turned over, carried into the day, and tested against life. One or two a day, pondered, will do more good than a chapter skimmed.

And the first tool is aimed at the family. A son's choices land on his parents. The father is made glad; the mother bears the sorrow. No one's wisdom or folly is private. Every young person who thinks "it is my life" should look at the faces of the two people who raised him. What he does, they will feel.

verseByVerse.quote: Treasures gained by wickedness do not profit, but righteousness delivers from death. The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, but he thwarts the craving of the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Treasures gained by wickedness do not profit, but righteousness delivers from death.

Treasures that were gained dishonestly are real treasures. The money is in the account; the house is built. But they do not profit. They cannot buy what matters, and they cannot save their owner from the one appointment he cannot avoid. Righteousness delivers from death. Jesus warned, one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions (Luke 12:15).

The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, but he thwarts the craving of the wicked.

Here is the first time the LORD himself appears in the sentence proverbs, and he appears as provider and as judge. The righteous are fed. The wicked have cravings that God thwarts: they get what they wanted and find it does not satisfy, or they never get it at all.

Is it true that no righteous person ever goes hungry? David said, I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken or his children begging for bread (Ps 37:25). That is the pattern of God's care. Yet Hebrews speaks of the faithful who went about destitute, afflicted, mistreated (Heb 11:37). A proverb states how God's world generally works, not a guarantee against every hardship. But even in hunger, the righteous are never abandoned, and the Father who knows what they need has promised to provide what they truly need (Matt 6:33).

verseByVerse.quote: A slack hand causes poverty, but the hand of the diligent makes rich. He who gathers in summer is a prudent son, but he who sleeps in harvest is a son who brings shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A slack hand causes poverty, but the hand of the diligent makes rich.

The picture is of two hands. One is slack, loose, not gripping the tool. The other is diligent, sharp, working. The same world gives very different results to them. This is not the only reason people are poor, and Proverbs will say much about the poor who are oppressed and the rich who are unjust. But it is one reason, and a young person can do something about it.

He who gathers in summer is a prudent son, but he who sleeps in harvest is a son who brings shame.

Harvest does not wait. There are a few weeks when the crop must be brought in, and a son who sleeps through them has lost the year. Life has harvests too: the years of study, the early career, the season when children are young and must be taught. They do not come back. And notice the word son again, twice. The lazy young man shames not only himself but the family that bears his name.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessings are on the head of the righteous, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence. The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessings are on the head of the righteous, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence.

Blessings rest on the righteous person's head, visibly, like a crown. The wicked man's mouth, by contrast, hides something. He talks pleasantly, and violence lies behind the words. The ESV notes that the line may also be read, "but violence covers the mouth of the wicked": the violence he planned will come back over his own face. The second line is repeated exactly in verse 11.

The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot.

Here is a proverb about what people leave behind. A righteous person's memory goes on blessing others after he has died: the grandmother whose prayers are still remembered, the father whose honesty is still quoted. Abel was killed at the beginning of history, and through his faith, though he died, he still speaks (Heb 11:4). He will be remembered forever (Ps 112:6).

The name of the wicked will rot, like meat left out. No one names his son after a notorious traitor. Ask what your name will smell like when you are gone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–21 — The Mouth of the Righteous
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Most of these sayings are about speech. The babbling fool comes to ruin (vv. 8, 10), but The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life (v. 11). Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses (v. 12). The rich trust their wealth as a fortress (vv. 15-16); the one who hides hatred lies (v. 18). When words are many, transgression is not lacking, but whoever restrains his lips is prudent (v. 19). The lips of the righteous feed many (vv. 20-21).
verseByVerse.theology: What comes out of a person's mouth either gives life to others or does them harm, and restraint is half of wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: The wise of heart will receive commandments, but a babbling fool will come to ruin. Whoever walks in integrity walks securely, but he who makes his ways crooked will be found out. Whoever winks the eye causes trouble, and a babbling fool will come to ruin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wise of heart will receive commandments, but a babbling fool will come to ruin.

The wise man takes in; the fool pours out. He receives commandments because he knows he needs them. The babbling fool, literally the fool of lips, is too busy talking to hear anything. And he talks himself into ruin.

Whoever walks in integrity walks securely, but he who makes his ways crooked will be found out.

Integrity means being whole, the same person in public and in private. And that person walks securely. He does not have to remember which story he told to whom. He does not lie awake afraid of what might come out. The man with a crooked way is living with a time bomb. He will be found out. It may take years. It will happen.

Whoever winks the eye causes trouble, and a babbling fool will come to ruin.

The winking eye is the signal of the schemer we met in 6:13. And the second line repeats verse 8 word for word: a babbling fool will come to ruin. The collection repeats itself deliberately. Some truths are important enough to say twice within a few lines, and the fool's mouth is one of them.

verseByVerse.quote: The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence. Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence.

A fountain in a dry land is where people come to live. The righteous person's speech is like that. People come away from talking with him refreshed, encouraged, set right. Think of the person in your life whose words you go to when you are dry.

Jesus promised that this fountain would flow from everyone who comes to him: Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water (John 7:38). A believer's mouth can become a fountain of life because the Spirit of life lives in him. And the second line comes back from verse 6, word for word: the wicked mouth hides violence.

Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses.

Hatred stirs up, like someone stirring embers back into flame. It keeps old grievances alive, brings them up again, retells them. Love covers. It does not pretend the offence did not happen, and it does not cover crimes that must be exposed. But it declines to keep uncovering what has been forgiven. Whoever covers an offense seeks love, but he who repeats a matter separates close friends (17:9).

Peter took this proverb straight into the life of the church: Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet 4:8). And behind every Christian's covering love stands the love of God, who covered our sins at the cost of his Son.

Is there an offence you keep stirring? What would it mean to cover it today?

verseByVerse.quote: On the lips of him who has understanding, wisdom is found, but a rod is for the back of him who lacks sense. The wise lay up knowledge, but the mouth of a fool brings ruin near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the lips of him who has understanding, wisdom is found, but a rod is for the back of him who lacks sense.

Two ways to learn. The person with understanding learns through words; wisdom is on his lips because it has gone in through his ears. The person who lacks sense will not learn through words, so he learns through the rod, through pain. Everyone learns eventually. The question is whether he learns from instruction or from consequences.

The wise lay up knowledge, but the mouth of a fool brings ruin near.

The wise man stores knowledge away like provisions, for later. The fool spends his words as fast as he gets them, and every sentence brings disaster a step closer. Some people are one remark away from losing a job or a friend, and they make the remark.

verseByVerse.quote: A rich man's wealth is his strong city; the poverty of the poor is their ruin. The wage of the righteous leads to life, the gain of the wicked to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A rich man's wealth is his strong city; the poverty of the poor is their ruin.

This proverb simply observes how life looks. Money does protect people. The rich can afford lawyers, doctors and a cushion against disaster. The poor have none, and one broken car can ruin them. Proverbs is not naive about that.

But the book does not leave it there. In 18:11 the same first line comes back with a second line added: A rich man's wealth is his strong city, and like a high wall in his imagination. The fortress is real, and it is also partly imaginary. Money protects against many things, but not against death, grief, judgment or a heart that is empty. That is why Paul tells the rich not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God (1 Tim 6:17).

The wage of the righteous leads to life, the gain of the wicked to sin.

What does a person's income lead to? The righteous man's wages go toward life: his family fed, his neighbour helped, God honoured. The wicked man's gain leads to more sin: more greed, more indulgence, more distance from God. Money is an amplifier. It makes a person more of what he already is.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever heeds instruction is on the path to life, but he who rejects reproof leads others astray. The one who conceals hatred has lying lips, and whoever utters slander is a fool.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever heeds instruction is on the path to life, but he who rejects reproof leads others astray.

A person who will not take correction does not only harm himself. He leads others astray. A father who never admits he was wrong teaches his children to do the same. A leader who will not be corrected takes a whole organisation down with him. Teachability is not a private virtue.

The one who conceals hatred has lying lips, and whoever utters slander is a fool.

Two ways to handle hatred, and both are wrong. Hide it behind a smile, and you are a liar. Let it out as slander, and you are a fool. The only real answer to hatred is not to hide it or voice it, but to have it removed from the heart, which only God can do.

verseByVerse.quote: When words are many, transgression is not lacking, but whoever restrains his lips is prudent. The tongue of the righteous is choice silver; the heart of the wicked is of little worth. The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of sense.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When words are many, transgression is not lacking, but whoever restrains his lips is prudent.

This is simple arithmetic. The more a person talks, the more chances there are to say something wrong. That is true in a meeting, in an argument, on social media, in a marriage. James says, let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger (Jas 1:19), and if anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man (Jas 3:2).

The wise person restrains his lips, like reining in a horse. Try it for a day: say less, and notice how many things you were about to say that you are glad you did not.

The tongue of the righteous is choice silver; the heart of the wicked is of little worth.

Notice the contrast: the tongue of one and the heart of the other. The righteous man's words are valuable because his heart is; the wicked man's heart is worth little, so his words are too. Speech is only as good as the heart it comes from.

The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of sense.

The righteous person's words are food, and they feed many: counsel, encouragement, truth, the gospel itself. The fool cannot feed even himself, and dies starving for the sense that was on offer. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt (Col 4:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–32 — The Blessing and the Stronghold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it (v. 22). The fool jokes about wrong, and the storm sweeps the wicked away while the righteous stand (vv. 23-25). The sluggard is vinegar to his employer (v. 26). The fear of the LORD lengthens life, and The hope of the righteous brings joy (vv. 27-28). The way of the LORD is a stronghold to the blameless; The righteous will never be removed, and their mouths bring forth wisdom (vv. 29-32).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter ends by looking to the future: what the righteous hope for will come, and what they stand on will hold.

verseByVerse.quote: The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it.

After many proverbs about human diligence, this one sets it in its place. Riches that last come from the blessing of the LORD. And that kind of wealth comes without the sorrow that so often attaches to money: the anxiety, the family fights, the guilt of how it was gained.

The ESV notes that the second line may be read, "and toil adds nothing to it". That does not contradict verse 4, which praised the diligent hand. It says that diligence without God's blessing achieves nothing lasting. It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep (Ps 127:2). Work hard, and rest in the knowledge that the increase is his. Godliness with contentment is great gain (1 Tim 6:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Doing wrong is like a joke to a fool, but wisdom is pleasure to a man of understanding. What the wicked dreads will come upon him, but the desire of the righteous will be granted. When the tempest passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous is established forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Doing wrong is like a joke to a fool, but wisdom is pleasure to a man of understanding.

What a person laughs at reveals what he loves. For the fool, wrongdoing is entertainment: the prank that humiliates someone, the joke about cheating, the laughter at sin on a screen. For the man of understanding, wisdom is where the pleasure is. Each finds joy in his own direction.

What the wicked dreads will come upon him, but the desire of the righteous will be granted.

The wicked man lives with a fear he pushes down: that one day he will have to answer for it. He is right. The righteous man lives with a desire, and his desire is also right: it will be granted. Both are headed toward what they expect.

When the tempest passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous is established forever.

The storm comes to both. The difference is not whether the tempest comes, but what is left when it has passed. Jesus told of two houses in the same storm; one did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock, and the other fell, and great was the fall of it (Matt 7:25, 27).

verseByVerse.quote: Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who send him. The fear of the LORD prolongs life, but the years of the wicked will be short.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who send him.

One of the book's comic pictures, and anyone who has managed people will recognise it. You send a lazy man on an errand, and the experience is like sour vinegar on your teeth, or smoke in your eyes: irritating, painful, and impossible to ignore. The job is not done, or done late, or done badly. A Christian employee's reliability is part of his witness, whether or not anyone thanks him for it.

The fear of the LORD prolongs life, but the years of the wicked will be short.

Again, the general pattern. A life lived in reverence toward God avoids a great many of the things that shorten lives: violence, addiction, reckless living, the stress of guilt. And ultimately the fear of the LORD leads to a life that has no end.

verseByVerse.quote: The hope of the righteous brings joy, but the expectation of the wicked will perish. The way of the LORD is a stronghold to the blameless, but destruction to evildoers. The righteous will never be removed, but the wicked will not dwell in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hope of the righteous brings joy, but the expectation of the wicked will perish.

Both the righteous and the wicked look forward to something. The difference is where their hopes are placed. The wicked expects a future built on his own plans, and it will perish. The righteous hopes in God, and that hope brings joy even now, before it is fulfilled. Hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts (Rom 5:5).

The way of the LORD is a stronghold to the blameless, but destruction to evildoers.

The same way of the LORD is two different things to two different people. To the blameless it is a fortress, a place of safety. To evildoers it is destruction. God's ways do not change; people's relationship to them does. The same sun that grows a plant withers one with no roots.

The righteous will never be removed, but the wicked will not dwell in the land.

The righteous are rooted. Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved, but abides forever (Ps 125:1). Circumstances will shake them; they will not be removed from God's hand.

verseByVerse.quote: The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, but the perverse tongue will be cut off. The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable, but the mouth of the wicked, what is perverse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, but the perverse tongue will be cut off.

The chapter ends as it spent most of its time: on speech. The picture in brings forth is of a tree bearing fruit. Wisdom grows out of the righteous person's mouth naturally. The perverse tongue, the tongue that twists truth, is like a branch that will be cut off.

The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable, but the mouth of the wicked, what is perverse.

The righteous person's lips know what is fitting: when to speak and when to be quiet, what will help and what will wound, how to say a hard thing kindly. That is a skill learned over years of listening to God and to people. The wicked mouth knows only what is twisted. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person (Col 4:6).

A chapter of thirty-two proverbs has given more attention to the mouth than to anything else. That is not an accident. The tongue is where wisdom and folly show themselves first and most often, every day.

10.text: <sup>1</sup>The proverbs of Solomon. 10.overview:
The main collection of Solomon's proverbs begins. The form changes from long discourse to short two-line contrasts between the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the foolish.

A wise son gladdens his parents (v. 1). Ill-gotten treasure does not profit, the LORD feeds the righteous, diligence brings plenty, and the memory of the righteous is a blessing (vv. 2-7). Most of the chapter concerns speech: the babbling fool comes to ruin, the mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, love covers offences, and many words bring transgression (vv. 8-21). The blessing of the LORD makes rich without sorrow; the righteous stand after the storm, their hope brings joy, and they will never be removed (vv. 22-32).
10.theology:
The two ways of chapters 1-9 are now applied to everyday life in compressed sayings. Proverbs describe the general pattern of God's world, not guarantees for every case (v. 3; Ps 37:25; Heb 11:37).

Human diligence matters (vv. 4-5), but lasting wealth is the LORD's blessing (v. 22; Ps 127:2). Speech reveals the heart (v. 20) and either gives life or does harm (vv. 11, 21). Love covers offences (v. 12; 1 Pet 4:8). Wealth is a real protection and a false security (v. 15; 18:11). The hope of the righteous will not perish (v. 28; Rom 5:5).
10.examples:
A son whose choices land on his parents' faces.

Sleeping through the harvest.

A name that smells when it is remembered.

Living with a time bomb that will be found out.

Stirring embers or covering them.

A fortress that is partly imaginary.

Saying less for a day.

Vinegar on the teeth: sending a sluggard on an errand.

11.overview:
God hates false scales and delights in honest weights; pride brings disgrace (vv. 1-2). Integrity guides the upright, while riches cannot save in the day of wrath and the wicked fall by their own wickedness (vv. 3-9). The righteous bless their city (vv. 10-11).

The wise do not belittle others or betray secrets, seek many counsellors, avoid guaranteeing strangers' debts, and are kind (vv. 12-17). The wicked earn deceptive wages and will not go unpunished; beauty without discretion is a gold ring in a pig's snout (vv. 18-22).

The generous grow richer and the one who waters is watered; the grain hoarder is cursed (vv. 23-26). Trust in riches falls, while the righteous flourish. The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, whoever wins souls is wise, and the wicked will surely be repaid (vv. 27-31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Honest Scales and a Rejoicing City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight (v. 1). Pride brings disgrace (v. 2). Integrity guides the upright, while the wicked fall by their own crookedness and riches cannot rescue them in the day of wrath (vv. 3-7). The righteous escape trouble and the wicked walk into it (vv. 8-9). When it goes well with the righteous, the city rejoices, and By the blessing of the upright a city is exalted (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Righteousness is public: it is measured in the marketplace and felt by a whole city.

verseByVerse.quote: A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight. When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight.

In the ancient market, goods were weighed on a balance against stones of a set weight. A dishonest trader kept two sets of stones in his bag: a heavy one for buying and a light one for selling. The law had forbidden it, You shall have just balances, just weights (Lev 19:36), and the prophets denounced merchants who were eager to make the ephah small and the shekel great and deal deceitfully with false balances (Amos 8:5).

Notice the strength of the language. God calls the rigged scale an abomination, the same word used for idolatry. And he calls an honest weight his delight. God cares about the till at the corner shop. He is pleased by an accurate invoice, an honest tax return, a fair price for a used car. Business is not a secular zone where God's standards do not apply. A just balance and scales are the LORD's (16:11).

What are the scales in your work? The timesheet, the expense claim, the product description, the grade you give a student? Each of them can be the LORD's delight.

When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom.

Pride and disgrace travel together; the second follows the first as surely as thunder follows lightning. The humble have wisdom because they are willing to learn. Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11).

verseByVerse.quote: The integrity of the upright guides them, but the crookedness of the treacherous destroys them. Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death. The righteousness of the blameless keeps his way straight, but the wicked falls by his own wickedness. The righteousness of the upright delivers them, but the treacherous are taken captive by their lust.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The integrity of the upright guides them, but the crookedness of the treacherous destroys them.

A person of integrity has a built-in guide. When a hard decision comes, he does not have to calculate what he can get away with; he already knows what he will do. His integrity decides for him. The treacherous man has no such guide, and his crookedness eventually turns on him.

Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death.

The second line is identical to 10:2. The first line names the moment when riches fail: the day of wrath. There is a day money cannot buy off. Zephaniah said, Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them on the day of the wrath of the LORD (Zeph 1:18). Many people spend their lives preparing financially for every day except that one.

The righteousness of the blameless keeps his way straight, but the wicked falls by his own wickedness. The righteousness of the upright delivers them, but the treacherous are taken captive by their lust.

Two proverbs in the same shape, making the same point: the wicked are not so much destroyed by God's thunderbolts as by their own choices. The wicked falls by his own wickedness. The treacherous are taken captive by their lust, their own cravings becoming the chains. Sin carries its own punishment inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: When the wicked dies, his hope will perish, and the expectation of wealth perishes too. The righteous is delivered from trouble, and the wicked walks into it instead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the wicked dies, his hope will perish, and the expectation of wealth perishes too.

Everything the wicked man hoped for was on this side of the grave, so at the grave it all ends. The ESV notes that wealth may also be read "his strength" or "iniquity". Whether he trusted his money, his strength or his wrongdoing, none of it goes further than the funeral. The righteous man's hope does not stop at death; that is where it is finally realised.

The righteous is delivered from trouble, and the wicked walks into it instead.

Sometimes the trouble meant for the righteous lands on the wicked. The book of Esther is a whole story built on this proverb. Haman built a gallows for Mordecai, and in the end they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai (Esth 7:10).

verseByVerse.quote: With his mouth the godless man would destroy his neighbor, but by knowledge the righteous are delivered. When it goes well with the righteous, the city rejoices, and when the wicked perish there are shouts of gladness. By the blessing of the upright a city is exalted, but by the mouth of the wicked it is overthrown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With his mouth the godless man would destroy his neighbor, but by knowledge the righteous are delivered.

The godless man's weapon is his mouth: slander, lies, rumour. Words can destroy a neighbour's reputation, marriage or career. The defence is knowledge: knowing the truth, knowing God, and being known for integrity, so that the lie does not stick.

When it goes well with the righteous, the city rejoices, and when the wicked perish there are shouts of gladness.

Here is a proverb about the public effect of character. When righteous people prosper, whole communities are better off, and people know it. When a corrupt official falls or a crime boss is jailed, the streets celebrate. A city can tell the difference, even if it could not explain why.

By the blessing of the upright a city is exalted, but by the mouth of the wicked it is overthrown.

The upright bless their city: they pay fair wages, keep their word, care for the poor, pray for their leaders. The wicked tear it down, and once again their instrument is the mouth: corruption, propaganda, lies. God told the exiles in Babylon, seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you, for in its welfare you will find your welfare (Jer 29:7). Christians are meant to be good for the places they live. Jesus called his disciples the salt of the earth (Matt 5:13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — The Neighbour, the Secret and the Kind Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The one who belittles his neighbour lacks sense; the trustworthy keep a secret (vv. 12-13). In an abundance of counselors there is safety (v. 14); do not guarantee a stranger's debt (v. 15). A man who is kind benefits himself, but a cruel man hurts himself (vv. 16-17). The wicked earn deceptive wages, and an evil person will not go unpunished (vv. 18-21). Like a gold ring in a pig's snout is a beautiful woman without discretion (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: How a person treats the people around him, in speech, trust and kindness, comes back to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever belittles his neighbor lacks sense, but a man of understanding remains silent. Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets, but he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever belittles his neighbor lacks sense, but a man of understanding remains silent.

To belittle is to make someone small: the sneer, the put-down, the joke at their expense. It feels clever. The proverb says it shows a lack of sense. The man of understanding, when he is tempted to cut someone down, keeps quiet. Do not speak evil against one another, brothers (Jas 4:11).

Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets, but he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered.

The slanderer goes about, from house to house, from group to group, passing on what he was told in confidence. The law had said, You shall not go around as a slanderer among your people (Lev 19:16). The trustworthy person is a vault. You can tell him your struggle and know it will not be at the church lunch on Sunday.

A test worth putting to yourself: if the people you have spoken about this week could hear everything you said, would they still trust you with a secret?

verseByVerse.quote: Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety. Whoever puts up security for a stranger will surely suffer harm, but he who hates striking hands in pledge is secure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety.

Nations fall, and companies, churches and families too, when decisions are made by one person who listens to no one. Safety lies in many counsellors. The wise leader surrounds himself with people who can tell him he is wrong. The same applies to personal decisions. Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed (15:22). Who are the counsellors you ask before a major decision, and do any of them disagree with you sometimes?

Whoever puts up security for a stranger will surely suffer harm, but he who hates striking hands in pledge is secure.

The warning of 6:1-5 again, compressed. Striking hands was the handshake that sealed a guarantee. To guarantee a stranger's debt is to hand your financial future to someone you do not know. The one who hates doing it is not stingy; he is wise.

verseByVerse.quote: A gracious woman gets honor, and violent men get riches. A man who is kind benefits himself, but a cruel man hurts himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A gracious woman gets honor, and violent men get riches.

The proverb sets two kinds of gain side by side. Violent, ruthless men do get rich; the book is not naive about that. But a gracious woman gets something they cannot take by force: honor. People respect her freely. The violent may have more money; she has more of what money cannot buy. And the reader is left to decide which he would rather have.

A man who is kind benefits himself, but a cruel man hurts himself.

Kindness looks like giving something away. The proverb says it comes back. The kind person has friends, peace of mind, a good name, a softer heart. The cruel person, who thinks he is winning, is damaging himself: his relationships, his conscience, his soul. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy (Matt 5:7).

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked earns deceptive wages, but one who sows righteousness gets a sure reward. Whoever is steadfast in righteousness will live, but he who pursues evil will die. Those of crooked heart are an abomination to the LORD, but those of blameless ways are his delight. Be assured, an evil person will not go unpunished, but the offspring of the righteous will be delivered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked earns deceptive wages, but one who sows righteousness gets a sure reward.

The wicked man's pay packet looks real, but his wages are deceptive. They promise more than they deliver, and they do not last. The righteous man's reward is sure. And notice the picture: he sows. Righteousness is like planting. The harvest comes later, but it comes.

Whoever is steadfast in righteousness will live, but he who pursues evil will die.

Two words matter: steadfast and pursues. The righteous man keeps going in one direction over years. The wicked man chases evil. Both are committed; both arrive.

Those of crooked heart are an abomination to the LORD, but those of blameless ways are his delight.

The same pair of words as verse 1: abomination and delight. There they described scales; here they describe hearts. God weighs the heart the way an honest trader weighs grain.

Be assured, an evil person will not go unpunished, but the offspring of the righteous will be delivered.

Be assured. God gives his word on it: evil will be punished. For the victim of injustice who has seen no justice yet, that is a comfort. For the wrongdoer who thinks he got away with it, it is a warning. He will render to each one according to his works (Rom 2:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Like a gold ring in a pig's snout is a beautiful woman without discretion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a gold ring in a pig's snout is a beautiful woman without discretion.

This is one of the most memorable pictures in the book, and it is meant to be a little shocking. A gold nose ring was a fine piece of jewellery. Put it in a pig's snout, and it is still gold, but it is wasted, rooting through the mud. Beauty without discretion, without good sense and moral judgment, is like that. The beauty is real, but it is attached to something that drags it through the dirt.

The proverb applies to men as well, and to every gift: intelligence without integrity, talent without character. Peter says the lasting beauty is the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious (1 Pet 3:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — One Who Waters Will Be Watered
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One gives freely, yet grows all the richer; another withholds what he should give, and only suffers want (v. 24). One who waters will himself be watered (v. 25), and the one who sells grain in a famine is blessed (v. 26). Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf (v. 28). The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and whoever captures souls is wise (v. 30), and the wicked will surely be repaid (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: The open hand is the wealthy one, and the greatest thing a wise person can win is another soul.

verseByVerse.quote: The desire of the righteous ends only in good, the expectation of the wicked in wrath. One gives freely, yet grows all the richer; another withholds what he should give, and only suffers want. Whoever brings blessing will be enriched, and one who waters will himself be watered. The people curse him who holds back grain, but a blessing is on the head of him who sells it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The desire of the righteous ends only in good, the expectation of the wicked in wrath.

Where do your desires end up? The righteous person's desires, because they are aimed at God and his ways, finish in good. The wicked person's expectations finish in wrath. Desire is a road, and every road ends somewhere.

One gives freely, yet grows all the richer; another withholds what he should give, and only suffers want.

Here is one of the great paradoxes of the book. By ordinary arithmetic, giving makes you poorer and keeping makes you richer. In God's economy it often runs the other way. The generous person grows all the richer, and the one who clutches what he should give suffers want. Not always in money, though often in that too, but always in joy, friendship and the favour of God.

Whoever brings blessing will be enriched, and one who waters will himself be watered.

A farmer who waters his neighbour's field in a drought finds that rain falls on his own. The picture is simple and generous. Paul put it this way: whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully (2 Cor 9:6). And Jesus: give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap (Luke 6:38). Paul reminded the Ephesian elders of the Lord's own words, It is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35).

The people curse him who holds back grain, but a blessing is on the head of him who sells it.

Now a specific case. In a famine, a merchant with a full warehouse can hold his grain back until the price rises. It is legal, and it is profitable. The people curse him, and rightly. Amos condemned those who trample on the needy (Amos 8:4). Modern forms of hoarding are not hard to find: price-gouging in a crisis, exploiting a shortage. The one who sells at a fair price when he could have squeezed people has a blessing on his head.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever diligently seeks good seeks favor, but evil comes to him who searches for it. Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever diligently seeks good seeks favor, but evil comes to him who searches for it.

People tend to find what they are looking for. The person who looks for ways to do good finds favour; the ESV notes it may be "acceptance", with God and with people. The person who goes looking for trouble, for a fight, for an opportunity to do wrong, finds it, and it finds him back.

Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf.

The key word is trusts. Having riches is not condemned; leaning on them is. A person who trusts in money will fall, because money is not strong enough to hold the weight. Jesus said, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God!, easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person (Mark 10:24-25), not because God hates wealth, but because wealth is so easy to trust.

The righteous flourish like a green leaf. A leaf is not strong, but it is alive, fed by a root the eye cannot see. The righteous are strong the same way, through the life of God flowing into them.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever troubles his own household will inherit the wind, and the fool will be servant to the wise of heart. The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and whoever captures souls is wise. If the righteous is repaid on earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever troubles his own household will inherit the wind, and the fool will be servant to the wise of heart.

A man who brings trouble into his own home, through anger, neglect, drunkenness or financial recklessness, will inherit the wind. At the end he will have nothing to hold. And the fool, who thought himself free and clever, ends up working for the wise man he despised.

The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and whoever captures souls is wise.

The righteous person's life produces fruit, and that fruit is a tree of life, the image from Eden and from 3:18. Other people are nourished and live because of what grows from his life.

And the second line: whoever captures souls is wise. To capture a soul is to win a person, to draw him to wisdom and life, and here it is the mark of the wise. Jesus called fishermen and said, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men (Matt 4:19). Those who turn many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever (Dan 12:3). The wisest investment a person can make is in another person's soul.

If the righteous is repaid on earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner!

If God disciplines and repays even his own people in this life, how much more certain is the judgment of the wicked. Peter quotes the verse in its Greek form to Christians under persecution: If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner? (1 Pet 4:18). The hardships of the righteous are a sign that God is serious about sin. That should drive every reader to the one place where sin has already been fully repaid: the cross.

11.theology:
God's standards apply in the marketplace; honest business is his delight (v. 1; Lev 19:35-36). Sin carries its own punishment (vv. 5-6), and God will certainly judge evil (v. 21; Rom 2:6).

Righteousness has public effects on a whole community (vv. 10-11; Jer 29:7). Generosity is enriched in God's economy (vv. 24-25; 2 Cor 9:6; Luke 6:38), and trust in riches fails (v. 28; Mark 10:24-25).

Winning others to wisdom is the mark of the wise (v. 30; Dan 12:3; Matt 4:19). The discipline of the righteous shows the certainty of judgment on the wicked (v. 31; 1 Pet 4:18).
11.examples:
Two sets of weights in one bag.

A timesheet or invoice that is God's delight.

Haman on his own gallows.

A city that cheers when a crook falls.

A friend who is a vault.

A gold ring in a pig's snout.

Watering a neighbour's field in a drought.

A merchant who sells grain at a fair price in a famine.

Fishers of men.

12.title: A Good Word Makes Him Glad
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid.<sup>2</sup>A good man obtains favor from the LORD, but a man of evil devices he
