astray.<sup>27</sup>Whoever is slothful will not roast his game, but the diligent man will get precious wealth.<sup>28</sup>In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death.
12.overview:
Loving discipline is loving knowledge. The righteous have a root that cannot be moved; an excellent wife is her husband's crown. The house of the righteous stands. Better to live modestly with bread than to pose and go hungry. The righteous care even for their animals, and diligent work brings bread (vv. 1-12).

The wicked are trapped by their own words, while good words and work come back to a man. The fool is right in his own eyes; the prudent ignore insults. Rash words wound like swords but the tongue of the wise heals. Truth lasts; lies are momentary and an abomination to the LORD (vv. 13-23).

The diligent rule. Anxiety weighs down the heart, but a good word makes it glad. The righteous guide their neighbours, the slothful do not finish what they start, and on the path of righteousness there is life and no death (vv. 24-28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Root of the Righteous
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge (v. 1). The LORD favours the good; the root of the righteous will never be moved (vv. 2-3). An excellent wife is the crown of her husband (v. 4). The thoughts, words and houses of the righteous stand, while the wicked are overthrown (vv. 5-8). Better to be humble and provided for than to pose and go hungry (v. 9); Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his beast (v. 10); the diligent farmer has bread, and the root of the righteous bears fruit (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Stability grows from what cannot be seen: a teachable heart, a good marriage, honest work and a root in God.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid. A good man obtains favor from the LORD, but a man of evil devices he condemns. No one is established by wickedness, but the root of the righteous will never be moved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid.

Proverbs does not often use a word as blunt as stupid. The word suggests something brutish, like an animal that cannot be taught. The point is simple. Nobody gains knowledge without being corrected, because learning means finding out you were wrong. So a person who loves knowledge must also love the discipline that brings it. A person who hates being corrected has shut the only door to learning, and that is not a small failing; it is a kind of stupidity.

Few people love correction naturally. But it is possible to learn to love it, by watching what it produces.

A good man obtains favor from the LORD, but a man of evil devices he condemns.

The LORD is not neutral about character. The good man obtains favor; the schemer is condemned. God looks past a person's success to his heart and his plans.

No one is established by wickedness, but the root of the righteous will never be moved.

Wickedness can build something that looks solid, but it has no foundation. The righteous have a root, and a root is what holds a tree when the wind comes. The picture is of the man in Psalm 1: like a tree planted by streams of water, whose leaf does not wither (Ps 1:3). The root is out of sight. What keeps a believer standing in a storm is what was growing in secret before it came.

verseByVerse.quote: An excellent wife is the crown of her husband, but she who brings shame is like rottenness in his bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An excellent wife is the crown of her husband, but she who brings shame is like rottenness in his bones.

A wife of strength and character is her husband's crown, the thing that honours him most in the eyes of others. The phrase An excellent wife is the same one that opens the great poem at the end of the book: An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels (31:10).

And the other side is painful: a wife who brings shame is like rottenness in his bones, a decay no one outside may see, eating away at his strength from inside. The proverb is honest that a marriage can be the greatest blessing or the deepest wound in a life.

Husbands should read it and ask whether they honour their wives as the crown they are. And the principle runs both ways. Every spouse is either a crown or a slow decay to the other, and most are some of each on different days. Which will you be this week?

verseByVerse.quote: The thoughts of the righteous are just; the counsels of the wicked are deceitful. The words of the wicked lie in wait for blood, but the mouth of the upright delivers them. The wicked are overthrown and are no more, but the house of the righteous will stand. A man is commended according to his good sense, but one of twisted mind is despised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The thoughts of the righteous are just; the counsels of the wicked are deceitful.

Before anyone acts, he thinks. The righteous person's thoughts are already bent toward what is fair. The wicked person's counsels, his plans and advice, are already deceitful before a word is spoken. Character is formed in the mind long before it shows in the hands.

The words of the wicked lie in wait for blood, but the mouth of the upright delivers them.

Words can ambush. A false accusation, a lie in court, a rumour that ruins someone: the wicked use words like an ambush from chapter 1. The upright use their mouths to rescue, both themselves and others. The same organ can be a weapon or a lifeline.

The wicked are overthrown and are no more, but the house of the righteous will stand.

A house in Proverbs is a family and its future as well as a building. The wicked may seem powerful, but they are overthrown and are no more. The house of the righteous stands, often for generations.

A man is commended according to his good sense, but one of twisted mind is despised.

In the long run, people recognise sense when they see it, and they recognise a twisted mind too. Reputation is not always fair in the short term, but over years it tends to settle on what a person actually is.

verseByVerse.quote: Better to be lowly and have a servant than to play the great man and lack bread. Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his beast, but the mercy of the wicked is cruel. Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits lacks sense. Whoever is wicked covets the spoil of evildoers, but the root of the righteous bears fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Better to be lowly and have a servant than to play the great man and lack bread.

This is one of the book's many "better than" proverbs, and it is sharply relevant. One man lives modestly and is well provided for. Another plays the great man, spends to look important, and has nothing to eat. The car on finance, the house beyond the budget, the credit card paying for the image. The proverb says: better to be thought ordinary and have bread on the table.

Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his beast, but the mercy of the wicked is cruel.

A righteous person's goodness reaches all the way down to his animals. He has regard for the life of his ox or donkey: he feeds it, rests it, does not beat it. The law said, You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain (Deut 25:4). God himself ended the book of Jonah by asking whether he should not pity Nineveh, and also much cattle (Jonah 4:11).

How a person treats creatures that cannot repay him or complain reveals his heart. And the wicked? Even their mercy is cruel. Their best kindness still has an edge of contempt in it.

Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits lacks sense.

The farmer who works the field in front of him eats. The man who chases worthless pursuits, get-rich schemes, fantasies, endless distractions, lacks sense. Many people neglect the ordinary work that would feed them because they are chasing something more exciting.

Whoever is wicked covets the spoil of evildoers, but the root of the righteous bears fruit.

The wicked man looks at what other crooks have stolen and wants it. The righteous man does not need to steal; his root bears fruit. The picture from verse 3 returns. The righteous man's provision grows from the inside, from what God has planted, while the wicked man's comes from grabbing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The evil man is caught by his own lips, but a man's words come back to him in good (vv. 13-14). The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but a wise man listens to advice, and the prudent ignores an insult (vv. 15-16). There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing. Truthful lips endure forever (vv. 17-19). Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD (vv. 20-22), and A prudent man conceals knowledge (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Words can cut or heal, and truth outlasts every lie.

verseByVerse.quote: An evil man is ensnared by the transgression of his lips, but the righteous escapes from trouble. From the fruit of his mouth a man is satisfied with good, and the work of a man's hand comes back to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An evil man is ensnared by the transgression of his lips, but the righteous escapes from trouble.

The ESV notes that the line may also be read, "In the transgression of the lips, there is an evil snare". Either way, the snare is made of his own words. The lie that needs another lie. The boast that gets checked. The angry email that gets forwarded. The righteous man escapes because he said nothing that needs escaping from.

From the fruit of his mouth a man is satisfied with good, and the work of a man's hand comes back to him.

Words and work both come back. A man's words are like seeds, and he eats what grows from them: kind words bring kindness back, harsh ones bring conflict. And the work of his hands comes back to him. What you give out in speech and effort is, largely, what you will live on.

verseByVerse.quote: The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but a wise man listens to advice. The vexation of a fool is known at once, but the prudent ignores an insult.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but a wise man listens to advice.

The fool's problem is that he is sure. Everything he does looks right to him. The book of Judges ends with a whole nation in that condition: Everyone did what was right in his own eyes (Judg 21:25), and the result was chaos. There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death (14:12).

The wise man is not the one who is always right. He is the one who listens to advice, who assumes he might be missing something. Before a big decision, who have you asked who might tell you no?

The vexation of a fool is known at once, but the prudent ignores an insult.

The fool's irritation is on his face and in his voice immediately. He cannot let anything pass. The prudent man ignores an insult. He is not a doormat; he simply does not need to answer every slight. There is great strength in that. The supreme example is Christ: When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Pet 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever speaks the truth gives honest evidence, but a false witness utters deceit. There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing. Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever speaks the truth gives honest evidence, but a false witness utters deceit.

The setting is a courtroom, but the principle reaches further. A person who is truthful in everyday speech will be an honest witness when it matters. The ESV notes that speaks is literally "breathes out": truth or lies come out of a person as naturally as breath, because they are what is inside.

There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing.

Few proverbs are more true to experience. Rash words, spoken without thinking, go in like a blade. Many people carry scars from a sentence said to them decades ago by a parent, a teacher or a spouse, a sentence the speaker has probably forgotten. James says, no human being can tame the tongue, and From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so (Jas 3:8, 10).

But the same tongue can heal. The tongue of the wise brings healing. A word of apology, of encouragement, of blessing, can reach a wound that nothing else touches. If you have wounded someone with words, the healing will very likely also have to come through words.

Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment.

Every lie has a short shelf life. It works for a moment, and then it has to be maintained, defended and eventually exposed. The truth does not need maintaining; it simply stays true. Behind every truthful word stands the God whose faithfulness endures forever (Ps 117:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Deceit is in the heart of those who devise evil, but those who plan peace have joy. No ill befalls the righteous, but the wicked are filled with trouble. Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who act faithfully are his delight. A prudent man conceals knowledge, but the heart of fools proclaims folly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deceit is in the heart of those who devise evil, but those who plan peace have joy.

Both the schemer and the peacemaker are making plans. One carries deceit in his heart as he plans, and there is no joy in that. The other plans peace, and joy comes with it. Planning a reconciliation, a kindness, a way to heal a rift, fills the heart in a way plotting never does.

No ill befalls the righteous, but the wicked are filled with trouble.

Read on its own, this seems plainly untrue. Righteous people get cancer, lose children and are persecuted. But the proverb is saying something deeper. Nothing that befalls the righteous is finally ill for them, because God turns it to good. For those who love God all things work together for good (Rom 8:28). The same event can be a disaster to a wicked man and a refining to a righteous one.

Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who act faithfully are his delight.

Abomination and delight again, the pair from 11:1 and 11:20. God hates lying because he is the God of truth, and lying is the native language of the enemy. Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self (Col 3:9). Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor, for we are members one of another (Eph 4:25).

That includes the small lies: the excuse for being late, the exaggerated story, the "I'm fine". God delights in those who act faithfully, people whose words and deeds can be relied upon.

A prudent man conceals knowledge, but the heart of fools proclaims folly.

The prudent man does not have to show everything he knows. He waits for the right moment, keeps confidences, and does not need to win every conversation. The fool announces whatever is in his head, and what is in his head is folly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–28 — The Path Where There Is No Death
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The diligent will rule and the lazy will serve (v. 24). Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad (v. 25). The righteous guides his neighbour, and the slothful will not even cook what he has caught (vv. 26-27). In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter moves from a weighed-down heart to a path on which death itself does not have the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: The hand of the diligent will rule, while the slothful will be put to forced labor. Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hand of the diligent will rule, while the slothful will be put to forced labor.

The irony is sharp. The lazy man avoids work to stay free, and ends up doing forced labor under someone else. The diligent man takes on work willingly, and ends up leading. Avoiding effort does not avoid work; it only decides who will be giving the orders.

Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad.

This is one of the most tender proverbs in the book. Anxiety is a weight. It sits on the heart and presses it down, and anyone who has lived with it knows how physical that feels. The proverb does not tell the anxious man to try harder or pull himself together. It says that a good word lifts him.

That has two applications. First, for the anxious: God has spoken a good word to you. Peter tells believers to humble themselves under God's hand, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (1 Pet 5:7). The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus (Phil 4:7).

Second, for everyone else: you can be the good word. Somebody you will see today is carrying a weight you cannot see. A sentence of encouragement from you may be exactly what lifts it. Think of one person and say it.

verseByVerse.quote: One who is righteous is a guide to his neighbor, but the way of the wicked leads them astray. Whoever is slothful will not roast his game, but the diligent man will get precious wealth. In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One who is righteous is a guide to his neighbor, but the way of the wicked leads them astray.

The righteous person shows others the way, simply by walking it. The ESV notes that the first line may be read, "The righteous chooses his friends carefully". Both readings belong together: the righteous choose friends wisely and help them, while the wicked lead their companions off the road. Do not be deceived: "Bad company ruins good morals" (1 Cor 15:33).

Whoever is slothful will not roast his game, but the diligent man will get precious wealth.

Another comic picture. The lazy man goes hunting, catches something, and then cannot be bothered to cook it. The effort is wasted at the last step. Unfinished degrees, half-built projects, good intentions never followed through: the sluggard is often not lazy about starting, only about finishing. The ESV notes that the second line may mean, "but diligence is precious wealth". The habit of finishing is itself a treasure.

In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death.

The chapter ends on one of the most hopeful lines in the book. On the path of righteousness there is life, and no death. The Old Testament does not often speak so directly about what lies beyond the grave, but this proverb reaches toward it. Death is not the end of the righteous man's path.

Jesus made the promise explicit: if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death (John 8:51). And at the tomb of Lazarus, I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this? (John 11:25-26). The path of righteousness leads through him, and on that path death has lost its sting.

12.theology:
Stability comes from being rooted in God (vv. 3, 12; Ps 1:3). Teachability is essential to wisdom (vv. 1, 15). Righteousness extends even to care for animals (v. 10; Deut 25:4; Jonah 4:11).

Speech wounds or heals (v. 18; Jas 3:8-10); God hates lies and delights in faithfulness (v. 22; Eph 4:25). The prudent absorb insults, as Christ did (v. 16; 1 Pet 2:23). Nothing is finally ill for the righteous (v. 21; Rom 8:28).

A good word lifts anxiety (v. 25; 1 Pet 5:7). The path of righteousness leads beyond death (v. 28; John 11:25-26).
12.examples:
A root that holds in the storm.

A crown or rottenness in the bones.

The car on finance and no bread.

Care for an animal that cannot repay.

A sentence that left a scar for decades.

The short shelf life of a lie.

One good word to someone carrying a weight.

The hunter who will not cook his game.

13.title: Hope Deferred Makes the Heart Sick
13.text: <sup>1</sup>A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke.<sup>2</sup>From the fruit of his mouth a man eats what is good, but the desire of the treacherous is for violence.<sup>3</sup>Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life; he who opens wide his lips comes to ruin.<sup>4</sup>The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is richly supplied.<sup>5</sup>The righteous hates falsehood, but the wicked brings shame and disgrace.<sup>6</sup>Righteousness guards him whose way is blameless, but sin overthrows the wicked.<sup>7</sup>One pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth.<sup>8</sup>The ransom of a man's life is his wealth, but a poor man hears no threat.<sup>9</sup>The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked will be put out.<sup>10</sup>By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom.<sup>11</sup>Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it.<sup>12</sup>Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life.<sup>13</sup>Whoever despises the word brings destruction on himself, but he who reveres the commandment will be rewarded.<sup>14</sup>The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.<sup>15</sup>Good sense wins favor, but the way of the treacherous is their ruin.<sup>16</sup>Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool flaunts his folly.<sup>17</sup>A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing.<sup>18</sup>Poverty and disgrace come to him who ignores instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is honored.<sup>19</sup>A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but to turn away from evil is an abomination to fools.<sup>20</sup>Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm.<sup>21</sup>Disaster pursues sinners, but the righteous are rewarded with good.<sup>22</sup>A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous.<sup>23</sup>The fallow ground of the poor would yield much food, but it is swept away through injustice.<sup>24</sup>Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him.<sup>25</sup>The righteous has enough to satisfy his appetite, but the belly of the wicked suffers want.
13.overview:
A wise son listens to his father. Guarding the mouth preserves life; the sluggard craves and gets nothing. Appearances of wealth deceive, wealth attracts threats, pride produces only strife, and hasty wealth dwindles while wealth gathered little by little grows (vv. 1-11).

Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life. Reverence for the word is rewarded; the teaching of the wise is a fountain of life; a faithful envoy brings healing; heeding reproof brings honour (vv. 12-19).

Walking with the wise makes a person wise, and the companion of fools suffers harm. A good man leaves an inheritance to his grandchildren; injustice sweeps away the harvest of the poor. The parent who loves his son disciplines him, and the righteous have enough (vv. 20-25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Guarded Mouth and the Honest Purse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A wise son hears his father's instruction (v. 1). Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life (vv. 2-3). The sluggard craves and gets nothing (v. 4); righteousness guards the blameless (vv. 5-6). Some pretend to be rich and have nothing, others the reverse (v. 7); wealth attracts threats (v. 8). The light of the righteous rejoices (v. 9); insolence breeds strife (v. 10). Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Mouth and money are both kept by restraint and patience, and both are ruined by haste.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke. From the fruit of his mouth a man eats what is good, but the desire of the treacherous is for violence. Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life; he who opens wide his lips comes to ruin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke.

The chapter opens where the book began: with a son and a father. The wise son hears. The scoffer does not even listen. He has made up his mind in advance that nothing his father says is worth his attention. Rebuke bounces off him because he has already dismissed the speaker.

From the fruit of his mouth a man eats what is good, but the desire of the treacherous is for violence.

A good man's words produce fruit he himself gets to eat: friendships, trust, peace. The treacherous man's appetite is for something else, violence, and that is what he feeds on.

Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life; he who opens wide his lips comes to ruin.

The picture of opens wide his lips is of a mouth with no gate at all. Whatever comes into his head comes out. The man who guards his mouth has a gatekeeper. A single unguarded sentence has ended careers, friendships and marriages. James goes further: If anyone thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his heart, this person's religion is worthless (Jas 1:26).

verseByVerse.quote: The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is richly supplied. The righteous hates falsehood, but the wicked brings shame and disgrace. Righteousness guards him whose way is blameless, but sin overthrows the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is richly supplied.

The sluggard is not a man without desires. He craves, often intensely. He wants the house, the qualifications, the fit body, the good marriage. He simply does not do what gets them. So he lives with constant wanting and nothing to show for it. Laziness does not kill desire; it only guarantees frustration.

The righteous hates falsehood, but the wicked brings shame and disgrace.

The righteous person does not merely avoid lies; he hates them, in himself and in others. The ESV notes that brings shame may be rendered "stench". The wicked man's life gives off a bad smell, and the people around him notice.

Righteousness guards him whose way is blameless, but sin overthrows the wicked.

Righteousness is pictured as a bodyguard, and sin as an enemy that knocks a man flat. A blameless life does not make a person invulnerable, but it removes a great many dangers that sin would have brought with it.

verseByVerse.quote: One pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth. The ransom of a man's life is his wealth, but a poor man hears no threat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth.

Appearances deceive both ways. One man drives the expensive car and is drowning in debt. Another lives quietly and has saved for decades. The ESV notes the lines may be read, "One makes himself rich", "another makes himself poor". Wealth is not always where it looks.

The deepest form of the proverb is spiritual. The church at Laodicea said, I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing, not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked (Rev 3:17). And Paul described the apostles as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything (2 Cor 6:10). Which is rich in the way that matters?

The ransom of a man's life is his wealth, but a poor man hears no threat.

Wealth is a mixed blessing. It can pay a ransom when a rich man is kidnapped or sued. But it is also why he is a target. The poor man hears no threat; nobody bothers to rob a man with nothing. There is a kind of freedom in having little that the rich never know.

verseByVerse.quote: The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked will be put out. By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom. Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked will be put out.

A righteous life is like a bright light that seems to shine gladly. The wicked man has a lamp, a smaller thing, and it will be put out. In the ancient world a lamp burning in a house meant the family was alive and present; a lamp going out meant the house was empty. The light of the wicked is put out, and the flame of his fire does not shine (Job 18:5).

By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom.

Nothing but strife. Pride produces only one crop. The proud person will not take advice, will not back down, will not admit fault, so every disagreement becomes a war. James asks, What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? (Jas 4:1). Where there is constant conflict, look for pride first, and look for it in the mirror.

Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it.

The ESV notes that hastily may be "by fraud". Quick money, whether from a scam, a gamble, an inheritance squandered or a get-rich-quick scheme, tends to disappear as fast as it came. But whoever gathers little by little will increase it, through honest work and patient saving. Whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished (28:20).

The same principle holds far beyond money. Character, knowledge, a marriage, a knowledge of Scripture: they are built little by little, and the person who wants them instantly rarely gets them at all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life (v. 12). Reverence for the word is rewarded, and The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life (vv. 13-14). Good sense wins favour, the prudent act with knowledge, and a faithful envoy brings healing (vv. 15-17). The one who heeds reproof is honoured, and A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The heart can sicken while it waits, and God's word is what keeps it alive until the desire is met.

verseByVerse.quote: Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life.

This is one of the most honest sentences in the Bible about what waiting does to a person. Hope deferred, hope postponed and postponed again, makes the heart sick. The infertile couple who hoped each month. The single person who hoped for marriage year after year. The parent praying for a child who has walked away. The job application, the medical result, the reconciliation that does not come. The heart grows sick. The proverb does not tell such a person to feel differently. It simply says: this is what happens, and God knows it.

The disciples on the road to Emmaus spoke with sick hearts: But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel (Luke 24:21). The psalmist talked to his own heart in the same condition: Why are you cast down, O my soul, Hope in God; for I shall again praise him (Ps 42:5).

And then the second line: a desire fulfilled is a tree of life. When hope finally comes true, it is like the tree of Eden, life-giving and full. The Christian's hope is sometimes deferred for a whole lifetime. The saints of Hebrews 11 all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar (Heb 11:13). But the tree of life stands at the end of the Bible, beside the river, and no hope placed in Christ will be disappointed there. If we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience (Rom 8:25).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever despises the word brings destruction on himself, but he who reveres the commandment will be rewarded. The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever despises the word brings destruction on himself, but he who reveres the commandment will be rewarded.

The ESV notes that this may be "a word" and "a commandment", any piece of good instruction. But in the whole Bible the supreme word is God's. The one who despises it destroys himself. God says, this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word (Isa 66:2).

The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.

Wise teaching is a fountain, and its purpose is practical: to help a person turn away from the snares of death. Good teaching shows where the traps are before you step in them. Think of the teachers, parents or pastors whose words kept you out of a snare you did not even see at the time.

verseByVerse.quote: Good sense wins favor, but the way of the treacherous is their ruin. Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool flaunts his folly. A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good sense wins favor, but the way of the treacherous is their ruin.

People are drawn to good sense; they trust it and like being around it. The ESV notes that the second line is a probable reading, and that the Hebrew says the way of the treacherous "is rugged" or "is an enduring rut". Either picture works: a rocky road, or a rut worn so deep a person cannot climb out.

Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool flaunts his folly.

The prudent man thinks before he acts. The fool flaunts his folly, spreading it out for display like a merchant with his goods. He does not hide his foolishness; he is proud of it.

A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing.

A messenger who distorts his message causes disaster. A faithful envoy brings healing, because he delivers the message as it was given. Paul described the ministry of the gospel this way: we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God (2 Cor 5:20). Every Christian who speaks of Christ is an envoy, and the healing comes when the message is told faithfully, without additions or subtractions.

verseByVerse.quote: Poverty and disgrace come to him who ignores instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is honored. A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but to turn away from evil is an abomination to fools.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Poverty and disgrace come to him who ignores instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is honored.

Ignoring instruction has a cost that shows up in two places: the bank account and the reputation. Heeding reproof leads to honour. The irony is that accepting correction feels humiliating at the time, and refusing it feels dignified. In the long run it is the other way round.

A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but to turn away from evil is an abomination to fools.

The first line echoes verse 12. The second explains why fools never taste that sweetness. They want the fulfilment, but they will not turn away from the evil that blocks it. The fool wants the good life and hates the very idea of giving up what ruins it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm (v. 20). Disaster pursues sinners (v. 21). A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children (v. 22), though injustice sweeps away the poor man's harvest (v. 23). Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him (v. 24). The righteous have enough (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: A life is shaped by the company it keeps, and it shapes the generations that come after it.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm. Disaster pursues sinners, but the righteous are rewarded with good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm.

This proverb may be the single most practical piece of advice a young person can be given. People become like the people they spend time with. Not immediately, but surely. Walk with the wise and you absorb their habits, their way of thinking, their instincts. Walk with fools and you will not merely be influenced; you will suffer harm, because fools bring their consequences on everyone near them.

Psalm 1 opens by describing the slide: Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers (Ps 1:1). Walking, standing, sitting.

A test worth running: list the five people you spend most time with. Are they making you wiser? And a question for parents: do you know who your children walk with?

Disaster pursues sinners, but the righteous are rewarded with good.

The ESV notes that Disaster may be "Evil". The picture is of something chasing a man. The sinner may outrun his consequences for a while, but they follow him. Moses warned, be sure your sin will find you out (Num 32:23).

verseByVerse.quote: A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous. The fallow ground of the poor would yield much food, but it is swept away through injustice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous.

A good man thinks two generations ahead. He leaves an inheritance to his grandchildren. That can be money, and planning well for a family's future is a godly thing to do. But the best inheritance is not financial: a name, a faith, a pattern of prayer and honesty that grandchildren remember. Timothy inherited a faith that dwelt first in his grandmother (2 Tim 1:5).

The sinner, meanwhile, is storing up wealth that will pass out of his hands, often to the very people he despised. What will your grandchildren inherit from you that cannot be spent?

The fallow ground of the poor would yield much food, but it is swept away through injustice.

Here is a proverb that refuses to blame all poverty on laziness. The poor man's field would yield much food. He has the land and he has worked it. But injustice sweeps his harvest away: unjust taxes, stolen land, corrupt officials, withheld wages. The book that praises diligence is honest that diligence is not always enough in a crooked world. James thunders against rich men whose laborers' wages were kept back by fraud and are crying out against you (Jas 5:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him. The righteous has enough to satisfy his appetite, but the belly of the wicked suffers want.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him.

This proverb is famous and often misunderstood, in both directions. It must be read carefully.

First, the point is love. The parent who never disciplines a child is not being kind; the proverb says he hates his son, because he is leaving him to grow up without the correction he needs. A child who is never told no, never faces consequences, never learns that his actions matter, is being set up for a painful life. The loving parent is diligent to discipline him, and the ESV notes that it may be read, "disciplines him early", before patterns harden.

Second, the rod stands for discipline as a whole: correction, consequences, and in the ancient world physical correction too. Whatever form discipline takes, the Bible never licenses cruelty, rage or abuse. The same Scriptures that say discipline your children also say, Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger (Eph 6:4), and Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged (Col 3:21). Discipline given in anger serves the parent. Discipline given in love serves the child.

And behind every parent stands the Father who disciplines his children: God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? (Heb 12:7).

The righteous has enough to satisfy his appetite, but the belly of the wicked suffers want.

The chapter ends on enough. The righteous man does not necessarily have a feast, but he has enough to be satisfied. That is a gift. Paul had learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content (Phil 4:11). The wicked man's belly suffers want, sometimes because he is poor, and often because nothing is ever enough for him.

13.theology:
Restraint in speech and patience with money are marks of wisdom (vv. 3, 11). True wealth and poverty are not always as they appear (v. 7; 2 Cor 6:10; Rev 3:17).

God knows the sickness of deferred hope, and the believer's hope, though sometimes deferred for a lifetime, ends at the tree of life (v. 12; Heb 11:13; Rom 8:25). God's word is to be revered (v. 13; Isa 66:2), and gospel messengers bring healing by faithfulness (v. 17; 2 Cor 5:20).

Companions shape character (v. 20; Ps 1:1). Poverty can be caused by injustice as well as laziness (v. 23; Jas 5:4). Loving discipline is essential to parenting, and never licenses harshness (v. 24; Eph 6:4; Heb 12:7).
13.examples:
A mouth with no gatekeeper.

The expensive car and the quiet saver.

Wealth that makes a man a target.

The monthly hope of an infertile couple.

"We had hoped" on the Emmaus road.

Listing the five people you spend most time with.

An inheritance grandchildren cannot spend.

A worked field swept away by injustice.

Discipline in love, not in anger.

Those who devise good meet steadfast love and faithfulness.<sup>23</sup>In all toil there is profit, but mere talk tends only to poverty.<sup>24</sup>The crown of the wise is their wealth, but the folly of fools brings folly.<sup>25</sup>A truthful witness saves lives, but one who breathes out lies is deceitful.<sup>26</sup>In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge.<sup>27</sup>The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.<sup>28</sup>In a multitude of people is the glory of a king, but without people a prince is ruined.<sup>29</sup>Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly.<sup>30</sup>A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot.<sup>31</sup>Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him.<sup>32</sup>The wicked is overthrown through his evildoing, but the righteous finds refuge in his death.<sup>33</sup>Wisdom rests in the heart of a man of understanding, but it makes itself known even in the midst of fools.<sup>34</sup>Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people.<sup>35</sup>A servant who deals wisely has the king's favor, but his wrath falls on one who acts shamefully.
14.overview:
A wise woman builds her house and folly tears it down. Fruitful work is messy, like a manger with oxen. The heart knows its own bitterness and joy; a way that seems right may end in death; laughter may hide an ache; each person is filled with the fruit of his ways (vv. 1-14).

The simple believe everything, while the prudent think carefully. The poor are disliked and the rich have many friends, but despising a neighbour is sin and generosity to the poor is blessed. Work profits; mere talk leads to poverty (vv. 15-24).

The fear of the LORD gives confidence and a refuge for one's children, and is a fountain of life. Slowness to anger shows understanding; envy rots the bones. Oppressing the poor insults their Maker. The righteous find refuge in death, and righteousness exalts a nation (vv. 25-35).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — Houses Built and Torn Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wisest of women builds her house, but folly with her own hands tears it down (v. 1). Uprightness shows the fear of the LORD, and the fool's own mouth brings the rod (vv. 2-3). Where there are no oxen, the manger is clean, but abundant crops come by the strength of the ox (v. 4). Leave the presence of a fool (vv. 5-9). The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy (v. 10). There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death (vv. 11-12); laughter can hide an aching heart, and every man is filled with the fruit of his ways (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Homes and lives are built or torn down by choices made from the inside, often out of sight of everyone else.

verseByVerse.quote: The wisest of women builds her house, but folly with her own hands tears it down. Whoever walks in uprightness fears the LORD, but he who is devious in his ways despises him. By the mouth of a fool comes a rod for his back, but the lips of the wise will preserve them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wisest of women builds her house, but folly with her own hands tears it down.

Chapter 9 said, Wisdom has built her house (9:1). Here a real woman does the same. A house in Proverbs means a household: a family, its atmosphere, its future. A wise woman builds it, day after day, through countless small acts of care, patience, prayer and good sense.

And folly tears it down with her own hands. No enemy is needed. Bitterness, a sharp tongue, contempt, neglect, the refusal to forgive: a person can dismantle her own home brick by brick without ever intending to. The proverb applies equally to husbands. Every day in a home, each person is either adding a brick or pulling one out.

Whoever walks in uprightness fears the LORD, but he who is devious in his ways despises him.

How can anyone tell whether a person fears God? By how he walks. Uprightness is the visible evidence of reverence. And the devious man, whatever he says in church, despises God. Crooked conduct is a statement about what someone thinks of the God who sees it.

By the mouth of a fool comes a rod for his back, but the lips of the wise will preserve them.

The fool's mouth makes the stick he will be beaten with. The ESV notes the line may read, "In the mouth of a fool is a rod of pride": his proud speech is itself the rod. Either way, his words turn on him, while the wise are protected by theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: Where there are no oxen, the manger is clean, but abundant crops come by the strength of the ox.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where there are no oxen, the manger is clean, but abundant crops come by the strength of the ox.

A farmer who wants a spotless barn can have one: get rid of the oxen. No animals, no mess, no feeding, no mucking out. But also no ploughing, and no harvest. Abundant crops come by the strength of the ox, and oxen come with a dirty manger.

This is a wonderfully practical proverb. Anything fruitful is messy. Children bring noise, broken things and sleepless nights. A church full of new believers brings problems a tidy, empty church never has. A growing business has complications a failing one does not. A person who wants a life with no mess must accept a life with no harvest.

Is there a mess in your life you resent, which is really the manger of something God is using to feed you and others?

verseByVerse.quote: A faithful witness does not lie, but a false witness breathes out lies. A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding. Leave the presence of a fool, for there you do not meet words of knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A faithful witness does not lie, but a false witness breathes out lies.

The honest witness does not lie; that is almost a definition. The false witness breathes out lies: they come as easily as breath because falsehood has become his nature.

A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding.

Here is a surprising proverb. The scoffer does seek wisdom, and does not find it. Why? Because he seeks it while mocking the very things that would teach him. He wants the benefits of wisdom without bowing to its source. For the man of understanding, who has begun with the fear of the LORD, knowledge comes easily, because he is humble enough to receive it.

Leave the presence of a fool, for there you do not meet words of knowledge.

Sometimes the wise thing is simply to leave. Some conversations produce nothing but folly, and staying in them only lets it rub off. There is no obligation to keep listening to a man who has nothing true to say.

verseByVerse.quote: The wisdom of the prudent is to discern his way, but the folly of fools is deceiving. Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wisdom of the prudent is to discern his way, but the folly of fools is deceiving.

The prudent man's wisdom is practical: he knows where he is going and why. The fool's folly is deceiving, and chiefly it deceives the fool himself. He does not merely lie to others; he believes his own story about where his road leads.

Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance.

The guilt offering was the sacrifice by which an Israelite acknowledged wrongdoing and made it right. Fools find the whole idea laughable. Guilt? Repentance? Making amends? They mock. The ESV notes that the second line is literally "but among the upright is acceptance": among people who take guilt seriously, there is reconciliation, with God and with each other.

Modern people mock guilt in their own ways, calling it repression or old-fashioned religion. But the person who cannot take his own guilt seriously can never know the joy of having it taken away. The whole Old Testament sacrificial system pointed to the final guilt offering, Christ himself.

verseByVerse.quote: The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy.

This is one of the loneliest and truest sentences in the Bible. Every human heart has depths no one else can reach. Your grief, no one else feels exactly as you feel it. Your joy, no one else can fully share. Friends can sit with you, and should, weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15). But there is a place inside each person where he is alone. Who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? (1 Cor 2:11).

That truth cuts two ways. It should make us slow to say "I know exactly how you feel" to a grieving person. We do not.

And it points to the one who does. The LORD looks on the heart (1 Sam 16:7). There is no bitterness so private that God does not see it, and no joy so personal that he does not share it. And Christ, who took on a human heart, is a high priest who is not unable to sympathize with our weaknesses (Heb 4:15). The place where no stranger can come is exactly where he comes.

verseByVerse.quote: The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish. There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish.

Notice the buildings. The wicked have a house, solid and impressive. The upright have a tent, flimsy and temporary. And yet the house is destroyed and the tent flourishes. What lasts is not determined by how strong it looks, but by who lives in it and whom they serve.

There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death.

This proverb appears twice in the book, word for word (here and at 16:25), and it deserves the repetition. It is one of the most important warnings anyone can hear. The road that leads to death does not look like it. It seems right. It feels reasonable, even good. Nobody walks toward destruction thinking, "This is the road to death." They think, "This is my road, and it is fine."

The ESV notes that the Hebrew says "ways of death", plural. There are many such roads: the respectable career that pushes God to the edge, the religion of good deeds that never needs a Saviour, the relationship everyone says is fine. Jesus said, what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God (Luke 16:15).

This is why feelings cannot be the final judge of a way. "It feels right" is exactly what the proverb says about the road to death. The only safe test of a road is God's word, not how it seems.

verseByVerse.quote: Even in laughter the heart may ache, and the end of joy may be grief. The backslider in heart will be filled with the fruit of his ways, and a good man will be filled with the fruit of his ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even in laughter the heart may ache, and the end of joy may be grief.

Behind many laughing faces is an aching heart. The life of the party may be the loneliest person in the room. The proverb is a call to look past appearances, and to be gentle. It is also honest about life in a fallen world: every earthly joy has an end, and many end in grief. Every wedding will one day have a funeral.

That is why the Christian hope matters so much. Jesus said, Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted (Matt 5:4). The proverb says earthly joy may end in grief. The gospel promises that for believers, grief ends in joy.

The backslider in heart will be filled with the fruit of his ways, and a good man will be filled with the fruit of his ways.

Both men are filled, and both are filled with the fruit of his ways. The same phrase for both. The backslider in heart, the person who has turned away inwardly, gets exactly what his way produces. So does the good man. Everyone eats what he grows.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — The Simple, the Prudent and the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The simple believes everything, but the prudent gives thought to his steps (v. 15). The wise are cautious and the quick-tempered act foolishly (vv. 16-18). The evil will bow before the good (v. 19). The poor is disliked even by his neighbor, but the rich has many friends, yet blessed is he who is generous to the poor (vv. 20-21). Those who plan good meet steadfast love; In all toil there is profit, but mere talk tends only to poverty (vv. 22-24).
verseByVerse.theology: The prudent person tests what he hears, does not follow the crowd in despising the poor, and works rather than talks.

verseByVerse.quote: The simple believes everything, but the prudent gives thought to his steps. One who is wise is cautious and turns away from evil, but a fool is reckless and careless. A man of quick temper acts foolishly, and a man of evil devices is hated. The simple inherit folly, but the prudent are crowned with knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The simple believes everything, but the prudent gives thought to his steps.

If any proverb speaks directly to an age of internet rumour and viral misinformation, it is this one. The simple believes everything: every forwarded message, every health scare, every conspiracy, every flattering salesman. The prudent person gives thought. He checks, weighs, waits.

The same applies to spiritual claims. Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God (1 John 4:1). The Bereans were praised because they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so (Acts 17:11). They even tested what an apostle told them. Christians should be the least gullible people in the world.

One who is wise is cautious and turns away from evil, but a fool is reckless and careless.

The ESV notes that is cautious may be "fears", meaning fears the LORD. The wise man is careful because he takes God and consequences seriously. The fool is reckless and careless, and often proud of it, calling his recklessness courage.

A man of quick temper acts foolishly, and a man of evil devices is hated.

Two kinds of trouble-maker: the hot-headed man who blows up, and the cold schemer who plots. The first acts foolishly in a moment; the second is hated over time. Both damage everyone around them.

The simple inherit folly, but the prudent are crowned with knowledge.

The simple person does not need to work to become a fool; he simply inherits it, by drifting. Folly is what you get by default. Knowledge is a crown, and crowns are earned.

verseByVerse.quote: The evil bow down before the good, the wicked at the gates of the righteous. The poor is disliked even by his neighbor, but the rich has many friends. Whoever despises his neighbor is a sinner, but blessed is he who is generous to the poor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The evil bow down before the good, the wicked at the gates of the righteous.

For now, the wicked often seem to be in charge. The proverb looks to the end, when the order is reversed and evil bows before good. History shows glimpses of it, and the last day will show it fully.

The poor is disliked even by his neighbor, but the rich has many friends.

This is a plain observation of how people behave, and it is not flattering. The poor man is avoided even by his neighbours, because he may ask for something. The rich man is surrounded by friends, many of whom are friends of his money. Proverbs is not approving of this. It is showing it to us so that we recognise it in ourselves.

Whoever despises his neighbor is a sinner, but blessed is he who is generous to the poor.

And here is the verdict. Despising a neighbour, including the poor neighbour everyone avoids, is sin. James rebuked a church that gave the rich visitor a good seat and told the poor man, You stand over there, and asked, have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts? (Jas 2:3-4). The blessing is on the one who is generous to the poor. Who is the person you tend to avoid because he might need something?

verseByVerse.quote: Do they not go astray who devise evil? Those who devise good meet steadfast love and faithfulness. In all toil there is profit, but mere talk tends only to poverty. The crown of the wise is their wealth, but the folly of fools brings folly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do they not go astray who devise evil? Those who devise good meet steadfast love and faithfulness.

Both kinds of people devise, make plans. Those who plan evil go astray. Those who plan good meet steadfast love and faithfulness, the two great covenant words from 3:3. The ESV notes that meet may be "show". Both are true: the one who plans good both receives and gives God's loyal love.

In all toil there is profit, but mere talk tends only to poverty.

Mere talk. Every workplace and every church knows the person who has endless ideas and opinions and does nothing. The proverb is blunt: talk without work leads to poverty. All toil, even the dull and unnoticed kind, produces something.

The crown of the wise is their wealth, but the folly of fools brings folly.

For the wise, wealth can be a crown, an honour that they use well. For fools, whatever they have only produces more foolishness. Folly in, folly out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–35 — The Fear of the LORD Is a Fountain of Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A truthful witness saves lives (v. 25). In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge; it is a fountain of life (vv. 26-27). Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, and envy makes the bones rot (vv. 28-30). Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him (v. 31). The righteous finds refuge in his death (vv. 32-33). Righteousness exalts a nation (vv. 34-35).
verseByVerse.theology: Reverence for God reaches into a person's temper, his view of the poor, his death, and the life of his nation.

verseByVerse.quote: A truthful witness saves lives, but one who breathes out lies is deceitful. In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge. The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A truthful witness saves lives, but one who breathes out lies is deceitful.

In a courtroom, one honest witness can save an innocent man's life. Truth is not a small matter. A lie in the wrong place can destroy a person; the truth told at cost can rescue one.

In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge.

Reverence for God produces strong confidence. The person who fears God fears nothing else in the same way. And the benefit reaches his children. A parent's fear of the LORD becomes a refuge for the next generation: a home where God is honoured, a model of faith, prayers offered for them for decades.

The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.

This proverb is nearly identical to 13:14, which said The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life. Here the fear of the LORD takes that place. The two are meant to be heard together: wise teaching is only a fountain because it flows from reverence for God.

verseByVerse.quote: In a multitude of people is the glory of a king, but without people a prince is ruined. Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly. A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a multitude of people is the glory of a king, but without people a prince is ruined.

A king's greatness is measured by his people, not merely by his palace. A leader without followers is nothing. That is a word for anyone who leads: your glory is the flourishing of the people entrusted to you. And the King of kings will be glorified by a people no one can number.

Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly.

Slow to anger is how God describes himself: a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger (Exod 34:6). The person who is slow to anger reflects God, and shows great understanding, because he takes time to see the whole situation. The hot-tempered man exalts folly. He puts it on display for everyone.

A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot.

Here the book notices how closely body and soul are bound together. A tranquil heart, at peace with God and content, gives life to the flesh; the ESV notes it may be "healing". Envy, or "jealousy", makes the bones rot. It eats a person from inside. The envious man thinks he is damaging the reputation of the one he envies. He is rotting his own bones. Where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice (Jas 3:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him.

This is one of the great theological proverbs of the book. Why does oppressing a poor man insult his Maker? Because the poor man was made by God, in God's image: So God created man in his own image (Gen 1:27). To crush him is to show contempt for the one whose image he bears. The same truth appears in 17:5, Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker.

And the other side: generosity to the needy honors God. Every act of kindness to a poor person is an act of worship. Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD (19:17).

Jesus took this to its fullest depth. As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matt 25:40). And John will not let anyone separate love for God from love for people: he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen (1 John 4:20).

How we treat the cleaner, the homeless man, the refugee, the employee who cannot afford to complain, is how we treat God.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked is overthrown through his evildoing, but the righteous finds refuge in his death. Wisdom rests in the heart of a man of understanding, but it makes itself known even in the midst of fools.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked is overthrown through his evildoing, but the righteous finds refuge in his death.

The second line is remarkable. The righteous finds refuge in his death. Death, the thing every human being dreads, becomes for the righteous a place of refuge. The Old Testament does not often say so much about what lies beyond the grave, but this proverb sees that the righteous man is not destroyed by death. He is sheltered in it.

The New Testament fills in the picture. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain (Phil 1:21). We would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord (2 Cor 5:8). The wicked is overthrown by his own evil; the believer walks through death into the arms of God.

Wisdom rests in the heart of a man of understanding, but it makes itself known even in the midst of fools.

Wisdom is at home, at rest, in the heart of a wise man. The ESV notes the line may mean that wisdom "rests quietly" there. It does not need to show off. And yet even among fools, wisdom makes itself known. A truly wise person cannot be completely hidden, even in a foolish crowd.

verseByVerse.quote: Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people. A servant who deals wisely has the king's favor, but his wrath falls on one who acts shamefully.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people.

Proverbs speaks mostly to individuals, but here it speaks to nations. A nation is lifted up not by military power or economic strength alone, but by righteousness: justice in its courts, honesty in its business, care for its weakest. And sin is a reproach to any people, any nation, whatever its size or history. No country is exempt. Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD (Ps 33:12).

That gives Christians a reason to care about the moral life of their nation, to pray for it and to live righteously in it, not in order to make it the kingdom of God, but because righteousness is good for every people.

A servant who deals wisely has the king's favor, but his wrath falls on one who acts shamefully.

The chapter ends in the royal court. A servant who acts wisely wins his king's favour; the one who acts shamefully faces his anger. Every Christian is a servant of a King. The question is not whether we serve, but whether we serve wisely.

14.theology:
Homes are built or destroyed by the character of those in them (v. 1). Human perception is unreliable: a way can seem right and lead to death (v. 12; 16:25), so every claim must be tested (v. 15; 1 John 4:1). The heart has depths only God fully knows (v. 10; 1 Sam 16:7; Heb 4:15).

Every human being bears God's image, so treatment of the poor is treatment of God (v. 31; Gen 1:27; Matt 25:40). The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life (v. 27) and a refuge for the next generation (v. 26). The righteous have hope in death (v. 32; Phil 1:21). Righteousness exalts nations (v. 34).
14.examples:
Adding a brick or pulling one out.

A clean manger and no harvest.

"I know exactly how you feel."

A road that feels fine and leads to death.

The life of the party who is loneliest in the room.

A forwarded rumour believed at once.

The neighbour everyone avoids.

Envy rotting the envier's bones.

The cleaner and the refugee as bearers of God's image.

15.overview:
A soft answer turns away wrath. The eyes of the LORD are everywhere; a gentle tongue is a tree of life. The LORD hates the sacrifice of the wicked but accepts the prayer of the upright. Sheol lies open before him, and so do human hearts; the scoffer will not go to the wise (vv. 1-12).

A glad heart makes a cheerful face and a continual feast. Better a little with the fear of the LORD than treasure with trouble, and a dinner of herbs with love than a fattened ox with hatred. The hot-tempered stir strife; plans succeed with many advisers; a word in season is good (vv. 13-23).

The path of life leads upward. The LORD tears down the proud and protects the widow. The righteous ponder their answers; the LORD hears their prayers; good news refreshes. The fear of the LORD is instruction in wisdom, and humility comes before honour (vv. 24-33).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Tongue and the Eyes of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger (v. 1). The wise tongue commends knowledge (v. 2). The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good (v. 3). A gentle tongue is a tree of life (vv. 4-7). The LORD hates the sacrifice of the wicked, but the prayer of the upright is acceptable to him (vv. 8-9). Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of the children of man!, and the scoffer will not go to the wise (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD who sees everything, down to the hidden heart, hears every word and every prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools pour out folly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

This may be the most useful single sentence in the book for daily life. Someone comes at you angry: a customer, a teenager, a spouse, a colleague. You have a choice. Answer in kind, and the anger doubles. Answer softly, and very often it drains away.

A soft answer is not a weak answer. It may say something hard. It simply refuses to add heat. It lowers the voice, acknowledges the other person's frustration, and does not reach for the sharpest word available. A harsh word is like petrol on a small fire. It feels satisfying for a second and costs a great deal afterward.

Peter tells Christians who are challenged about their faith to answer with gentleness and respect (1 Pet 3:15). Try it the next time you feel a sharp reply rising. Lower your voice and see what happens.

The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools pour out folly.

The wise man makes knowledge attractive; people want to hear more. The fool pours out folly, like water from an overturned jar, with no control and no end. The contrast is not only in content but in manner: one serves truth well, the other just empties himself.

verseByVerse.quote: The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good.

There is nowhere God does not see. Not the locked office, the hotel room on a business trip, the browser in private mode, the thought no one will ever hear. Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? (Ps 139:7).

The verse is a warning and a comfort at once. For the evil, it means nothing is hidden and nothing will be forgotten. No creature is hidden from his sight (Heb 4:13). For the good, it means no act of faithfulness goes unnoticed: the prayer said alone, the kindness nobody thanked you for, the temptation resisted with no one watching. God was watching.

How would today change if you lived it knowing, really knowing, that the LORD's eyes are on this room?

verseByVerse.quote: A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but perverseness in it breaks the spirit. A fool despises his father's instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is prudent. In the house of the righteous there is much treasure, but trouble befalls the income of the wicked. The lips of the wise spread knowledge; not so the hearts of fools.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but perverseness in it breaks the spirit.

Once more, the tree of life. A gentle tongue, and the ESV notes this may be a "healing" tongue, gives life to the people around it. And a twisted tongue breaks the spirit. Some people have been broken inside by years of harsh, mocking or manipulative words from someone close to them. Words can build a person up for a lifetime or crush him for one.

A fool despises his father's instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is prudent.

The fool's contempt starts at home. He despises his father's teaching. The prudent man, whatever his age, heeds reproof. Teachability, again, is the dividing line.

In the house of the righteous there is much treasure, but trouble befalls the income of the wicked.

The righteous man's house holds treasure, not necessarily money, but everything that makes a home rich: peace, love, faith, stability. The wicked man has income, perhaps a large one, and trouble comes with it: legal battles, family conflict, anxiety, the constant need for more.

The lips of the wise spread knowledge; not so the hearts of fools.

Wise people are like farmers scattering seed; knowledge spreads out from them. Fools spread nothing worth having. The ESV notes the second line may be read, "the hearts of fools are not steadfast". A fool's heart is unstable, so his words are too.

verseByVerse.quote: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is acceptable to him. The way of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but he loves him who pursues righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is acceptable to him.

This is a startling verse. A wicked man comes to worship and brings a costly sacrifice. God calls it an abomination. An upright man simply prays, with nothing in his hands, and God finds it acceptable. God is not impressed by religious activity that is cut off from a changed life. He said through Isaiah, What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? (Isa 1:11), and through Samuel, Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Sam 15:22).

That is a warning for anyone who uses church attendance, giving or religious duty as a cover for a life he has no intention of changing. And it is an encouragement to the person who feels he has nothing to offer God but a simple prayer. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise (Ps 51:17). The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working (Jas 5:16).

The way of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but he loves him who pursues righteousness.

Verse 8 spoke of worship; verse 9 speaks of the whole way of life. God's verdict on worship depends on his verdict on the life. And notice the verb: he loves the one who pursues righteousness. Not the one who has fully arrived, but the one who is chasing it. God loves the direction of a heart, not only its achievements.

verseByVerse.quote: There is severe discipline for him who forsakes the way; whoever hates reproof will die. Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of the children of man! A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is severe discipline for him who forsakes the way; whoever hates reproof will die.

A person who leaves God's way does not escape discipline; the discipline gets severe. God corrects gently at first, and more firmly if gentle correction is ignored. And a person who hates reproof altogether cuts himself off from the correction that could save him. The end is death.

Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of the children of man!

Sheol is the realm of the dead; Abaddon is a word for destruction, the deepest place of ruin. They are the most hidden places imaginable. Yet they lie open before the LORD, like a book on a table. If God sees the depths of death, how much more does he see the human heart?

No motive is hidden from him, no secret resentment, no self-deception. That is terrifying for anyone trying to hide from God. It is freeing for anyone who has stopped trying. There is no point pretending to the one who already knows everything, and no need to, because he loved us knowing it.

A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise.

The scoffer avoids the very people who could help him. He will not seek out a wise friend, a pastor, a counsellor, because they might tell him something he does not want to hear. So he surrounds himself with people who agree with him, and stays a scoffer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Better a Dinner of Herbs
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A glad heart makes a cheerful face, and the cheerful of heart has a continual feast (vv. 13-15). Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it. Better is a dinner of herbs where love is than a fattened ox and hatred with it (vv. 16-17). The hot-tempered stir strife and the sluggard's path is a hedge of thorns (vv. 18-19). Without counsel plans fail, and a word in season, how good it is! (vv. 20-23).
verseByVerse.theology: What makes a table or a life rich is not what is on it, but reverence for God and love around it.

verseByVerse.quote: A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but by sorrow of heart the spirit is crushed. The heart of him who has understanding seeks knowledge, but the mouths of fools feed on folly. All the days of the afflicted are evil, but the cheerful of heart has a continual feast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but by sorrow of heart the spirit is crushed.

The face shows the heart. A glad heart lights up a face, and a sorrowful one crushes the spirit. Proverbs does not pretend the believer is never crushed. But it shows how much the inner life matters to everything else. A joyful heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones (17:22).

The heart of him who has understanding seeks knowledge, but the mouths of fools feed on folly.

Everyone is hungry for something. The man of understanding goes looking for knowledge. The fool feeds on folly: gossip, trivia, scandal, entertainment that empties the mind. What a person feeds on, he becomes. What has your mind been eating this week?

All the days of the afflicted are evil, but the cheerful of heart has a continual feast.

Two people can live through similar circumstances and experience them completely differently. For one, all the days are bad. For the other, life is a continual feast. The difference is not always what happens to them, but what is in their hearts. A cheerful heart is not the same as denial. It is a heart that has found something to rejoice in that circumstances cannot take. Rejoice in the Lord always; again I will say, rejoice (Phil 4:4). Paul wrote that from prison.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it. Better is a dinner of herbs where love is than a fattened ox and hatred with it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it.

Two "better than" proverbs side by side, and they belong together. First: a small income with the fear of the LORD beats a fortune with trouble attached. The trouble may be anxiety, family fights, a guilty conscience, the constant fear of losing it. Many wealthy people would give much of their money for the peace a poor believer has. Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, "I will never leave you nor forsake you." (Heb 13:5).

Better is a dinner of herbs where love is than a fattened ox and hatred with it.
