Reconciliation within families is hard and urgent (v. 19; Matt 18:15). Marriage is a gift of God's favour (v. 22), and Christ is the friend who sticks closer than a brother (v. 24; John 15:15; Heb 13:5).
18.examples:
Withdrawal that protects a habit no one may see.

Posting before reading.

Refusing the plate of gossip.

Running to the tower when the bad news comes.

A wall that exists only in the imagination.

Hearing exactly half of the story.

Iron bars between brothers.

The friend who holds on when the crowd drifts.

19.title: Whoever Is Generous to the Poor Lends to the LORD
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Better is a poor person who walks in his integrity than one who is crooked in speech and is a fool.<sup>2</sup>Desire without knowledge is not good, and whoever makes haste with his feet misses his way.<sup>3</sup>When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the LORD.<sup>4</sup>Wealth brings many new friends, but a poor man is deserted by his friend.<sup>5</sup>A false witness will not go unpunished, and he who breathes out lies will not escape.<sup>6</sup>Many seek the favor of a generous man, and everyone is a friend to a man who gives gifts.<sup>7</sup>All a poor man's brothers hate him; how much more do his friends go far from him! He pursues them with words, but does not have them.<sup>8</sup>Whoever gets sense loves his own soul; he who keeps understanding will discover good.<sup>9</sup>A false witness will not go unpunished, and he who breathes out lies will perish.<sup>10</sup>It is not fitting for a fool to live in luxury, much less for a slave to rule over princes.<sup>11</sup>Good sense makes one slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense.<sup>12</sup>A king's wrath is like the growling of a lion, but his favor is like dew on the grass.<sup>13</sup>A foolish son is ruin to his father, and a wife's quarreling is a continual dripping of rain.<sup>14</sup>House and wealth are inherited from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD.<sup>15</sup>Slothfulness casts into a deep sleep, and an idle person will suffer hunger.<sup>16</sup>Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his life; he who despises his ways will die.<sup>17</sup>Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed.<sup>18</sup>Discipline your son, for there is hope; do not set your heart on putting him to death.<sup>19</sup>A man of great wrath will pay the penalty, for if you deliver him, you will only have to do it again.<sup>20</sup>Listen to advice and accept instruction, that you may gain wisdom in the future.<sup>21</sup>Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand.<sup>22</sup>What is desired in a man is steadfast love, and a poor man is better than a liar.<sup>23</sup>The fear of the LORD leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied; he will not be visited by harm.<sup>24</sup>The sluggard buries his hand in the dish and will not even bring it back to his mouth.<sup>25</sup>Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence; reprove a man of understanding, and he will gain knowledge.<sup>26</sup>He who does violence to his father and chases away his mother is a son who brings shame and reproach.<sup>27</sup>Cease to hear instruction, my son, and you will stray from the words of knowledge.<sup>28</sup>A worthless witness mocks at justice, and the mouth of the wicked devours iniquity.<sup>29</sup>Condemnation is ready for scoffers, and beating for the backs of fools.
19.overview:
Better poor with integrity than crooked and foolish. Zeal without knowledge misses the way, and the fool who ruins himself rages against the LORD. Wealth attracts friends and poverty drives them away; false witnesses will not escape (vv. 1-10).

It is a person's glory to overlook an offence. A prudent wife is from the LORD. Keeping the commandment keeps life, and whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, who will repay. Discipline a son while there is hope, but never in destructive anger (vv. 11-19).

Many are a man's plans, but the purpose of the LORD will stand. Steadfast love is what is desired in a person. The fear of the LORD leads to life and satisfied rest. The sluggard will not feed himself; a son who mistreats his parents brings shame; whoever stops listening to instruction will stray (vv. 20-29).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Integrity, Haste and Fair-Weather Friends
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Better is a poor person who walks in his integrity than one who is crooked in speech and is a fool (v. 1). Zeal without knowledge misses the way, and the fool blames God for his own ruin (vv. 2-3). Wealth brings many new friends, but a poor man is deserted by his friend; everyone befriends the generous, and the poor man's brothers go far from him (vv. 4, 6-7). False witnesses will not escape (vv. 5, 9). Whoever gets sense loves his own soul (v. 8), and luxury does not suit a fool (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Poverty with integrity beats wealth with folly, even though the crowd follows the money.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is a poor person who walks in his integrity than one who is crooked in speech and is a fool. Desire without knowledge is not good, and whoever makes haste with his feet misses his way. When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Better is a poor person who walks in his integrity than one who is crooked in speech and is a fool.

The chapter opens with a "better than" that cuts against how the world ranks people. The world would take the crooked, successful man over the honest poor one. Proverbs reverses the ranking. A poor person with integrity has something no amount of money can buy and no reversal can take away. Would you rather be respected for your wealth or trusted for your word?

Desire without knowledge is not good, and whoever makes haste with his feet misses his way.

Enthusiasm is not enough. The ESV notes that Desire may be "A soul": a person full of zeal but empty of knowledge. He rushes, and misses the road. Many a young believer has burned with zeal and done damage because he did not stop to learn. Paul said of his own people, they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Rom 10:2).

Haste is often the partner of folly: the quick marriage, the sudden career move, the rash purchase, the angry email sent at once. Slow down long enough to know where the road goes.

When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the LORD.

Here is one of the most psychologically acute verses in the book. A man ruins his own life by his own foolish choices. And then, rather than admit it, he gets angry at God. "Why did God let this happen to me?" The debt was his; the affair was his; the drinking was his. But his heart rages against the LORD.

Cain did it: his offering was not accepted, and Cain was very angry (Gen 4:5). James forbids it: Let no one say when he is tempted, "I am being tempted by God" (Jas 1:13). And Lamentations asks, Why should a living man complain, a man, about the punishment of his sins? (Lam 3:39). The first step out of the ruin is to stop blaming God for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Wealth brings many new friends, but a poor man is deserted by his friend. A false witness will not go unpunished, and he who breathes out lies will not escape. Many seek the favor of a generous man, and everyone is a friend to a man who gives gifts. All a poor man's brothers hate him; how much more do his friends go far from him! He pursues them with words, but does not have them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wealth brings many new friends, but a poor man is deserted by his friend.

Proverbs is realistic about human nature. Money attracts friends. When a person wins the lottery, relatives he has not seen in years appear. When he loses everything, even his friend drifts away. This is not how things should be, but it is how they often are, and the wise person knows it before he needs to.

A false witness will not go unpunished, and he who breathes out lies will not escape.

Placed in the middle of proverbs about fair-weather friends, this is a reminder that lies do not pay. It will be repeated almost word for word in verse 9, with a sharper ending.

Many seek the favor of a generous man, and everyone is a friend to a man who gives gifts.

The ESV notes a generous man may be "a noble". Everyone wants to be close to the important man and the man with gifts to give. Crowds form around generosity and power. The wise person asks, of his own friends: which of them would still be here if I had nothing?

All a poor man's brothers hate him; how much more do his friends go far from him! He pursues them with words, but does not have them.

The ESV notes that the meaning of the last sentence is uncertain, but the picture is painful enough. The poor man is avoided even by his family. He calls after his friends, and they are gone. That is loneliness of the deepest kind.

These verses are a call to be different. The church is meant to be the one place where the poor man is not deserted, where brothers do not go far away when someone loses his job. Who in your church has quietly been left behind since his circumstances changed?

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever gets sense loves his own soul; he who keeps understanding will discover good. A false witness will not go unpunished, and he who breathes out lies will perish. It is not fitting for a fool to live in luxury, much less for a slave to rule over princes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever gets sense loves his own soul; he who keeps understanding will discover good.

Getting wisdom is the truest form of self-love. Not self-indulgence, but genuinely caring for your own soul. The person who pursues sense is doing the best thing he can for himself.

A false witness will not go unpunished, and he who breathes out lies will perish.

Verse 5 said the liar will not escape. Now it says he will perish. The repetition within a few verses deepens the warning. Lying is not a minor fault.

It is not fitting for a fool to live in luxury, much less for a slave to rule over princes.

Some things are out of place. A fool surrounded by luxury does not know how to use it; it only magnifies his folly. And a person suddenly lifted into power he is not fit for can do great harm. The proverb warns against putting people where their character cannot carry them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Good sense makes one slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense (v. 11). The king's wrath roars and his favour refreshes (v. 12). A foolish son and a quarrelsome wife wear a man down, but a prudent wife is from the LORD (vv. 13-14). Laziness brings hunger, and keeping the commandment keeps life (vv. 15-16). Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed (v. 17). Discipline a son while there is hope, and do not keep rescuing the hot-tempered (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Wisdom lets small wrongs go, treats giving as a loan God himself repays, and corrects while correction can still help.

verseByVerse.quote: Good sense makes one slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense. A king's wrath is like the growling of a lion, but his favor is like dew on the grass.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good sense makes one slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense.

This is a beautiful proverb. Good sense slows anger down. It stops to think: what did he mean? What is he going through? Does this really matter? And there is glory, real honour, in overlooking an offence, in choosing not to take it up.

The world often sees letting things go as weakness. Scripture sees it as glory. Love is not irritable or resentful (1 Cor 13:5). And the Christian has the strongest reason of all to overlook offences: as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive (Col 3:13). When Peter asked how often he should forgive, Jesus said, I do not say to you seven times, but seventy-seven times (Matt 18:22).

Not every wrong should be overlooked; some must be confronted. But a great many should. Is there a small offence you have been holding that it would be your glory to let go today?

A king's wrath is like the growling of a lion, but his favor is like dew on the grass.

A king's anger is terrifying, like a lion's growl before it attacks. His favour is gentle and refreshing, like dew on dry grass in the morning. A similar picture appeared at 16:14-15. Those with power over others should remember how their anger and their kindness land.

verseByVerse.quote: A foolish son is ruin to his father, and a wife's quarreling is a continual dripping of rain. House and wealth are inherited from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A foolish son is ruin to his father, and a wife's quarreling is a continual dripping of rain.

Two sorrows in a home. A foolish son brings ruin. And a quarrelsome spouse is like a continual dripping: a leaking roof in the rainy season, drip, drip, drip, never stopping. It is not a single crash; it is the wearing effect of constant complaint. The picture returns at 27:15. Husbands can drip too, and the proverb is a mirror for both.

House and wealth are inherited from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD.

A father can leave his son a house and money. But no father can hand down a good wife. She is a gift from the LORD. That is a word of gratitude to every man with a prudent wife: she did not come from your cleverness or your inheritance, but from God. And it is a reason for a young man to pray about marriage, not merely to plan it (compare 18:22).

verseByVerse.quote: Slothfulness casts into a deep sleep, and an idle person will suffer hunger. Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his life; he who despises his ways will die. Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Slothfulness casts into a deep sleep, and an idle person will suffer hunger.

Laziness is like a drug that sends a person into a deeper and deeper sleep. The more he rests, the less he wants to wake up. And the end is hunger.

Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his life; he who despises his ways will die.

There is a play on the word keeps. Keep God's commandment, and it keeps you. Despise the direction of your life, treating your choices as if they did not matter, and you will die. Jesus said, If you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15). Obedience is not a cage but a lifeline.

Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay him for his deed.

This is one of the most remarkable promises in Proverbs. When you give to a poor person, you are not only giving; you are lending to the LORD. God treats the gift as a loan made to him personally, and he pays his debts. He will repay him.

That changes how to think about generosity. Giving to the poor is not throwing money away. It is putting it in the safest hands there are. The repayment may not come in cash, or on this side of death, but it will come. And it fits what we saw at 14:31: God so identifies with the poor that kindness to them is kindness to him. As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matt 25:40).

verseByVerse.quote: Discipline your son, for there is hope; do not set your heart on putting him to death. A man of great wrath will pay the penalty, for if you deliver him, you will only have to do it again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Discipline your son, for there is hope; do not set your heart on putting him to death.

Two sides again. First, discipline while there is hope, while the child is young enough to be shaped. There is a window, and it closes. The parent who waits until the teenage years to start correcting has waited too long.

Second, the discipline must never become destruction. Do not set your heart on putting him to death. Discipline aims at the child's life, never at crushing him. A parent who disciplines in rage, or whose discipline leaves a child broken, has crossed a line the Bible draws clearly. The goal is hope. Later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it (Heb 12:11).

A man of great wrath will pay the penalty, for if you deliver him, you will only have to do it again.

Some people's anger keeps getting them into trouble, and there is always someone rescuing them: paying the fine, smoothing things over, making excuses. The proverb says that rescue does not help. You will only have to do it again. Sometimes love means letting a person face the consequences of his own temper, because that is the only thing that will teach him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–29 — The Purpose of the LORD Will Stand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Listen to advice (v. 20). Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand (v. 21). What is desired in a man is steadfast love (v. 22). The fear of the LORD leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied (v. 23). The sluggard will not lift food to his mouth, and the simple learn from the punishment of scoffers (vv. 24-25). A son who mistreats his parents brings shame; Cease to hear instruction, my son, and you will stray (vv. 26-27). Worthless witnesses and scoffers face judgment (vv. 28-29).
verseByVerse.theology: Behind all human planning stands the purpose of the LORD, and the one who fears him rests.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen to advice and accept instruction, that you may gain wisdom in the future. Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Listen to advice and accept instruction, that you may gain wisdom in the future.

Wisdom is a long-term investment. Listening to advice now pays off in the future. The advice you take at twenty shapes who you are at fifty.

Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand.

A man's mind is busy with many plans: careers, houses, retirements, projects. God has one purpose, and it is the one that will stand. That is humbling for anyone who has built his life around his own plans. It is deeply comforting for anyone whose plans have fallen apart. The plans failed; the purpose of the LORD did not.

Joseph's life is the great illustration: a boy with dreams, sold, imprisoned, forgotten. Every human plan went wrong. And the purpose of the LORD stood, to save many lives. The same God holds the purpose of every believer's life, including the parts that make no sense yet.

verseByVerse.quote: What is desired in a man is steadfast love, and a poor man is better than a liar. The fear of the LORD leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied; he will not be visited by harm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is desired in a man is steadfast love, and a poor man is better than a liar.

What makes a person truly desirable, as a friend, a spouse, a leader? Not wealth or charm, but steadfast love, hesed, loyal love that keeps its commitments. And a poor man who is honest is better than a rich man who lies. Loyalty and truth are worth more than money.

The fear of the LORD leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied; he will not be visited by harm.

Three gifts to those who fear the LORD: life, rest and satisfaction. Many people are restless and never satisfied, always wanting more, never at peace. The fear of the LORD brings a person to rest. It is not that he has everything; it is that he has the one who is everything.

He will not be visited by harm does not mean no hardship ever touches him. It means no harm that can finally destroy him. Jesus said, I came that they may have life and have it abundantly (John 10:10).

verseByVerse.quote: The sluggard buries his hand in the dish and will not even bring it back to his mouth. Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence; reprove a man of understanding, and he will gain knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sluggard buries his hand in the dish and will not even bring it back to his mouth.

A cartoon of laziness, and one of the funniest verses in the Bible. The sluggard reaches into the bowl of food, and then cannot be bothered to lift his hand to his mouth. The picture returns at 26:15. It is exaggerated to make the point memorable: laziness can grow so great that a person will not even do what is in his own obvious interest.

Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence; reprove a man of understanding, and he will gain knowledge.

Three kinds of learners. The scoffer probably will not learn from being punished, but the simple watching will. The man of understanding needs only a word of reproof. Consequences teach even those who are not directly involved. And the wise need far less of them.

verseByVerse.quote: He who does violence to his father and chases away his mother is a son who brings shame and reproach. Cease to hear instruction, my son, and you will stray from the words of knowledge. A worthless witness mocks at justice, and the mouth of the wicked devours iniquity. Condemnation is ready for scoffers, and beating for the backs of fools.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who does violence to his father and chases away his mother is a son who brings shame and reproach.

A shocking picture: a son who mistreats his aged father and drives his mother out of the house, perhaps to take the property. It happens, in more polished forms, when grown children exploit elderly parents or abandon them. The commandment says, Honor your father and your mother (Exod 20:12), and Paul calls it the first commandment with a promise (Eph 6:2). How are you treating the parents who are growing old?

Cease to hear instruction, my son, and you will stray from the words of knowledge.

A verse with a twist. It sounds almost like permission: stop listening. But it is irony. Stop listening to instruction, and you will drift. Drifting takes no effort. It only requires that you stop paying attention. That is how most people wander from God: not by a decision to leave, but by ceasing to hear.

A worthless witness mocks at justice, and the mouth of the wicked devours iniquity.

The wicked man gulps down evil like food. He consumes it and wants more. And the worthless witness treats justice as a joke.

Condemnation is ready for scoffers, and beating for the backs of fools.

The chapter ends with a warning that judgment is ready, already prepared, waiting. The scoffer thinks he has escaped because nothing has happened yet. It is only that the moment has not come.

19.theology:
Human folly must not be blamed on God (v. 3; Jas 1:13). Integrity is worth more than wealth, and the church must not imitate the world's desertion of the poor (vv. 1, 4, 7).

Overlooking offences reflects God's forgiveness (v. 11; Col 3:13). God identifies with the poor so fully that generosity to them is a loan to him (v. 17; Matt 25:40). God's purpose stands over every human plan (v. 21), and the fear of the LORD brings rest (v. 23; John 10:10). Honouring parents remains a lifelong duty (v. 26; Eph 6:2).
19.examples:
Relatives who appear after a lottery win.

A man who wrecked his life and is angry at God.

The glory of letting a small offence go.

A roof dripping in the rainy season.

A gift to the poor as a loan to the LORD.

Rescuing a hot-tempered man over and over.

Joseph's plans and God's purpose.

The sluggard's hand in the dish.

Drifting by ceasing to hear.

20.title: The Spirit of Man Is the Lamp of the LORD
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise.<sup>2</sup>The terror of a king is like the growling of a lion; whoever provokes him to anger forfeits his life.<sup>3</sup>It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife, but every fool will be quarreling.<sup>4</sup>The sluggard does not plow in the autumn; he will seek at harvest and have nothing.<sup>5</sup>The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out.<sup>6</sup>Many a man proclaims his own steadfast love, but a faithful man who can find?<sup>7</sup>The righteous who walks in his integrity— blessed are his children after him!<sup>8</sup>A king who sits on the throne of judgment winnows all evil with his eyes.<sup>9</sup>Who can say, "I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin"?<sup>10</sup>Unequal weights and unequal measures are both alike an abomination to the LORD.<sup>11</sup>Even a child makes himself known by his acts, by whether his conduct is pure and upright.<sup>12</sup>The hearing ear and the seeing eye, the LORD has made them both.<sup>13</sup>Love not sleep, lest you come to poverty; open your eyes, and you will have plenty of bread.<sup>14</sup>"Bad, bad," says the buyer, but when he goes away, then he boasts.<sup>15</sup>There is gold and abundance of costly stones, but the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel.<sup>16</sup>Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger, and hold it in pledge when he puts up security for foreigners.<sup>17</sup>Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.<sup>18</sup>Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war.<sup>19</sup>Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets; therefore do not associate with a simple babbler.<sup>20</sup>If one curses his father or his mother, his lamp will be put out in utter darkness.<sup>21</sup>An inheritance gained hastily in the beginning will not be blessed in the end.<sup>22</sup>Do not say, "I will repay evil"; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you.<sup>23</sup>Unequal weights are an abomination to the LORD, and false scales are not good.<sup>24</sup>A man's steps are from the LORD; how then can man understand his way?<sup>25</sup>It is a snare to say rashly, "It is holy," and to reflect only after making vows.<sup>26</sup>A wise king winnows the wicked and drives the wheel over them.<sup>27</sup>The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts.<sup>28</sup>Steadfast love and faithfulness preserve the king, and by steadfast love his throne is upheld.<sup>29</sup>The glory of young men is their strength, but the splendor of old men is their gray hair.<sup>30</sup>Blows that wound cleanse away evil; strokes make clean the innermost parts.
20.overview:
Wine is a mocker and strong drink a brawler. It is honourable to keep out of strife; the sluggard does not plow and has nothing at harvest. The heart's purposes are deep water that understanding draws out. Faithful men are rare. No one can say he has made his heart pure. God hates unequal weights, and even a child is known by his acts (vv. 1-11).

The LORD made the seeing eye and the hearing ear. The buyer runs down what he boasts of later. Bread gained by deceit turns to gravel. Plans need counsel; avoid the babbler (vv. 12-19).

Cursing parents ends in darkness; hasty inheritances are not blessed. Do not repay evil but wait for the LORD. A man's steps are from the LORD; rash vows are a snare. The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD. Steadfast love upholds a throne; young and old each have their glory; and painful blows can cleanse the heart (vv. 20-30).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Wine, Strife and the Deep Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise (v. 1). Do not provoke a king (v. 2). It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife (v. 3). The sluggard does not plow and has nothing at harvest (v. 4). The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out (v. 5). A faithful man is rare, and the righteous bless their children (vv. 6-7). Who can say, "I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin"? (vv. 8-9). God hates unequal weights, and even a child is known by his acts (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: No one sees all the way into his own heart, and no one can make it clean.

verseByVerse.quote: Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise.

Wine is personified, and the portrait is sharp. It is a mocker: it promises cheer and then makes a fool of the drinker. Strong drink is a brawler: it starts fights, loosens tongues, and turns ordinary men into violent ones. Noah, the righteous survivor of the flood, drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent (Gen 9:21). Chapter 23 will give a whole painting of the drunkard's misery (23:29-35).

The Bible does not forbid wine. Jesus made it at Cana, and the psalmist thanks God for wine that gladdens the heart. What the proverb condemns is being led astray by it. The ESV notes the last phrase may be read "will not become wise": a person in the grip of drink stops growing. Do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18).

For anyone who has seen alcohol destroy a family, this verse is not abstract. And for anyone who is beginning to need a drink rather than enjoy one, the mocker has already started laughing. Tell someone.

verseByVerse.quote: The terror of a king is like the growling of a lion; whoever provokes him to anger forfeits his life. It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife, but every fool will be quarreling. The sluggard does not plow in the autumn; he will seek at harvest and have nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The terror of a king is like the growling of a lion; whoever provokes him to anger forfeits his life.

Nearly the same picture as 19:12. A king's anger can be deadly, and the wise do not provoke it carelessly. There is a place for respect toward those who hold real power.

It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife, but every fool will be quarreling.

The world often thinks the man who wins every argument is the strong one. The proverb says the honour belongs to the man who stays out of it. Keeping aloof from strife is not cowardice. It takes more self-control to walk away than to fight. And every fool, without exception, will be quarrelling. It is almost a way of identifying one.

The sluggard does not plow in the autumn; he will seek at harvest and have nothing.

In Israel the plowing was done in autumn, when the rains came and the weather turned cold and unpleasant. The sluggard stays indoors. Then at harvest he goes out to his field looking for a crop, and there is nothing, because nothing was planted. Every harvest in life requires an unpleasant plowing season: study before the exam, saving before retirement, discipline before maturity.

verseByVerse.quote: The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out. Many a man proclaims his own steadfast love, but a faithful man who can find? The righteous who walks in his integrity— blessed are his children after him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out.

A person's real motives and intentions lie deep, like water at the bottom of a well. Most people cannot see them, and often the person himself cannot. But a man of understanding will draw it out, like someone lowering a bucket on a long rope.

This is the skill of a good counsellor, pastor, parent or friend: asking the questions that help another person discover what is really going on inside. Not telling him, but drawing it out. Who has done that for you? And whose deep water could you patiently draw up this week by listening rather than talking?

Many a man proclaims his own steadfast love, but a faithful man who can find?

Talk about loyalty is cheap. Many people advertise their faithfulness. Finding one who actually is faithful, who keeps his word when it costs him, is rare. Jesus asked a sobering question of the same kind: when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth? (Luke 18:8).

The righteous who walks in his integrity— blessed are his children after him!

A father's integrity blesses the next generation. His children inherit a good name, a model to follow, and the fruit of his prayers. The most lasting thing a parent gives is not money but a life of integrity lived in front of them.

verseByVerse.quote: A king who sits on the throne of judgment winnows all evil with his eyes. Who can say, "I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin"?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A king who sits on the throne of judgment winnows all evil with his eyes.

A wise judge sees through a case the way a farmer winnows grain, tossing it in the wind so the chaff blows away. With a look he separates the truth from the lies. Earthly kings do this imperfectly. The King who will sit on the final throne does it perfectly.

Who can say, "I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin"?

And straight after the king who sees all evil comes the question that silences everyone. Who can say he is clean? The answer is no one. Not the most moral, not the most religious. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Rom 3:23). If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8).

Notice the words I have made. The problem is not only that no one is pure, but that no one can make himself pure. Self-improvement cannot clean a heart. That can only be done by God: Create in me a clean heart, O God (Ps 51:10). And the good news is that he does. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). The question of this verse has no answer in man, and a full answer in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Unequal weights and unequal measures are both alike an abomination to the LORD. Even a child makes himself known by his acts, by whether his conduct is pure and upright.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unequal weights and unequal measures are both alike an abomination to the LORD.

The ESV notes that the Hebrew is "Two kinds of" weights: one set for buying, one for selling. The same verse comes back almost exactly at verse 23, and the principle already appeared at 11:1. Double standards in business are detestable to God. So are double standards in life: one rule for me and another for everyone else, one set of weights for my faults and another for yours.

Even a child makes himself known by his acts, by whether his conduct is pure and upright.

Character shows early. A child's actions reveal what kind of person he is becoming. Parents should watch not only what their children say but what they do. The ESV notes a different reading is possible: "Even a child can dissemble in his actions, though his conduct seems pure and upright". Both are true of children, and of adults. Actions reveal, and actions can also disguise. You will recognize them by their fruits (Matt 7:16), given enough time to see the fruit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — The Seeing Eye and the Mouth Full of Gravel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hearing ear and the seeing eye, the LORD has made them both (v. 12). Love not sleep (v. 13). "Bad, bad," says the buyer, but when he goes away, then he boasts (v. 14). The lips of knowledge are a precious jewel (v. 15). Secure your loans against rash guarantors (v. 16). Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel (v. 17). Make plans by counsel, and avoid the babbler (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who made eyes and ears sees the haggler's lie and the cheat's sweet bread turning to gravel.

verseByVerse.quote: The hearing ear and the seeing eye, the LORD has made them both. Love not sleep, lest you come to poverty; open your eyes, and you will have plenty of bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hearing ear and the seeing eye, the LORD has made them both.

A simple and wonderful statement. Every eye that sees and every ear that hears was made by God. That is a reason for gratitude: sight and hearing are gifts, not rights. And it is a reason for sober thought. The God who made the eye sees; the God who made the ear hears. And he intends the ears and eyes he made to be used for what he made them for. When Moses complained that he could not speak, the LORD answered, Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD? (Exod 4:11).

Love not sleep, lest you come to poverty; open your eyes, and you will have plenty of bread.

Sleep is good; loving it is dangerous. The sleepy man is poor. Open your eyes, get up, face the day, and there will be bread. The eyes God made are for opening.

verseByVerse.quote: "Bad, bad," says the buyer, but when he goes away, then he boasts. There is gold and abundance of costly stones, but the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Bad, bad," says the buyer, but when he goes away, then he boasts.

Here is a scene from any market in the world. The buyer picks up the item and frowns. "Poor quality. Far too expensive. I could get it cheaper elsewhere." The seller lowers the price. And the buyer walks away and tells his friends what a bargain he got.

The proverb does not condemn bargaining. It exposes the lie. Many people who would never tell an outright lie think nothing of misrepresenting a car they are selling or running down a house they want to buy. The God who hates unequal weights (v. 10) also hears the buyer's "Bad, bad".

There is gold and abundance of costly stones, but the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel.

Gold and gems are plentiful enough in the market. What is truly rare is a mouth that speaks knowledge. Wise speech is the rarest jewel there is.

verseByVerse.quote: Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger, and hold it in pledge when he puts up security for foreigners. Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger, and hold it in pledge when he puts up security for foreigners.

A piece of hard-headed financial advice, repeated at 27:13. If a man is foolish enough to guarantee a stranger's debts, do not lend to him without collateral. Take his cloak as security. The ESV notes that the last phrase may be "for an adulteress". Either way, a man with such poor judgment is a bad risk.

Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.

Imagine biting into a loaf of fresh bread and finding your mouth full of grit and stones. That is what dishonest gain becomes. At first it is sweet: the money from the fraud, the promotion won by lying, the grade from cheating. Afterward, it turns to gravel: guilt, exposure, broken trust, a conscience that grinds.

Moses chose rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin (Heb 11:25). Sin's pleasure is real, but it is fleeting, and it leaves gravel.

verseByVerse.quote: Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war. Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets; therefore do not associate with a simple babbler.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war.

No sensible king goes to war on a whim. He takes counsel. The same is true of the battles of ordinary life: starting a business, confronting a problem, making a big move. Plans are established by counsel (compare 24:6).

Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets; therefore do not associate with a simple babbler.

The first line is from 11:13. The second draws the practical conclusion: do not keep company with a person who cannot keep his mouth shut. The ESV notes that the Hebrew is "with one who is simple in his lips". If he is telling you other people's secrets, he is telling other people yours.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The one who curses his parents will see his lamp go out, and a hasty inheritance is not blessed (vv. 20-21). Do not say, "I will repay evil"; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you (v. 22). A man's steps are from the LORD; how then can man understand his way? (vv. 23-24). Beware rash vows (v. 25). The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts (vv. 26-27). Steadfast love upholds the throne; strength is the glory of the young and gray hair of the old; and Blows that wound cleanse away evil (vv. 28-30).
verseByVerse.theology: Leave vengeance and direction to God, and let him search the heart with the lamp he has put inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: If one curses his father or his mother, his lamp will be put out in utter darkness. An inheritance gained hastily in the beginning will not be blessed in the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If one curses his father or his mother, his lamp will be put out in utter darkness.

Under the law, cursing a parent was a capital crime: Whoever curses his father or his mother shall be put to death (Exod 21:17). God takes the honour of parents that seriously. The proverb uses the image of a lamp going out: the life of the one who curses his parents ends in darkness.

An inheritance gained hastily in the beginning will not be blessed in the end.

Think of the prodigal son demanding his inheritance before his father was dead. Wealth grabbed early, before it is rightly due, or wealth acquired too quickly, rarely brings blessing. What comes fast often goes fast, and brings ruin with it.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not say, "I will repay evil"; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you. Unequal weights are an abomination to the LORD, and false scales are not good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not say, "I will repay evil"; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you.

When someone wrongs us, the instinct is immediate: I will get him back. The proverb forbids even saying it. Instead: wait for the LORD. That is not passivity. It is trust that God sees the wrong, cares about justice, and will act. And it is freedom: you do not have to carry the weight of evening the score.

Paul quotes the principle in Romans: Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord." (Rom 12:19). Is there a wrong you have been planning to repay? Hand it over.

Unequal weights are an abomination to the LORD, and false scales are not good.

The repetition of verse 10, placed right after the call not to take revenge, may be deliberate. Revenge is a kind of false scale: we weigh the other person's offence heavily and our own lightly. God's scales are true.

verseByVerse.quote: A man's steps are from the LORD; how then can man understand his way? It is a snare to say rashly, "It is holy," and to reflect only after making vows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man's steps are from the LORD; how then can man understand his way?

If God directs every step, no human being can fully understand his own path. We see a few steps ahead at best. Jeremiah prayed, I know, O LORD, that the way of man is not in himself, that it is not in man who walks to direct his steps (Jer 10:23).

That is a relief rather than a burden. You do not have to understand your whole life to walk it faithfully. The confusing season, the closed door, the unexpected turn: you may not understand your way, but the one directing your steps does.

It is a snare to say rashly, "It is holy," and to reflect only after making vows.

Some people make promises to God in a moment of emotion, "I dedicate this to you", "If you get me through this, I will...", and only think about what they have promised afterward. It becomes a trap. Jephthah vowed that whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me would be offered up, and his daughter came out (Judg 11:31). It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay (Eccl 5:5). Think first. Then promise.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise king winnows the wicked and drives the wheel over them. The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts. Steadfast love and faithfulness preserve the king, and by steadfast love his throne is upheld.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wise king winnows the wicked and drives the wheel over them.

The picture comes from the threshing floor: a heavy wheel rolled over the grain to separate it from the husk. A wise ruler separates out the wicked and deals with them firmly. Justice is not soft on evil.

The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts.

God has placed a lamp inside every human being. The ESV notes the Hebrew word is "breath", the breath of life God breathed into man. With it he searches all his innermost parts. That is the conscience, and more than the conscience: the human capacity to know oneself, which God uses to shine light into the corners we would rather keep dark.

When you feel that inner discomfort about something you have done, that may be the lamp of the LORD. Do not blow it out. Who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? (1 Cor 2:11). And God searches deeper than we can ever search ourselves.

Steadfast love and faithfulness preserve the king, and by steadfast love his throne is upheld.

A king is not ultimately kept on his throne by armies but by steadfast love and faithfulness, the two great covenant words. Rulers who are loyal and true to their people last. Steadfast love and faithfulness meet (Ps 85:10). And the one King whose throne is upheld forever is the one who is full of both.

verseByVerse.quote: The glory of young men is their strength, but the splendor of old men is their gray hair. Blows that wound cleanse away evil; strokes make clean the innermost parts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glory of young men is their strength, but the splendor of old men is their gray hair.

Every age has its own glory. The young have strength, energy and courage. The old have gray hair, the sign of experience, wisdom and a long life (16:31). Neither should despise the other. The young need the wisdom of the old; the old need the energy of the young. A church or family that honours both is strong.

Blows that wound cleanse away evil; strokes make clean the innermost parts.

The chapter ends on a hard truth. Pain can cleanse. Discipline that hurts, the wound of correction, the painful consequence, can reach the innermost parts and make them clean in a way that gentle words sometimes do not. No one enjoys it at the time. For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness (Heb 12:11).

A believer going through a painful season may be in exactly this place: the strokes of a loving Father, cleansing something deep.

20.theology:
No one can make his own heart pure (v. 9; Rom 3:23); cleansing comes from God (Ps 51:10; 1 John 1:9). God sees deep motives (vv. 5, 27) and hates double standards (vv. 10, 23).

Vengeance belongs to God, and believers wait for him (v. 22; Rom 12:19). Human steps are directed by God beyond our understanding (v. 24; Jer 10:23). Vows must be made thoughtfully (v. 25; Eccl 5:5). Drunkenness leads astray (v. 1; Eph 5:18). Painful discipline can cleanse (v. 30; Heb 12:11).
20.examples:
Noah uncovered in his tent.

Plowing in the cold autumn rain.

A bucket lowered into the deep water of a heart.

"Bad, bad," and then the boast.

A mouthful of gravel.

Handing over a wrong you planned to repay.

Jephthah's rash vow.

The lamp of conscience you should not blow out.

21.title: The Victory Belongs to the LORD
21.text: <sup>1</sup>The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will.<sup>2</sup>Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the heart.<sup>3</sup>To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.<sup>4</sup>Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, are sin.<sup>5</sup>The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty.<sup>6</sup>The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapor and a snare of death.<sup>7</sup>The violence of the wicked will sweep them away, because they refuse to do what is just.<sup>8</sup>The way of the guilty is crooked, but the conduct of the pure is upright.<sup>9</sup>It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife.<sup>10</sup>The soul of the wicked desires evil; his neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes.<sup>11</sup>When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise; when a wise man is instructed, he gains knowledge.<sup>12</sup>The Righteous One observes the house of the wicked; he throws the wicked down to ruin.<sup>13</sup>Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered.<sup>14</sup>A gift in secret averts anger, and a concealed bribe, strong wrath.<sup>15</sup>When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers.<sup>16</sup>One who wanders from the way of good sense will rest in the assembly of the dead.<sup>17</sup>Whoever loves pleasure will be a poor man; 21.overview:
The king's heart is like water in the LORD's hand. The LORD weighs the heart, and righteousness and justice are more acceptable than sacrifice. Diligent plans lead to abundance; treasure gained by lying is a vanishing vapor (vv. 1-8).

A quarrelsome home is worse than a corner of the roof. The Righteous One brings down the wicked. Whoever closes his ear to the poor will not be heard. Justice brings joy to the righteous and terror to evildoers; lovers of pleasure grow poor (vv. 9-19).

The wise save and the fool devours. Pursuing righteousness and kindness finds life and honour. The sluggard craves while the righteous give generously. No wisdom can succeed against the LORD: the horse is prepared for battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD (vv. 20-31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The King's Heart in the LORD's Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will (v. 1). Every way seems right to a man, but the LORD weighs the heart (v. 2). To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice (v. 3). Pride is sin (v. 4). The diligent plan well and the hasty grow poor; treasure gained by lying is a fleeting vapor (vv. 5-6). The violence of the wicked sweeps them away (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: No heart, not even a king's, is outside God's direction, and no religious act replaces a just life.

verseByVerse.quote: The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will. Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will.

Picture a farmer irrigating his field. He digs small channels, and with a movement of his hoe he sends the water this way or that, wherever the crop needs it. The proverb says the heart of a king is like that water in God's hand. The most powerful person in the land, whose decisions seem to shape history, is himself being directed.

Scripture shows it again and again. God put it into the heart of a Persian king to help rebuild the temple: Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king (Ezra 7:27). Nebuchadnezzar, the proudest king on earth, was humbled until you know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will (Dan 4:32).

That is enormous comfort in a world of frightening leaders and elections. No president, dictator or board of directors is outside God's hand. And it is why Paul urges prayer for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life (1 Tim 2:2). Pray for the leaders who worry you. Their hearts are water in God's hand.

Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the heart.

Almost the same as 16:2. Placed right after the king's heart, it applies the same truth to everyone. Each person thinks his way is right. God weighs what is actually inside. The scales we use on ourselves are always flattering.

verseByVerse.quote: To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice. Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, are sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.

God commanded sacrifices in the law. But he never wanted them as a substitute for a righteous life. A worshipper who cheats his workers on Monday and brings an offering on Saturday has misunderstood God completely. Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Sam 15:22). For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hos 6:6). Micah asked what the LORD really wants, and answered: to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God (Mic 6:8).

The modern form of sacrifice is religious activity: attendance, giving, serving on committees. All good. None of it can cover for a life of injustice. God looks first at how we treat people.

Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, are sin.

Pride shows in the eyes and lives in the heart. It is the lamp the wicked walk by, the light they steer their lives with. The ESV notes that lamp may be "the plowing": pride is what the wicked cultivate, the work of their fields. Either way, the verdict is simple: it is sin.

verseByVerse.quote: The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty. The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapor and a snare of death. The violence of the wicked will sweep them away, because they refuse to do what is just. The way of the guilty is crooked, but the conduct of the pure is upright.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty.

Two paths to wealth, and only one works. The diligent plan carefully and work steadily, and it leads surely to abundance. The hasty want it now: the shortcut, the gamble, the scheme. Everyone who goes that way ends poor. Patience is not only a virtue; it is a financial strategy.

The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapor and a snare of death.

Money made by lies is like breath on a cold morning: visible for a second and gone. The ESV notes that many manuscripts read "a vapor for those who seek death". The liar thinks he is seeking treasure; he is seeking death. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes (Jas 4:14). If life itself is a vapor, riches gained by lying are a vapor within a vapor.

The violence of the wicked will sweep them away, because they refuse to do what is just.

The violence the wicked use against others becomes the flood that carries them off. And the root cause is named: they refuse. Their problem is not that they do not know what is just; they will not do it.

The way of the guilty is crooked, but the conduct of the pure is upright.

Guilt bends a person's path. The guilty must twist and turn to avoid being found out. The pure can walk in a straight line because they have nothing to hide.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–19 — The Cry of the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Better a corner of the roof than a house with a quarrelsome wife (v. 9). The wicked show no mercy (v. 10); the simple learn from punished scoffers (v. 11); the Righteous One brings the wicked down (v. 12). Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered (v. 13). A secret gift calms anger (v. 14); justice is joy to the righteous (v. 15). Wandering from sense ends among the dead; lovers of pleasure grow poor (vv. 16-17). The wicked become a ransom for the upright, and a desert is better than a fretful home (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: A person who will not hear the poor will one day find that he is not heard.

verseByVerse.quote: It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife. The soul of the wicked desires evil; his neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes. When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise; when a wise man is instructed, he gains knowledge. The Righteous One observes the house of the wicked; he throws the wicked down to ruin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife.

Houses in Israel had flat roofs, and a man could build a small shelter up there. The proverb says he would be better off living in that cramped corner, exposed to the weather, than sharing a spacious house with constant conflict. It appears again word for word at 25:24, and in a different form at verse 19.

The proverb is written for young men, and it is honest about a real misery. But the point applies to husbands as much as wives. A home can be large and comfortable and unbearable because of the atmosphere in it. What kind of atmosphere do you create at home: the kind people want to come in from the roof to, or escape to it from?

The soul of the wicked desires evil; his neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes.

Wickedness is ultimately a matter of desire. The wicked man does not merely do evil; he wants it. And people who live near him get no mercy.

When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise; when a wise man is instructed, he gains knowledge.

A near repeat of 19:25. The simple learn by watching consequences land on others. The wise learn by being taught. Better to be the second kind of learner.

The Righteous One observes the house of the wicked; he throws the wicked down to ruin.

The ESV prints The Righteous One with capitals: this is God himself. He observes the house of the wicked, watches closely, and in his time brings it down. The wicked man thinks no one is watching his house. Someone is.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered. A gift in secret averts anger, and a concealed bribe, strong wrath. When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered.

This is one of the most sobering proverbs in the book. A person hears the cry of someone in need and deliberately closes his ear. The day will come when he is the one crying out, and no one will answer.

Jesus told the story of a rich man who feasted sumptuously every day, while at his gate lay a poor man named Lazarus who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table (Luke 16:19-21). After death the rich man cried out for mercy, and none came. For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy (Jas 2:13). And John asks, if anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him? (1 John 3:17).

The poor are not always at the gate. Sometimes they are in an email appeal, a news story, a colleague whose family is struggling. Is there a cry you have closed your ear to?

A gift in secret averts anger, and a concealed bribe, strong wrath.

This is an observation, not a recommendation. The ESV notes the Hebrew is "a bribe in the bosom". A quiet gift can calm an angry person, and a bribe can buy off wrath. There is a legitimate form of this: Jacob sending gifts ahead to Esau. And a corrupt form, which Proverbs condemns elsewhere (17:23). The proverb describes how people work, and leaves the reader to use it rightly.

When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers.

The same event, a just verdict, a crime exposed, a corrupt official jailed, produces joy in one group and terror in another. How a person reacts when justice is done shows which group he belongs to. And the final day of justice will be exactly this: joy for those who belong to the Judge, terror for those who do not.

verseByVerse.quote: One who wanders from the way of good sense will rest in the assembly of the dead. Whoever loves pleasure will be a poor man; he who loves wine and oil will not be rich. The wicked is a ransom for the righteous, and the traitor for the upright. It is better to live in a desert land than with a quarrelsome and fretful woman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One who wanders from the way of good sense will rest in the assembly of the dead.

He wandered: not a dramatic rebellion, just a drift off the path. And he ends up resting, but among the dead. The rest he wanted was the rest of the grave. Folly offers rest and delivers death.

Whoever loves pleasure will be a poor man; he who loves wine and oil will not be rich.

Wine and oil were the luxuries of the ancient world. God gave them as good gifts: wine to gladden the heart of man, oil to make his face shine (Ps 104:15). The problem is not enjoying them but loving them. A person who lives for pleasure, spending on every comfort and experience, will be poor, and often poor in more than money.

The wicked is a ransom for the righteous, and the traitor for the upright.

This does not describe atonement. It describes God's justice reversing the plans of the wicked, so that the trouble they planned for the righteous falls on them instead, as Haman hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai. God said to Israel, I give Egypt as your ransom (Isa 43:3).

And the gospel reverses even this proverb in the most astonishing way. There, the Righteous One became the ransom for the wicked. Christ, who was not a traitor, took the place of traitors.

It is better to live in a desert land than with a quarrelsome and fretful woman.

Verse 9 said a corner of the roof; now it is the desert. The picture escalates: better the wilderness, with its heat and loneliness, than a home full of anger and fretting. Constant complaint makes any home a wilderness.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wise store up and the fool devours (v. 20). Whoever pursues righteousness and kindness will find life, righteousness, and honor (v. 21). Wisdom takes strong cities; the guarded mouth avoids trouble; the scoffer is named (vv. 22-24). The sluggard craves and craves, but the righteous gives and does not hold back (vv. 25-26). God hates the sacrifice of the wicked; false witnesses perish (vv. 27-29). No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD. The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD (vv. 30-31).
verseByVerse.theology: Prepare the horse, and trust the LORD for the victory, for no plan can succeed against him.

verseByVerse.quote: Precious treasure and oil are in a wise man's dwelling, but a foolish man devours it. Whoever pursues righteousness and kindness will find life, righteousness, and honor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Precious treasure and oil are in a wise man's dwelling, but a foolish man devours it.

The wise man saves; his house has reserves. The fool devours everything as soon as it comes in. Whatever the income, the fool spends it all. The difference between them is not how much they earn, but what they do with it.

Whoever pursues righteousness and kindness will find life, righteousness, and honor.

A beautiful promise. The person who pursues righteousness and kindness finds three things: life, honour, and righteousness itself. The pursuit is rewarded with more of what was pursued. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied (Matt 5:6). Most people chase honour and miss it. Those who chase righteousness find honour as well.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise man scales the city of the mighty and brings down the stronghold in which they trust. Whoever keeps his mouth and his tongue keeps himself out of trouble. "Scoffer" is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wise man scales the city of the mighty and brings down the stronghold in which they trust.

Strength is not everything. A wise man can capture a city that trusted in its walls. Wisdom beats brute power, in war, in business and in life. The strong trust their strongholds; the wise find a way over.

Whoever keeps his mouth and his tongue keeps himself out of trouble.

A near repeat of 13:3. Most of the trouble a person gets into could have been avoided by keeping quiet.

"Scoffer" is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride.

The proverb gives a definition, piling up words for pride: arrogant, haughty, arrogant pride. That is what a scoffer is. His mockery is not wit; it is pride wearing a smile.

verseByVerse.quote: The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor. All day long he craves and craves, but the righteous gives and does not hold back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor.

The sluggard is not killed by lack of desire. He is killed by desire itself, desire that never gets turned into work. He wants and wants, and his hands will not move. The unfulfilled craving eats him alive.

All day long he craves and craves, but the righteous gives and does not hold back.

Two people. One spends his whole day craving: wanting more, wishing he had it. The other spends his day giving, and does not hold back. What a contrast. The craver never has enough. The giver, who seems to have less because he gives it away, is the one who is full. Jesus said, It is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35).

Which describes your average day: craving or giving?

verseByVerse.quote: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination; how much more when he brings it with evil intent. A false witness will perish, but the word of a man who hears will endure. A wicked man puts on a bold face, but the upright gives thought to his ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination; how much more when he brings it with evil intent.

Verse 3 said justice is better than sacrifice. This goes further. A wicked man's sacrifice is already an abomination (15:8). It is worse still when he brings it with evil intent: using religion to cover a crime, buy favour, or look respectable. Religious show that serves a wicked purpose is doubly offensive to God.

A false witness will perish, but the word of a man who hears will endure.

The liar perishes (compare 19:5, 9). The man who hears, who listens carefully before he speaks, gives testimony that lasts. Careful listening makes for truthful speaking.

A wicked man puts on a bold face, but the upright gives thought to his ways.

The wicked man bluffs. He looks confident, puts on a brave face, and brazens it out. The upright man does something harder: he gives thought to his ways. The ESV notes it may be "establishes" his ways. Bluster hides; reflection builds.

verseByVerse.quote: No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD. The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD.

The chapter builds to its climax. All human wisdom, all understanding, all the counsel of experts: none of it can succeed against the LORD. Three nouns, three denials. When the rulers gathered against Jesus, they thought they were in control, and the church prayed that they had only done whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:28). The greatest crime in history accomplished God's plan of salvation.

The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD.

The war horse was the tank of the ancient world. A wise king prepares his cavalry. The proverb does not say, do not prepare the horse. It says, prepare it, and know that the victory belongs to the LORD. Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God (Ps 20:7). David said to Goliath, the battle is the LORD's (1 Sam 17:47).

Here is the balance of the whole book. Work hard, plan well, study, prepare, get advice, saddle the horse. Then trust God with the outcome, because it is his. The student prepares for the exam and prays. The surgeon trains and trusts. The farmer plows and waits for rain. What is the horse you need to make ready this week, and have you handed its victory to the LORD?

21.theology:
God is sovereign over the hearts of rulers (v. 1; Ezra 7:27; Dan 4:32) and over every plan against him (v. 30; Acts 4:27-28). Human preparation is right, but the outcome belongs to God (v. 31; Ps 20:7).

A just life matters more to God than religious ritual (vv. 3, 27; Mic 6:8; Hos 6:6). Refusing mercy to the poor brings judgment without mercy (v. 13; Luke 16:19-25; Jas 2:13). Righteousness and generosity are pursued and rewarded (vv. 21, 26; Matt 5:6).
21.examples:
A farmer directing irrigation water with his hoe.

Praying for the leaders who worry you.

Cheating on Monday and giving on Saturday.

Breath on a cold morning.

A corner of the roof, and a desert.

The rich man and Lazarus at the gate.

Craving all day, or giving all day.

Saddling the horse and trusting the LORD for the victory.

22.title: A Good Name
22.text: <sup>1</sup>A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold.<sup>2</sup>The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the Maker of them all.<sup>3</sup>The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it.<sup>4</sup>The reward for humility and fear of the LORD is riches and honor and life.<sup>5</sup>Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them.<sup>6</sup>Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it.<sup>7</sup>The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender.<sup>8</sup>Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity, and the rod of his fury will fail.<sup>9</sup>Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor.<sup>10</sup>Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease.<sup>11</sup>He who loves purity of heart, and whose speech is gracious, will have the king as his friend.<sup>12</sup>The eyes of the LORD keep watch over knowledge, but he overthrows the words of the traitor.<sup>13</sup>The sluggard says, "There is a lion outside! I shall be killed in the streets!"<sup>14</sup>The mouth of forbidden women is a deep pit; he with whom the LORD is angry will fall into it.<sup>15</sup>Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him.<sup>16</sup>Whoever oppresses the poor to increase his own wealth, or gives to the rich, will only come to poverty.<sup>17</sup>Incline your ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply your heart to my knowledge,<sup>18</sup>for it will be pleasant if you keep them within you, if all of them are ready on your lips.<sup>19</sup>That your trust may be in the LORD, I have made them known to you today, even to you.<sup>20</sup>Have I not written for you thirty sayings of counsel and knowledge,<sup>21</sup>to make you know what is right and true, that you may give a true answer to those who sent you?<sup>22</sup>Do not rob the poor, because he is poor, or crush the afflicted at the gate,<sup>23</sup>for the LORD will plead their cause and rob of life those who rob them.<sup>24</sup>Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man,<sup>25</sup>lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.<sup>26</sup>Be not one of those who give pledges, who put up security for debts.<sup>27</sup>If you have nothing with which to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you?<sup>28</sup>Do not move the ancient landmark that your fathers have set.<sup>29</sup>Do you see a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings; he will not stand before obscure men.
22.overview:
Chapter 22 opens the collection's most famous verse — "a good name is to be chosen rather than great riches" (v.1) — and then pivots to "the thirty sayings of the wise" (vv.17–24:22), a section with remarkable parallels to the Egyptian wisdom text Instruction of Amenemope. That such wisdom appeared across cultures does not diminish Scripture; it shows that general revelation seeds wisdom broadly, while special revelation perfects and redeems it.

The chapter holds together two great themes: reputation rightly ordered (vv.1–9) and instruction rightly received (vv.17–29). A good name is not a brand to manage but a life poured out in integrity before God. The rich and poor alike bear the LORD's image (v.2) — a leveling that should dismantle both pride and contempt.

Timothy Keller notes that "fear of the LORD" (v.4) is the engine beneath all genuine wisdom. Humility before God produces the kind of person whose name becomes, almost accidentally, a good one. The one who grasps for reputation loses it; the one who fears God gains it freely.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 22 — A Good Name, Train Up a Child, and the Thirty Sayings of the Wise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 22 is transitional: vv.1-16 continue the Solomonic antithetical proverbs, then v.17 introduces 'The Words of the Wise' (22:17-24:22), which bears resemblance to the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope. This section is more extended and instructional in form, addressed directly to the son. The thirty sayings (v.20) are a distinct literary unit within this section.
verseByVerse.theology: The opening verse—a good name chosen over riches—is one of Proverbs' most foundational value statements. Reputation built on integrity is more valuable than wealth. The training of children (v.6) is a call to individualized formation: 'the way he should go' may carry the sense of 'the way suited to him.' The promise is covenantal: faithful formation has reliable results over the long arc of a life.
verseByVerse.examples: The thirty sayings begin with the most urgent social ethics (v.22: do not rob the poor; v.24: avoid the angry man) before moving toward financial wisdom and the skill of the craftsman (v.29). The pedagogy is practical and urgent: these are not theoretical principles but survival wisdom for a young man entering public life.

verseByVerse.quote: A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold. The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the Maker of them all. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold.

The verb is chosen, which means the two are being offered as alternatives. Proverbs is not saying a man may have both; it is putting them on a table and telling him to pick, because in practice there are moments when he must.

And the reason a name is worth more is in its economics. Money can be replaced — men have lost everything at fifty and rebuilt it. A name cannot. It is assembled over decades out of small consistencies and can be spent in a single afternoon, and the man who spends it discovers that there is no market in which to buy another.

Then v. 2, which is one of the great levelling sentences of the Old Testament: the rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the Maker of them all.

They meet. In a village they could not avoid each other — the same well, the same gate, the same road — and Proverbs says the meeting itself is instructive, because the one thing that is true of both of them is the thing neither arranged.

And it is the deepest ground there is for how a Christian treats people. Not that the poor man is virtuous, and not that the rich man is guilty. Both were made, by the same hand, and neither had any say in which of the two he turned out to be — which is why contempt in either direction is finally a remark about the Maker.

verseByVerse.quote: The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it. The reward for humility and fear of the LORD is riches and honor and life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it.

Two men and one hazard, and the difference is entirely in the first verb: one of them sees. Everything else follows from that, and it is why this book spends so much time on perception rather than on courage.

And note that the prudent man’s response is not to confront the danger or to prepare for it. He hides. There is no heroism anywhere in the verse — Proverbs regards getting out of the way as an entirely respectable outcome, which is a useful corrective in a Christian culture that often mistakes exposure for faith.

The simple, meanwhile, does the most natural thing in the world. He goes on. He does not decide to walk into it; he simply continues, because continuing requires no decision, and the verse says he pays for it.

Then v. 4: the reward for humility and fear of the LORD is riches and honor and life. Read with the whole book this is the ordinary shape of things rather than a contract — and note which qualities are named. Not competence. Humility, and the fear of God, which are the two things a man cannot fake for long and cannot acquire by wanting the reward.

verseByVerse.quote: Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them. Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them. The crooked road is not merely wrong, it is unpleasant — snagged and trapped, the hedge of thorns of 15:19. And the counsel is distance again: not vigilance on that road, but staying off it.

Then v. 6, and this verse has done more damage to more godly parents than any other sentence in Proverbs: train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it.

Take the promise first and take it seriously, because it is real. The years of a childhood are formative in a way nothing later is; what a child absorbs before he can evaluate it goes in deeper than anything argued into him at thirty. Proverbs is telling parents that the work repays doing and that it lasts, and that is true and ought to be believed.

And take the word train. The Hebrew root has to do with dedicating something — the same root as the word for the dedication of a house or the temple. It is not primarily instruction. It is the setting apart of a child for a purpose, which is a much larger and more patient activity than teaching him things.

Now the pastoral matter, and it must be said plainly, because a great many people reading this verse are reading it with a grown child in mind who has walked away.

This is a proverb. It is not a promise with God’s name attached and it never was. Everything in this book speaks of how life generally runs, and every reader has already accepted that elsewhere — that the diligent generally prosper, that the righteous are generally delivered — while knowing Job exists. It is only at this verse that people suddenly demand it be a guarantee, and then conclude, when it fails, that the fault must have been theirs.

Consider what that conclusion actually requires. It requires that no child raised well ever rebels, which the Bible itself contradicts on nearly every page. God is the perfect Father. His instruction was flawless, his household was Eden, and his children walked out of it — Children have I reared and brought up, but they have rebelled against me (Isaiah 1:2). Whatever Proverbs 22:6 means, it cannot mean that a departed child proves a failed parent, or the charge lands first on God.
