Some readers take the Hebrew to say according to his way — according to the child’s own bent, his particular making — and that reading has a long history and a good deal to commend it. Either way the verse stands as it always did: an encouragement to do the work, not a receipt issued in advance.

And to the parent whose child is gone: the training was not wasted, and it is not finished. What was put in early does not evaporate; it waits. There is a long list in Scripture of people who came back much later, and the man who wrote the parable of a son who went into a far country was not describing a father who had failed.

verseByVerse.quote: The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender. Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity, and the rod of his fury will fail. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender.

No comment is attached. Proverbs simply states the mechanics of debt in the plainest language available and lets the word slave sit there.

And it is not an exaggeration, as anybody in real debt will confirm. What is lost is not money — the money was spent and enjoyed. What is lost is the ability to decide. A man in debt cannot leave the job, cannot take the risk, cannot say no to the client, cannot move, cannot give what he wants to give. Somebody else’s schedule now governs a large part of his life, and it will do so for a determined number of years.

Note that borrowing is not called sin here. Scripture regulates lending rather than forbidding borrowing, and there are debts a wise man takes on with his eyes open. What the verse insists on is that the transaction has a second half that is never printed on the advertisement: the money arrives now, and a portion of his freedom leaves with the same post.

Then v. 8: whoever sows injustice will reap calamity, and the rod of his fury will fail. The image is a man whose weapon breaks in his hand — which is the whole doctrine of this book about violence, delivered in one clause.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor. Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor.

The Hebrew is literally a good eye, and it is an idiom for generosity — the opposite of the evil eye, which is the grudging, calculating look. Which locates generosity somewhere surprising: not in the hand, and not in the bank balance, but in how a man sees.

That is why generosity cannot be produced by a decision about percentages. A man with a good eye notices things — that somebody is short, that a coat is thin, that a family has gone quiet about money — and the noticing happens before any giving is considered. A man without one can walk past the same information for years and be entirely sincere in saying that nobody asked.

Then v. 10: drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease.

An uncomfortable verse and a necessary one. It says that some conflict in a community is not a systemic problem or a failure of process. It is one person, and it will continue for exactly as long as he is there, and it will stop when he goes.

The uncomfortable part is what that requires of a leader, since removing somebody is the hardest thing anybody in a church or a team ever has to do, and there is always a case for one more conversation. Proverbs says the arithmetic plainly: while he stays, everybody else pays. And 9:8 has already ruled out the gentler option, because this man cannot be reproved into changing.

verseByVerse.quote: He who loves purity of heart, and whose speech is gracious, will have the king as his friend. The eyes of the LORD keep watch over knowledge, but he overthrows the words of the traitor. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who loves purity of heart, and whose speech is gracious, will have the king as his friend. Two qualities, one internal and one visible, and the promise attached is access — which is exactly the currency of a royal court, where everybody was manoeuvring for it.

And the route named here is the one nobody attempts. Purity of heart and gracious speech are not strategies; they cannot be adopted for the purpose without ceasing to be themselves. Which is the quiet joke in the verse: the way to the king’s friendship turns out to be available only to the man who was not working on getting it.

Then v. 12: the eyes of the LORD keep watch over knowledge, but he overthrows the words of the traitor.

Truth is described as having a guard on it. Not that lies are prevented — the second half concedes that the traitor speaks, and history is largely a record of successful falsehood. What is promised is that God is keeping watch over the truth itself, so that it survives the people who suppress it and is still there when they are not.

Remember that in an age of manufactured accounts. A lie has to be maintained by somebody. The truth is being looked after.

verseByVerse.quote: The sluggard says, "There is a lion outside! I shall be killed in the streets!" The mouth of forbidden women is a deep pit; he with whom the LORD is angry will fall into it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sluggard says, There is a lion outside! I shall be killed in the streets!

This is the funniest verse in Proverbs and one of the most penetrating, and everything is in the excuse.

He does not say he is tired. He does not say he would rather not. He produces a reason of the highest possible seriousness — a lion, in the street, and mortal danger — which is unanswerable if true and cannot be checked without going outside, which is precisely what he is declining to do.

And the sluggard has not chosen a small excuse, because a small one could be dealt with. He has chosen a magnificent one. Anybody who has managed people, or been part of a family, knows the shape: the reason offered for not doing the thing is always larger and more principled than the thing itself, and to question it would seem unkind.

Which yields a diagnostic anybody may run on himself. When you have not done something you intended to do, listen to the size of the reason. If it is a matter of principle, or of health, or of somebody else’s failure, and it has grown noticeably since last week, there may be a lion in it.

Then v. 14: the mouth of forbidden women is a deep pit. The mouth again, as in chs 5 to 7 — never the face. And a pit is not a wall a man collides with. It is under the surface, and he is walking normally right up until the moment there is nothing beneath him.

verseByVerse.quote: Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him. Whoever oppresses the poor to increase his own wealth, or gives to the rich, will only come to poverty. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him.

The first half is a doctrine of human nature stated in one clause, and it is the most realistic sentence about children in the Bible. Folly is not learned from bad company; it is bound up — tied in, native, present before any influence arrives. Every parent discovers this at about eighteen months and no parent had to teach it.

Which settles a question the modern world keeps reopening. Children are not blank and they are not naturally good and gradually corrupted. They arrive with something in them, and the loveliest child anybody has ever had is included in the description.

The second half is the rod of 13:24, and it carries the same guard: godly readers differ on whether this requires corporal punishment today, and the argument on both sides was set out there. What is not in dispute is the direction of the verse. Something native has to be driven out, and it will not leave on its own, and a parent who does nothing is not being gentle — he is leaving his child bound up with it.

Then v. 16: whoever oppresses the poor to increase his own wealth, or gives to the rich, will only come to poverty. The two halves are the same instinct in opposite directions — taking from those with no power and flattering those with plenty — and both are described as bad business.

verseByVerse.quote: Incline your ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply your heart to my knowledge, for it will be pleasant if you keep them within you, if all of them are ready on your lips. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Incline your ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply your heart to my knowledge.

Something has changed here. The Solomonic collection has ended, and a new section begins — the words of the wise, running to 24:22 — and the voice returns to the personal address of chs 1 to 9 after twelve chapters of impersonal sayings.

Which is a small thing with a large implication. Wisdom keeps returning to a person talking to a person. It can be collected into sentences and stored, and every so often somebody has to sit down opposite somebody and say listen to me.

Then v. 18 gives the reason, and it is not the one expected: for it will be pleasant if you keep them within you, if all of them are ready on your lips.

Pleasant. Not useful, not safe. And take the two conditions seriously as instructions: kept within you, which is memory and meditation, and ready on your lips, which is the ability to produce the thing at speed — because wisdom that must be looked up is not available in the four seconds when it is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: That your trust may be in the LORD, I have made them known to you today, even to you. Have I not written for you thirty sayings of counsel and knowledge, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
That your trust may be in the LORD, I have made them known to you today, even to you.

Here is the purpose of the whole book, stated once, plainly, and it is not what a casual reader would guess. Not that you may be prudent. Not that your life may go well. That your trust may be in the LORD.

Which reframes everything that has come before it. All the practical counsel — the money, the speech, the ant, the scales, the sluggard, the quarrelsome household — was aimed at producing trust. Wisdom in this book is not an alternative to faith and it is not a supplement to it. It is the shape a trusting life takes on a Tuesday.

And the last three words are a surprise: even to you. The teacher stops in the middle of a sentence to make sure the reader knows the address on it. A book of general maxims turns and looks at one person.

Then v. 20: have I not written for you thirty sayings of counsel and knowledge? The number is not decorative. There survives an Egyptian collection called the Instruction of Amenemope, arranged in thirty chapters, and several sayings in this section run remarkably close to it — which has troubled some readers and should not. Scripture has never been embarrassed to take what is true wherever it is found and set it in the fear of the LORD, and the borrowing, if that is what it is, has been converted by v. 19: that your trust may be in the LORD. No Egyptian sage wrote that line.

verseByVerse.quote: to make you know what is right and true, that you may give a true answer to those who sent you? Do not rob the poor, because he is poor, or crush the afflicted at the gate, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
To make you know what is right and true, that you may give a true answer to those who sent you.

The aim is a man who can be sent — trusted with a message, and relied on to bring back an accurate one. That is the faithful envoy of 13:17, and it is still the rarest quality in any organisation.

Then v. 22 opens the thirty sayings, and it is remarkable what comes first: do not rob the poor, because he is poor, or crush the afflicted at the gate.

Of everything the collection could have begun with, it begins here. And the phrase because he is poor is the sting. That is the reason he was chosen — not that he is dishonest, or difficult, or in the way, but that he is the one who cannot do anything about it. Robbing him carries no risk, which is the entire attraction.

And at the gate puts it in the courthouse. This is not burglary; it is the legal system, working correctly in every visible respect, operated by people who can afford it against a man who cannot. Which is how most injustice has always been done — not by breaking the law but by being better resourced inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: for the LORD will plead their cause and rob of life those who rob them. Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the LORD will plead their cause and rob of life those who rob them.

The poor man had no advocate at the gate — that was the whole problem in v. 22. So God takes the brief himself, and the legal language is exact: he pleads their cause, which is what a counsel does, standing up in court on behalf of a party who cannot speak for himself.

And the reciprocity in the second half is deliberate: those who rob him will be robbed. He is not merely punished; he is treated in the currency he chose.

Which puts anybody in a position of advantage on notice. The person on the other side of the transaction may have no representation, no leverage and no realistic prospect of complaint. He has counsel, and the counsel has never lost.

Then v. 24: make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man. The verse assumes what people deny — that character is contagious — and it does not suggest arguing with him. It says do not be around him, which is the same counsel as 14:7 and for the same reason.

verseByVerse.quote: lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare. Be not one of those who give pledges, who put up security for debts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.

The verb is learn, and it is passive learning — nobody sets out to acquire a temper. It is picked up, the way an accent is picked up, by proximity and repetition and without any moment at which a decision was made.

And the mechanism should be named, because it explains something people find puzzling in themselves. A man who spends two years around somebody who is quick to take offence will find, gradually, that his own threshold has moved. Things that would not have registered now register. He has not adopted a philosophy; he has been re-tuned, and he will experience the change as having become more discerning.

Then v. 26: be not one of those who give pledges, who put up security for debts. The fourth time this book has warned about surety (6:1; 11:15; 17:18), and the phrasing here is about identity rather than action — do not be one of those. It is describing a type of man who does this repeatedly, generously, and never learns.

verseByVerse.quote: If you have nothing with which to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you? Do not move the ancient landmark that your fathers have set. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you have nothing with which to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you?

The picture is precise and domestic. Not the house, not the field — the bed, taken out from under a sleeping man. That is what the last stage of an unpayable guarantee looked like, and the verse asks the only question that matters about it: why.

Because there is no good answer. He gained nothing; he was not even the borrower. He is losing the last object in the house for a transaction that never benefited him at all, and the whole thing began with a handshake he did not want to refuse in front of somebody.

Then v. 28: do not move the ancient landmark that your fathers have set.

A boundary stone marked where one man’s land ended and another’s began, and moving one at night was the perfect crime — silent, deniable, and it stole from a neighbour by inches. It was forbidden in the law with a curse attached (Deuteronomy 19:14; 27:17), and Proverbs adds one word to it: ancient.

Which is where the verse reaches past land. Some things were settled a long time ago by people who are not here to argue for them, and a generation which finds the reason for a boundary unobvious is not thereby entitled to move it. The stones were put there by men who had seen what happened without them.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you see a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings; he will not stand before obscure men. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you see a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings; he will not stand before obscure men.

The chapter ends with a question, an observation, and no moral attached — and it is one of the most encouraging sentences in the book for ordinary people.

The man is not described as ambitious, well connected, or eloquent. He is skilful in his work, which is a thing anybody in any trade can become by doing the same thing carefully for long enough. And the promise is not that he will be famous. It is that he will end up in rooms his position does not entitle him to, because competence is scarce and eventually somebody looks for it.

That is the same claim as 18:16 — a man’s gift makes room for him — and it is a thing to have in a culture that assumes advancement is a matter of self-presentation. Proverbs says the doors open from the other side, to people who were busy getting good at something.

And it stands as a quiet dignity given to every trade. The joiner, the nurse, the accountant, the woman who runs a small office properly — this book puts them in front of kings, on the strength of nothing but having done the work well. Which is finally a statement about God, who made a world in which excellence tells, and who spent the first thirty years of his own life in a workshop before anybody heard him speak.

22.theology:
The LORD as Maker of Rich and Poor. Verse 2 is theologically dense. To say that the LORD made both rich and poor is not to endorse economic inequality as divinely ordained but to strip class of ultimate significance. Both are equally creatures, equally sinners, equally in need of grace. Christian theology presses further: both are equally candidates for redemption, equally called to table fellowship. The cross is the great leveling — "there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free" (Gal. 3:28).

Humility and the Fear of the LORD (v.4). Proverbs keeps returning to this pair. Humility is not self-deprecation; it is accurate sight — seeing oneself as creature before Creator. The fear of the LORD is the relational disposition that keeps that sight clear. Together they produce a life of remarkable freedom: freed from status anxiety, freed from the grasping that destroys the soul. "Riches and honor and life" are given, not seized.
22.examples:
Then: Israelite parents would teach children in the rhythms of daily life — working, eating, traveling (Deut. 6:7). The craftsman's workshop was also a school of character. The "gate" was where elders like Boaz administered justice publicly (Ruth 4:1). Chapter 22's advice was entirely practical for a society where reputation, work quality, and economic justice were intertwined in visible community life.

Now: In an age of curated digital personas, "a good name" (v.1) has never been more misunderstood. The proverb cuts against impression management — the good name Proverbs values cannot be manufactured online. Verse 6 speaks to parents worried their children will abandon the faith: wisdom-shaped formation is deeper than we know, even when the season of apparent departure is long. And verses 22–23 call the church to advocate concretely for economic justice — not as political performance, but as the natural overflow of fearing the God who defends the poor.

23.title: Do Not Wear Yourself Out to Get Rich
23.text: <sup>1</sup>When you sit down to eat with a ruler, observe carefully what is before you,<sup>2</sup>and put a knife to your throat if you are given to appetite.<sup>3</sup>Do not desire his delicacies, for they are deceptive food.<sup>4</sup>Do not toil to acquire wealth; be discerning enough to desist.<sup>5</sup>When your eyes light on it, it is gone, for suddenly it sprouts wings, flying like an eagle toward heaven.<sup>6</sup>Do not eat the bread of a man who is stingy; do not desire his delicacies,<sup>7</sup>for he is like one who is inwardly calculating. "Eat and drink!" he says to you, but his heart is not with you.<sup>8</sup>You will vomit up the morsels that you have eaten, and waste your pleasant words.<sup>9</sup>Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, for he will despise the good sense of your words.<sup>10</sup>Do not move an ancient landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless,<sup>11</sup>for their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you.<sup>12</sup>Apply your heart to instruction and your ear to words of knowledge.<sup>13</sup>Do not withhold discipline from a child; if you strike him with a rod, he will not die.<sup>14</sup>If you strike him with the rod, you will save his soul from Sheol.<sup>15</sup>My son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will be glad.<sup>16</sup>My inmost being will exult when your lips speak what is right.<sup>17</sup>Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day.<sup>18</sup>Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off.<sup>19</sup>Hear, my son, and be wise, and direct your heart in the way.<sup>20</sup>Be not among drunkards or among gluttonous eaters of meat,<sup>21</sup>for the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty, and slumber will clothe them with rags.<sup>22</sup>Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old.<sup>23</sup>Buy truth, and do not sell it; buy wisdom, instruction, and understanding.<sup>24</sup>The father of the righteous will greatly rejoice; he who fathers a wise son will be glad in him.<sup>25</sup>Let your father and mother be glad; let her who bore you rejoice.<sup>26</sup>My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes observe my ways.<sup>27</sup>For a prostitute is a deep pit; an adulteress is a narrow well.<sup>28</sup>She lies in wait like a robber and increases the traitors among mankind.<sup>29</sup>Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaining? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes?<sup>30</sup>Those who tarry long over wine; those who go to try mixed wine.<sup>31</sup>Do not look at wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and goes down smoothly.<sup>32</sup>In the end it bites like a serpent and stings like an adder.<sup>33</sup>Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart utter perverse things.<sup>34</sup>You will be like one who lies down in the midst of the sea, like one who lies on the top of a mast.<sup>35</sup>"They struck me," you will say, "but I was not hurt; they beat me, but I did not feel it. When shall I awake? I must have another drink."
23.overview:
Chapter 23 is a series of urgent parental instructions addressing three great idols: wealth, food and pleasure, and intoxication. The framing device — a son being warned before a meal with a ruler (vv.1–3) and warned again before wine (vv.29–35) — is deliberate. What we eat and drink, and with whom, shapes character more than we imagine.

The center of the chapter is a pair of commands that belong together: "Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day. Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off" (vv.17–18). The antidote to the fool's prosperity is not resignation but eschatological confidence — a hope rooted in the character of God, not the circumstances of the moment.

Keller reads verse 23 — "Buy truth, and do not sell it" — as the heart of the chapter. Truth is not a commodity; it is a person (John 14:6). The wisdom tradition points toward One whose price was infinite and whose gift is freely given.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 23 — Table Manners, Ambition, Parental Formation, and the Last Woe
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 23 contains some of Proverbs' most memorable passages: the dinner table with a ruler (vv.1-3), the wealth that sprouts wings (v.5), the appeal to the heart ('give me your heart,' v.26), the parents' joy in the wise child (vv.24-25), and the devastating portrait of the drunkard (vv.29-35). The chapter is more discursive and extended than the short antithetical couplets of chapters 10-22.
verseByVerse.theology: The extended parent-child address of vv.15-25 is one of the emotional high points of the book: 'My son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will be glad' (v.15). The father's joy in the child's wisdom is the goal of all the instruction. The mother's teaching appears explicitly in v.22 alongside the father's; the formation of wisdom is a shared parental project.
verseByVerse.examples: The portrait of the drunkard (vv.29-35) is one of the most vivid character studies in the Bible: the woe questions, the progression of symptoms (redness of eyes, strange sights, perverse speech), and the self-defeating conclusion: 'I will seek it yet again.' This is addiction described with psychological precision two millennia before modern science.

verseByVerse.quote: When you sit down to eat with a ruler, observe carefully what is before you, and put a knife to your throat if you are given to appetite. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you sit down to eat with a ruler, observe carefully what is before you, and put a knife to your throat if you are given to appetite.

The scene is a young man invited to dine somewhere above his station, and the counsel is startlingly violent for a dinner party. A knife at your own throat, over food.

What makes the moment dangerous is not the meal but what the meal is doing. In that world a great man’s table was a mechanism: the invitation created an obligation, and the guest who ate freely and enjoyed himself had, without any agreement being spoken of, become somebody who owed something. Which is exactly how it still works, and everybody who has been taken to an expensive lunch by somebody who wanted something knows the feeling.

And the phrase observe carefully what is before you is doing more than telling him to look at the plate. It means: understand the situation you are sitting in. The food is the visible part.

The knife, then, is a picture of how much self-command the moment requires — because a man given to appetite will not think about any of this. He will simply enjoy the meal, and find out later what it cost.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not desire his delicacies, for they are deceptive food. Do not toil to acquire wealth; be discerning enough to desist. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not desire his delicacies, for they are deceptive food. The word is literally bread of lies. Nothing is wrong with the food; the lie is in what the food is saying, which is that this is hospitality and there is nothing else in it.

Then vv. 4 and 5 turn from a rich man’s table to a man’s own ambition, and they contain one of the most quietly devastating instructions in the Bible: do not toil to acquire wealth; be discerning enough to desist.

Note that toil is not the same as work. Proverbs commends work in almost every chapter. The Hebrew here is about wearying oneself, driving oneself — and the object is wealth as such, pursued for its own sake, with no figure at which the pursuit ends.

And the command is one nobody ever expects to find in Scripture: desist. Stop. Not redirect the money, not give more of it away, not hold it loosely while continuing to chase it. Have the discernment to stop chasing.

Which requires a man to answer a question he has probably never put to himself — what the figure is. Almost nobody has one. Ask a man what amount would be enough and he will say he has not thought about it, and the reason he has not thought about it is that thinking about it would end the pursuit, and the pursuit is the part he cannot give up.

verseByVerse.quote: When your eyes light on it, it is gone, for suddenly it sprouts wings, flying like an eagle toward heaven. Do not eat the bread of a man who is stingy; do not desire his delicacies, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
When your eyes light on it, it is gone, for suddenly it sprouts wings, flying like an eagle toward heaven.

The picture is deliberately absurd, and the absurdity is the argument. Money is described as a bird that grows wings while you are looking at it — not stolen, not spent, not lost through foolishness. It simply goes, upward, at speed, and there is a man standing in a field watching it get smaller.

And the striking part is the timing: when your eyes light on it. The moment of arrival is the moment of departure. Which is the exact experience of anybody who has finally reached a financial target — the odd flatness of the week it happened, and the discovery, within a month or two, that the figure has quietly moved.

Then v. 6 begins a second table scene, and this host is worse than the ruler: do not eat the bread of a man who is stingy; do not desire his delicacies. The Hebrew is a man with an evil eye — the exact opposite of the good eye of 22:9. He is giving you dinner and counting it.

verseByVerse.quote: for he is like one who is inwardly calculating. "Eat and drink!" he says to you, but his heart is not with you. You will vomit up the morsels that you have eaten, and waste your pleasant words. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he is like one who is inwardly calculating. Eat and drink! he says to you, but his heart is not with you.

There is the whole thing in one sentence, and it is one of the most exact descriptions of insincere hospitality ever written. He says the right words. The words are warm and generous and correctly chosen. And the sums are running the entire time.

Everybody has sat at that table and most people could not have said what was wrong. That is what makes the verse valuable: it names an experience people routinely dismiss as their own oversensitivity. Something is off, the welcome does not land, and there is no evidence whatever, because nothing has been said or done wrong.

Then v. 8: you will vomit up the morsels that you have eaten, and waste your pleasant words.

The physical image is coarse and it is chosen with care. The meal will not stay down. But the second loss is the one to notice — the pleasant words, wasted. The guest was generous back. He was appreciative, he opened up, he said the warm true things a good guest says, and every one of them went into a man who was calculating.

Which is a real cost and a rarely counted one. Genuine warmth spent on somebody who is not there to receive it is not merely unreciprocated. It is spent, and a person only has so much.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, for he will despise the good sense of your words. Do not move an ancient landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not speak in the hearing of a fool, for he will despise the good sense of your words.

The same counsel as 9:8, and the reason given is a warning about what will happen to what is said. He will despise it — not disagree, not fail to understand. He will take a good thing and hold it cheap, and once he has done so it cannot be un-cheapened.

Which is why the Lord’s warning about pearls before swine (Matthew 7:6) is a mercy toward the pearls rather than a judgment on the pigs. Some things ought not to be said in some rooms, not because the hearers are unworthy of them but because saying them there destroys them.

Then v. 10: do not move an ancient landmark or enter the fields of the fatherless. The boundary stone of 22:28, and now the victim is named: the fatherless, who has no man to stand at the gate for him and no prospect of being believed against an adult.

The crime is chosen for its safety. It is quiet, it moves a line by inches, and there is nobody at all to complain — which is exactly the sort of wrong most likely to be committed, and exactly the sort about to be answered in the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: for their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you. Apply your heart to instruction and your ear to words of knowledge. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For their Redeemer is strong; he will plead their cause against you.

The word is go’el, and it is one of the great words of the Old Testament. The go’el was the nearest male relative, and his job was everything an orphan in v. 10 has nobody to do: to buy back land the family had lost, to redeem a relative sold into slavery, to stand up in court and take the case, to avenge a killing. He was the family member who had the standing to act when you had none.

And the whole force of this verse is that the fatherless boy, who by definition has no such relative, turns out to have one — and he is strong. Which was the entire calculation of the man moving the stone: that there was nobody. He was wrong about the only thing that mattered.

This is the word Job reached for in the worst hour of his life: I know that my Redeemer lives (Job 19:25). It is what Boaz became for a destitute foreign widow. It runs the whole length of Scripture and it is not a metaphor about God being kind. It is a legal office, and God takes it.

And it required, in the end, that the Redeemer be a relative — which is why the letter to the Hebrews labours the point that he had to be made like his brothers in every respect (Hebrews 2:14-17). He took flesh in order to have the standing. The go’el of the fatherless became one of us so that he could buy back what we had lost, and he paid for the field with his own blood.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not withhold discipline from a child; if you strike him with a rod, he will not die. If you strike him with the rod, you will save his soul from Sheol. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not withhold discipline from a child; if you strike him with a rod, he will not die. If you strike him with the rod, you will save his soul from Sheol.

The rod passage of 13:24 and 22:15, at its strongest, and the argument in it is one of scale. The father is answering a parent’s natural flinch — the fear of doing harm — and he answers it by comparing two harms. Correction hurts and does not kill; what is being prevented is the road that ends in Sheol.

Which is the reasoning underneath all discipline properly understood. A parent who will not cause a small pain now is choosing a larger one later, on his child’s behalf, and describing the choice to himself as gentleness.

On the question of whether the rod requires corporal punishment today, the two readings were set out at 13:24 and both are held by people who love Scripture and their children. What is not in question here is the direction of the passage, and it is not really about method at all: it is about a parent who will not act, and a road that goes somewhere.

And the line must be repeated because these verses have been abused. Nothing here permits a parent to strike a child in anger, or to injure, or to frighten. The verse says explicitly he will not die, which sets a limit rather than granting a licence, and the New Testament adds the other half in the same breath as the command to train: do not provoke your children to anger (Ephesians 6:4). Discipline in Scripture is calm, consistent and costly to the parent. A household where a child is afraid is not obeying this verse; it is the thing this verse exists to prevent.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will be glad. My inmost being will exult when your lips speak what is right. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, if your heart is wise, my heart too will be glad. My inmost being will exult when your lips speak what is right.

After the rod, this. And the placing is not accidental — the two passages are four verses apart and they belong to the same man.

What is being disclosed here is the motive underneath everything the father has said since ch. 1. He is not managing his son’s behaviour, and he is not protecting his own reputation. He wants his boy to be wise because it would make him glad, and the language he uses for the gladness is the strongest available: my inmost being will exult — literally his kidneys, which in Hebrew are the seat of the deepest feeling, and a verb meaning to leap.

Which is a considerable thing for a father to say to a son, and most sons never hear it. A great many men grew up entirely certain of what their father wanted them to do and never once suspected that their father’s happiness was tied to how they turned out.

And it is the note the whole Bible ends on, applied upward. God is not described as satisfied by his people’s obedience. He is described as rejoicing over them with gladness, and exulting over them with loud singing (Zephaniah 3:17).

verseByVerse.quote: Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day. Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day.

Here is the oldest difficulty in the life of faith, named without embarrassment. Not doubt about God’s existence — envy. The wicked are doing well, and the person who is trying to live rightly can see it, and something in him wants what they have.

The psalmist said the same thing and was more explicit about how far it went: he almost slipped, he says, because he was envious of the arrogant when he saw the prosperity of the wicked (Psalm 73:2-3). This is not a minor temptation for the immature. It nearly took a man who wrote Scripture.

And the counter offered is deliberately unglamorous: continue in the fear of the LORD all the day. Not resolve the question. Not obtain an explanation. Continue — keep going, today, without the answer, which is what faith mostly is.

Then v. 18, and it is the answer, though a small one: surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off.

That is all the Old Testament can say here, and it is enough to stand on. The word is aharit — an afterward, a latter end. Whatever is visible now is not the finished account. The psalmist got the same answer and got it in the same place: he could not work it out until he went into the sanctuary of God, and then he discerned their end (Psalm 73:17).

Envy is finally a failure of perspective rather than of morals. It is what happens when a man prices two lives at the halfway point.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, my son, and be wise, and direct your heart in the way. Be not among drunkards or among gluttonous eaters of meat, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear, my son, and be wise, and direct your heart in the way. The verb is a navigational one — set your heart straight down the road — and it assumes what the whole book assumes: that a heart has a direction and can be pointed.

Then v. 20 introduces the chapter’s last and longest subject: be not among drunkards or among gluttonous eaters of meat.

Two appetites, and it is worth noticing that they are named together and that only one of them is ever preached about. Gluttony is the sin the modern church has quietly retired, and Proverbs puts it in the same sentence as drunkenness without any sense that it is the lesser item.

And the counsel is again about company rather than conduct. Not do not get drunk — do not be among them. Because appetite is social: it is learned, normalised, and calibrated by the people a man eats with, and nobody has ever developed a serious drinking problem alone.

verseByVerse.quote: for the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty, and slumber will clothe them with rags. Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty, and slumber will clothe them with rags.

The image in the second half is the memorable one. Slumber is described as clothing — something that goes on a man, gradually, garment by garment, until it is what he is wearing and what everyone sees.

And the mechanism is honest. It is not that drink costs money, though it does. It is that both appetites produce sleep, and sleep is the thing that quietly removes the mornings, and a life is made of mornings.

Then v. 22: listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old.

The second clause is the one that stops a reader, because it names a moment nobody plans for. When she is old. Not when she is teaching you and you are twelve — when she is diminished, repeating herself, slower than the room, and no longer of any practical use to anybody.

Contempt at that stage is easy and almost invisible. It is in the tone of the answer, the impatience at the third telling, the speaking about her over her head as though she were not present. And Proverbs, which spends nine chapters telling a son that his mother’s teaching is worth his life, comes back at the end to say: and when there is nothing left in it for you, do not despise her.

verseByVerse.quote: Buy truth, and do not sell it; buy wisdom, instruction, and understanding. The father of the righteous will greatly rejoice; he who fathers a wise son will be glad in him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Buy truth, and do not sell it; buy wisdom, instruction, and understanding.

Four things to acquire and one absolute prohibition, and the prohibition is the striking half: do not sell it.

Which means the truth a man holds is saleable, and that there is a market. Nobody sells the truth for money; the price is nearly always something else. A position that requires him not to say the thing he knows. A friendship that would not survive it. Peace in a household, purchased by agreeing with something he does not believe. Standing among people whose approval he wants.

And the transaction is rarely experienced as a sale. It feels like tact, or like humility, or like choosing his battles — and one of those may be the right word, since Proverbs itself commends holding the tongue. The test the verse implies is a simple one: was the silence for the sake of somebody else, or for the sake of what it would have cost me?

Then v. 24: the father of the righteous will greatly rejoice; he who fathers a wise son will be glad in him. The theme of vv. 15-16 again, and this time in public. The gladness is not merely private relief; there is a man in a village who is visibly pleased about his son, and everybody can see it.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your father and mother be glad; let her who bore you rejoice. My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes observe my ways. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let your father and mother be glad; let her who bore you rejoice. The son is told to make it happen — the gladness is presented as something within his gift, and it is. Almost nothing a grown man does costs less and returns more than the deliberate provision of joy to the two people who raised him.

Then v. 26, which is the summit of this chapter and one of the great sentences of the Old Testament: my son, give me your heart, and let your eyes observe my ways.

After twenty-three chapters of instruction, this is what the father actually wants, and it is not obedience. He asks for the boy’s heart — and having asked, he offers something in return that is much more costly than a lecture: let your eyes observe my ways. Watch me. He is putting his own life on the table as the exhibit.

Nobody says that who is not willing to be looked at closely. It is the most exposing sentence a father can utter, and it is the only one that ever works.

And the reason it belongs at the summit is that it is the shape of everything God asks. He does not ask first for behaviour, and he never asked for religion — my son, give me your heart is the whole law under one sentence, and it is what the first and greatest commandment says with more words. And the second half, which no human father can honestly offer without qualification, was offered without any: follow me, said the Son of God, and learn from me, and whoever has seen me has seen the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: For a prostitute is a deep pit; an adulteress is a narrow well. She lies in wait like a robber and increases the traitors among mankind. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For a prostitute is a deep pit; an adulteress is a narrow well.

Two shapes, and both are about getting out rather than falling in. A pit is deep and a well is narrow — and anybody who has thought about the second image will feel it. The problem with a narrow well is not the descent. It is that a man in one cannot get his arms out to climb, and there is nothing to push against.

Which is the accurate description of what chs 5 to 7 have been saying all along. The danger is not that the thing is attractive; the danger is the geometry of the exit.

Then v. 28: she lies in wait like a robber and increases the traitors among mankind. The ambush language of 7:12 — and then the second clause, which widens the damage in an unexpected direction.

She increases the traitors. The result of this sin is not primarily ruined men; it is more traitors in the world — because every man involved has to become one. He has to keep a second account of his own life, and lie fluently to people who trust him, and practise the skill until it is unremarkable. And that skill does not stay in one room. A man who has learned to be a traitor domestically is a different man at work, and in church, and with his friends.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaining? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes? Those who tarry long over wine; those who go to try mixed wine. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaining? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes?

Six questions in a row, and the passage that follows is the most vivid portrait of drunkenness in ancient literature. It runs to the end of the chapter, and it is written with more sympathy than readers usually notice.

Look at the list before the answer arrives. Woe and sorrow, which are inward. Strife and complaining, which are the household. Wounds without cause — injuries he cannot account for, from things that happened while he was not present to himself. And then the small physical detail that gives the whole thing away, the one thing anybody in the room can see: redness of eyes.

Then v. 30 answers all six at once: those who tarry long over wine.

And the diagnosis is in the verb. Not those who drink — those who tarry, who stay, whose relation to the evening is that they do not want it to end. Proverbs is not describing a quantity. It is describing a man who has nowhere else he would rather be, and that is the honest line between drinking and something else, and it is a line a man crosses before anybody notices including himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not look at wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and goes down smoothly. In the end it bites like a serpent and stings like an adder. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not look at wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and goes down smoothly.

Three clauses, and every one of them is a compliment. The colour, the sparkle in the cup, the ease of the first mouthful. Scripture is describing exactly what is good about it, and doing so lovingly, because there would be no danger if the thing were not genuinely delightful.

That honesty is what makes this passage useful, and its absence is what makes most warnings about alcohol useless. A man who is told that drink is grim knows from experience that it is not, and having caught the speaker in one falsehood he discounts the rest.

Then v. 32: in the end it bites like a serpent and stings like an adder.

In the end is aharit again, the word from 5:4 and 23:18 — the afterward. And the image is a snake in the cup, which is the truest picture of addiction anybody has drawn. It does not bite at the top. It is quiet, and lower down, and by the time it moves the man has already been drinking from that cup for years and the cup is where he goes for comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart utter perverse things. You will be like one who lies down in the midst of the sea, like one who lies on the top of a mast. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your eyes will see strange things, and your heart utter perverse things.

The two halves name the two real losses, and neither is the hangover. Perception goes first — the world stops looking the way it is. Then speech, and the phrase is your heart utters, which is precise: what comes out is not invented, it is what was underneath, arriving without the usual doors.

Which is the thing families remember. Not the drinking. The sentence said at eleven o’clock that everybody has to go on living with afterwards, and that cannot be withdrawn by the explanation that he did not mean it — because in a sense he did, and everyone in the room knows it.

Then v. 34: you will be like one who lies down in the midst of the sea, like one who lies on the top of a mast.

Two images of a man asleep in a place where sleep is impossible. The middle of the sea, and — the more extraordinary — the top of a mast, swaying, in the dark, thirty feet up. That is the physical sensation of the room turning, rendered by somebody who had plainly seen it.

And under the comedy is something serious: he is asleep in mortal danger and entirely at ease. The verse is not describing discomfort. It is describing a man who cannot feel where he is.

verseByVerse.quote: "They struck me," you will say, "but I was not hurt; they beat me, but I did not feel it. When shall I awake? I must have another drink." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
They struck me, you will say, but I was not hurt; they beat me, but I did not feel it. When shall I awake? I must have another drink.

The chapter ends inside the man’s own mouth, and it is the most terrible sentence in Proverbs.

Take the parts in order. They struck me… but I was not hurt. He was in a fight. He does not remember it, and he is reporting it as though it happened to somebody else. There is no shame in the line and no alarm — only a flat curiosity about an event he was present for and absent from.

Then: when shall I awake? A man asking, from inside a fog, when he will be able to think again.

And then the last five words, and everything the chapter has been building for lands on them: I must have another drink. The end of the sentence is the beginning of the next one. He has just recited the whole case against it — the woe, the sorrow, the wounds, the lost hours — and the conclusion he draws from all of it is that he needs the thing that did it.

That is not weakness of will and Proverbs does not present it as a joke. It is the exact description of an addiction, written three thousand years before the word existed: the man is not choosing badly between options, he has one option, and the evidence has stopped functioning as evidence.

So a word must be said to anybody who has recognised himself in this chapter, and it must not be a lecture, because the man in v. 35 has heard them all and can recite them better than the person delivering them. What he needs is not information. He needs somebody to be told — one person, today, out loud, which is the single hardest and most necessary act available to him — and he needs help of a kind that includes a doctor, because this is a condition of the body as well as of the soul and Scripture never sneers at ordinary means.

And he needs to know what this book cannot tell him, because Proverbs stops at the diagnosis. There is one who came for people at the bottom of a narrow well and was called a friend of drunkards by his enemies, who meant it as an insult and were describing his ministry accurately. He did not come to improve the strong. Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick (Mark 2:17). The man in v. 35 cannot get out, and that is exactly the qualification.

23.theology:
The God Who Redeems. The title goel (v.11) is loaded with covenantal meaning. Ruth's story turns on it; Isaiah uses it for God's redemption of Israel from exile (Isa. 41:14; 43:14); the New Testament sees Christ as the ultimate Redeemer who pays the price no family member could afford. That God is the Redeemer of the fatherless means no one is truly without a defender — which is why the church must embody that advocacy in concrete, particular acts of care.

Eschatological Hope as Wisdom. Verses 17–18 show that wisdom is inseparable from eschatology. To fear the LORD is to orient yourself toward a future guaranteed by the character of God, not by present circumstances. This is not optimism (a temperamental preference for good outcomes) but hope (a theologically grounded confidence in the One who controls the end). The resurrection of Jesus is the anchor of that hope — "your hope will not be cut off" because death itself was cut off at the cross.
23.examples:
Then: A meal with a ruler in the ancient world was a political event — gifts and flattery were expected. The son is warned to see past the knife at his throat and not lose himself to ambitious social climbing (vv.1–3). Landmark boundaries were sacrosanct in Israelite law (Deut. 19:14); moving them was theft dressed as nothing. The wine section (vv.29–35) addressed a culture where wine was the primary social lubricant — wisdom does not prohibit it but demands mastery over it.

Now: The wealth section (vv.4–5) speaks directly to the professional-class anxiety that drives overwork and portfolio obsession. The eschatological correction (vv.17–18) is the only real cure for envy of the successful fool: a longer view. And the wine section remains searingly contemporary — addiction affects every demographic, and Proverbs' anatomical description of it is more clinical than moralistic. The gospel adds to wisdom's diagnosis: the heart craves what only God can give, and the disordered craving for any substance is finally a spiritual hunger misdirected.

24.title: Do Not Envy the Wicked
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Be not envious of evil men, nor desire to be with them,<sup>2</sup>for their hearts devise violence, and their lips talk of trouble.<sup>3</sup>By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is established;<sup>4</sup>by knowledge the rooms are filled with all precious and pleasant riches.<sup>5</sup>A wise man is full of strength, and a man of knowledge enhances his might,<sup>6</sup>for by wise guidance you can wage your war, and in abundance of counselors there is victory.<sup>7</sup>Wisdom is too high for a fool; in the gate he does not open his mouth.<sup>8</sup>Whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer.<sup>9</sup>The devising of folly is sin, and the scoffer is an abomination to mankind.<sup>10</sup>If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small.<sup>11</sup>Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter.<sup>12</sup>If you say, "Behold, we did not know this," does not he who weighs the heart perceive it? Does not he who keeps watch over your soul know it, and will he not repay man according to his work?<sup>13</sup>My son, eat honey, for it is good, and the drippings of the honeycomb are sweet to your taste.<sup>14</sup>Know that wisdom is such to your soul; if you find it, there will be a future, and your hope will not be cut off.<sup>15</sup>Lie not in wait as a wicked man against the dwelling of the righteous; do no violence to his home;<sup>16</sup>for the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in times of calamity.<sup>17</sup>Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles,<sup>18</sup>lest the LORD see it and be displeased, and turn away his anger from him.<sup>19</sup>Fret not yourself because of evildoers, and be not envious of the wicked,<sup>20</sup>for the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be put out.<sup>21</sup>My son, fear the LORD and the king, and do not join with those who do otherwise,<sup>22</sup>for disaster will arise suddenly from them, and who knows the ruin that will come from them both?<sup>23</sup>These also are sayings of the wise. Partiality in judging is not good.<sup>24</sup>Whoever says to the wicked, "You are in the right," will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations,<sup>25</sup>but those who rebuke the wicked will have delight, and a good blessing will come upon them.<sup>26</sup>Whoever gives an honest answer kisses the lips.<sup>27</sup>Prepare your work outside; get everything ready for yourself in the field, and after that build your house.<sup>28</sup>Be not a witness against your neighbor without cause, and do not deceive with your lips.<sup>29</sup>Do not say, "I will do to him as he has done to me; I will pay the man back for what he has done."<sup>30</sup>I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense,<sup>31</sup>and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns; the ground was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down.<sup>32</sup>Then I saw and considered it; I looked and received instruction.<sup>33</sup>A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest,<sup>34</sup>and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man.
24.overview:
Chapter 24 returns to the theme of envy with fresh urgency (vv.1, 19–20) and surrounds it with wisdom's great affirmations: the wisdom-built house (vv.3–4), the resilience of the righteous (v.16), the warning against schadenfreude (v.17), and the sweetness of wisdom itself (vv.13–14). The chapter also contains one of Proverbs' most striking ethical demands: rescue those being led to slaughter (vv.11–12), with the sobering reminder that pleading ignorance before the God who weighs hearts will not stand.

The key structural move is the contrast between two futures. The wicked may prosper now, but "the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be put out" (v.20). Wisdom sees what is coming. The righteous, by contrast, may fall repeatedly — but they rise (v.16). Resurrection hope is embedded in Proverbs' anthropology long before Easter morning.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 24 — Do Not Envy the Wicked, Rescue the Perishing, and the Sluggard's Field
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 24 closes the thirty sayings (vv.1-22), adds a brief section of further sayings of the wise (vv.23-29), then closes with the extended portrait of the sluggard's field (vv.30-34). The chapter is rich in practical ethics: do not envy evildoers, rescue those being led to death, do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and the devastating image of the vineyard overgrown with weeds.
verseByVerse.theology: The rescue-those-being-led-to-death passage (vv.11-12) is one of the most searching ethical demands in Proverbs. The person who says 'I did not know' is explicitly warned that God who weighs the heart knows the truth. Willful ignorance is not innocence. The prophetic tradition (Isa. 58; Amos 5) and the New Testament (James 4:17) make the same point: knowing what is right and failing to do it is sin.
verseByVerse.examples: The sluggard's field (vv.30-34) is Proverbs' most extended narrative vignette: the wise man walks by the field of the sluggard, sees the ruin, and draws a moral lesson. Poverty does not come suddenly but through the gradual accumulation of small decisions to sleep a little longer. The lesson is learned not from a text but from observation—wisdom is drawn from the seen world.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not envious of evil men, nor desire to be with them, for their hearts devise violence, and their lips talk of trouble. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be not envious of evil men, nor desire to be with them, for their hearts devise violence, and their lips talk of trouble.

The chapter opens on the theme it will return to twice more (vv. 19-20; 23:17), which suggests that envy of the wicked is not an occasional temptation but the standing one.

And the second command is the interesting one: nor desire to be with them. That is not about their money. It is about the room — the pull of being included among people who are getting away with things, who seem more alive than the careful, and whose company confers a kind of standing.

Then the reason, and it is deflating on purpose. What actually goes on in that room? Their hearts devise violence, and their lips talk of trouble. That is the whole conversation. Strip away the atmosphere and what is left is a group of men whose subject matter is other people’s destruction — which is not glamorous, it is merely loud, and anybody who has spent an evening in it knows how quickly the shine comes off.

verseByVerse.quote: By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is established; by knowledge the rooms are filled with all precious and pleasant riches. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
By wisdom a house is built, and by understanding it is established; by knowledge the rooms are filled with all precious and pleasant riches.

Three stages, three words, and they are in the right order. Wisdom builds — gets the thing up. Understanding establishes — makes it stand, which is a different operation and comes later. And knowledge fills the rooms, which is the last stage and the one everybody wants to start with.

The house here is the household of 14:1: a family, a marriage, a life together. And the sequence is the correction of a common mistake. Most people build the rooms and hope the household will happen inside them — the house, the furnishings, the arrangements — and Proverbs says the order runs the other way. Wisdom first, and the pleasant things arrive last and by themselves.

And the word pleasant deserves keeping. This is not an ascetic book. It expects a wisely built household to end up with good things in it and sees no need to apologise for them. What it will not allow is the belief that the good things are what makes it a home.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise man is full of strength, and a man of knowledge enhances his might, for by wise guidance you can wage your war, and in abundance of counselors there is victory. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wise man is full of strength, and a man of knowledge enhances his might, for by wise guidance you can wage your war, and in abundance of counselors there is victory.

The claim of 21:22 stated as a principle: wisdom is a form of power. Not a consolation for people who lack power — power itself, and the sort that decides outcomes.

And the illustration is war, because war is where a society finds out what actually works. In the field, charm is useless and confidence is worse than useless, and the man who wins is the one who knew the ground.

Then the second half repeats what this book has now said three times (11:14; 15:22): the abundance of counsellors. Three occurrences is Proverbs shouting, and the shouting is directed at the one thing every leader believes he already does. He asks people. What he does not do is ask people who might say no.

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom is too high for a fool; in the gate he does not open his mouth. Whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wisdom is too high for a fool; in the gate he does not open his mouth.

The gate is the courthouse and the council chamber, where the town’s serious business is settled — and the fool, who is voluble everywhere else, has nothing to say there.

That is an acute observation, and anybody who has sat on a committee will recognise it. There are people who talk fluently in every setting except the one where a decision has to be made and defended, and who fall silent precisely when it matters. Not because they have become humble. The material at the gate is too high — it requires weighing consequences, holding two considerations at once, and being answerable — and the fool has never developed any of it, because he has spent his life expressing opinions rather than forming them.

Then v. 8: whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer. The Hebrew is roughly master of plots — a title, and the point is that it sticks. A man may do this quietly for years and then discover that it has become his name, and that everybody had it before he did.

verseByVerse.quote: The devising of folly is sin, and the scoffer is an abomination to mankind. If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devising of folly is sin, and the scoffer is an abomination to mankind.

Note where the sin is located: in the devising. It is a sin before it is an act, at the stage where a man is turning something over and telling himself he is only thinking.

And the second clause is unusual, because Proverbs almost always says a thing is an abomination to the LORD. Here the scoffer is an abomination to mankind. Everybody has had enough of him. He believes he is feared or admired; he is merely disliked, universally, by people who are careful not to show it.

Then v. 10, and it is a hard sentence: if you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small.

The Hebrew has a wordplay — tsarah and tsar, a narrowness and a narrow strength — so the sense is that trouble is the measurement rather than the cause. Adversity does not make a man weak. It tells him, accurately and for the first time, how much he had.

Which sounds unsympathetic and is not, once the use of it is clear. Nobody knows the state of his own strength until it is tested; every man overestimates it in good weather; and the point of having it measured is not condemnation but the chance to do something about it before the next time. And the New Testament supplies what Proverbs does not — that the man whose strength is small is precisely the one to whom it is said, my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter. If you say, "Behold, we did not know this," does not he who weighs the heart perceive it? Does not he who keeps watch over your soul know it, and will he not repay man according to his work? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter.

This is the most demanding verse in Proverbs, and it is not an appeal to feeling. It is a command, with two verbs of physical intervention: rescue, and hold back — take hold of somebody and stop him going.

The original setting is judicial: people condemned unjustly, walking to an execution nobody in the town is preventing. It has since been applied to the unborn, to the trafficked, to the condemned, to the man about to walk out of his marriage, to the friend on the edge of something irreversible — and every one of those applications is legitimate, because the verse is not narrow. It describes anybody whose destruction is currently in progress and is currently preventable.

And then v. 12 removes the only defence anybody ever uses. If you say, Behold, we did not know this — and Proverbs does not even bother to argue. It asks three questions. Does not he who weighs the heart perceive it? Does not he who keeps watch over your soul know it? And will he not repay man according to his work?

The plea of ignorance is dismissed because God is described as reading the plea rather than the statement — he weighs the heart, which is where the not-knowing was manufactured. And that is the uncomfortable accuracy of it. Almost nobody in this position lies outright. What happens is that a man arranges not to find out, declines to ask the question whose answer would oblige him, and is then able to say quite sincerely that he did not know.

And the middle question is the tender one, sitting in the middle of a rebuke: he who keeps watch over your soul. The God who will hold a man accountable for the neighbour he did not rescue is described, in the same breath, as the one who has been guarding him the whole time.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, eat honey, for it is good, and the drippings of the honeycomb are sweet to your taste. Know that wisdom is such to your soul; if you find it, there will be a future, and your hope will not be cut off. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, eat honey, for it is good, and the drippings of the honeycomb are sweet to your taste. Know that wisdom is such to your soul.

An instruction to enjoy something, which is rarer in this book than the warnings, and it is put first as the comparison. The father tells his son to eat honey — it is good, with no qualification attached — and then says: that is what wisdom is like.

The comparison is doing careful work. Honey is not medicine and it is not fuel. Nobody eats it because he ought to. And the claim is that wisdom is that sort of thing to the soul: not a discipline endured for later benefit but something with an actual taste, which a person can come to want.

Which is the difference between two Christians who behave identically. One has decided to obey; the other has developed an appetite. From outside they look the same for about a decade.

Then the promise of 23:18 returns word for word: if you find it, there will be a future, and your hope will not be cut off. The repetition is deliberate, and both occurrences sit next to a passage about envying the wicked — because that is the argument. There is an afterward, and it belongs to the man who looks least likely to have one.

verseByVerse.quote: Lie not in wait as a wicked man against the dwelling of the righteous; do no violence to his home; for the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in times of calamity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lie not in wait as a wicked man against the dwelling of the righteous; do no violence to his home; for the righteous falls seven times and rises again.

The logic of the second half is not what a reader expects, and following it is the whole point. Do not attack the righteous man — because he gets up. Not because it is wrong, though it is. Because it does not work.

And this is one of the most encouraging sentences in Scripture, provided it is read correctly. It does not say the righteous man does not fall. It says he falls seven times, which is the Hebrew number for completeness — as often as it is possible to fall.

So the difference between the two men in this verse is not that one of them is steady. Both go down. The difference is entirely in what happens next, and it is stated in the plainest possible verb: rises again.

Which is a definition of the righteous life that a great many discouraged Christians have never been given. Not a record without falls — a pattern of getting up. And the getting up is not self-generated either, since the same Scripture says it is God who upholds a man with his hand when he stumbles (Psalm 37:24). Seven falls and seven risings, and only one of the seven pairs was ever in doubt.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles, lest the LORD see it and be displeased, and turn away his anger from him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles.

Both clauses have to be there, and the second is the one that catches everybody. Do not rejoice covers the visible behaviour — no gloating, no remark, no forwarding of the news. And then: let not your heart be glad, which is the same event conducted silently and with a straight face.

Note that Proverbs assumes the man has an enemy. Scripture is not naive about this; there are people who wish a person harm, and the Bible does not require pretending otherwise. What it forbids is the pleasure.

Then the reason in v. 18, which is one of the strangest in the book: lest the LORD see it and be displeased, and turn away his anger from him.

Read that carefully. Your gloating might cause God to go easier on your enemy. The falling was God’s business, and delighting in it is an interference — as though a man had joined in with somebody else’s discipline of his own child, which stops the discipline instantly and turns the parent round to face the interferer.

Which is the most efficient cure for gloating anybody has ever devised. A man who wants his enemy dealt with is told, in effect, that his own satisfaction is the one thing capable of getting in the way.

verseByVerse.quote: Fret not yourself because of evildoers, and be not envious of the wicked, for the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be put out. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fret not yourself because of evildoers, and be not envious of the wicked, for the evil man has no future; the lamp of the wicked will be put out.

The theme of v. 1 returns, and now with the word fret alongside envy — because they are the same emotion in two moods. Envy wants what the wicked man has; fretting is furious that he has it. Both are the same act of comparison, and both keep the man who is doing it occupied.

And the answer given is the same as at v. 14 and 23:18, in the negative: the evil man has no future. No aharit, no afterward. Which is exactly the calculation envy fails to make. It looks at a man at forty and prices the whole life from a single reading.

Then the lamp, and the image is domestic and final. A lamp going out in an Israelite house at night was the end of the day and, in the language of that world, the end of a family line. Not extinguished violently. Simply out, and the room dark, and nobody there.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, fear the LORD and the king, and do not join with those who do otherwise, for disaster will arise suddenly from them, and who knows the ruin that will come from them both? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, fear the LORD and the king, and do not join with those who do otherwise.

Two authorities named in one breath, and Peter says the same pair in the same order: fear God. Honour the emperor (1 Peter 2:17). The order is the whole of Christian political teaching. The king is genuinely to be feared, and he is second.

Which is what keeps the verse from being a charter for whatever government happens to be in power. Proverbs has already said that a throne is established by righteousness and that a king who does evil is sawing at his own legs (16:12), and the same Bible has Daniel’s friends declining a statue and the apostles telling a council that they must obey God rather than men. Ordinary obedience is commanded; unlimited obedience is not, because the second authority is under the first.

And then v. 22 gives the reason for the warning, and it is not moral but practical: disaster will arise suddenly from them, and who knows the ruin that will come from them both? Anybody who joins a faction against constituted authority is attaching himself to something whose outcome he cannot see — and revolutions have a long history of consuming the people who began them.

verseByVerse.quote: These also are sayings of the wise. Partiality in judging is not good. Whoever says to the wicked, "You are in the right," will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
These also are sayings of the wise. Partiality in judging is not good.

A new heading, a further collection, and it opens on the understatement of 18:5 — not good, which in this book is the flattest way of saying something is monstrous.

Then v. 24 makes the specific case, and the language escalates without warning: whoever says to the wicked, You are in the right, will be cursed by peoples, abhorred by nations.

That is an extraordinary reaction to a single sentence spoken in a courtroom. But the response is not out of proportion, because what has been broken is not one man’s case. A community can survive a great deal of private wickedness; what it cannot survive is the discovery that its judgments are for sale — since after that nothing anybody says about right and wrong means anything, and every citizen becomes his own enforcement.

Which is why the whole world hates it, in every culture, without needing to be taught. Nations that agree on nothing else agree on this, and Proverbs treats that universal instinct as evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: but those who rebuke the wicked will have delight, and a good blessing will come upon them. Whoever gives an honest answer kisses the lips. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
But those who rebuke the wicked will have delight, and a good blessing will come upon them.

The other side of v. 24, and note what is promised to the man who stands up: delight. Not vindication, not safety, not thanks — delight, which is a word about pleasure.

Which is a promise most people would not believe, because rebuking the wicked is a thoroughly unpleasant business at the time. It is done in a room where everybody would rather it were not happening, and it costs the man who does it. The delight in this verse is not concurrent. It is what a person has afterwards for the rest of his life, and its opposite — the memory of the meeting where he said nothing — is one of the more durable regrets available.

Then v. 26, one of the loveliest images in Proverbs: whoever gives an honest answer kisses the lips.

A kiss on the mouth in that culture was the mark of the closest affection, and it is used here of plain speech. Telling somebody the truth is described as an act of intimacy — which reverses the usual instinct entirely, since most people withhold honesty in the name of kindness.

And it is exactly right. The people who tell you the truth are the ones who are close to you, and the ones who tell you only what you want to hear have quietly decided you are not worth the risk.

verseByVerse.quote: Prepare your work outside; get everything ready for yourself in the field, and after that build your house. Be not a witness against your neighbor without cause, and do not deceive with your lips. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prepare your work outside; get everything ready for yourself in the field, and after that build your house.

The most practical verse in the chapter, and it is about sequence. Field first, house second — because the field produces the income and the house consumes it, and a man who reverses the order has built something he cannot maintain.

In its own setting this is advice to a young man about to marry: get the livelihood established before you take on the household. Which is not the counsel of a book that despises romance; it is the counsel of a book that has watched a great many marriages strained by a mortgage taken on the strength of hope.

And the principle runs everywhere. Build the capacity before the commitment. Ministries, businesses and families all fail in the same way — not from lack of vision but from a house built before the field was ready, and then a decade spent servicing it.

Then v. 28: be not a witness against your neighbor without cause, and do not deceive with your lips. The phrase is without cause — testimony given not because it was necessary but because there was an opportunity, and the man had something he could say.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not say, "I will do to him as he has done to me; I will pay the man back for what he has done." I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not say, I will do to him as he has done to me; I will pay the man back for what he has done.

This is 20:22 again, and once more the prohibition is on the saying. And what makes this version sharper is the reasonableness of the sentence being forbidden.
