The dripping of 19:13 returns with a detail added — on a rainy day — and the addition is the misery of it. There is already rain outside; the house was the one place that was supposed to be dry, and it is coming through the roof.

Then two images for the impossibility of stopping it, and both are chosen for the same quality. Wind cannot be held because there is nothing to grip; oil cannot be held because it goes through the fingers of a closed hand. Neither is strong. Both are simply not the sort of thing a hand can close on — which is exactly the frustration of arguing with a contention that is not about anything, since every specific point is answered and the atmosphere does not shift.

And the guards from 19:13 and 21:9 stand here: the same fault is charged against men elsewhere in this book (26:21; 15:18; 29:22), the sin has no sex, and the verse is a measurement of a real misery rather than counsel to leave. What it adds is honesty about the method — this cannot be gripped, and a man who keeps trying to grip it is going to exhaust himself on the wrong problem.

verseByVerse.quote: Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another. Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who guards his master will be honored. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another.

One of the best known verses in the book, and its picture is nearly always softened. Sharpening is not encouragement. Two blades are brought together hard, at an angle, with friction and noise and sparks, and metal comes off — and it comes off both.

Which is the part that gets left out. This is not a description of a mentor improving a protégé. Both pieces of iron are changed by the encounter, and both lose something, and neither is comfortable during it.

And it requires the same material. Iron sharpens iron; it does not sharpen wood, and iron is not sharpened by a cushion. Which means this kind of friendship is only available between people who are prepared to be hard with each other — and it explains why so few Christians have any, since it requires a relationship in which both parties have agreed, in advance, that they would rather be sharpened than soothed.

The practical test is short. Name the person who is currently allowed to tell you that you are wrong. If nobody has that standing, no sharpening is happening, and the edge that was there at twenty-five is going quietly blunt.

Then v. 18: whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who guards his master will be honoured. A fig takes years to bear and the man who tends it is not paid in the meantime, and the same is true of faithfulness to a person. Both are long, unwitnessed, and pay at the end.

verseByVerse.quote: As in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man. Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
As in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man.

The Hebrew is compressed and has been read two ways, and both are useful. The plainer sense is that a man’s heart shows him what he is, the way a pool shows him his face — self-knowledge, of the kind he cannot get from anywhere else.

The older reading takes it of two people: as water gives back a face, so one man’s heart answers another’s. Which is the experience of any real friendship — the discovery that what you thought was peculiar to you is in somebody else as well, and the enormous relief of it.

Either way the instrument is a still surface. Running water reflects nothing. Which is a small and serious observation about self-knowledge and about friendship alike: neither happens at speed, and a life with no still moments in it will show a man nothing at all.

Then v. 20: Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man.

The comparison is between the grave and a man’s eyes, and the shared quality is that neither has ever said enough. The grave has taken every human being who ever lived and shows no sign of being full; and the eye, having got what it was looking at, immediately looks at something else.

Which is the most honest sentence about consumption ever written, and it goes deeper than shopping. The eye is not a stomach; there is no mechanism in it for fullness. Nothing seen has ever concluded the wanting, and anybody waiting for the acquisition that will finally settle him is waiting for a thing that has never once occurred in the history of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: The crucible is for silver, and the furnace is for gold, and a man is tested by his praise. Crush a fool in a mortar with a pestle along with crushed grain, yet his folly will not depart from him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crucible is for silver, and the furnace is for gold, and a man is tested by his praise.

17:3 used this image of God testing hearts. Here the same furnace is fired for a different purpose, and the fuel is compliments.

That is a shrewder test than adversity, and less commonly noticed. Trouble tests a man, and everybody knows it. Praise tests him more finely, because he does not know it is happening. Watch what a compliment does to a person over five years: whether he begins to need it, whether he arranges his work to attract it, whether he can hear one about somebody else without something tightening.

And the honest form of the test is not how a man responds to praise in the moment — everybody can produce a modest sentence. It is what he does when it stops.

Then v. 22, and it is one of the grimmest and most comic images in Proverbs: crush a fool in a mortar with a pestle along with crushed grain, yet his folly will not depart from him.

A mortar and pestle separates the husk from the grain by force; it is the most thorough method of breaking something down that a household possessed. And the verse says: do that to a fool, and what comes out of the bowl is a smaller fool.

Which is Proverbs at its most sober about the limits of consequence. Suffering does not automatically improve people. The same hard year that makes one man wise makes another man bitter, and the difference is not in the pestle.

verseByVerse.quote: Know well the condition of your flocks, and give attention to your herds, for riches do not last forever; and does a crown endure to all generations? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Know well the condition of your flocks, and give attention to your herds, for riches do not last forever; and does a crown endure to all generations?

The chapter turns here into its closing passage, and it is one of the most unexpected endings in the book: five verses of farm management.

And the instruction is precise. Know well the condition — literally know the face of your flock. Not the number. The face: which ewe is limping, which one is off her food, which part of the wall needs seeing to. It is intimate, unglamorous, ongoing knowledge of the thing actually in your care.

Then the reason, and it is the argument of the whole passage: riches do not last forever; and does a crown endure to all generations? Even a crown, the most permanent thing a man could imagine, is put in the form of a question.

So the counsel is this: since nothing accumulated can be relied on, attend to what is alive and in front of you. A flock is not a store of value. It is a thing that has to be kept, and it feeds you because it is kept, and the man who looks after it eats every year while the man with the treasure eventually discovers that riches have wings (23:5).

verseByVerse.quote: When the grass is gone and the new growth appears and the vegetation of the mountains is gathered, the lambs will provide your clothing, and the goats the price of a field. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the grass is gone and the new growth appears and the vegetation of the mountains is gathered, the lambs will provide your clothing, and the goats the price of a field.

Three stages of a year in half a verse, and the shepherd is in all of them. The old grass eaten, the new growth coming, the mountain hay gathered — and every one of those is work done at a particular time that cannot be done at another.

Then the return: clothing from the lambs, and from the goats the price of a field. Which is the striking phrase, because a field is capital. The flock, properly kept, does not merely feed the household. It buys land.

That is the argument the whole passage has been making, quietly, against the way most people think about money. There is a slow, ordinary, entirely unremarkable way of getting on in the world: attend to the living thing you have, through its seasons, for years — and it turns into something you could not have bought outright.

And it stands against the hasty wealth of 13:11 and 20:21 as the alternative. Not a scheme. A flock, and a man who knows their faces.

verseByVerse.quote: There will be enough goats' milk for your food, for the food of your household and maintenance for your girls. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
There will be enough goats’ milk for your food, for the food of your household and maintenance for your girls.

The chapter ends on a word this book has used before at its most contented: enough.

And look at what it covers. Food for the man, food for his household, and maintenance for the servant girls — who are the last and least people in that establishment, and who are named. The provision reaches all the way to the bottom of the house.

Nothing here is a fortune. There is no crown in this picture and no treasure; v. 24 has already said that neither lasts. What there is, is a working flock, a household that eats, and everybody in it accounted for — and Proverbs presents it, after twenty-six verses about friendship and jealousy and praise and fools, as the picture of a life that has gone well.

Which is a very unfashionable definition of success and a durable one. Most people, offered it at twenty-five, would decline. Most people at sixty would take it.

And the Shepherd who knows the condition of his flock by face said the same thing in the first person, and he did not mean goats. I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me (John 10:14) — one at a time, by name, the limping one included. He did not count them from a distance. He went out after the one that had strayed from the nest, and he laid down his life for the flock, and there is enough in his house, and everybody in it is provided for down to the last.

27.theology:
Friendship as Means of Grace. Chapter 27 treats friendship as one of God's primary instruments for human formation. The friend who wounds faithfully (v.6), the counsel that gladdens (v.9), the iron sharpening iron (v.17) — these are not merely social goods but spiritual mechanisms. The Reformers called preaching, sacraments, and prayer the "means of grace"; Proverbs adds to this the faithful friend whose love is too serious to be merely pleasant. The church at its best is a community of faithful wounders.

Creatureliness and Humility. Verse 1 ("you do not know what a day may bring") and the closing pastoral image (vv.23–27) together present a vision of creaturely wisdom: know your limits, tend what is given, plan humbly. The theological virtue behind this is not pessimism but trust — trust in a God who holds the future and who is worthy to hold it. Christian hope does not eliminate planning; it transforms its spirit from grasping to stewardship.
27.examples:
Then: Proverbs' audience would have known the pastoral life intimately — flocks, herds, seasonal rhythms. The closing section (vv.23–27) is not romantic but practical: attend to what you have, do not speculate beyond your means, sustainable abundance is preferable to volatile wealth. The friendship section spoke to a culture where patronage and flattery were the social currency of court life; genuine friendship of the kind Proverbs describes was rare and precious precisely because it was so counter-cultural.

Now: Verse 17 (iron sharpens iron) is widely quoted in men's ministries and leadership circles — rightly so, though its cutting edge is often dulled into something merely motivational. The real application is uncomfortable: who in your life is allowed to wound you faithfully? Who will tell you what your spouse, your employees, and your therapist might not? The Christian who cannot answer that question is almost certainly growing softer, not sharper. And verse 1 is a direct rebuke of the five-year planning culture that imagines the future as essentially controllable — wisdom builds plans lightly held.

28.title: The Wicked Flee When No One Pursues
28.text: <sup>1</sup>The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion.<sup>2</sup>When a land transgresses, it has many rulers, but with a man of understanding and knowledge, its stability will long continue.<sup>3</sup>A poor man who oppresses the poor is a beating rain that leaves no food.<sup>4</sup>Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep the law strive against them.<sup>5</sup>Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD understand it completely.<sup>6</sup>Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man who is crooked in his ways.<sup>7</sup>The one who keeps the law is a son with understanding, but a companion of gluttons shames his father.<sup>8</sup>Whoever multiplies his wealth by interest and profit gathers it for him who is generous to the poor.<sup>9</sup>If one turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination.<sup>10</sup>Whoever misleads the upright into an evil way will fall into his own pit, but the blameless will have a goodly inheritance.<sup>11</sup>A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man who has understanding will find him out.<sup>12</sup>When the righteous triumph, there is great glory, but when the wicked rise, people hide themselves.<sup>13</sup>Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.<sup>14</sup>Blessed is the one who fears the LORD always, but whoever hardens his heart will fall into calamity.<sup>15</sup>Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a poor people.<sup>16</sup>A ruler who lacks understanding is a cruel oppressor, but he who hates unjust gain will prolong his days.<sup>17</sup>If one is burdened with the blood of another, he will be a fugitive until death; let no one help him.<sup>18</sup>Whoever walks in integrity will be delivered, but he who is crooked in his ways will suddenly fall.<sup>19</sup>Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits will have plenty of poverty.<sup>20</sup>A faithful man will abound with blessings, but whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished.<sup>21</sup>To show partiality is not good, but for a piece of bread a man will do wrong.<sup>22</sup>A stingy man hastens after wealth and does not know that poverty will come upon him.<sup>23</sup>Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than he who flatters with his tongue.<sup>24</sup>Whoever robs his father or his mother and says, "That is no transgression," is a companion to a man who destroys.<sup>25</sup>A greedy man stirs up strife, but the one who trusts in the LORD will be enriched.<sup>26</sup>Whoever trusts in his own mind is a fool, but he who walks in wisdom will be delivered.<sup>27</sup>Whoever gives to the poor will not want, but he who hides his eyes will get many a curse.<sup>28</sup>When the wicked rise, people hide themselves, but when they perish, the righteous increase.
28.overview:
Chapter 28 is one of Proverbs' most theologically concentrated chapters, weaving together themes of conscience, confession, justice, and integrity. The opening verse sets the tone: the wicked flee even when unpursued — they are haunted by a conscience that cannot be quieted. The righteous are bold as a lion — not because they are braver by temperament, but because they have nothing to hide before God.

The chapter's pastoral center is verse 13: "Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy." This is Proverbs' most direct statement about confession and forgiveness, and it anticipates the New Testament's fuller development: 1 John 1:9, the prodigal son, the ministry of reconciliation. Concealment breeds shame and shame breeds the restless flight of verse 1; confession brings the boldness that only forgiveness can give.

Keller identifies this chapter as showing that integrity is not merely an ethical preference but a structural feature of a well-ordered soul. The person of integrity is not trying to avoid getting caught; they have nothing to manage, because they live openly before God.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 28 — The Righteous Are Bold, the Wicked Are Exposed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 28 is dominated by the contrast between the righteous and the wicked in the context of power and poverty. The wicked ruler who oppresses the poor (v.15-16), the poor person who walks in integrity (v.6), the one who confesses sins versus the one who conceals them (v.13), and the warning against rushing to be rich (v.20-22). The chapter is political, social, and deeply theological.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 is one of Proverbs' most pastorally significant: 'Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.' The connection between honest confession and divine mercy is proto-evangelical; 1 John 1:9 makes the same claim with the blood of Christ as the basis. The person who covers sin is not protecting himself but preventing the mercy he desperately needs.
verseByVerse.examples: The poor who walk in integrity (v.6) are contrasted with the rich who are crooked (v.6) and those who oppress the poor (vv.3,8,15). Proverbs' consistent concern for justice to the poor runs through this chapter: God sides with the poor against the exploiter, and the person who honors God cannot oppress those God honors.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion. When a land transgresses, it has many rulers, but with a man of understanding and knowledge, its stability will long continue. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion.

Nobody is chasing the man in the first half. That is the whole verse — the pursuit is imaginary, and he is running anyway.

Which is an exact account of what guilt does to a person, and it is not primarily fear of being caught. It is a permanent readiness to be. Footsteps behind him mean something. An unexpected call from the office is a matter for two minutes of rapid thinking. A letter with an official mark on it is opened standing up. Nothing has happened, and he has been running for years.

And the second half is not what most people expect the opposite to be. Not calm, not at peace — bold as a lion, which is an active and forward quality. A clear conscience does not merely remove anxiety; it releases a man to do things, because a great deal of what passes for caution in the world is simply a man protecting something he cannot afford to have looked at.

Then v. 2: when a land transgresses, it has many rulers — the political instability of a corrupt society, described in five words. Nobody stays in office, because there is no settled ground for anybody to stand on.

verseByVerse.quote: A poor man who oppresses the poor is a beating rain that leaves no food. Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep the law strive against them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A poor man who oppresses the poor is a beating rain that leaves no food.

The image is a downpour so hard that it destroys the crop it should have watered — rain doing the work of drought. And the shock in the verse is the subject: a poor man oppressing the poor.

That is a truth Proverbs is honest enough to record and which is rarely preached. Oppression is not confined to the wealthy. Much of the worst of it is done at the bottom, by people with a very little power over people with none — the foreman, the landlord of one house, the man who lends small sums at the end of the week — and it is more merciless than what comes from above, because he knows exactly how little they have and precisely where the pressure will tell.

Then v. 4: those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep the law strive against them.

Two responses to the same person, and the second is the striking one. Keeping the law is not described here as personal compliance. It produces striving against — active opposition — so that a man’s obedience is measured not only by what he does not do but by what he will not let pass in silence.

verseByVerse.quote: Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD understand it completely. Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man who is crooked in his ways. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD understand it completely.

The claim is about comprehension rather than compliance, and it goes further than most people would. It is not that the evil man knows what justice is and disregards it. He does not understand it, and this is what makes such men so hard to argue with.

Anybody who has tried to explain to a certain sort of person why a thing was wrong knows the sensation. The facts are agreed. The principle is stated. And the reply comes back showing that the whole argument was received as a move in a negotiation, because that is the only category available. He is not being obstinate; he genuinely has no faculty for the thing being described.

And the second half tells where the faculty comes from, and it is not education. Those who seek the LORD understand it completely — because justice is not a human convention to be worked out but the character of somebody, and a man who is coming to know him is being given the sense of it by acquaintance.

Then v. 6 restates 19:1 with the contrast sharpened to poor-against-rich: better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man who is crooked in his ways. Both men are real, and Proverbs is not pretending the second is unhappy. It says only that if a man could have one of the two, he should take the first — which is easy to affirm and very hard to choose at the moment of choosing.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who keeps the law is a son with understanding, but a companion of gluttons shames his father. Whoever multiplies his wealth by interest and profit gathers it for him who is generous to the poor. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who keeps the law is a son with understanding, but a companion of gluttons shames his father. The company again — and note that the young man is not described as a glutton. He is a companion of them, which is where it starts and is entirely enough to do the damage (13:20).

Then v. 8, and it is one of the most satisfying sentences in the book: whoever multiplies his wealth by interest and profit gathers it for him who is generous to the poor.

The verb is the joke. He gathers — works at it, accumulates, adds to the pile with considerable skill — and Proverbs says that what he is actually doing is collecting on somebody else’s behalf.

He does not know this. That is the whole flavour of the verse: a man spending thirty years building something, in the settled belief that it is his, and the arrangement all along was that it would end up in the hands of a person who gives it away.

Which is how it commonly goes, and not by any miracle. Money got by squeezing people is frequently lost, or dispersed at a death, or passed to somebody who does not share the temperament that acquired it. The pile changes hands. Proverbs has simply noticed who it tends to reach in the end, and found it funny.

verseByVerse.quote: If one turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination. Whoever misleads the upright into an evil way will fall into his own pit, but the blameless will have a goodly inheritance. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
If one turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination.

One of the most severe verses in the Bible about religion, and the logic is uncomfortable and exact. A man declines to listen to God, and then addresses him — and the address is called an abomination.

The offence is not that he is unworthy to pray; nobody is worthy, and this book knows it. It is the structure of the transaction. He has established that this is a one-way relationship in which he does the talking, and he only turns up when he wants something. Anybody who has had a friend like that recognises exactly what is being described and how it feels.

And it gives an uncomfortable diagnostic for the Christian life, since the two disciplines are usually thought of as a matched pair and are not equally practised. A man who prays a great deal and reads almost nothing has arranged precisely the relationship this verse describes.

Then v. 10: whoever misleads the upright into an evil way will fall into his own pit. The pit of 26:27 again, and the specific crime should be named — not doing evil but recruiting somebody else to it, which is what the gang in ch. 1 was doing, and it has been in this book from the first page.

verseByVerse.quote: A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man who has understanding will find him out. When the righteous triumph, there is great glory, but when the wicked rise, people hide themselves. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man who has understanding will find him out.

An observation about how money affects a man’s self-assessment, and it is not that wealth makes him arrogant. It is subtler. Everybody has agreed with him for years — because they wanted something, or because his success looked like an argument — and after a decade of that a man concludes that his judgment is excellent, on evidence that was never evidence.

And the one who sees through him is the poor man who has understanding, which is a lovely arrangement. He has no stake, nothing to gain by agreeing, and no reason to be impressed — and he is therefore the only person in the room able to see clearly. He will also, of course, never be asked.

Then v. 12: when the righteous triumph, there is great glory, but when the wicked rise, people hide themselves.

The measure of a government offered here is not its policy but the behaviour of ordinary people under it. Are they visible? Do they speak in a shop? Is the town out in the square, or is everybody indoors, saying less?

Which is a test any person can apply anywhere, and it works on a household or a church as readily as on a country. Where somebody wicked has risen, people go quiet and become hard to find, and they will not be able to tell you why.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy. Blessed is the one who fears the LORD always, but whoever hardens his heart will fall into calamity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.

This is the clearest gospel sentence in the book, and it should be taken a clause at a time.

Conceals. Not denies — conceals, which is the ordinary state of most people. A man who covers a thing is doing something continuous: keeping it out of view, managing the conversations, maintaining a version of himself for public use. It is not a single act but a job, and it is never finished.

And the promise attached to it is a very odd one: he will not prosper. Not that he will be found out — Proverbs says that elsewhere, and here it says something quieter and worse. He will simply not thrive. The thing sits in him and everything else grows around it slightly wrong.

Then the two verbs on the other side, and both are required. Confesses — says it out loud, which is where nearly everybody stops, because there is a kind of confession that has become a substitute for change. And forsakes — leaves it, which is the half that costs something. A man who confesses without forsaking has told the truth about a life he intends to go on living; a man who tries to forsake without confessing is fighting in the dark and alone.

And then the sentence that makes this the gospel in a verse: he will obtain mercy. Which is exactly the reverse of what anybody would expect, and it is the thing that keeps people concealing. Everyone assumes that disclosure brings judgment and that silence buys safety, and Proverbs says the arrangement runs the other way round: the covering forfeits mercy, and the telling obtains it.

David spent a year on the first half and wrote down what it did to him — when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long — and then the second half, in one line: I said, I will confess my transgressions to the LORD, and you forgave the iniquity of my sin (Psalm 32:3-5). And 1 John says the same thing to Christians as a standing promise: if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive them (1 John 1:9). Nobody has ever been turned away at that door. The only people who fail to obtain mercy are those who did not come because they were busy covering.

verseByVerse.quote: Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a poor people. A ruler who lacks understanding is a cruel oppressor, but he who hates unjust gain will prolong his days. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a poor people.

Two animals, and both are chosen for the same reason: neither can be reasoned with, and neither can be escaped by a man on foot. And the victims are specified — a poor people, who have nowhere to go and no means of appeal, which is what makes the combination so deadly. A wicked ruler over a wealthy people is merely resisted.

Then v. 16: a ruler who lacks understanding is a cruel oppressor, but he who hates unjust gain will prolong his days.

Note the causation, because it is not the obvious one. Cruelty is traced to a lack of understanding rather than to malice. The oppressive ruler in this verse is not necessarily wicked by temperament; he is stupid — he cannot see how his decisions land, has no picture of the household at the other end of the policy, and does harm on a large scale while intending nothing.

Here is a warning for anybody with authority, at any scale, and it is more searching than a warning about cruelty would be. Nobody in a church or a business believes himself cruel. Plenty of people make decisions without ever finding out what happens downstream of them, and Proverbs calls the result oppression regardless of the intent.

verseByVerse.quote: If one is burdened with the blood of another, he will be a fugitive until death; let no one help him. Whoever walks in integrity will be delivered, but he who is crooked in his ways will suddenly fall. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
If one is burdened with the blood of another, he will be a fugitive until death; let no one help him.

The hardest sentence in the chapter, and it must be read for what it is. This is not counsel for private individuals about how to treat guilty people; it is about a murderer and the machinery of justice, and the instruction let no one help him means: do not shelter him from the law. Israel had cities of refuge for the man who killed accidentally, and no refuge at all for the man who did it deliberately (Numbers 35:16-21), and this verse is that provision in proverb form.

And the phrase to sit with is a fugitive until death. Even where the law never reaches him, something else does. He is running for the rest of his life — which is v. 1 again, at its worst: nobody pursuing, and no possibility of rest.

The verse cannot be turned into a rule about forgiveness, and a Christian should be clear about why. The New Testament is emphatic that the blood of Christ reaches murderers; the man who held the coats at Stephen’s stoning wrote a third of it. What Proverbs is refusing is the confusion of mercy with the obstruction of justice — because forgiveness is God’s to give, and a criminal court is not the place where it is administered.

Then v. 18: whoever walks in integrity will be delivered, but he who is crooked in his ways will suddenly fall. Suddenly is the word. The crookedness took years; the fall takes an afternoon.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits will have plenty of poverty. A faithful man will abound with blessings, but whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits will have plenty of poverty.

12:11 again, with one word changed and the change is the wit of it: he will have plenty of poverty. The chaser does get an abundance. It is simply an abundance of the wrong thing, and the sentence is built so that both men end up with plenty.

Then v. 20: a faithful man will abound with blessings, but whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished.

Two men, and the comparison is not between honesty and dishonesty. It is between faithfulness and haste — which is a strange pairing until it is seen that they are opposites in practice. Faithfulness is a quality that only exists over time; it cannot be demonstrated quickly, because it consists precisely in still being there.

And haste is not merely impatient. It is the thing that makes faithfulness impossible, because every shortcut a man takes is a place where he stopped being reliable in order to get somewhere sooner. The two cannot be held together, and a man who is in a hurry to be rich has already decided which of them he is giving up.

verseByVerse.quote: To show partiality is not good, but for a piece of bread a man will do wrong. A stingy man hastens after wealth and does not know that poverty will come upon him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
To show partiality is not good, but for a piece of bread a man will do wrong.

The understatement of 18:5, and then a second clause that does something unexpected: it names the price.

A piece of bread. Not a fortune, not a career, not enough to change a life. Proverbs has watched people carefully and observed that a great deal of wrongdoing is done for almost nothing — a small advantage, a minor convenience, a favour returned — and that men who would refuse a large bribe with real indignation will bend for something trivial without noticing they have.

That is a more useful warning than one about corruption on a grand scale. Nobody reading this is likely to be offered a fortune to pervert a judgment. Everybody will be offered a piece of bread.

Then v. 22: a stingy man hastens after wealth and does not know that poverty will come upon him. Literally a man with an evil eye, the grudging look of 23:6 — and the diagnosis is that he cannot see what is coming. The eye that is fixed on getting is not available for looking ahead.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than he who flatters with his tongue. Whoever robs his father or his mother and says, "That is no transgression," is a companion to a man who destroys. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than he who flatters with his tongue.

The word to hold is afterward. Proverbs is entirely honest about the short run: at the time, the flatterer is preferred, and the man who told the truth is not thanked and may not be spoken to for a fortnight.

So the verse asks for a particular kind of nerve — the willingness to be, for a period, misunderstood by somebody whose good opinion you want. And it makes a promise that can only be collected later: eventually, and often years later, a man knows exactly who told him the truth, and he knows what it cost them, and the account is settled in his estimation permanently.

Everybody can name the person who did this for them. Almost nobody thanked them at the time.

Then v. 24: whoever robs his father or his mother and says, That is no transgression, is a companion to a man who destroys.

The sting is in the quoted sentence. He is not defending himself against an accusation; he does not think there is one to answer, because within a family the categories go soft. It was going to come to him anyway. They will not miss it. It is not really stealing.

And Proverbs, which is generally moderate, puts him in the company of a destroyer — because the thing that has been damaged is not the money.

verseByVerse.quote: A greedy man stirs up strife, but the one who trusts in the LORD will be enriched. Whoever trusts in his own mind is a fool, but he who walks in wisdom will be delivered. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A greedy man stirs up strife, but the one who trusts in the LORD will be enriched.

The connection between the two halves is not obvious and it is the point. Greed is presented here as a failure of trust — which is why it produces conflict. A man who believes there is not enough, and that nobody is coming to supply him, must secure his own portion, and securing it means taking it from somewhere. Every quarrel over an estate, a contract or a promotion has this at the bottom of it.

Then v. 26, which is the sentence a modern reader is least prepared for: whoever trusts in his own mind is a fool.

Every instinct of the age is against it. Trusting your own judgment is the definition of maturity in most of what people read, and the alternative sounds like the surrender of the intellect.

It is not. Proverbs has spent twenty-eight chapters demanding hard thinking, and it is not now recommending that a man stop using his mind. It is saying that he should not trust it — should not lean his weight on it (3:5), because it is the instrument that was wrong the last four times, and it is the same instrument he would have to use to assess whether it is wrong now.

The alternative given is not blind obedience but walking in wisdom: a man with counsel around him, a fixed word above him, and a settled suspicion of his own certainty — which turns out to be the only arrangement under which a mind can be used safely at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever gives to the poor will not want, but he who hides his eyes will get many a curse. When the wicked rise, people hide themselves, but when they perish, the righteous increase. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever gives to the poor will not want, but he who hides his eyes will get many a curse.

The phrase in the second half is the exact one: hides his eyes. Not refuses, not argues, not says no. Looks away — which is the actual mechanism, and it takes about a second, and it is nearly always done without any conscious decision at all.

And it is worth noticing that the verse assumes the seeing came first. The eyes had to be hidden because they had already found something, which means the man in this verse is not ignorant. He is managing his attention, and Proverbs regards that as the point at which the sin was committed.

Then the last verse repeats v. 12 with one change, and the change is the chapter’s final word: when the wicked rise, people hide themselves, but when they perish, the righteous increase.

The verb is increase. Not: the righteous celebrate, or are vindicated. They multiply — because they were there all along, hiding, and what looked like their absence was only their silence.

Take that as encouragement, if you have looked at an institution, or a country, or a church, and concluded that the good people have gone. Elijah made exactly that mistake and was told there were seven thousand he had not counted (1 Kings 19:18). They do not increase by arriving. They increase by coming out.

And that is finally what the day of Christ is for. The whole creation is described as waiting on tiptoe for the revealing of the sons of God (Romans 8:19) — a world in which the righteous have been hidden for a very long time, and the wicked have risen and risen, and the ending is not that the good are rewarded but that they are at last revealed, and there turn out to be a great many more of them than anybody could see.

28.theology:
Conscience, Confession, and the Mercy of God. Verse 13 is Proverbs' most direct engagement with the mechanics of mercy. The theological claim is that God's mercy is available — "will obtain mercy" is not conditional on sinlessness but on confession and forsaking. This is not a works-righteousness framework but a grace framework: mercy is given freely to those who stop hiding. The gospel deepens and perfects this: the confession that obtains mercy is made to a God who has already borne the penalty in Christ. Confession is not appeasement; it is homecoming.

The Boldness of Integrity. Verse 1 presents courage not as a gift of temperament but as a fruit of character. The righteous person is bold as a lion because integrity creates a kind of structural fearlessness — nothing to hide, nothing to protect, no secret that could be exposed. This is the "freedom of a Christian" Luther described: the person who lives before God without pretense is free from the anxiety that haunts those who manage appearances. Paul could say "I am not ashamed of the gospel" (Rom. 1:16) because the gospel had done precisely this work in him.
28.examples:
Then: Ancient Israelite legal culture required witnesses and public testimony; concealment was a constant temptation in legal disputes, land transactions, and communal life. Verse 13 spoke into that culture's pressure to manage reputation through concealment rather than facing consequences through confession. The poor man of verse 6 would have been a recognizable figure: the day laborer with an unblemished reputation in a world where bribery and corruption were available to those with means.

Now: Verse 13 is the most directly applicable verse in this chapter for pastoral ministry. The epidemic of unconfessed sin — hidden addiction, secret financial failure, private moral collapse — produces precisely the restlessness of verse 1. The church that creates a culture of safe confession (not therapeutic oversharing, but covenant honesty) creates the conditions for the boldness of verse 1. And verse 27 ("hides his eyes") describes the posture of studied indifference to need — the averted gaze that has learned, through habit, not to see the homeless person on the corner, not to read the email from the struggling church, not to answer the call from the difficult family member.

29.title: Where There Is No Vision
29.text: <sup>1</sup>He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing.<sup>2</sup>When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan.<sup>3</sup>He who loves wisdom makes his father glad, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth.<sup>4</sup>By justice a king builds up the land, but he who exacts gifts tears it down.<sup>5</sup>A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet.<sup>6</sup>An evil man is ensnared in his transgression, but a righteous man sings and rejoices.<sup>7</sup>A righteous man knows the rights of the poor; a wicked man does not understand such knowledge.<sup>8</sup>Scoffers set a city aflame, but the wise turn away wrath.<sup>9</sup>If a wise man has an argument with a fool, the fool only rages and laughs, and there is no quiet.<sup>10</sup>Bloodthirsty men hate one who is blameless and seek the life of the upright.<sup>11</sup>A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back.<sup>12</sup>If a ruler listens to falsehood, all his officials will be wicked.<sup>13</sup>The poor man and the oppressor meet together; the LORD gives light to the eyes of both.<sup>14</sup>If a king faithfully judges the poor, his throne will be established forever.<sup>15</sup>The rod and reproof give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother.<sup>16</sup>When the wicked increase, transgression increases, but the righteous will look upon their downfall.<sup>17</sup>Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will give delight to your heart.<sup>18</sup>Where there is no prophetic vision the people cast off restraint, but blessed is he who keeps the law.<sup>19</sup>By mere words a servant is not disciplined, for though he understands, he will not respond.<sup>20</sup>Do you see a man who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him.<sup>21</sup>Whoever pampers his servant from childhood will in the end find him his heir.<sup>22</sup>A man of wrath stirs up strife, and one given to anger causes much transgression.<sup>23</sup>One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor.<sup>24</sup>The partner of a thief hates his own life; he hears the curse, but discloses nothing.<sup>25</sup>The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe.<sup>26</sup>Many seek the face of a ruler, but it is from the LORD that a man gets justice.<sup>27</sup>An unjust man is an abomination to the righteous, but one whose way is straight is an abomination to the wicked.
29.overview:
Chapter 29 gathers some of Proverbs' most quotable and weighty political and social wisdom, while returning constantly to the themes that have threaded through the whole book: the righteous vs. the wicked, the teachable vs. the stubborn, pride vs. humility. The famous verse 18 — "Where there is no prophetic vision the people cast off restraint" — is frequently misread as a vision-casting management principle, but its Hebrew context is far richer: without divine revelation, without the word of the LORD, human community loses its moral and social coherence.

The chapter also addresses the twin temptations of leadership: listening to falsehood (v.12) and the fear of man (v.25). The ruler who wants to be loved rather than just will tolerate flattery and generate corruption. The person who fears what others think becomes a snare to themselves — and a danger to those they lead. The antidote in both cases is the fear of the LORD, which is its own kind of freedom.

Keller reads verse 25 as one of Proverbs' most penetrating diagnoses of the human condition: the fear of man is not merely a social anxiety but a form of idolatry, a misplaced trust that enslaves precisely because it demands everything and delivers nothing lasting.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 29 — Correction, Justice for the Poor, and the Snare of People-Pleasing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 29 covers the son who accepts correction (v.1,15), the ruler who is just to the poor (v.14), the vision without which people perish (v.18), and one of Proverbs' most theologically searching statements: the fear of man is a snare, but the one who trusts in the LORD is safe (v.25). The chapter builds toward this climax, showing how justice, correction, and governance all depend on whether one fears God or fears men.
verseByVerse.theology: The fear of man (v.25) is the pastoral problem that underlies much of what Proverbs has diagnosed throughout. Every form of flattery, false witness, partiality, and sycophancy is an expression of the fear of man. The antidote is not courage in the conventional sense but the fear of God—a reverence so complete that it eclipses the terror of human disapproval.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 18—where there is no prophetic vision, the people cast off restraint—has been quoted in countless contexts. In its original meaning it concerns the absence of God's word through his prophets; where the word of God is not heard, social restraint dissolves. The connection between the word of God and civil order is theological and empirical.

verseByVerse.quote: He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing. When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing.

The whole book is compressed into that one sentence, and the two words that carry it are often and suddenly.

Often reproved. Not once, not ignorantly. This is a man who has been told, repeatedly, over years, by different people who cared enough to say it — and every time, the neck went hard. The image is a draught animal refusing the yoke: not arguing, since an ox cannot argue, simply setting the muscles and declining to turn.

And then suddenly. After all that duration, the end has no duration at all. Which is the consistent testimony of anybody who has watched a man go down: the collapse took a weekend, and everybody was astonished, and the warnings had been arriving since 2011.

Beyond healing is the phrase of 6:15, and it needs the same guard: this is not a denial that God forgives. It is a statement about a particular fracture. Some things, once they finally break, do not go back to what they were — the marriage, the ministry, the trust of a child — and the man may be entirely forgiven and still be living among the pieces.

Then v. 2: when the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan. The groan is involuntary and it is the truest indicator of a regime, because nobody organises it and nobody can be prosecuted for it.

verseByVerse.quote: He who loves wisdom makes his father glad, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth. By justice a king builds up the land, but he who exacts gifts tears it down. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who loves wisdom makes his father glad, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth. The two halves of the prodigal son, three hundred years before the parable — a father’s gladness, and a young man in a far country with the money gone.

Then v. 4: by justice a king builds up the land, but he who exacts gifts tears it down.

The word for gifts is the bribe word, and the contrast is architectural: one man is building and the other is pulling the same structure down.

And the mechanism explains why corruption is so much more destructive than theft. What a corrupt official takes is small compared to what he destroys, and what he destroys is the thing everything else rests on — the assumption that outcomes are related to merit. Once a country stops believing that, every citizen begins behaving rationally in a corrupt system, and the damage is no longer traceable to anybody.

verseByVerse.quote: A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet. An evil man is ensnared in his transgression, but a righteous man sings and rejoices. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet.

The Hebrew leaves it deliberately ambiguous whose feet are in the net, and the ambiguity is a gift, because both readings are true.

Read one way, the flatterer is trapping his neighbour — and this is the plain sense. Praise is laid on the ground like a net, the man walks into it feeling excellent, and by the time he notices he is committed to something.

Read the other way, the net is under the flatterer’s own feet, which is the sharper reading. A man who has made his way by telling people what they want to hear is not free. He is now required to keep doing it; he cannot afford an honest sentence with anybody he has flattered, and the network of small untruths he has laid down around himself is exactly the thing he will trip over.

Then v. 6: an evil man is ensnared in his transgression, but a righteous man sings and rejoices. Two men in the same world, and the comparison is not between one who is caught and one who escapes. It is between a man tangled in something and a man singing — which is a strange and lovely thing to set against a snare, and it is the more accurate picture of what a clear conscience actually produces.

verseByVerse.quote: A righteous man knows the rights of the poor; a wicked man does not understand such knowledge. Scoffers set a city aflame, but the wise turn away wrath. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A righteous man knows the rights of the poor; a wicked man does not understand such knowledge.

The word is knows, and it is not sympathy. It is information: what the poor man is actually entitled to, what the law provides, what is owed him and by whom.

Which sets a considerably higher bar than feeling sorry for people. It is possible to be moved by poverty in general and to know nothing whatever about the specific case in front of you — the tenancy, the benefit, the wage, the debt — and Proverbs says the righteous man has taken the trouble to find out.

And the second half explains why so little changes. The wicked man does not merely disregard the poor man’s rights; he does not understand such knowledge, and the phrase is dismissive. The whole category is unintelligible to him. He is not being asked to be generous and refusing; he cannot see what is being talked about.

Then v. 8: scoffers set a city aflame, but the wise turn away wrath. The fire imagery of 26:20-21, and note the disproportion — a city, set alight by men who have done nothing but talk. Mockery is being credited with the power to burn a place down, which anybody who has watched a community turn will not consider an exaggeration.

verseByVerse.quote: If a wise man has an argument with a fool, the fool only rages and laughs, and there is no quiet. Bloodthirsty men hate one who is blameless and seek the life of the upright. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
If a wise man has an argument with a fool, the fool only rages and laughs, and there is no quiet.

Both reactions in one sentence, and that is the exactness of it: rages and laughs. Not alternately in some ordered way — both, unpredictably, sometimes within a minute, so that a serious point is met with fury and then with amusement and the man asking cannot tell which is coming.

And the last clause is the verdict: there is no quiet. No resolution, and no settlement. The argument does not end, because ending requires somebody to concede something, and raging and laughing are precisely the two responses that never do.

Which is why 26:4 said what it said. There are conversations that cannot reach a conclusion, and the wise man’s error is not that he argues badly. It is that he keeps going, believing that one more attempt will produce quiet, and it will not.

Then v. 10: bloodthirsty men hate one who is blameless. Not envy — hate. The existence of an honest man is an accusation to a dishonest one, and it requires no words. Which is why the innocent are so often the target rather than the powerful, and it is finally why a man who had done nothing at all was killed outside a city wall.

verseByVerse.quote: A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back. If a ruler listens to falsehood, all his officials will be wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back.

This verse has been in a long argument with the modern world and has quietly won it. An entire century has been taught that expressing everything is healthy and holding back is repression — and Proverbs says the man who gives full vent is a fool.

Note that neither man in this verse is described as feeling less. The wise man has exactly the same thing in him; the difference is that he holds it, and the word for it is quietly, which means nobody in the room knows the holding is happening.

And the reason is not that feelings do not matter. It is that a feeling voiced in full, at volume, at the moment it is hottest, is almost never what the man will think in the morning — and by then it has been said, and cannot be recalled, and everybody heard it.

Then v. 12: if a ruler listens to falsehood, all his officials will be wicked.

The word is all, and it is a claim about how organisations work. A leader does not need to be corrupt to corrupt everything under him; he need only be receptive to a certain kind of report. Everybody beneath him learns within a month what sort of information is welcome, and within a year nobody is bringing him anything else — and he will sincerely believe he is well informed.

verseByVerse.quote: The poor man and the oppressor meet together; the LORD gives light to the eyes of both. If a king faithfully judges the poor, his throne will be established forever. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poor man and the oppressor meet together; the LORD gives light to the eyes of both.

A near-twin of 22:2, and this version is more startling. There the rich and poor met and God was Maker of both; here it is the poor man and the man who is grinding him down — and God gives light to the eyes of both.

Light to the eyes is a Hebrew way of saying life itself; it is what a man has when he is alive. So the verse says that the oppressor is being kept in existence, this morning, by the God of the man he is oppressing.

Which is the common grace of God stated without comfort. The sun rises on the evil and the good, said the Lord Jesus, and he said it as an argument for loving enemies (Matthew 5:45). The man doing harm is breathing air that is being given to him.

Then v. 14: if a king faithfully judges the poor, his throne will be established for ever. The whole security of a reign is attached to its treatment of the people with the least ability to affect it — which is the one group a ruler can safely ignore, and the verse says the throne stands or falls there.

verseByVerse.quote: The rod and reproof give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother. When the wicked increase, transgression increases, but the righteous will look upon their downfall. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rod and reproof give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother.

The phrase that carries this is left to himself, and it names something that does not feel like a decision. Nobody sets out to abandon a child. What the verse describes is the absence of attention — a child who is fed, clothed, and left, because the parent is tired, or busy, or frightened of the confrontation.

And the two instruments are named together: the rod and reproof. Words as well as correction. The two readings of the rod set out at 13:24 stand here, and what is not in dispute is that a child needs both something said and something done, and that a household with neither is not being gentle.

Then v. 16: when the wicked increase, transgression increases, but the righteous will look upon their downfall. The first half is a claim about atmosphere: wrongdoing is not a fixed quantity in a society but multiplies with the number of people visibly doing it — which is why the tone of a workplace, a school or a church changes so quickly once a few people set it.

verseByVerse.quote: Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will give delight to your heart. Where there is no prophetic vision the people cast off restraint, but blessed is he who keeps the law. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will give delight to your heart. Note what is promised, and to whom. Rest, to the parent — which is the honest currency, because the alternative is a decade of not sleeping.

Then v. 18, the most misquoted verse in Proverbs: where there is no prophetic vision the people cast off restraint, but blessed is he who keeps the law.

The older rendering — where there is no vision, the people perish — has been used for a century to mean that organisations need ambitious goals, and that is not remotely what the verse says. The word is hazon, and it means prophetic revelation: God speaking. Not a strategy. A word from outside.

And the result of its absence is not that people fail. It is that they cast off restraint — the verb used of a mob, or of cattle out of a broken pen. Where God is not speaking, the fences come down; and it is not that people become miserable, but that nothing is holding them.

Which is why the second half is the answer, and it is deliberately unglamorous. Against a whole society running loose stands he who keeps the law — one man, doing what he was told, staying inside the fence when it no longer appears to be attached to anything. And he is called blessed.

verseByVerse.quote: By mere words a servant is not disciplined, for though he understands, he will not respond. Do you see a man who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
By mere words a servant is not disciplined, for though he understands, he will not respond.

The observation is uncomfortable and it is not about servants only. There are people in whom words do nothing — and the verse is careful to say why, because it is not comprehension. Though he understands, he will not respond. He heard it, he took it in, and nothing followed.

Which is a real limit on what teaching can do, and anybody who has managed, parented or pastored has met it. The instinct in that situation is to explain again, at greater length and more clearly, on the assumption that the message failed. Proverbs says the message arrived. Something else is missing, and more words will not supply it.

Then v. 20: do you see a man who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him.

This is 26:12 with one substitution, and the substitution is startling. There the man worse than a fool was the one wise in his own eyes. Here it is the man who speaks too quickly — which sets a very ordinary fault in extremely serious company.

And the two are more closely related than they look. A man who speaks before he has thought has, in that moment, treated his first reaction as reliable — which is what being wise in one’s own eyes consists of, performed at speed and a dozen times a day.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever pampers his servant from childhood will in the end find him his heir. A man of wrath stirs up strife, and one given to anger causes much transgression. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever pampers his servant from childhood will in the end find him his heir.

The Hebrew of the last word is uncertain and the sense is not: something has gone wrong in the household. A relationship that should have been one thing has, through years of indulgence, become another, and the man who did the indulging did not choose the outcome and cannot now undo it.

That is the general shape of the warning, and it applies well past servants. Indulgence is not a neutral kindness; it establishes something. Every concession makes the next one expected, and by the time a man notices that the arrangement has changed, it changed some years ago and there was no moment at which it could have been objected to.

Then v. 22: a man of wrath stirs up strife, and one given to anger causes much transgression.

The second half is the one to weigh, because it counts a cost angry men never count. He causes much transgression — in other people. His temper is not merely a fault he has; it is a generator, and the sins committed around him because of it are on his account too: the lies told to avoid setting him off, the resentment cultivated by people who cannot answer him, the children who learned that this is how a man behaves.

That is the answer to the standing defence of the short-tempered, that it is over quickly and he means nothing by it. It is over quickly for him.

verseByVerse.quote: One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor. The partner of a thief hates his own life; he hears the curse, but discloses nothing. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
One’s pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor.

The book has said this at 11:2, 15:33, 16:18 and 18:12, and it says it once more before the collection ends. Five times is Proverbs at its most emphatic, and the reason is that this is the one error nobody detects in himself.

And the mechanics are in the verbs. Pride does not lead to being brought low by somebody else; it brings him low, and it is his own. Humility does not achieve honour either — the lowly man obtains it, receives it, from hands that are not his.

Then v. 24: the partner of a thief hates his own life; he hears the curse, but discloses nothing.

The setting is a court. When something was stolen, a public adjuration was pronounced over the community — a curse laid on anyone who knew and would not say — and the man in this verse is standing there, hearing it, saying nothing.

He has not stolen anything. That is the point of the verse. He is guilty by silence, and Proverbs says of him that he hates his own life — because he has bound himself to a man who will eventually be caught, and he will go down with him, and he chose it in a room where all he had to do was speak.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe. Many seek the face of a ruler, but it is from the LORD that a man gets justice. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe.

Of all the verses in this chapter this is the most useful, because it names the thing that actually governs most people’s decisions and that almost nobody would list as a motive.

Ask a man why he did not say the thing at the meeting, or why he agreed to the arrangement, or why he has not raised the matter with his brother for four years, and the reasons offered will be prudential. Underneath nearly all of them is this verse. He was afraid of a person: of what would be thought, of the atmosphere, of a particular face going cold.

And the image is a snare, which is the right one, because a snare does not stop a man where he stood. It takes him somewhere. The fear of one person’s opinion has made people move house, change churches, keep silent about abuse, marry, stay married, sign documents and lose decades — and at every stage it felt like a series of small reasonable accommodations.

The cure offered is not courage. Proverbs does not tell him to care less what people think, which is advice nobody has ever successfully taken. It moves the object: whoever trusts in the LORD is safe. The fear does not go by being resisted; it goes by being displaced, when a man becomes more concerned with one opinion than with all the others.

Then v. 26: many seek the face of a ruler, but it is from the LORD that a man gets justice. Which is the same lesson applied to hope rather than to fear. The queue outside the great man’s door is long, and everybody in it is seeking a face — and Proverbs notes, drily, that the decision they are all waiting for is not being made in that room.

verseByVerse.quote: An unjust man is an abomination to the righteous, but one whose way is straight is an abomination to the wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
An unjust man is an abomination to the righteous, but one whose way is straight is an abomination to the wicked.

The Hezekiah collection closes on a perfectly balanced sentence, and the balance is the point. The revulsion runs both ways.

Which is a more honest ending than a warm one would have been. Proverbs has spent five chapters describing two kinds of life, and it finishes by observing that they cannot be reconciled and that each finds the other genuinely repellent. Not disagreeable — abomination, the strongest word available, used of both.

And the second half is the one Christians need and rarely expect. A straight life is offensive to crooked people, and it is offensive precisely because it is straight; the offence is not caused by tactlessness and cannot be removed by better manners. A man who has decided to live this way and is puzzled that certain people cannot stand him has not been badly advised. He has been read correctly.

Which is exactly what the Lord Jesus told his disciples to expect, and he put it in the same terms: if the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you (John 15:18). He was the one man in history whose way was entirely straight, and the reaction to him was not indifference. It was the reaction this verse describes, and it ended at a cross.

So the collection ends without resolving the tension, because it does not resolve in this world. There is no arrangement under which a man is both straight and universally liked, and the honest thing — which is what this book has been from the first verse — is to say so plainly and let the reader choose which abomination he would rather be.

29.theology:
Revelation as Social Foundation. Verse 18 makes a claim that should trouble both secular and religious complacency: human society cannot sustain itself by human wisdom alone. It needs the word of God — not as a political imposition but as the moral grammar that makes community coherent. The history of every society that has tried to build order on human reason alone is the history of ideologies that eventually devour themselves. The church is, among other things, the community that keeps the word of God alive in the world — not for its own sake, but for the world's sake.

The Fear of the LORD vs. the Fear of Man. Verses 25 and 23 together present Proverbs' final pastoral diagnosis: pride (placing the self at the center) and fear of man (placing human opinion at the center) are two versions of the same disorder — life organized around anything other than the LORD. Both lead to a snare. Only trust in the LORD is safe, and only humility before the LORD leads to honor. This is the fear of the LORD in its final, practical form.
29.examples:
Then: The ruler who listens to falsehood (v.12) was an immediate practical concern in the ancient Near East — courtiers who told kings what they wanted to hear were a perennial danger, one that the prophets constantly opposed. The fear of man (v.25) was particularly acute for anyone in a patronage society: your livelihood, safety, and social standing all depended on powerful people's approval. Proverbs' call to trust the LORD rather than manage human opinion was countercultural in every ancient context.

Now: Verse 25 is the pastoral verse of the chapter — perhaps of the entire book — for contemporary application. The epidemic of anxiety, people-pleasing, cancel-culture terror, and social-media performance is Proverbs' "fear of man" writ large in digital ink. The pastor who preaches what the congregation wants to hear, the employee who never challenges injustice, the friend who flatters rather than wounds — all are in the snare. The antidote is not indifference but a stronger fear: the fear of the LORD that makes every other fear small.

30.title: The Words of Agur
30.text: <sup>1</sup>The words of Agur son of Jakeh. The oracle. The man declares, I am weary, O God; I am weary, O God, and worn out.<sup>2</sup>Surely I am too stupid to be a man. I have not the understanding of a man.<sup>3</sup>I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One.<sup>4</sup>Who has ascended to heaven and come down?
