30.overview:
Chapter 30 is the most distinctive unit in the book of Proverbs — the words of Agur son of Jakeh, an otherwise unknown figure whose opening confession is one of the most startling passages in wisdom literature. He begins not with a proverb but with an admission of total inadequacy: "I am too stupid to be a man. I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One" (vv.2–3). This is the fear of the LORD in its most radical form — a profound epistemic humility before the mystery of God.

The rhetorical questions of verse 4 — "Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists?" — echo God's speech from the whirlwind in Job 38–39 and anticipate the Prologue of John: the One who descended and ascended, who commands wind and wave, is the Son of God, the Word made flesh (John 3:13; Eph. 4:9–10). "What is his name, and what is his son's name? Surely you know!" is charged with irony — Agur does not know, but the reader of the whole canon does.

The prayer of verses 7–9 is one of the most theologically mature prayers in Scripture: give me neither poverty nor riches, only enough. It is the prayer of someone who understands the spiritual dangers of both extremes — the arrogance of abundance and the desperation of want. Keller calls it the perfect antidote to prosperity theology and poverty mysticism alike.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 30 — Agur's Confession of Ignorance, Four-Things Sayings, and the Limits of the Creature
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 30 introduces Agur son of Jakeh, whose opening confession is one of the most startlingly humble passages in the Bible: 'I am too stupid to be a man. I have not the understanding of a man' (v.2). From this posture of radical epistemic humility, Agur moves to praise the reliability of God's word (v.5), requests for moderation in wealth and poverty (vv.7-9), and a series of numerical observations (the 'four things') that celebrate the wonder of creation.
verseByVerse.theology: Agur's theology begins with what he does not know (vv.2-4): a series of impossible questions about the cosmic creator, reminiscent of God's speech to Job (Job 38-41). The answer implicit in the questions is: only God knows, and only God has done these things. The creature who begins with this humility is properly positioned to receive wisdom from above.
verseByVerse.examples: The numerical sayings (threes and fours) are not mere curiosity but a poetic strategy for enlarging perception: the world is full of wonders that the person of limited vision misses. The leech that never says enough, the four never-satisfied things, the four things too wonderful, the four things too little but exceeding wise—all call the reader to attend more carefully to the creation that God made.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of Agur son of Jakeh. The oracle. The man declares, I am weary, O God; I am weary, O God, and worn out. Surely I am too stupid to be a man. I have not the understanding of a man. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of Agur son of Jakeh. The oracle. The man declares, I am weary, O God; I am weary, O God, and worn out.

A new voice, and nobody knows who he was. Agur is named nowhere else in Scripture, and after twenty-nine chapters of Solomon and the wise men the book gives its penultimate chapter to a man about whom nothing is known at all.

And listen to how he begins. Not with a maxim — with exhaustion, said twice: I am weary, O God; I am weary, O God, and worn out. The Hebrew of this verse is famously difficult and translators have divided over it for centuries, but the ESV’s reading has the ring of the man who follows, and it is remarkable that it is here at all.

Because this is the last thing a book of wisdom would be expected to contain. Proverbs has been supremely confident for twenty-nine chapters — the world is ordered, folly is self-defeating, wisdom can be got — and then it hands the microphone to somebody who is tired out by the whole business and says so before he says anything else.

Then v. 2, and he goes further: surely I am too stupid to be a man. I have not the understanding of a man. The word he uses of himself is ba‘ar, the brutish, cattle word of 12:1 — the very insult this book throws at people who will not learn, turned round and applied by a wise man to himself.

Which is not false modesty and it is not depression. It is what happens to an honest mind that has gone far enough. A man who has really looked at the world does not end up impressed with his own grasp of it, and Agur is the proof that the wisdom tradition knew this about itself.

verseByVerse.quote: I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One. Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has wrapped up the waters in a garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son's name? Surely you know! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One. And then, out of that admission, comes the most extraordinary passage in the book.

Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has wrapped up the waters in a garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth?

Four questions, and each names something no human being has ever done. They are the questions God asks Job out of the whirlwind, asked here by a man who has arrived at the same place from below. And notice their shape: they are not about God’s power in the abstract but about action — going up, coming down, holding, wrapping, establishing.

Then the fifth question, and it stops the reader: what is his name, and what is his son’s name? Surely you know!

The last clause is heavy with irony. Agur has just said he knows nothing, and he asks a question he is certain his hearer cannot answer either. Somebody did all this. He has a name, and — this is the astonishing part — he has a son, and Agur knows neither.

The Old Testament nowhere else comes so close to asking the question outright. And the answer, when it came, used Agur’s own words: no one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man (John 3:13). Somebody has come down; the name is Jesus; and the son’s name Agur could not supply is the name at which every knee will bow.

Which means the wisest thing in this chapter is a confession of ignorance that turns out to be a question with an answer — and the answer was a person who had not yet arrived, and who would one day stand in a boat and speak to the wind that only God could gather in his fists.

verseByVerse.quote: Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him. Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him.

After the four questions, this. Agur cannot ascend to heaven and does not know the name — and what he has instead is a word that has been tested and holds.

The verb is a metalworker’s word: refined, assayed, put through fire to see what it actually is. So the claim is not that God’s word sounds impressive but that it has been examined and no dross came off — which is exactly what a man in Agur’s condition needs. He has stopped trusting his own understanding, and he must therefore have something outside himself that survives testing.

Then v. 6, and it follows necessarily: do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar.

The prohibition is on adding, which is the more interesting error. Taking things away is obvious vandalism and everybody recognises it. Adding looks like devotion — a further requirement, a detail supplied where Scripture was silent, a certainty about something God did not say — and it is almost always done by the most serious people, out of a wish to be more careful than God was.

And the verdict is severe: the man who does it will be found a liar, because he has put his own sentence inside somebody else’s speech and let it be taken for theirs. Moses said it (Deuteronomy 4:2), and the last chapter of the Bible says it again over the whole book (Revelation 22:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Two things I ask of you; deny them not to me before I die: Remove far from me falsehood and lying; give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things I ask of you; deny them not to me before I die.

This is the only prayer in the book of Proverbs, and there is something moving about where it falls: at the very end, from the man who said he was weary and understood nothing.

And the framing is that of a man who knows he is running out of time. Before I die — this is not a young man’s prayer. He has narrowed a whole life’s wanting down to two requests, and what he asks for is nothing anybody would put on a list.

Remove far from me falsehood and lying — not that he may never be lied to, but that there may be none in him. And then the second, and it is one of the strangest petitions in Scripture: give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me.

Nobody prays this. Everybody prays the first half — deliver me from poverty — and nobody has ever asked to be spared wealth, because it does not occur to us that wealth is a danger requiring deliverance.

Agur is asking for the middle: enough, and no more. And the phrase the food that is needful for me is precisely the request the Lord Jesus put into the model prayer, in the same shape: give us this day our daily bread (Matthew 6:11). Not this year’s. Today’s — which requires a man to come back tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: lest I be full and deny you and say, "Who is the LORD?" or lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lest I be full and deny you and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God.

And here is his reasoning, and it is the most self-aware sentence in the Old Testament.

He knows exactly what wealth would do to him. Not that he would become greedy — that he would become self-sufficient, and that a full man asks who is the LORD? not in defiance but in genuine puzzlement, because nothing in his week requires God for anything. That is the danger of plenty, and it is invisible from inside it. Nobody notices the moment prayer became optional.

And he knows what poverty would do to him too, and he is equally honest about it: he would steal, and in stealing would drag God’s name through it, since a thieving believer does more damage to the name than an honest unbeliever ever could.

What makes the prayer great is that he does not claim to be above either. He is not asking God to help him handle wealth well. He is saying, in effect, that he knows himself well enough not to trust himself with it — which is a level of self-knowledge almost nobody reaches, and the only sane response to it is exactly the one he makes: to ask God to arrange his circumstances so that his weakness is not tested.

Which is also, word for word, what the Lord taught us to pray: lead us not into temptation (Matthew 6:13). Not make me strong enough. Do not take me there.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not slander a servant to his master, lest he curse you, and you be held guilty. There are those who curse their fathers and do not bless their mothers. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not slander a servant to his master, lest he curse you, and you be held guilty.

The specific case is a man with no standing being reported to the one person who can ruin him, and the reason given is startling: lest he curse you. The servant has no power, no appeal and no defence — and his cry against you counts, which is the same principle as 22:23. God attends to the complaints of people nobody else has to listen to.

Then v. 11 opens a sequence of four there are those sayings, and they form a portrait of a generation: there are those who curse their fathers and do not bless their mothers.

The first mark of a society going wrong is not violence or greed; it is contempt at home. And the second half is the quieter half — not cursing the mother, simply not blessing her, which is an omission and not an act, and is how most of it is actually done.

verseByVerse.quote: There are those who are clean in their own eyes but are not washed of their filth. There are those—how lofty are their eyes, how high their eyelids lift! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are those who are clean in their own eyes but are not washed of their filth.

The second of the four, and it is the most searching sentence in the chapter. Two things are true of this man at once: he is genuinely filthy, and he genuinely believes he is clean.

And the verb is washed — passive. He has not been washed, which is a different claim from saying he has not washed himself. Cleansing here is something done to a man from outside, and the reason he does not have it is not that he refused. It is that he never applied, because he did not think he needed it.

That is the exact condition of religious respectability, and it is why the Lord Jesus made so little progress with the Pharisees and so much with prostitutes. The publican who could not lift his eyes went home justified (Luke 18:14); and it is this verse the Lord had in mind when he told men who were scrupulous about cups that they were full of greed and self-indulgence inside (Matthew 23:25).

Then v. 13: there are those — how lofty are their eyes, how high their eyelids lift! The third mark, and it is not a sentence but an exclamation. Agur is describing a look, and everybody knows it: the very slight raising of the eyelids that measures a person and finds him not worth the trouble. It requires no words at all, and it is completely unmistakable to whoever receives it.

verseByVerse.quote: There are those whose teeth are swords, whose fangs are knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, the needy from among mankind. The leech has two daughters: Give and Give. Three things are never satisfied; four never say, "Enough": (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are those whose teeth are swords, whose fangs are knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, the needy from among mankind.

The fourth and last of the generation, and the imagery has become predatory. Teeth like swords, and the object is not conquest but eating — devour the poor, which reduces people to food and describes exactly what an exploitative arrangement does to those inside it.

And note the progression across the four. It began with contempt for parents, went to a false conscience, then to a look, and ends with cannibalism of the poor. That is a sequence rather than a list, and it is the sober suggestion that the last item is what the first one becomes when nothing interrupts it.

Then v. 15 changes gear completely: the leech has two daughters: Give and Give.

It is a joke, and a grim one. The leech’s children are named after the only word she knows, and Proverbs has just described a whole class of people whose entire vocabulary is a request.

And then the numerical saying begins: three things are never satisfied; four never say, Enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Sheol, the barren womb, the land never satisfied with water, and the fire that never says, "Enough." The eye that mocks a father and scorns to obey a mother will be picked out by the ravens of the valley and eaten by the vultures. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sheol, the barren womb, the land never satisfied with water, and the fire that never says, Enough.

Four insatiable things, and the second is not like the others. Sheol takes everybody, dry ground absorbs any amount of rain, and fire consumes whatever it is given — three appetites that swallow. And in the middle of them, a woman who cannot have a child.

Which is an act of considerable tenderness on Agur’s part, and it is easily missed. He is not accusing her of anything. He has put childlessness on a list of the four great unfillable hungers in the world, alongside death itself — which is a truer estimate of that grief than most people who have not carried it would ever make.

And any reader who is living it will recognise the exactness. It is not a disappointment that diminishes with time. It is a wanting with no floor, and every month is a fresh one, and nothing else supplied has ever filled the place.

Then v. 17, and the tone snaps back: the eye that mocks a father and scorns to obey a mother will be picked out by the ravens of the valley.

The image is a corpse left unburied on open ground, which to an Israelite was the most degrading end imaginable. And the punishment is aimed at the offending organ — the eye of v. 13, that lifted its lids at a parent, taken by birds. It is deliberately grotesque, and it is answering v. 11: the contempt that began the chapter’s catalogue is here at the end of it, and Agur wants it seen for what it comes to.

verseByVerse.quote: Three things are too wonderful for me; four I do not understand: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship on the high seas, and the way of a man with a virgin. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three things are too wonderful for me; four I do not understand: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship on the high seas, and the way of a man with a virgin.

Agur, who began by saying he understood nothing, now says it again — and this time it is not lament. It is delight.

The four have one thing in common and it takes a moment to see: none of them leaves a track. The eagle goes through the air and the air closes; the snake crosses bare rock without a mark; the ship passes and the sea is exactly as it was. Motion with no trace of the passage.

And then the fourth, which is the one the list was built for: the way of a man with a virgin. The mystery of how two people come to love each other. There is no track there either. Nobody can reconstruct it afterwards, including the two of them — how it began, why her, what happened between an ordinary acquaintance and the day everything was different.

Which is why this is a verse to give to anyone inclined to reduce love to chemistry or to strategy. Agur was a wise man and this is his considered position: it cannot be explained, and he does not want it explained. He calls it too wonderful, and puts it beside an eagle.

And there is something to be learned from a man whose response to what he cannot understand is not frustration but wonder. That is a rare temperament and it is close to the heart of what this book means by the fear of the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the way of an adulteress: she eats and wipes her mouth and says, "I have done no wrong." Under three things the earth trembles; under four it cannot bear up: (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the way of an adulteress: she eats and wipes her mouth and says, I have done no wrong.

Immediately after the fourth wonderful thing comes its counterfeit, and the placing is deliberate. The way of a man with a virgin is a mystery. This is the way of the adulteress — the same word, way, and no mystery at all.

And the picture is the most casual in the book. She eats, she wipes her mouth, she says she has done nothing. Three actions, and the third is as untroubled as the other two — the wiping of the mouth is the gesture of a person finishing an ordinary meal and thinking about something else.

That is what the passage is for. It is not describing defiance; a defiant conscience at least knows what it is refusing. This is a conscience that has stopped registering. She is not lying when she says she has done no wrong, which is exactly the horror of it, and it is where the road of chs 5 to 7 finally arrives.

Then v. 21 opens a new numerical saying: under three things the earth trembles; under four it cannot bear up.

verseByVerse.quote: a slave when he becomes king, and a fool when he is filled with food; an unloved woman when she gets a husband, and a maidservant when she displaces her mistress. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A slave when he becomes king, and a fool when he is filled with food; an unloved woman when she gets a husband, and a maidservant when she displaces her mistress.

Four situations the earth cannot carry, and modern readers often mistake the point. Agur is not saying that servants should stay servants. Proverbs itself has just said that a servant who deals wisely will rule (17:2), and God’s own habit throughout Scripture is to raise the lowly.

What all four have in common is a sudden reversal with no formation behind it. Each of these people has come into something they longed for and were never prepared for — and the trouble is not their origin but the speed.

The slave made king has been under authority and has learned nothing about exercising it, and has usually learned a great deal about resenting it. The fool with a full stomach has had the one restraint on him removed. The unloved woman who finally marries carries into the marriage everything the years of not being wanted put into her. And the maid who has displaced her mistress is in possession of a house she used to clean.

The observation is compassionate rather than snobbish, and it names something anybody can watch happening: getting what you wanted, before you were the sort of person who could hold it, is one of the more efficient ways to be ruined — and it is exactly why God so often makes people wait.

verseByVerse.quote: Four things on earth are small, but they are exceedingly wise: the ants are a people not strong, yet they provide their food in the summer; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four things on earth are small, but they are exceedingly wise.

The loveliest of Agur’s lists, and after the four that made the earth tremble it is the perfect answer: four creatures that could be stepped on, each of which has solved a problem that ought to have defeated it.

And the framing tells the reader what to do. Agur is not drawing morals from nature at random. He is doing what the father did at 6:6 — sending a man outside to look at something smaller than himself.

Then the first: the ants are a people not strong, yet they provide their food in the summer.

Their answer to weakness is timing. An ant cannot fight anything, cannot outrun a winter, and cannot carry much — and it does not need to, because it acts in the season when the work is possible. Which is the whole strategy available to anybody who is not strong, and it is a considerable one: you cannot beat the winter, and you can be ready before it.

verseByVerse.quote: the rock badgers are a people not mighty, yet they make their homes in the cliffs; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rock badgers are a people not mighty, yet they make their homes in the cliffs.

The second small creature, and its solution is different from the ant’s. The hyrax — a small furry animal about the size of a rabbit, with no speed, no weapons and no strength — lives where nothing can get at it.

It has not become strong. It has chosen its ground, and the cliff does the work. Everything that would eat it is bigger and faster and cannot climb, so its entire defence consists of being somewhere.

That is the strategy this whole book has been recommending, and here it is with fur on. The weak creature that survives is not the one that learns to fight. It is the one that knows where the rock is and does not go far from it — and the Psalms use exactly this animal’s habitat for God himself: the LORD is my rock and my fortress, the high mountains are for the wild goats; the rocks are a refuge for the rock badgers (Psalm 18:2; 104:18).

A Christian is not asked to be formidable. He is asked to live in the cliffs.

verseByVerse.quote: the locusts have no king, yet all of them march in rank; the lizard you can take in your hands, yet it is in kings' palaces. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The locusts have no king, yet all of them march in rank.

The third, and its answer is coordination. A single locust is nothing; a swarm strips a country. And the astonishing part, which Agur has noticed exactly, is that there is no king — no command, no order given, and yet every one of them moves in formation.

Here is a picture of what a body can do when nobody has to be persuaded. In most human organisations the ranks are held by authority; the locusts hold theirs because of what they are. Paul reaches for the same idea when he describes a church as a body whose parts do not require instructions to serve each other.

Then the fourth: the lizard you can take in your hands, yet it is in kings’ palaces.

The joke is perfect and it is the best of the four. This creature is so unimpressive that a man can pick it up — and it lives in the palace. It has no rank, no invitation and no business being there, and there it is on the wall of the throne room, having got in past every guard by being too small to stop.

Which is the last word of the list and the point of the whole set: none of these four is powerful, and all four are exactly where they need to be. Smallness is not the obstacle a man thinks it is. It is very often the method.

verseByVerse.quote: Three things are stately in their tread; four are stately in their stride: the lion, which is mightiest among beasts and does not turn back before any; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three things are stately in their tread; four are stately in their stride: the lion, which is mightiest among beasts and does not turn back before any.

The counterpart to the previous list, and the arrangement of the two is the wit of the chapter. Four small things that are wise, and then four stately things that are — well, the reader is invited to notice what happens to this list as it goes on.

The lion begins it and deserves the place. Does not turn back before any is a real description: an animal with nothing above it in the world, whose composure is not performed.

And the word for all four is about bearing rather than power — the way a thing walks, the confidence in the tread. Which is a quality men have always admired and always tried to imitate, and the next verse is about to say something quietly devastating about the imitation.

verseByVerse.quote: the strutting rooster, the he-goat, and a king whose army is with him. If you have been foolish, exalting yourself, or if you have been devising evil, put your hand on your mouth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The strutting rooster, the he-goat, and a king whose army is with him.

And there is the joke, and it is not gentle. The list of stately things began with a lion, and it ends with a cockerel, a goat, and a king — in that order, in the same sentence, as though there were nothing to choose between them.

The rooster struts magnificently and is a small bird in a farmyard. The he-goat leads the flock and is a goat. And the king is stately, Agur says, whose army is with him — which is the clause that undoes him. His bearing is borrowed. Remove the army and the walk changes, which cannot be said of the lion.

Which is as neat a piece of satire as the Old Testament contains, and it is aimed at everybody who has ever walked into a room differently because of what was standing behind him — the title, the money, the institution, the people who agree with him.

Then v. 32, and Agur turns from watching to instructing, for the only time: if you have been foolish, exalting yourself, or if you have been devising evil, put your hand on your mouth.

The gesture is physical and immediate. Not reflect, not repent in the abstract — put your hand over your mouth, which is what a man does when he has realised something mid-sentence and needs to stop before the sentence finishes.

verseByVerse.quote: For pressing milk produces curds, pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For pressing milk produces curds, pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife.

The chapter — and Agur — ends on three examples of one principle, and the Hebrew makes the joke that English cannot: the same verb runs through all three. Squeeze milk, and you get butter. Squeeze a nose, and you get blood. Squeeze anger, and you get a fight.

The first is a good outcome, the second is an injury, and the third is the one being taught — and setting them side by side makes the argument without an argument. Pressure produces. That is what it does. The only question is what is being pressed.

And the counsel is the same as v. 32 and it is entirely practical. Anger is already present in most difficult situations; nobody is being told to have none. What produces the strife is the pressing — the extra sentence, the point pursued past the moment it was made, the wanting to be agreed with as well as right. Take the hand off and there is no fight, and the anger, unpressed, mostly evaporates by the following week.

So the man who began by saying he was weary and understood nothing finishes by telling the reader to put a hand over his mouth and stop squeezing. Which is a strange end to a chapter that has held the wind in its fists and asked for the name of the Son of God — and it is exactly right, because Agur has arrived where the whole book has been going: the man who knows how little he knows is the one who can be quiet.

30.theology:
Agur's Confession and the Knowledge of God. Verses 2–4 present what theologians call the via negativa — the approach to God through what cannot be said rather than what can. Agur knows that the gap between human knowledge and divine reality is infinite. The only bridge is revelation — "every word of God proves true" (v.5). This epistemological structure is precisely what Paul describes in 1 Corinthians 1–2: human wisdom cannot know God; God reveals himself through the "foolishness" of the cross. The wise person is the one who, like Agur, knows what they do not know and receives what God has given.

Contentment as Theology. The prayer of verses 8–9 embodies what Paul calls "learned contentment" (Phil. 4:11). Contentment is not a natural temperament but a theological achievement — the fruit of trusting that God's provision, whatever its form, is sufficient. It requires a prior conviction about God's goodness and sovereignty that prosperity theology undermines and asceticism misunderstands. Agur's prayer is the wisest financial philosophy in Scripture: enough, by the hand of a good God.
30.examples:
Then: Agur's confession (vv.2–4) would have been startling in a culture of competing wisdom schools, each claiming to have the key to the good life. A sage who begins by confessing ignorance is subverting the genre from within. The numerical sayings (three things / four things) were a recognized teaching form — the pattern held attention and the final item delivered the punch. The prayer of vv.8–9 addressed a society in which both the prosperity of the few and the poverty of the many were daily realities.

Now: Agur's prayer (vv.8–9) is the most direct rebuke of the prosperity gospel available in the Old Testament — and it also rebukes the romanticization of poverty. "Give me neither" is the prayer of someone who has seen clearly what both do to the soul. In an age of financial anxiety and comparison culture, "feed me with the food that is needful for me" is a radical act of trust. And verse 4's cascading questions ("What is his name, and what is his son's name?") invite the reader who knows the New Testament to feel the full weight of the answer: the name that is above every name (Phil. 2:9).

31.title: The Excellent Wife
31.text: <sup>1</sup>The words of King Lemuel. An oracle that his mother taught him:<sup>2</sup>What are you doing, my son? What are you doing, son of my womb? What are you doing, son of my vows?<sup>3</sup>Do not give your strength to women, your ways to those who destroy kings.<sup>4</sup>It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine, or for rulers to take strong drink,<sup>5</sup>lest they drink and forget what has been decreed and pervert the rights of all the afflicted.<sup>6</sup>Give strong drink to the one who is perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress;<sup>7</sup>let them drink and forget their poverty and remember their misery no more.<sup>8</sup>Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute.<sup>9</sup>Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy.<sup>10</sup>An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels.<sup>11</sup>The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will have no lack of gain.<sup>12</sup>She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life.<sup>13</sup>She seeks wool and flax, and works with willing hands.<sup>14</sup>She is like the ships of the merchant; she brings her food from afar.<sup>15</sup>She rises while it is yet night and provides food for her household and portions for her maidens.<sup>16</sup>She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard.<sup>17</sup>She dresses herself with strength and makes her arms strong.<sup>18</sup>She perceives that her merchandise is profitable. Her lamp does not go out at night.<sup>19</sup>She puts her hands to the distaff, and her hands hold the spindle.<sup>20</sup>She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy.<sup>21</sup>She is not afraid of snow for her household, for all her household are clothed in scarlet.<sup>22</sup>She makes bed coverings for herself; her clothing is fine linen and purple.<sup>23</sup>Her husband is known in the gates when he sits among the elders of the land.<sup>24</sup>She makes linen garments and sells them; she delivers sashes to the merchant.<sup>25</sup>Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come.<sup>26</sup>She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue.<sup>27</sup>She looks well to the ways of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness.<sup>28</sup>Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her:<sup>29</sup>"Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all."<sup>30</sup>Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.<sup>31</sup>Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.
31.overview:
Chapter 31 is the crown of the book of Proverbs — and it is breathtaking in its literary architecture. The final poem (vv.10–31) is an acrostic: each verse begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to taw. The entire alphabet is enlisted to praise this woman. Nothing has been left out; she is the complete embodiment of wisdom.

The poem must be read in light of the whole book. Proverbs 1–9 introduced Lady Wisdom and Lady Folly as two great feminine figures calling to humanity. Lady Folly was seductive, loud, and ultimately fatal (ch.7). Lady Wisdom called from the heights, offered life, and pointed to the fear of the LORD (ch.8–9). Now, in the book's final movement, Lady Wisdom is embodied in a particular woman whose life is the concrete shape of wisdom incarnate: she fears the LORD (v.30), she opens her hand to the poor (v.20), she speaks with wisdom (v.26), she is clothed with strength and dignity (v.25).

This woman is not a job description for wives but a portrait of wisdom as it appears in an actual human life. She is also, for the Christian reader, a type of the church — the bride who fears the Lord, who does good rather than harm, who is praised at the gates. And she points ultimately to Christ himself, the Wisdom of God in whom all the treasures of wisdom are hidden, who "surpasses them all" (v.29).

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 31 — The Queen Mother's Instruction and the Poem of the Excellent Wife
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 31 closes Proverbs with two remarkable pieces: the words of King Lemuel taught to him by his mother (vv.1-9) and the acrostic poem of the excellent wife (vv.10-31). The queen mother's instruction (vv.1-9) focuses on two dangers for the king: women and wine. The excellent wife poem is an alphabetic acrostic (each verse beginning with successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet), a form that signals comprehensiveness: this is the A to Z of wisdom embodied in a woman.
verseByVerse.theology: The excellent wife (eshet chayil—woman of valor or strength) is the culmination of Proverbs' vision of wisdom. She is the embodiment of everything chapters 1-9 commended as the goal of wisdom's formation. She is also Lady Wisdom made flesh—the personification of wisdom encountered in 1:20-33 and 8:1-36 now taking human form in a household. Waltke: the poem is not a job description for wives but a vision of human flourishing.
verseByVerse.examples: The poem's closing verses (vv.28-31) give the excellent wife what she has not sought: public praise from her husband and children, and honor at the gates. She who worked faithfully without seeking recognition receives it. The woman who fears the LORD (v.30) is contrasted with the woman of beauty who is vain—fear of God outlasts physical beauty and produces lasting honor.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of King Lemuel. An oracle that his mother taught him: What are you doing, my son? What are you doing, son of my womb? What are you doing, son of my vows? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words of King Lemuel. An oracle that his mother taught him.

The book of Proverbs ends with a woman speaking. After twenty-nine chapters of a father talking to his son, and a chapter from a man nobody can identify, the final word in Israel’s book of wisdom is a queen mother instructing her boy — and the whole of it, including the great poem at the end, is hers.

Lemuel is unknown outside this chapter, and it hardly matters. What matters is that Scripture troubled itself to say where these words came from, and the source is a mother who evidently thought her son needed telling and had the standing to tell him.

Then v. 2, and it is one of the most extraordinary sentences in the Bible, because it is barely a sentence at all: what are you doing, my son? What are you doing, son of my womb? What are you doing, son of my vows?

Three times, escalating, and the Hebrew is broken — it reads like somebody who has begun to speak before deciding what to say. This is not composed rhetoric. It is a mother in a doorway.

And follow the three names she gives him. My son — the ordinary word. Son of my womb — she is reminding him, and herself, that this large man in front of her was carried. And then son of my vows, which is the phrase that opens the whole thing up: she promised something about him to God, before or after he was born, in the way Hannah did over Samuel (1 Samuel 1:11).

So a woman who dedicated a child to God is now watching him do something she cannot bear, and she has no argument left except the three ways she can name him. Every praying parent of a grown child knows the position exactly: no authority left, no leverage, and one thing still true — that this person was asked for and given and promised, and the promise is not hers to release.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not give your strength to women, your ways to those who destroy kings. It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine, or for rulers to take strong drink, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not give your strength to women, your ways to those who destroy kings.

She begins where the book began, and she is more concise than the father of chs 5 to 7 because she is speaking about it as a woman, and to a king.

The word is strength — the same root as the hayil that will name the excellent wife at v. 10, and the connection is deliberate. A man has a fixed amount of this, and what she is warning against is not pleasure but expenditure. Given here, it is not available there. The king who spends himself in a series of women arrives at the throne room with nothing left for it.

Then vv. 4 and 5, and she turns to the other appetite: it is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine.

Note the repetition. It is not for kings, said twice, and the argument is entirely about office. She does not say wine is evil — the same Bible has it gladdening the heart of man, and ch. 31 will end by recommending it to somebody else four verses later. She says it is not for him, because of what he is responsible for.

Here is a category most Christians have lost and badly need: things that are permissible in themselves and not permissible for a particular man, because of what he is carrying. A surgeon, a pilot and a father of small children are not in the same position as everybody else, and the question is not whether a thing is allowed but whether it is allowed to somebody with these people’s lives in his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: lest they drink and forget what has been decreed and pervert the rights of all the afflicted. Give strong drink to the one who is perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lest they drink and forget what has been decreed and pervert the rights of all the afflicted.

And there is her reason, and it is not about the king’s dignity. It is about the poorest people in his kingdom.

Follow the chain. He drinks; he forgets the decree; the case comes before him; the rights of the afflicted are perverted — and he will never know he did it. He will not remember the hearing, and the man who lost is not in a position to complain to anybody. That is why she raises it: a king’s private indulgence is never private, because it is paid for at the other end of the kingdom by somebody with no name.

Then vv. 6 and 7, and they are among the most surprising verses in Scripture: give strong drink to the one who is perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress; let them drink and forget their poverty and remember their misery no more.

Having removed wine from the king, she prescribes it — to the dying, and to those in bitter distress. This is anaesthesia, and it is a work of mercy: in a world with no medicine, strong drink was what could be done for somebody in unbearable pain, and it was offered as compassion.

And the verses are not a licence for drowning ordinary sorrows; ch. 23 has already dealt at length with the man who tarries long over wine. What is being described is the deathbed and the last extremity, and the mother of a king is instructing him to see that they get it.

There is one more thing, and it is worth the whole chapter. At Golgotha they offered the Lord Jesus wine mixed with myrrh — the customary mercy, the drink of Proverbs 31:6, given to men who were perishing. He did not take it (Mark 15:23). The one man in history entitled to that cup refused it, and drank the other one to the bottom, undulled and entirely conscious, so that nothing of what he bore should be blunted.

verseByVerse.quote: let them drink and forget their poverty and remember their misery no more. Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute. Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute. Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy.

The command is given twice — open your mouth, and then open your mouth — and it is the last instruction a mother gives her son before she describes the woman he should marry. Of everything a queen could tell a king, this is what she chose.

And the phrase for the mute is the heart of it. It does not mean people who cannot physically speak. It means those who have no voice in the place where their case is decided — who cannot get a hearing, cannot afford representation, cannot make anybody listen, and whose situation is therefore settled by people who will never meet them.

Which makes this one of the sharpest political sentences in the Bible, and it belongs to nobody’s party. The man with the power to speak is told that his mouth is not his own: it exists to be used on behalf of people who have none, and the measure of his reign will be taken there rather than in his buildings or his armies.

It also settles a question Christians argue about, and settles it in a woman’s voice at the end of the wisdom literature. Personal righteousness and public justice are not two agendas. The mother who has just warned her son about women and wine goes straight on to the courts, in the same breath, as though they were obviously the same subject — because they are: what a man does at night decides what he is worth in the morning, and both are finally about the destitute.

And the Lord Jesus opened his mouth for the mute in the most literal way available, and then opened it once more where it counted most — for people who could not speak a word in their own defence, before a court that had already decided, and he did it by saying nothing at all and letting the sentence fall on him.

verseByVerse.quote: An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels. The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will have no lack of gain. She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels.

And now the last twenty-two verses of the book, and three things need saying before a single line of the portrait, because this passage has done more damage to more Christian women than any other page of Scripture, and none of the damage was intended.

First: it is a poem, and its form is the key to it. These twenty-two verses are an acrostic — each begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, in order, from aleph to tav. Which is to say the poem is deliberately an A to Z, a complete survey, and no more a description of one woman’s Tuesday than a hymn of praise is a description of a church service. It is a portrait of a whole life, gathered up and set out in twenty-two panels. Nobody does all of this at once, and the poem never suggests anybody does.

Second: the word. Excellent is hayil, and it is not a domestic word at all. It is a military one — strength, force, valour, the word used of an army, and of the mighty men of David. It is used of Boaz, where the ESV renders it a worthy man. So the opening line is closer to a woman of valour, who can find? — and everything that follows is a description not of a tidy household but of formidable competence.

Third: what the poem is for. It stands at the end of a book written to a young man, and it is placed there as the answer to the woman of ch. 7, who called from her doorway in the dark. Lady Wisdom has been personified since ch. 1; here she walks into a house and gets on with things. The son is being told what to look for, and what to be — because everything praised in this woman is what the book has spent thirty chapters commending to him.

Then the first two lines, and both are about her husband, and both are astonishing. The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will have no lack of gain. He does not supervise her; he trusts her — with the money, with the decisions, with the household — and the poem is already, in its second line, describing a marriage that most of its readers across the centuries would not have recognised.

And v. 12: she does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life. The measurement is a lifetime. Anybody can do good for a season, and this is the only line in the poem that could not be true of a single impressive year.

verseByVerse.quote: She seeks wool and flax, and works with willing hands. She is like the ships of the merchant; she brings her food from afar. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
She seeks wool and flax, and works with willing hands.

The portrait begins with raw material, which is where any real work begins, and with two verbs worth having. She seeks — she goes out and sources it, which means judgment about quality and price before anything is made. And she works with willing hands, literally with the delight of her hands, which is a phrase about pleasure in the doing.

Wool and flax are the beginning of the two great textile industries of that world, and this is the first hint of what the poem is actually describing. She is not mending clothes for her family. She is at the head of a supply chain, and by v. 24 she will be selling into a market.

Then v. 14: she is like the ships of the merchant; she brings her food from afar.

The comparison is with international trade, and the ancient reader would have felt the reach of it. Merchant ships were the most sophisticated commercial operation in existence — capital, distance, risk, timing, and a return that could not be guaranteed.

And what she does with all that competence is bring home food. Which is the shape of the whole poem and the reason it is so easily undersold: enormous ability, deployed entirely toward the flourishing of a household, and Scripture presents that not as a waste of her gifts but as their proper use.

verseByVerse.quote: She rises while it is yet night and provides food for her household and portions for her maidens. She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
She rises while it is yet night and provides food for her household and portions for her maidens.

Before dawn, and the detail that matters is at the end of the line: her maidens. She has staff. She is not doing this because there is nobody else; she is up before the people who work for her, organising their day as well as her family’s.

And the word portions is an allocation — she has decided what each of them gets, which is a manager’s decision made at four in the morning before anybody else is awake.

Then v. 16, and this is the verse that ought to have prevented several centuries of misunderstanding: she considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard.

Three separate acts, and every one of them is commercial. She considers — surveys the land, weighs it, works out whether it is worth the money. She buys it, on her own authority, with no suggestion that she consulted anybody. And then she plants a vineyard, which is a capital investment with a four-year wait before the first serious crop.

This is a woman making a long-term acquisition with her own earnings and her own judgment, and the poem records it as one item on a list of her ordinary virtues.

verseByVerse.quote: She dresses herself with strength and makes her arms strong. She perceives that her merchandise is profitable. Her lamp does not go out at night. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
She dresses herself with strength and makes her arms strong.

The Hebrew is literally that she girds her loins with strength — the gesture of gathering up a long robe and tying it at the waist before hard physical work, and it is a man’s idiom, used of soldiers and labourers.

And the second half is the one people skip. She makes her arms strong, which is a process rather than a condition: she got that way, deliberately, over time, because the work required it.

That is a piece of the portrait most devotional treatments quietly leave out, and it should not be left out. Nothing about this woman is fragile. The poem is describing physical capability as part of her excellence, and it does so without the least embarrassment.

Then v. 18: she perceives that her merchandise is profitable. Her lamp does not go out at night.

She checks the margin — that is the plain sense of the first clause: she knows whether the business is making money, which is not a thing anybody knows by accident.

And the lamp is not romantic. It is the same woman who was up before dawn in v. 15, still working after dark. The poem is honest about the cost of what it is describing, and it does not pretend that a life like this is achieved in ordinary hours.

verseByVerse.quote: She puts her hands to the distaff, and her hands hold the spindle. She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
She puts her hands to the distaff, and her hands hold the spindle.

The two tools of spinning, and their presence in the poem is significant precisely because they are unglamorous. After the merchant ships and the vineyard, she is sitting with a spindle doing the slow, repetitive work that the raw wool of v. 13 requires before it can become anything.

She has not delegated the craft. The woman who buys fields still knows how to make the thread, which is worth noticing about every kind of leadership: the ones who are trusted are usually the ones who can still do the work.

Then v. 20, and the poem turns outward for the first time: she opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy.

The verb opens is set against the closed hand of 21:13, and the second half adds distance — she reaches out, which means going to somebody rather than waiting to be approached.

And the placing of this verse in the poem is deliberate. It comes immediately after two verses about her earning capacity, and immediately before four about her household’s prosperity, so that generosity sits in the middle of the account of her wealth rather than at the end of it. What she makes is not hers first and given away second. The opening of the hand is one of the things the money is for.

verseByVerse.quote: She is not afraid of snow for her household, for all her household are clothed in scarlet. She makes bed coverings for herself; her clothing is fine linen and purple. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
She is not afraid of snow for her household, for all her household are clothed in scarlet.

The absence of fear is the point, and it has a reason attached. She is unafraid of winter not because she is brave but because the coats were made in August — which is the ant of 6:8, at work in a household.

And scarlet is a detail with money in it. Dyed cloth was expensive; she has not merely provided against the cold but provided well, and the servants of v. 15 are included in all.

Then v. 22: she makes bed coverings for herself; her clothing is fine linen and purple.

Purple was the most costly dye in the ancient world, made from sea-snails and reserved in most societies for royalty. And the poem says, without a flicker of apology, that she wears it.

Read that line to every Christian woman who has been taught that godliness requires her to be drab. This is the same woman who gives to the poor two verses earlier and rises before dawn. Scripture does not present her fine clothing as a compromise or as a concession. It is in the list, as one of the good things about her, and it was paid for out of what she made herself.

verseByVerse.quote: Her husband is known in the gates when he sits among the elders of the land. She makes linen garments and sells them; she delivers sashes to the merchant. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her husband is known in the gates when he sits among the elders of the land.

The only verse in the poem about what he does, and it sits in the middle of what she does — which is exactly the point, and the ancient reader would have felt it as a compliment to her.

The gate was the place of judgment and public business, and a man sat there because he had standing. And the poem locates the reason for his standing in the previous twelve verses. He is respected because of the household behind him, and everybody in that town knows who built it.

It is a quiet and rather lovely reversal of what the reader expects. This is not a woman whose significance derives from a notable husband. It is a husband whose position is underwritten by a notable wife, and the poem says so in the one line it gives him.

Then v. 24: she makes linen garments and sells them; she delivers sashes to the merchant. Manufacture, and then wholesale — she is not selling at a market stall, she is supplying a trader. The wool and flax of v. 13 have completed their journey, and the enterprise that began with sourcing raw material ends with a delivery to a middleman.

verseByVerse.quote: Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come. She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come.

The poem has just described her linen and her purple; now it describes what she is actually wearing, and the metaphor is deliberate — strength and dignity are the garments people notice.

And then one of the most beautiful clauses in the Old Testament: she laughs at the time to come.

Not that she is unaware of it. This is a woman who has thought about winter in August and knows exactly what the future can do. She laughs because she has looked at it, and because everything that can be prepared has been prepared, and because what cannot be prepared for is in somebody else’s hands.

Set that against the anxiety of 12:25 which bows a man down, and the contrast is the whole argument of this book about wisdom and fear. The laughter is not optimism. It is the noise a person makes who has done the work and settled the question of who is in charge of the rest.

Then v. 26: she opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue.

The phrase is torat hesed — the law, or instruction, of covenant love. She teaches, and what she teaches is not merely accurate but kind, and the two are held in one phrase as though it were obvious that they belong together.

And the echo is unmistakable: open your mouth was her own command to her son in v. 8. The woman being described does with her tongue what the king was told to do with his.

verseByVerse.quote: She looks well to the ways of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness. Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her: (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
She looks well to the ways of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness.

The verb is a watchman’s word — she keeps a lookout over her household, which means she notices things: which child has gone quiet, what is wrong between two of the servants, what needs attending to before it becomes a problem.

That is not administration. It is the same faculty the book has been calling wisdom since ch. 1 — seeing what is actually there — applied to the people she is responsible for.

Then v. 28, and after eighteen verses of activity the poem finally lets somebody else speak: her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her.

They rise up, which is the gesture of standing when somebody of rank enters a room, and they do it in the house. And this is the first response recorded in the whole poem. Everything until now has been what she does; here is what she gets, and it comes from the four or five people who know exactly what it cost.

Strike that note for anybody doing this kind of work now, largely unwitnessed. The praise in this poem does not come from the town. It comes from inside the house, from people who were there when it was done, and Scripture treats that as the highest form of it available.

verseByVerse.quote: "Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all." Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all.

Her husband’s words, quoted directly — the only line of his speech in the Bible — and the first half is as important as the second. Many women have done excellently. He is not saying there is one good woman in the world. He is naming a category, a great many of them, and then saying what a husband should say about his own.

Then v. 30, which is the verse the whole poem has been walking toward: charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.

Neither charm nor beauty is called wicked. Deceitful means it tells you something that is not the case, and vain is hevel — breath, vapour, the word of Ecclesiastes. So the complaint against them is not that they are bad but that they are unreliable as evidence and they do not last, which anybody who has watched a marriage built on them will confirm.

And what is praised instead is the one thing this book has praised from 1:7: the fear of the LORD. Twenty-two verses of competence, industry, commerce and strength, and the summary line attributes none of it to temperament or talent. It was all coming from there.

Now the pastoral matter, and it must be said plainly, because a great many women read this chapter annually and finish it feeling condemned.

This poem is not a job description and it was never issued as a standard to be met. It is an acrostic — an A to Z — and it is sung, in Jewish households to this day, by a husband to his wife on a Friday evening. It is a song of praise. Whatever else it is doing, it is not a list against which a woman is to be measured on a Tuesday when the house is a mess and she has achieved four of the twenty-two.

And v. 30 is the poem’s own defence against that misuse, because it tells the reader where to look. Not at the vineyard, or the purple, or the lamp burning at midnight — at the fear of the LORD, which is available to a woman with no capital, no staff, no health and no strength in her arms whatever. Every other verse in this chapter describes what that fear happened to produce in one woman’s particular circumstances. It is her portrait, not a uniform.

verseByVerse.quote: Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.

The last verse of the book of Proverbs, and it is an instruction to the reader.

Give her. Somebody is being told to do something, and it is not the woman. After twenty-one verses of what she has done, the poem turns and addresses whoever is listening, and requires of them a response — not admiration, but payment: the fruit of her hands, which is what is owed rather than what is generous.

And then the gates. She has been in the house for the whole poem; her husband was the one who sat in the gate at v. 23. The final line takes her works out to the public square where the town’s serious business is done, and says: let them be praised there.

Which is a striking way for this book to end. Proverbs began with Wisdom standing in the street crying aloud at the entrance of the city gates (1:20-21), and it finishes with a woman’s works being praised in exactly that place. Wisdom went out into the town in ch. 1 and asked to be heard; in ch. 31 she is at the gate again, and this time everybody can see what she made.

So the book closes on the practical question its readers will actually face, and the answer is a person rather than a principle. It began by asking a young man to get wisdom, and it ends by showing him what wisdom looks like when it has been got — not a philosophy, not a temperament, but a woman up before dawn, buying a field, feeding her servants, giving to the poor, laughing at the future.

And the question of v. 10 still stands over the whole poem: an excellent wife who can find? Proverbs asks it and does not answer it, in the same way that Agur asked for the Son’s name and could not supply it. But the New Testament finishes the sentence, and it does so in the only direction that could have worked. There is a bride of such value that she is described as a treasure a man sold everything to buy — and she was not found excellent. She was found ruined, and was made excellent by a husband who gave himself up for her, that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25-27).

The excellent wife of Proverbs 31 is what he is making. Her strength is his, her works are his gift, and on the last day her deeds will follow her (Revelation 14:13) — praised at the gates of a city that has twelve of them, by a husband who found her when there was nothing precious about her at all, and who has been saying ever since that many have done excellently and she surpasses them all.

31.theology:
Lady Wisdom Embodied. The structural genius of Proverbs is now fully visible: the book opens with a father urging his son to seek wisdom and avoid folly (chs.1–9), personified as two women. The book closes with wisdom embodied in a particular woman whose final credential is the fear of the LORD (v.30). The frame is complete. Lady Wisdom is not an abstraction; she is what a human life looks like when it is ordered toward God. For the Christian reader, Christ is the fullness of this embodiment: "Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption" (1 Cor. 1:30).

The Fear of the LORD as Crown. Proverbs 1:7 begins: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." Proverbs 31:30 ends: "a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised." The book is a vast unfolding of what lies between these two statements — the practical wisdom of a life lived in the fear of God. That fear is not dread but the relational posture of the creature before the Creator, the redeemed before the Redeemer. It issues in generosity, diligence, faithful speech, care for the poor, and the peculiar joy of the woman who laughs at the time to come. This is Proverbs' final word, and it is the beginning of the gospel.
31.examples:
Then: The acrostic form (aleph to taw) was a literary statement: this is everything, the complete alphabet of a wise life. Israelite readers would have recognized the woman of chapter 31 as the antithesis of Lady Folly (ch.7) and the embodiment of Lady Wisdom (ch.8). Her economic activity — buying fields, trading, making linen garments — was entirely realistic for a woman of means in the ancient Near East, where women managed households that were also small enterprises. Her praise "at the gates" was public honor in the place where civic life happened.

Now: Chapter 31 has sometimes been weaponized as a productivity checklist for Christian women. The poem resists this. It is not a job description but a portrait — and its crown is not efficiency but the fear of the LORD. Any reading that focuses on the woman's activities while ignoring verse 30 has misread the poem. More broadly, the chapter invites readers to ask: what does wisdom look like in a full, concrete human life? The answer is not a set of rules but a person — generously open-handed, dignified under pressure, laughing at the future, speaking with wisdom and kindness. The church is called to embody this portrait collectively: the community that fears the LORD, opens its hand to the poor, and lets its works praise it in the gates of the city it inhabits.
